Tri-screen portable monitors aren’t for the faint of heart

Ars Technica November 23, 2026

Three extra screens boost multitasking but can distract and overwhelm.

Living in New York City means making the most of limited space. As a result, I’m always interested in tools that can boost my productivity at a small desk, in a cramped office, or working on the go.

I’ve experimented with dual-screen laptops in multiple form factors and numerous portable monitors, including ones with projection capabilities. I’ve had particularly good results with dual-screen portable monitors.

Naturally, a portable monitor with three full-size screens was the next logical step.

To get a four-screen (including my laptop’s screen) experience, I tested KYY’s X90G ($360 as of this writing). It’s a portable monitor with three 15.6-inch IPS screens. Each screen has 1920×1080 resolution, its own control buttons, and is specced for up to 400 nits of brightness.

The X90G isn’t the only tri-screen monitor available, but it stood out to me because of its design. Some of the X90G’s rivals place the three displays above the laptop screen, which would require you to look away from the laptop screen repeatedly.

Instead, the X90G places one screen on the left and right sides of the laptop screen and one above the laptop display for a more cohesive—but not completely unified—visual workspace.

The X90G also has better compatibility than its rivals by supporting Linux and Android in addition to Windows and macOS (on systems using an M1 processor or better).

Most laptops should fit in the X90G’s designated area, but many workstations and gaming laptops won’t, since it doesn’t support laptops larger than 17.3 inches.

Let’s get something out of the way: If you hate bezels, a triple-portable-monitor isn’t for you.

The X90G never felt like one large screen; it always felt like four disparate displays. The screens aren’t perfectly aligned in a row, meaning you sometimes have to move the mouse awkwardly to get from one display to the next.

The gadget’s back panel, where the connected laptop’s screen sits, has a kickstand, so the X90G can be set upright on a tabletop or tilted back. But even with my PC’s lid flush against the monitor’s back panel, parts of the monitor remained visible and distracted me at times.

Sometimes the lit-up screen above my laptop’s lid would inadvertently pull my eyes from my laptop’s display. Worsening matters, I tested the X90G with a 13-inch laptop that, when open, doesn’t cover the opening on the back panel that serves as the monitor’s handle. That means that north of the laptop’s screen was a hole, part of the back panel, a display bezel, and then the extra display.

For some workloads, having four distinct screens is very beneficial. Each of the X90G’s screens supports independent tilting and has its own on-screen display menus, controls, and power buttons. I could keep the screen I was using to write or read an article dimmer while boosting the brightness of the screen displaying an image I was editing, for instance.

The X90G’s design also made it relatively easy to view content on the two side panels and the laptop’s screen simultaneously. This helped me keep things like reports, photos, blogs, spreadsheets, and other documents nearby while conducting research. In these cases, I reserved the northern screen for secondary tasks, like email, chat, or displaying the popular Finnish puppy cam Pentulive.

I try to keep my workspaces uncluttered to minimize distractions. A tri-screen monitor makes it easier to manage multiple tasks simultaneously but doesn’t allow for the cleanest layout or setup, which presents its own challenges.

It’s also worth noting that you need a decent amount of space to fully extend a triple-portable-monitor setup. The X90G measures about 46 inches across with the side panels flattened out. That’s wider than my desk. You’ll also need some clearance if you want to fold the side panels in toward the laptop more, perhaps for a closer view.

Tri-portable monitors are geared toward people with minimal space who want the flexibility to carry three screens on the go. But these devices are bound to have some bulk. The X90G weighs 6.4 pounds, more than twice the weight of the Dell XPS ultralight laptop I tested it with. That’s a reasonable weight for three displays, but it still inevitably compromises portability.

Alternatively, on days when I could leave the monitor set up and just plug in my laptop, it felt pretty magical to be instantly rewarded with three additional screens by plugging a USB-C cable into my PC.

For someone seeking to maximize small spaces, a three-screen portable monitor sounds reasonable. In practice, though, it’s hard to strike the right balance between portability and screen space with this many displays.

With devices like the X90G, you can quadruple the number of pixels at your disposal. But when I used the X90G, the screens all felt like separate entities, partially because one of them isn’t in line with the laptop’s screen at all. A triple portable monitor can’t moonlight as a larger, unified display, like some dual monitors can.

That said, a tri-screen monitor can do things others can’t, including making it easier to share information with other people.

But if you want a portable monitor for more traditional reasons, such as needing an easily transportable way to get more screen real estate, or if you prefer clear spaces for working, a triple monitor may be overkill, if not overwhelming.

Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI

Ars Technica November 23, 2026

The new Asus ProArt laptop costs up to $7,000, but it can run a gaggle of local AI agents.

Buying a new computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense. Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia’s new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models.

While it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16, with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you’re looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error.

Before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia’s pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn’t skimp on the specs.

Asus has released numerous ProArt laptops, but this one is notable for including the new Nvidia Spark RTX chip in its most powerful configuration. The Spark N1X has a 20-core Grace CPU, divided between 10 high-performance Arm Cortex-X925 cores and 10 power-efficient Arm Cortex-A725 cores. The performance cluster reaches boost speeds between 4.0 and 4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores peak at 2.8 GHz. Memory caching on the processor totals 49MB, split between 24MB of shared L3 cache and 25MB of L2 cache.

Graphics and AI are the purview of the Nvidia GB20B Blackwell GPU. It packs 6,144 cores in this configuration across 48 streaming multiprocessors, backed by its own 24MB L2 cache. These 5th-generation Tensor Cores support the full suite of Nvidia technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, and NVFP4. In all, you’re looking at up to 31 TFLOPS of FP32 graphical performance and about 1,000 TOPS of FP4 AI compute.

Asus will sell this device in two memory configurations (plus some lower-specced retailer-specific SKUs), but the one I’ve been testing (and the one that makes the most sense alongside the RTX Spark) has 128GB of LPDDR5x RAM. It supports up to 300GB/s of raw bandwidth, which is fast for shared system memory. However, using a dedicated GPU typically gets you higher throughput with a GDDR7 memory interface. Still, you get several times more memory than a gaming GPU in this machine.

This is essentially an Nvidia Spark DGX workstation with a screen and keyboard. It also runs Windows 11, which lowers the barrier to entry if you want local AI agents. While many local AI setups focus on 27-billion-parameter models that will fit on a video card, the Asus ProArt P16 can easily load models with 100-plus billion parameters, with enough left over for lighter background AI tasks.

Nvidia and Asus say the Spark’s AI compute and ample memory are enough power to run frontier-level AI models locally. That means you can get powerful AI compute without running through your allotment of expensive tokens or sending all your data to a server in the cloud. Ignoring the AI angle, the ProArt P16 has to be a good laptop before it makes sense for even the most AI-obsessed buyers to consider it. Luckily, it gets all the basic laptop things right.

It’s nice to see a wide array of ports on this machine. There are three USB-C ports with USB4 support, and they’re split between the left and right sides. That makes connecting devices and charging much easier. There’s also a legacy USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 port, full HDMI, a 3.5 mm jack, and an SD card reader.

The machine comes with a beefy 140 W USB-C charger, which can get you a few hours of use in just a minute or two of charging. Asus says you can get up to 12 hours of use per charge, but that depends very much on what you’re doing. Watching video at low brightness might get you even more than 12 hours, but expect somewhat less for mixed use and even less for heavy AI workloads. In my (unscientific) testing, after a full workday and tinkering with AI on the side, the P16 usually has about 30 percent of its battery left.

The 16-inch 120Hz OLED display is overall very good, sporting a 4K+ resolution of 3840 x 2400. The stacked (tandem) pixels mean you get an incredibly high 1,600 nits of peak brightness. However, tandem OLEDs do tend to look a bit grainy with solid colors at lower brightness levels. I’ve laid eyes on two P16 units, one of which was noticeably more grainy than the other—so that’s something to look out for. However, the texture is easy to ignore at normal viewing distances and mid-to-high brightness.

The trackpad is enormous (150.3 x 99.5 mm) and relies on haptic clicks instead of a physical mechanism. This is a relatively new thing for Windows laptops, which are still catching up to Apple’s trackpads. That said, the ProArt’s pad works very well. It’s appropriately sensitive, and you can adjust the click intensity and detection threshold.

The keyboard is a little on the narrow side for a larger laptop, but the keys feel great. There’s ample travel, the tactility is sharp, and the firm keyboard deck ensures no flex at the bottom of each keystroke. The aluminum chassis is overall very solid, but it only comes in white or black, with the latter being your only option for the high-end model. The matte case looks great, but it is a magnet for smudges (particularly the plastic of the keys).

Unlike previous ProArt laptops that had standard GPUs, there’s no dedicated memory for the RTX Spark’s graphics and AI cores. Windows sees the machine as having 64GB of system RAM and 64GB of video memory, but in reality, this shared 128GB of memory is adjusted dynamically based on what you’re doing.

Since this is a Windows machine, there is some overhead that limits your AI workloads. On a DGX Spark box with the same underlying hardware, all the memory is available for AI. Here, you’re capped at about 110GB. That’s still a huge amount of memory for AI, far surpassing what you can get on even the most expensive consumer-level GPUs.

There are a few clear advantages to making the ProArt P16 your AI hub. Running an AI model locally on the Spark’s Blackwell cores lets you keep all your data private. When you interact with ChatGPT or Gemini, your interactions and data become training and advertising fodder. You’re also trusting the AI provider to run your workloads on the right model, and they’ll often route requests to cheaper ones to save money.

With an RTX Spark laptop, you have total control over how the AI operates. That also means you have to do all the setup and management yourself. The ProArt comes with a few Asus apps, which will streamline setup for a subset of AI-powered tasks, but installing a third-party agent is where things get interesting (but not always good).

Nvidia’s laptop AI chip is optimized for desktop clients like OpenClaw and Hermes, allowing you to download the AI models of your choice in a fairly simple graphical UI. I tested various models in different size ranges. Asus recommends starting with Qwen 27B, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that splits the difference between size and efficiency. I also loaded a few versions of Google’s Gemma open models in the same size range.

But these are all small enough that you could run them on a high-end GPU. To push the Spark, I grabbed a few larger models like the Qwen Flash Next, a 90GB download with 125 billion parameters. This model occupies almost all the shared memory when active, whereas the smaller ones won’t even go beyond the GPU’s reserved 64GB.

The nice (and scary) thing about setting up a local agent on Windows is that it can control the PC. Once the model is loaded in your preferred AI framework, you can just ask it to handle additional configuration. Need to set up access for your online accounts? Just ask. Manage installed tools and apps? Just ask. Surely nothing could go wrong, right?

In short order, I set up agent workflows to access and analyze data from test email accounts, manage local files, update a coding project, and analyze the content of images in my photo library. I also used ComfyUI workflows to generate images and videos locally without worrying about running through a limited allotment of tokens in the cloud. I’ll admit, I don’t have much use for media generation, but some of these local image models have gotten surprisingly good. Of course, the machine itself is expensive enough that you could pay for the most extravagant AI plans for a few years before breaking even. Still, the data and compute are all yours.

A few tragic tales about local agents nuking file directories or exposing data have made the rounds, and that’s a real concern when you start giving these things access to your PC—these models can do whatever you can do while sitting at the keyboard. I tested the P16’s AI capabilities with that in mind, ensuring I had no irreplaceable or sensitive data on the machine. Agents are supposed to seek authorization before taking action, but mistakes may happen, even if you’re being careful.

The agents didn’t make any huge mistakes in my testing, but watching the chain of thought bounce around can be maddening, like an unguided robot vacuum bouncing into walls. But like a vacuum, today’s AI agents usually get to the right place.

Sometimes, it does feel very futuristic. You give the machine a problem or tell it to troubleshoot something, and it does it without sharing any data with anyone. It’s a different way of using a PC. That’s cool, but it’s also not without frustration. Even though these models are often able to arrive at the correct result, they may not do so very quickly.

During normal operation, the Asus ProArt P16 is whisper-quiet. As soon as you start running inference for AI, though, the fans kick into high gear. The machine absolutely burns through the enormous 100 Wh battery, which is the largest cell you can legally bring on an airplane in the US. You really only get about two hours of inference without the power cable, and you might not get as much done as you’d think in that time. For example, scanning a day’s emails and generating action items takes around five minutes with a mid-weight model.

With simple tasks, models like Qwen 27B can churn through 20 or so tokens per second (with default “medium” effort mode). That’s a bit slower than you’ll get with cloud-based frontier models, which are also more capable thanks to their powerful server hardware. As long as you don’t need to ask it if Taiwan is a country, Qwen seems like the best option for local AI currently. Google’s mid-weight Gemma models can occasionally hit up to 40 tokens per second, but that figure tends to come down to a quarter of that speed for more complex tasks.

While Qwen Flash Next does produce better results, it takes so long I usually stick with the smaller models—it chugs along at just a few tokens per second unless you drop its thinking level. You can still make use of all that RAM by running multiple concurrent agents, though. That may be the real promise of RTX Spark machines, but that requires you to have a lot of AI-powered projects in mind. If you’re just using a Spark laptop as an alternative to keeping a ChatGPT window open, you should probably pay for ChatGPT Pro instead of buying a $7,000 PC.

While the RTX Spark is aimed at AI workloads, it’s also an all-around speedy Windows platform. It is, however, an Arm-based chip with 20 Nvidia Grace CPU cores. Microsoft has a sordid history with Windows on Arm, but things are finally in a better place.

The Windows Prism emulator can run x86 and x64 programs well enough that you won’t usually notice the difference, and some past software gaps, like Google Drive and VPN apps, have been addressed with native Arm versions. So you don’t need to fear Arm chips on Windows anymore unless you have very specific legacy software and hardware needs.

In daily use, the ProArt P16 with RTX Spark is extremely responsive. It’s still usable even when you fill up the memory with AI agents running inference in the background. There are very few systems that directly compare to the RTX Spark right now, but here are some system benchmarks of the Asus ProArt P16.

Nvidia has pushed the idea that Spark can be your primary gaming machine, too. But here, emulation is more of a bother. There are virtually no native Arm games for Windows, and emulation takes a bite out of your performance. Titles that require system-level anti-cheat measures may not run because those cannot be emulated. However, Nvidia has made progress here, collaborating with some major vendors like Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, and Denuvo to support their technology on Spark. It’s still early, though, and you may encounter errors.

The GPU component of the Spark N1X is equivalent to the most powerful Blackwell-based gaming GPUs on the market, but emulation means performance won’t quite measure up. You also have to remember that the ProArt P16 has an incredibly high-resolution OLED screen. Running games at native resolution, even without the emulation overhead, is already pushing the limits of the hardware.

Aside from the benchmark numbers, I put the ProArt P16 to work playing some games. While they ran well enough to play, it’s not as simple as cranking the settings to max like you would on an x86 system with a Blackwell GPU. For example, Baldur’s Gate 3 is not exactly a graphical tour de force, and it’s more CPU-bound than some other AAA games.

I had to make some compromises to maintain 60 fps, even in less busy areas of the game. It was basically a trade-off between lowering detail and using aggressive DLSS or dropping the game below native resolution. You can expect Spark-based machines like this to run most games with high graphical settings, but ultra settings will be out of reach if you want to maintain good frame rates.

In a purely technical way, it’s cool that you can run powerful 100GB AI models on a laptop. Devices like the DGX Spark and DIY GPU clusters can perform similar tasks, but having everything centralized on one machine makes it more appealing as a way to get things done with AI, and Windows makes it easy to get started.

The ProArt P16 can be your one and only computer, handling gaming, productivity, and AI inference. However, it can be hard to really take advantage of all the AI capabilities of the machine. You’re looking at running either one or two large, powerful agents at very slow speeds or a collection of smaller models much faster. That means you need to have plenty of AI applications in mind. Otherwise, you might as well get a standard laptop.

You probably already know if that’s something you want. The kind of person running multiple concurrent agentic tasks using cloud systems might benefit from a PC like the ProArt P16, and in some extreme instances, they might want to spend $7,000 on the machine with 128GB of RAM. However, you could also step down to the 64GB model to save a few thousand dollars and still get some useful AI capabilities as models get more efficient.

The Asus ProArt P16 is really a niche machine. If you want something primarily for gaming, an x86 system with a discrete GPU makes more sense, and a lighter, productivity-focused laptop is better for most buyers. The ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of how a local AI-powered future could work, but it’s not a good purchase for anyone but the most fervent AI boosters right now.

Trump FCC declares California isn’t allowed to enforce phone service rules

Ars Technica November 20, 2026

FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says that its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”

Gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

SpaceX’s Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

Ars Technica November 20, 2026

“Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026.”

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

“SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U. S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U. S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has said that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

“My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U. S. Government official.”

The communications from Himes suggest that congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

“It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

Various options are open to congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

It seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or launches, as the company is currently providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button

Ars Technica November 20, 2026

Google search is making it even easier to access AI tools on the search page.

Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google. com. A redesign that has been in testing for the past few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image-generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that sat next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

The other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged in to Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”

It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

This change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

Ars Technica November 20, 2026

Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

Ars Technica November 20, 2026

Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.

Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat. com.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router to another one. Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U. S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

Moore said that the most effective means for preventing leakage is to host models using on-premises servers. That option is expensive, though. For those who can’t afford a self-hosted system, the next best option, Moore said, is to receive service directly from a first-tier provider that provides “one contract and a privacy policy to read.” Moore said that even then, there’s no guarantee no data will leak, but that the measure minimizes the chances. AI users should also avoid accepting default provider or reseller pools and instead pick upstream providers themselves.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded

Ars Technica November 20, 2026

A recent brightening turned out to be from a star orbiting inside another.

In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”

Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

Karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system where this might be happening while searching Andromeda for stars changing in brightness, using the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA’s Near-Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (NEOWISE) mission. One giant had been brightening for seven years. “When a star first swallows its companion, it has a very subtle effect on its brightness,” Karambelkar said. “It slowly brightens, and a lot of light comes out in the infrared.”

In April 2025, Karambelkar’s team published a paper suggesting that this system, named AT 2025abao, was undergoing an engulfment in progress. Back then, though, they couldn’t rule out a competing explanation: a single star with instabilities deep within its core. So, they kept watching.

The researchers reconstructed the history of the system using observations from about a dozen telescopes and surveys, going back to photographic sky plates from 1989. Until 2018, the star barely changed. Modeling those quiet years revealed a giant late in its life, about 350 times wider than the Sun. Its companion was impossible to see, however. “The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000,” Karambelkar said.

To get around it, the team estimated the mass of the smaller companion based on the amount of dust the system had shed before the engulfment. The estimates suggested a star of roughly 0.7 solar masses.

Between 2018 and early 2025, the giant brightened two- to threefold in visible light, swelling while its temperature stayed nearly constant. Karambelkar compares the process to a spacecraft reentering Earth’s atmosphere. The companion, skimming through the giant’s outer layers, was gradually seeing its orbit shrink, and the friction was heating up the envelope. The energy released by that drag matched the extra light the team observed.

Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half while its infrared glow kept rising. NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope happened to catch it in July 2025, revealing that the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun’s width and wrapped itself in fresh dust.

In October 2025, the star brightened roughly 100-fold in just 25 days, shining like 1.5 million Suns at its peak. “At one point, the rate at which the orbit was decaying became very, very fast,” Karambelkar said, comparing the release of the gravitational energy to an explosion. “The companion just fell very quickly, very deep inside the envelope of the star, and it crashed into the core. That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material.”

The eruption had all the hallmarks of a luminous red nova, a type of outburst known to come from merging stars—but an event the researchers weren’t expecting. “Honestly, our minds were blown,” Karambelkar said. He said that this was evidence that this explosion was a consequence of the inspiraling of a binary companion. What made AT 2025abao special, though, was the giant itself.

All previously known luminous red novae came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound outer layers, which inevitably drive both stars toward a merger. This one was an old giant with a loose, churning envelope—the setup that can also leave behind a surviving tight binary. To find out if the companion actually survived, the team looked at how AT 2025abao’s energy was spent.

To predict how such events end, astronomers use a formula with an efficiency parameter describing how much of the energy lost by the sinking companion goes into blowing the envelope away. AT 2025abao showed that the energy goes to different places at different stages.

During the slow spiral, most of the energy escaped as light. In the final plunge, the companion released about a hundred times more energy, but only around 1 percent of it was radiated away. Nearly all the rest went into hurling a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times the speed needed to escape the giant’s gravity. The rest of the envelope stayed put, which suggests the companion merged with the giant’s core instead of surviving as a tight partner.

“Initially, when the rate of energy deposition is low, the star is able to puff up and adjust to this new energy source inside it,” Karambelkar said. “But once the energy deposition rate increases very quickly as the companion spirals even closer, the star can no longer adjust itself. At that point, it needs to throw out some of its material.”

The efficiency the team calculated fits values inferred from known post-engulfment binaries. But the formula assumes the energy is mostly spent expelling lots of the envelope. Here, most of it went into flinging a small amount of gas at high speeds. It turned out the formula works as a rule of thumb but misses some of the physics.

In AT 2025abao, gas shed during the slow spiral piled up in the plane of the binary’s orbit, so the explosion’s ejecta could expand freely toward the poles even though it was blocked around the equator. That, Karambelkar argues, explains the hourglass-shaped nebulae seen around dying stars. “It had been an idea for a very long time that those hourglass shapes are shaped by binary interactions,” he said. “It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.”

The team admits it can’t yet be sure the stars merged, because dust formed from the ejected material hides whatever is left inside. “We want to continue monitoring the system for several years, possibly even decades, to watch the dust clear out and whatever is remaining inside emerge,” Karambelkar said. “That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.” In the meantime, the team hopes to find many more such events involving stars of different masses and types.

Telescopes we have today can detect them only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should spot them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years. “We can have an influx of several of these events per year,” Karambelkar said.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z

NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain

Ars Technica November 20, 2026

“We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”

SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

The Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.

Other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.

Ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.

For Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a New Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.

Then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.

So, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a big reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.

“The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech said. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.

“With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech said. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”

Artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.

“I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech said. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”

The Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.

“With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech said. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”

While there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a new milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.

NASA levied new test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The company plans to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.

“One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech said. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.

This year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight plan for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated plans will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion.

“Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech said. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”

The new concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.

“One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech said. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”

The six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.

Now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.

What’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.

“We’re still working that out,” Creech said. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”

For missions using Blue Moon, the lander will connect with Orion in orbit around the Moon. Blue Origin’s updated plans do away with the requirement for in-space refueling but will still require four launches of the company’s New Glenn rocket, one for the Blue Moon lander itself and three with transfer stages to boost it out of Earth orbit to the Moon.

A new stretched Centaur upper stage for the Space Launch System should give the rocket energy to send Orion to low-lunar orbit, which it could not reach with the current version of SLS. NASA has not determined if the new Centaur exploration stage will be ready in time for Artemis IV. If not, Artemis IV could fly with the last of NASA’s in-stock SLS upper stages.

NASA is also waiting to decide which lander to use on Artemis IV. In either case, two of Orion’s four astronauts will transfer into the landers for the final descent to the lunar surface for a four-day stay, then take off and return to Orion.

Starship and Blue Moon must each complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. The landing demos are targeted for late 2027 or early 2028, Creech said, but they won’t necessarily test everything crews will need when they head for the lunar south pole.

Starship’s elevator, for example, is not part of SpaceX’s uncrewed landing demonstration. Engineers will use a test lab at Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama to check the elevator’s performance in a simulated lunar environment.

NASA did not initially require SpaceX or Blue Origin to prove their landers could take off from the Moon before a crew mission. Government officials later added the lunar takeoff requirement for each company’s uncrewed landing demos.

For now, NASA is leaving the details of the uncrewed takeoff demo up to SpaceX and Blue Origin. During Apollo, NASA’s lunar lander never landed on the Moon before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. NASA did, however, fly a dress rehearsal around the Moon on Apollo 10 that included a test of the lunar module’s landing abort capability.

“Where we are today is, Blue will land and then do a full ascent back to the rendezvous point with Orion,” Creech said. “With SpaceX. They will land, they will take off again, get to main stage on the engines, and then they will do another landing on the surface.”

That could change. Today’s plan gives SpaceX two shots at proving Starship can safely land on the Moon, but it comes with trade-offs.

“When I came into the program, I was like, ‘Why are we not going all the way to the rendezvous point?’” said Creech, who took over as HLS program manager in 2025. “Some of my key people felt strongly we would get more out of the way we’re doing it now. There are others that have different opinions… We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”

For Starship, orbital refueling remains the key to the Moon. SpaceX’s propellant transfer demonstration will involve two Starships, one launched from Florida and another from Texas, docking together in low-Earth orbit and transferring a “meaningful” amount of propellant from one ship to the other, Creech said.

“The first quarter of next year, we will see a long-awaited propellant transfer test from SpaceX, where they launch two Starships in pretty close proximity, actually dock, and transfer, we’re calling it a meaningful amount, of propellant,” Creech told Ars. “That is going to be a big learning point if they pull that off, because their architecture depends on propellant aggregation and multiple propellant flights.”

The propellant transfer test will mark the first time one spacecraft has offloaded a significant quantity of cryogenic propellants—in this case, methane and liquid oxygen—onto another vehicle in space. It is the culmination of decades of government and commercial research on cryogenic orbital refueling. The results will tell engineers how much of the propellant will be lost from boil-off during the transfer.

That is one reason why there’s still so much ambiguity about how many Starship refueling tankers SpaceX will need to launch to give the Starship lunar lander enough gas to fly to the Moon. Without refueling, Starships are restricted to flights in low-Earth orbit.

The low end of the estimate for Starship tankers is six to eight refueling flights to support a Starship lunar mission. Those numbers come from Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, and fall below NASA’s own conservative planning figure of 20 refueling launches. Musk’s figures hinge on future Starship upgrades to reach the vehicle’s full potential. SpaceX’s goal is to get Starship’s lift capacity up to 100 to 200 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit. Today’s version of Starship, known as Starship V3, is still far short of 100 metric tons of payload capacity.

For context, a Starship carries 1,600 metric tons of propellant with its tanks full. Refueling flights using future, fully optimized Starships might be able to fill those tanks with as few as six tankers. That is not the case today.

SpaceX is working on a taller, heavier Starship called Starship V4. It will fly with nine Raptor engines, an upgrade over the six-engine variant flying today. In 2025, Musk said Starship V4’s first launch was targeted for 2027. There hasn’t been a recent update to the schedule for Starship V4.

The initial Artemis lunar missions will use Starship V3, Creech said.

The past, present, and future share a show floor at Pinball Expo 2026

Ars Technica Long form October 21, 2026

Flipping through the highlights in and around Pinball Expo 2026.

It’s October in the Midwest, which means it’s time for the pinball world to descend on a convention center in Chicagoland for the annual Pinball Expo. Once thought to be an entertainment sector slowly bleeding out, pinball has come back in a big way in recent years. I visited one of Chicago’s last old-school manufacturers before heading down the road to see what’s new in the silver-ball universe.

Hundreds gathered on a brisk fall Friday morning outside Stern Pinball’s headquarters in Elk Grove, Illinois, waiting to enter a Wonka-like wonder factory where piles of raw parts become licensed creations from Jaws to the brand-new Fallout. Stern invited me to tour its offices and factory floor before heading off to the convention in nearby Schaumburg, Illinois.

As I stood with my tour group in Stern Pinball’s HQ lobby, mouth agape at the dozens of machines lining the walls, we were greeted by the man himself, Gary Stern, who gave us some background on the company’s 40-year history. After a stop at Gary’s podium, we were ushered to the factory floor entrance, where Stern employee and legendary game designer George Gomez briefed us on the tour rules and answered questions. According to Gomez, “at any given time, Stern controls 90 percent of the current pinball market, and everybody else splits the rest.”

While the industry may be expanding toward something more reminiscent of its glory days, there’s no doubt who still rules the market. With a steady stream of new license releases, Stern has cemented itself as the brand in modern pinball.

What I saw on the expo floor, though, showed me that the remaining 10 percent of the market is doing some really interesting things, and hobbyist projects are booming. From modular home setups to open development kits that let anyone with silver-ball dreams try their hand at game design, there was something for everyone. In short, it’s a very exciting time to be a pinball fan.

Stern’s latest offering, Fallout, stood near the entrance of a convention floor packed with the latest machines from manufacturers like Jersey Jack, Barrels of Fun, Spooky Pinball, and others. I’ve attended this show for the last four years, and each year seems to bring new companies into the fold. Despite more than 25 years of advances in home entertainment, nothing quite matches the tactile thrill of launching a metal ball around a wooden cabinet.

Several companies showed off their latest attempts to bring pinball into virtual reality without abandoning physical controls, letting players wear a VR helmet while pressing real buttons on a pedestal setup. It’s a fun novelty that demonstrates what’s possible, but if the lines at the expo were any indication, most people still prefer walking up to a physical machine and enjoying the tactile controls, visuals, and sounds that come with it.

One of the biggest questions facing anyone buying a pinball machine for home use is what to do when you get bored with a $10,000 game. Until recently, the options were to sell it, find someone willing to trade, or build your own virtual pin setup with screens instead of physical playfields. The Multimorphic P3 team saw an opportunity for another approach.

According to Multimorphic co-creative director Stephen Silver, “The way the P3 is designed is that the lower two-thirds is a ball-tracking interactive display… We have floating mechanisms above the screen, floating flippers, floating slings, floating targets. And the upper third is a swappable play field. We’ve got 10 different play fields now that we can swap and change the entire game.”

As demonstrated by the much-hyped Dungeon Crawler Carl prototype (whose lines never seemed to get shorter), the P3 system uses a playfield screen that can react to ball movement in real time, and the game can change to match player choices. In Dungeon Crawler Carl, for instance, the display layout changes based on which book in the series the player chooses.

“We’re planning on doing seven books in the game… you can play them in any order you want,” Silver explained. ” The idea being that you get to Faction Wars—the events of the seventh book—it’s a perfect wizard mode. When we started this, Faction Wars was the last book in the series. It still feel(s) like a good wrapping-up point for this story that we’re telling. In the future, we could always be open to adding more books, but right now that’s the plan.”

The first two entries in the book series had playable pin versions on the show floor, and Silver says that “every single book itself is the equivalent depth of a ’90s Williams game… It’s like seven really solid games in one,” Silver said.

Dungeon Crawler Carl will enter production “at the end of the year, and then it should be rolling out to delivery early next year,” he said.

The platform’s versatility extends beyond in-house designs. Multimorphic offers a free software development kit (SDK) that lets community members design and distribute their own table creations for the P3 system. Machine owners can swap physical overlay kits or remove them entirely to play original games on the reactive screen.

“There are 30 different games available on the system now because you can do software-only games,” Silver said. “It’s the only third-party development platform in pinball. So anybody can download the free SDK and develop third-party software games… and release it through our store to an audience of P3 owners that are hungry for new content.”

Sitting on one of the more unassuming tables of the PinExpo show floor was Pocket Pinball, a free Android APK that lets users load any Visual Pinball X (VPX) table on their phone or tablet. But the project’s developer, Johnny Zen, had something else to show off: a closed beta for his Pinball Construction Set. An homage to the 1982 classic Bill Budge Apple II game of the same name, the browser-based tool lets users design their own pinball machine with an easy drag-and-drop interface. Multimorphic may have the only free pinball SDK for now, but if Zen has his way, that won’t be true for long.

Whereas most modern pinball designs start at the CAD desk, the upcoming Pinball Construction Set keeps the process entirely within a browser. Zen compares the system to building a coaster in Roller Coaster Tycoon: Users can choose between three styles or start with a blank slate. After selecting a template, such as a standard or wide-body layout, they can add traditional design elements like ramps, targets, and scoops by clicking and dragging them into place.

The program is still in closed beta, but aspiring pinball developers can register their interest to be notified when it becomes publicly available. Zen also plans to add a marketplace where users can commission artwork from freelance artists. “If you needed some artwork for your apron or playfield, you basically look at the artist profiles, then the app will send the artist’s team the exact measurements of what you need,” he said.

One of the most exciting trends in pinball’s modern resurgence is the rise of homebrew design, with passionate hobbyists turning basement-built machines into careers with some of the industry’s biggest players. Often serving as playable resumes, homebrew games give aspiring designers a chance to flex their creative muscles without the licensing restrictions that come with producing commercial machines.

One of this year’s homebrew highlights was Shaolin Flow, an ode to the great Hong Kong action movies that those of us who grew up in the ’90s watched on Saturday afternoon network TV. Complete with an optional Wu-Tang soundtrack, Shaolin Flow lets players choose between traditional flipper-button controls and a more punchy approach. Two fist-shaped sensors sit atop the playfield, to the left and right of the flippers. Players activate the flippers by throwing punches over the sensor.

What initially looked like a gimmick quickly proved to be a great time. Adding a physical element to an already physical game felt more natural than I expected, and the absence of any perceptible input lag made the experience seamless.

As the tools for designing and building pinball machines become more accessible, the homebrew scene continues to grow. Each year brings more entries to the floor, transforming what was once a smaller corner of proudly displayed projects into a dedicated, walled-off section featuring games from the future stars of pinball design. This year’s homebrew showstopper could see its creator designing a licensed table for one of the industry’s major manufacturers by the following year’s show.

Pinball Expo isn’t just an industry trade event; it’s also a celebration of every era of pinball history. Volunteers haul machines from their personal collections to the show floor, where the general public can play them all weekend. And it’s not just balls and flippers. Walk the aisles, and you’ll see artists, merch and crafts vendors, accessories, retro video games, traditional arcades, and enough aftermarket mod kits to turn any pinball machine into a second hobby.

For decades, pinball production was concentrated among a handful of major manufacturers in the Chicagoland area. While the region might still be the industry’s epicenter, newer challengers to Stern’s dominance, like Texas-based Barrels of Fun or European producers like Dutch Pinball, show that things are changing.

Today, aspiring developers can turn a good idea into a playable VPX table without ever putting down their phone. Whether it’s a bedroom developer working with a free SDK or one of the industry’s biggest players, pinball is being made by more people in more places, and fans are all the better for it.
