Teenage girl stabbed multiple times by 14-year-old boy, murder trial told

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:24:13 GMT

Warning: This article contains details readers may find distressing

A teenage girl was stabbed "around 55 times" by a 14-year-old boy, a murder trial has been told.

Lilly Jones, from Blaina, in Blaenau Gwent, left home at about 18:30 on 20 June, telling her father she was "popping out for a bit".

Her body was discovered face down in woodland close to Duffryn Park two days later.

A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be named because he is under 18, denies her murder.

He and Lilly shared an interest in Pokémon and were "in some kind of relationship", the court heard.

The boy was dressed in a white short-sleeved shirt and tie as he sat in the dock at Newport Crown Court on Monday.

Anna Pope KC, prosecuting, told the jury a camping knife containing a complete DNA profile had been found in the boy's bedroom drawer.

"It was calculated to be a billion times more likely if this DNA had come from Lilly Jones than if it had come from someone else," she said.

Pope said the boy had not given an explanation as to why Lilly's DNA was on the knife.

She added scratch marks were discovered on the inside of his arm and forensic swabs taken from Lilly's fingernails identified his DNA.

She had been stabbed in the heart, both lungs and an artery in her neck. There were 17 stab wounds to her neck, and knife wounds were found on her face, jaw, chest and bottom.

Lilly's phone has never been found.

Newport Crown Court was told Lilly and the boy became friends in March this year after a chance meeting in the street.

They were captured on CCTV cameras in Blaina and were last seen together at 18:50 as they walked towards a footbridge leading to the park, near to where her body was later found.

At 22:19 that evening, Lilly's family contacted the police to report her missing. It was the day after her 14th birthday.

Police searching for Lilly spoke to the teenager the following day. He told officers he was supposed to meet up with Lilly at the Red Lion pub in Blaina, but she never arrived.

He later told police they had been together for part of the previous night, before they separated. He said he came home after she told him she was going to meet up with someone else.

In a further conversation with police on the day Lilly's body was found, he said she had told him she wanted to show him a disused park, before leaving.

When he was arrested he told police he did not murder Lilly and did not know where her phone was.

The trial heard that, when a phone belonging to the defendant was examined, he was found to have searched for Gwent Police, and similar terms, about 30 times the morning after Lilly disappeared, between 05:49 and 10:02.

Pope added: "The phone also showed that photographs had been taken by someone using [the defendant's] phone, we say that's [the defendant]."

She added it was "of note" that one of the photographs "is looking back towards the scene where we say Lilly's body was later found".

Addressing the jury, Pope said: "We will ask you to consider why it is that [the defendant] would take a photograph of some distance, of the area where we know Lilly to have died that night? Particularly if, as he suggests, he left her alive, when she was going to meet a friend."

The trial continues.

Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:14:50 GMT

Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.

The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.

Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.

"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.

"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.

He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."

There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.

"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.

The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's support for Trump.

They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media.

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.

In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:11:58 GMT

There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.

Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.

The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.

And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.

This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.

Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.

There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.

Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.

This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres.

A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.

The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment.

The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics.

Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.

Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:07:25 GMT

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".

In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".

Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".

Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.

"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.

She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.

UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".

It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.

Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.

"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."

Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

'People were screaming in pain' during Co-op Live evacuation

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:43:42 GMT

Rap music fans who were evacuated from a concert after an unknown substance was released have said there was a "burning" feeling in their throat and they started to "cough and splutter" and some people were "screaming in pain".

Some 12,000 people were evacuated from Co-op Live Arena after the incident at US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live in Manchester at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday.

One person was taken to hospital, and more than 80 were assessed by paramedics.

Concertgoers have described feeling "unsafe" and seeing "distressing" scenes and people "coughing up blood", with some claiming the venue's security was lax.

Leon Douzi said he was "right next to" where the substance was released, and "there was this gas coming out of a can" and someone holding it and then "it just hit me in the throat" and it felt like "burning", like pepper spray.

He said it was scary and "there was a bit of panic. Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."

Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing, both 19, who had travelled from Cambridge to see the concert, said it was not immediately clear what had happened.

Sophie said: "I thought something had gone wrong with smoke coming off stage.

"We started to suffer, coughing and spluttering and feeling tight-chested. A member of staff said it was tear gas.

"Security rushed in and went straight to the pit. We only left as we were starting to feel unsafe and not 100 per cent well."

She said there was "no communication", adding: "You would think Manchester would be extra vigilant, given what's happened in the past."

A 16-year-old from Manchester, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "The lack of any sort of urgency from the staff was incredibly concerning.

"After the gas was set off and the lights came on, it was more than 40 minutes until we were finally told the show was off.

"And even then, we were just told to leave the arena. We were not rushed, we were not 'evacuated', just told to leave after having sat in the presence of a toxic gas for 40 minutes."

Joey Howe, a football journalist who was also at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester: "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue.

"The lights have come on and he is being rushed off stage.

"That horrible smell just hit you."

The 22-year-old added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking - it was really distressing," Howe said.

"We then decided to leave the venue. It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see."

Carol from Bolton, who was sitting in Block 108 of the arena, said: "About 40 minutes into the show, we saw some sort of smoke and a red flare going off.

"Don Toliver left the stage. From where we were sitting, we saw people rushing out of GA (ground access) and security staff wandering around looking lost.

"We sat for a further 45 minutes before finally hearing an announcement at 11pm to leave the arena.

"At no point was there an announcement to evacuate from our level. Very disappointed."

Harper, who was also there, told BBC Radio 5Live: "I was right on the opposite side and I was seeing people cough up blood - I mean, that's when it was really scary for some of us, especially my girlfriend and I.

"I was in shock because I had no idea what was going on because it just stopped and all the lights came on.

"I saw people getting wheelchairs out... I was fearful it was something even worse."

Jessica Moult-Boffey, 23, of Wigan, said she went to the exit and saw "lads on the bridge" which leads into Medlock Square "crying and screaming in pain".

The music fan added that they were "asking for help" but there were only two stewards outside.

She said she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".

Poppy said: "I just cannot believe it.

"When we went in, no-one checked my bag.

"I held it up and said, 'Do you need to check my bag?'

"The security staff member said: 'No, it's okay.'

"Every single other person I spoke to didn't have their bag checked either."

Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".

It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Greater Manchester Police said it was investigating what the substance was and what had caused the incident.

The force said a major incident had been declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.

Anyone who left the event and has since become unwell is urged to attend their local hospital.

The rapper, whose real name is Caleb Zackery Toliver, was performing at the Manchester venue as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.

He is due to perform at London's O2 Arena on Monday, and at Wembley Arena on 24 November.

Last week the 32-year-old musician received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, including for Best New Artist.

He recently released new track TF, which features on the album for blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto VI and on Friday appeared at Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival in Miami alongside Travis Scott.

Toliver has more than six million followers on Instagram. His sixth album, Nitrous, is set to release on 4 December and he is due to appear on US sketch show Saturday Night Live on 5 December.

'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:30:59 GMT

Manchester United lost 4-0 at Liverpool in their opening match under Mauricio Pochettino

Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.

But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.

By that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.

A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.

The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.

United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.

"We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us," said the 21-year-old.

"There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good.

"It's all about character now."

Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half-year contract

United are giving little away about their plans for the January transfer window.

For now, it is being stressed, Pochettino's priority is to get the most from the players currently at his disposal.

However, there was sympathy with former boss Michael Carrick's belief he had been let down in the summer window and there was a plan to address that.

That situation remains. A striker is thought to be Pochettino's priority given United's only recognised number nine, Benjamin Sesko, is out at least until January with a shin issue that has bothered him since March.

United have a long-standing issue at left-back. First choice Luke Shaw missed his eighth successive game on Sunday and the only other orthodox left-back in senior ranks is England Under-20 international Harry Amass, who didn't even make the bench at Anfield.

However, Pochettino worked with Shaw at the start of his career at Southampton and feels the 31-year-old can be a positive influence on his group.

The reality though is United still have nine games to play before they can make any changes to their squad.

Among those fixtures are home games against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland.

Newly promoted Coventry are four points ahead of United, who are second from bottom. Forest and Sunderland are in the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford club.

A trip to Crystal Palace - the one side below United, and the other Premier League club to replace their coach during the international break - looms on 13 December.

After Wednesday's encounter with Sporting, Pochettino's side have one Champions League game before the end of the year - against RB Leipzig on 8 December.

Any solutions to be found to the current mess over the next five weeks have to come from within. If they don't, light-hearted discussions about a first relegation since 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty start to get serious.

"They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three," Ashley Young - a Premier League winner with United - told Match of the Day.

"They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat.

"It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them. I am sure he will be able to do that when he has been longer in the job."

This video can not be played

Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation right now - Young

Pochettino shut down a question about United's terrible recent defensive record when he spoke to the media immediately after the game at Anfield.

"Tell me only about the circumstance today," he said. "I wasn't [here] in the past."

That is true - and may also have been a useful diversion exercise in avoiding a dissection of a defensive unit he is still getting to know.

However, Pochettino knows United have kept one clean sheet all season - against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. He will also know United have now conceded 19 goals in their past six games.

Pochettino's big decision at Liverpool was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire.

"He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," said the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss.

It was not clear when Pochettino meant.

In the 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October, De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months following major back problems that eventually required surgery, largely because Leny Yoro was suspended and Lisandro Martinez was injured. He then played for two minutes against Roma on 3 November, when he was thrown on as then manager Carrick searched desperately for a winner.

Most goals can be broken down into a number of mistakes that compound to make an eventual negative outcome.

Team positioning has been mentioned as a reason De Ligt found himself exposed under a high ball at Anfield. However, his failure to deal with it presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.

But United have been conceding bad goals all season. Numerous players have been culpable.

There is a limit to what Pochettino can do in the time available. However, he wants to maximise what he can do.

Whereas Carrick tended to let his starting players have a day off after matches, the new regime has decided a warm-down session at Carrington is the better option.

And defensive organisation was surely one of the key points his coaching team had on their list of things to work on when the players began preparations to face Sporting on Wednesday.

Midfielder Andrey Santos has started three out of 10 Premier League games since the opening-day defeat at Hull

With £70m summer arrival Carlos Baleba injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, Pochettino must find a way to protect United's goal, which might require additional support in midfield.

The strengths of Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are with the ball. Either with three in the middle of defence or a third man in midfield, a way needs to be found to stop opposition attacks running straight at the defence.

In his recent interview with Sky Sports, United chief executive Omar Berrada said the club needed to be "disciplined" in the transfer market and avoid spending huge sums on players who would not necessarily make the squad better.

But the fact former Chelsea midfielder Andrey Santos went five games between Premier League starts under Carrick from the opening-day defeat at Hull - and was only introduced for the final three minutes at Anfield - suggests there are doubts over the Brazilian, who cost £48m in the summer.

Underneath that is the knowledge United borrowed from their revolving credit facility around all their major summer purchases and did the same again earlier this month when Pochettino was hired at a cost of just over £7.5m.

In public accounts released last week, United confirmed there was another £160m available in credit - but also they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £236m of which is due within 12 months.

Neither before nor after the transfer window opens do any simple solutions to United's predicament present themselves.

Last season, fellow 'big-six' club Tottenham did not save themselves until the final day of the season.

Confidence remains high at Old Trafford the situation will not be quite so dire for them, but it could be a very bumpy ride.

Raya to miss Dortmund game but injury 'not serious'

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:23:09 GMT

David Raya is Arsenal's first choice goalkeeper and has won the Golden Glove for the last three seasons in the Premier League.

Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya's shoulder injury "doesn't look too serious", but he will miss Tuesday's Champions League against Borussia Dortmund, says Mikel Arteta.

Raya was helped off the pitch in the 70th minute of Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle on Saturday.

He hurt his left shoulder while claiming a cross and making contact with Newcastle forward William Osula.

"We need some more tests [on Tuesday] but it is quite encouraging," said Gunners boss Arteta.

"He is not fit [to face Dortmund] but it doesn't look too serious."

Arteta said that while the incident looked pretty innocuous the pain his keeper was in made him fear it was a serious injury.

"With the pain that he was showing immediately after the action we were all quite worried but it seems to be better than what we expected," said Arteta.

"When you look at the action it doesn't seem to be much but the extent of the pain that he had and how he was struggling, it was quite worrying.

"We expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain he had in that moment.

"The first tests that we have done have shown something that is much more encouraging. He does not need to have surgery which was the worry as that would rule him out for months so let's see."

Raya set to have scan on injury - how much would Arsenal miss him?

Arsenal face Borussia Dortmund, Manchester City, Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid in their next tranche of matches.

And Raya is huge part of the way that Arsenal play because of his ability with the ball at his feet.

When asked if losing Raya for a long period of time would be the biggest blow to his team, Arteta said: "We have seen what David brings to the team but as well that is why we are very protective with Kepa [Arrizabalaga] and Illan [Meslier].

"Everybody needs to be ready because these things unfortunately happen and now we need to show everyone how well we are protected and the good keepers that we have in Kepa and Illan."

UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:09:50 GMT

Spain beat England 1-0 to win the 2023 World Cup

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.

It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.

The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.

The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.

Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

The news comes on the same day the UK government announced a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place.

This video can not be played

Fifa announces UK will host 2035 Women's World Cup

England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.

But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.

England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.

"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."

The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.

If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.

Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.

Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.

A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff is one of two Welsh venues, along with the Cardiff City Stadium

The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.

However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions.

Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football.

"We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them.

"In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt."

Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country".

"Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."

Fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

The bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."

IFA 'positive' over upgrades needed for World Cup

Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 14:54:03 GMT

Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.

Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.

The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.

In a statement published on social media, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.

It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.

The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.

It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".

Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.

They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.

Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued, in which four soldiers and 16 "members of organised crime" were killed, according to the latest figure released by the defence minister on Monday.

Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "Serafín", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.

As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.

There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.

US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".

"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".

The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.

He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.

As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.

The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".

It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.

According to think tank Insight Crime, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.

The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".

His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

Friends were wary of me holidaying with my ex's former wife and kids - but our blended family works

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 14:30:04 GMT

When TV personality Laura Anderson announced she was going on holiday with her ex-partner's ex-wife Natasha Gray and their children, some friends were sceptical.

"They'd say to be wary of that relationship and not see it as genuine," she says.

While there is no formal title for the mums and dads of your child's half-siblings, Laura says she thinks of Natasha as her friend.

Laura, a radio host and former Love Island contestant, has a three-year-old daughter, Bonnie, with her ex, actor Gary Lucy.

Natasha, a nurse, was with Gary for 14 years prior to Laura's relationship with him and they have four children.

Laura tells CBeebies Parenting Download how she and Natasha built a friendship to enable their children to spend time with their half-siblings.

Also on the podcast, co-parenting expert Aaron Dale shares his experience of getting to know his son's stepfather and gives tips to other parents in a similar situation.

Laura was 14 when she found out she had a half-sister from her father's previous relationship and now the two are "very close".

She felt a responsibility to make sure her own daughter didn't "miss out on that sibling bond" and the idea of spending time with Natasha and her children developed naturally.

"Maybe there was a point that I wasn't fully ready when Bonnie was younger and I was still navigating my break-up," she says.

"But I became more comfortable with the idea and I thought, 'No, she's right. We need to make an effort'... It felt like a chance to give [Bonnie] more than just me and her."

Aaron - author of The Co-Parent: A Toolkit for Parenting Together, Apart - grew up on the same estate as his half-siblings but says his father never introduced them. His two sons have different mums.

"I made a promise to myself that my sons would never feel like they were 'half' anything. My sons are brothers, full stop."

Aaron co-parents with his ex-partners and says he has a "great relationship" with the stepdad to one of his sons. He says a blended family creates "a wider circle of love" for children.

"I've seen this first hand with my son's stepfather. Not only does he have an amazing relationship with my son, but so does his daughter and their wider family."

He acknowledges it's not always straightforward but says it's the responsibility of parents to "put differences aside".

"Whatever the dynamic looks like between the adults involved, your children's relationships with their siblings deserve to be a priority."

Aaron says it's important to take time to get to know the other adults in your child's family including their values, personality, interests and what they want from life.

"Don't become so consumed with how this person might fit into your child's world that you forget to consider whether they fit into yours," he says.

He advises having a conversation about the roles you would like each other to play, what you're comfortable with and where boundaries need to be established.

You should also respect "existing bonds", he adds. "You are becoming an extension of a child's existing family, not a replacement for somebody else.

"Don't enter a child's life feeling that you have to take somebody else's place, and don't make them feel that loving you somehow means being disloyal to another parent."

Laura's advice for getting to know your blended family is to "make it about the children".

"Be as selfless as possible and remove any negative feelings you might have towards your ex," she says.

Even if you initially feel rejected when trying to establish a blended family, she urges you not to "give up at the first hurdle".

Despite scepticism from friends, Laura says she and Natasha have proven their blended family works.

"I think they definitely changed their minds once they saw pictures of us all together. They'd say, "You look so comfortable and so happy.'"

Laura says the trip she had in the summer with Natasha and their children was "one of the best holidays" she had been on.

"I felt really comfortable and it was just love all round."

Laura and Natasha have booked a staycation in the Cotswolds to celebrate Christmas with their children.

"I've got matching PJs and someone's going to come in and cook for us - and we've got a Santa coming in."

She adds: "We want to have those memories, we just want to soak it all up."

England's tearaway quick bowler reinvented as a top-order batter

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 14:26:27 GMT

George made her England debut against Australia in 2018

Sportspeople are faced with a question when injuries hit again and again. Do I try one more time or should I walk away?

England's Katie George came really close to choosing the latter option last year.

"I had a couple of conversations with my close family and partner about whether it was taking too much out of me and whether I was happy with the person I was," she says. "I was pretty miserable."

George made her England debut in 2018 aged 18 as a tearaway fast bowler. She was quick. Some coaches believed generationally so.

She played seven internationals between March and July before the injuries first hit that summer. George is matter of fact about how many have followed. The list is enough to make the rest of us wince.

"Nine stress fractures in my back," she says. "I tore the cartilage off my rib.

"Bits and bobs. Ankle surgery. I have missed a lot of cricket."

Unable to bowl because of her back and little more than a tailender with the bat, George got into sides purely for her athleticism and a penchant for stunning catches. She was occasionally referred to as a 'specialist fielder'.

The label was meant as a compliment, but it still stung. She says she felt like an "empty uniform".

"For a long time I was worried about being the [injury prone ex-Liverpool and England striker] Daniel Sturridge - what could have been, all of that talent wasted," says George, who played football for Portsmouth in her youth.

"I found that really difficult. I didn't want to be that person.

"Over a period of time you get told you are really resilient and you have been through so much. Then when it keeps happening there is pressure and it gets harder.

"You need to look brave and be resilient and show less emotion than you are feeling. Anyone knows when you bottle that up it can get quite tricky."

This video can not be played

The injury-hit bowler back with England as a batter

Then came George's end-of-year appraisal at Warwickshire - that uncomfortable question. Quit or change something. George opted the latter.

Alongside coach Ali Maiden, an unlikely plan was hatched. George had more ducks than fifties at that point in her professional career but why not try and build on flashes of potential. Why not try and become a frontline batter?

Even George did not really believe.

"I always knew I was half decent at bowling but I never had that feeling for batting," she says.

"Right the way through age groups and my first fifty at Western Storm, there were moments where in a game it would come off but I would have no idea how to replicate it.

"I would always put it down to a fluke."

The turnaround has been extraordinary. Batting most regularly at number three, George topped the average tables for this season's One-Day Cup with a figure of 77.55.

A 98 against Blaze in April was followed by a first professional century against Lancashire in June. An unbeaten ton against Durham rounded off the campaign. She even opened in the T20 Blast.

"It is crazy it happened but there was a lot of hard work and I am very grateful to Ali," she says.

"He pushed me and challenged me as to why couldn't I change the narrative a little bit. I want to impact games.

"I don't want to sit on the bench. I can do that from my sofa."

As a result, George will travel to India for an England A tour that begins later this month.

She is there alongside youngsters tipped for bright futures but also established names like Lauren Filer and Tilly Corteen-Colman. Her partner Issy Wong was named in the squads but has withdrawn because of injury.

"We were doing a team thing a couple of weeks ago and we were asked what we are most proud of," George says.

"Until the last few months it probably would have been my England debut but, once I thought about it, it was actually being stood in that team room as a batter and wearing this kit again.

"If you said I would be here as a batter in England kit I would definitely have laughed and said you were smoking something."

Given her past, George would be wise not to look too far into the future. She has not given up on bowling again regularly, nor is she ready to listen to advice to stop.

"It would fall on deaf ears," she says.

More immediately, England coach Charlotte Edwards, selector Lydia Greenway and England's new managing director of women's cricket Leah Poulton will all be in India for the upcoming tour, providing George the chance to impress.

"My dream would be to play a red-ball game for England," she says. "That is what I set out for do.

"It is what I watched as a kid with my dad. I vividly remember my first ever Test match watching Jimmy Anderson running in and bowling.

"Whether I am able to, I don't know. Maybe it will be as a batter - that would be the biggest plot twist ever."

George was given her first 50-over cap by Charlotte Edwards, who is now England coach

GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 14:08:50 GMT

A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.

Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."

The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.

Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.

He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.

City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".

He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.

He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.

Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.8m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.

The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

When he was sentenced he stood and smiled.

He had short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt without a tie.

The hacker blinked frequently during the hearing.

The Judge Mr Justice Turner told him "you are a very talented young man," and warned him: "Don't let this happen again."

Kurtaj's defence team said he found the online world a more comfortable way of interacting with other people.

"The restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests that are a core feature of ASD [autism spectrum disorder] led him to become preoccupied with the online world where he felt better able to function and exist," they said.

They said he was exposed to people who showed him how to cheat at games and then to "people who were involved in hacking".

During the pandemic, he was "very isolated" and his "connection to Lapsus$ provided him with a sense of community and self-worth that had been absent in his life previously," they added.

Kurtaj and the gang's other hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber used social engineering techniques - tricking people into clicking malicious links or giving up sensitive information - to gain access to internal systems.

Previously, the court heard that during his hack on Uber he posted a picture of a penis as part of his attempts to force the company to pay a ransom.

His hacks on the companies are estimated to have caused around £10m of damage.

Using the data stolen from the firms, he and other members of the gang targeted cryptocurrency investors.

The prosecution argued that the gang stole at least $300,000 (£230,000) from individual victims.

Kurtaj also pleaded guilty to physical assaults on workers while in custody, including multiple biting incidents.

In prison, he was caught with a mobile phone after sending a taunting text message to police and posting updates on Snapchat.

Will it snow this week? Mild Atlantic air collides with cold air across the UK

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 12:41:42 GMT

The UK is in the grip of the coldest spell of autumn so far.

Yellow cold health alerts from the UK Health Security Agency remain in force until 09:00 GMT on Tuesday, warning of possible impacts to health services and vulnerable people.

The cold Arctic air is clashing with mild Atlantic air that arrived in the south-west of the UK over the weekend - a meteorological setup that provides the ingredients for possible snow.

However, there remains uncertainty in where the boundary between the cold and mild air masses will sit.

Even small shifts in temperature could make a significant difference to what falls from the sky and, crucially, the chances of snow.

Weather battleground for the week ahead

A clash between the air masses is already underway, as weather systems arrived from the Atlantic overnight into Sunday, bringing milder air with them.

The coming days will see the UK caught between lingering cold air, held in place by a dominant area of high pressure over Norway, and milder, wetter conditions associated with Sunday's weather fronts.

For many, the main hazards will be freezing fog and icy stretches, particularly where skies clear overnight.

Further west, rain could still bring a risk of disruption, while uncertainty remains over the potential for snow.

The key question is whether the cold air can hold its ground or whether milder Atlantic conditions will steadily push eastwards.

A cold and frosty start on Monday

Monday will begin on a cold note, with temperatures widely below freezing, bringing frost along with patches of ice and freezing fog.

Blue skies and just a few fair-weather clouds will follow the frost.

Any patchy fog will clear, but with winds a little fresher than on Sunday, temperatures will reach 8 to 10C.

Meanwhile, Sunday's bands of rain will gradually weaken over southwest England and Wales, where conditions will remain grey, damp and blustery.

At times, cloud and light rain will also spread into Northern Ireland.

Tuesday afternoon pressure chart

By midweek, the battleground will shift further eastwards.

Early on Tuesday, the weather front - which by then will mainly consist of a band of cloud - will have edged further east.

As a result, it will be a little less chilly to start the day, but cloudier for most.

Another, more active weather front will quickly follow, moving eastwards across Northern Ireland on Tuesday morning.

It is then forecast to spread into northern and western England, Wales and much of Scotland through the day, bringing the first chance of snow to the Highlands and Grampians.

Tuesday night and Wednesday will be dominated by cloudy skies, with weather fronts bringing rain at times.

The situation could be complicated by another area of low pressure developing in the English Channel.

This would not only bring more rain to the south but also strengthen easterly winds, which would begin to push the cold air back westwards.

The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.

Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

"Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."

Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m.

This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions.

Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation".

Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 10:09:25 GMT

The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

How have we got here?

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.

Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."

She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."

However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

It had frozen about £50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.

Gordon Brothers released around £21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.

Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid, although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.

A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer.

Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

For now, Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended by 10 days to find a rescue deal.

Shuttleworth says the future of Poundland is "really unclear, with the owners and the management at loggerheads about its future".

Palmer says there are two ways forward for Poundland - either a solvent deal, where the company gets bought and carries on trading, or a collapse followed by a break-up.

"The immediate make-or-break issue is Christmas: a value retailer that can't get stock on its shelves in November and December is in serious trouble, whatever its full-year results say," says Palmer.

There has been political pressure on Gordon Brothers from both Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. They have called for answers over why the Martin Property Group offer to buy the business, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

A committee of MPs also questioned Gordon Brothers last week, adding to pressure.

But Shuttleworth says that as a US firm Gordon Brothers appears "unmoved" by the arguments that the UK government has put forward.

Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 09:53:52 GMT

Tyson Fury will fight Anthony Joshua on 11 December in Cardiff

Tyson Fury says he was diagnosed with schizophrenia soon after his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.

British heavyweight Fury, 38, says he heard voices in his head threatening to hurt him and his family.

In a documentary which will be released by Netflix on Friday, Fury and wife Paris describe how he was diagnosed after being admitted to hospital with a suspected heart attack in June 2016.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury says.

"It was like a living version of the pits of hell. I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.

"The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder."

Doctors said Fury had suffered an anxiety attack.

Fury recalls hearing the radio talking to him, and begging Paris to get him out of the hospital because "the Illuminati" wanted him.

In the period after his victory over Klitschko, Fury gained weight and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.

"It got that bad I was hearing voices in my mind," he says.

"I wouldn't be able to sit and have a conversation because I'd be hearing stuff in my mind.

"I didn't know where to turn and no-one knew what to do. I really needed help, or check into rehab or something.

"I never got a break from it for years. I wanted to be what I thought was normal again."

This video can not be played

How Tyson Fury's mental health unravelled after conquering Wladimir Klitschko

After Fury was released from hospital, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder was confirmed, according to the documentary.

The NHS describes schizophrenia, external as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech. It says the main symptom of bipolar disorder, external is extreme changes to your mood.

Fury describes a "turning point" in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween.

"I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked," he says.

"I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on.

"I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, 'I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I'm a fat mess addicted to alcohol'."

He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training.

It resulted in another world title when he beat Deontay Wilder in 2020.

Fury is preparing for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December.

The fight will be broadcast live on Netflix.

De Villiers claims ball-tampering from first 2018 Test

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:08:13 GMT

AB de Villiers played 114 Tests for South Africa between 2004 and 2018, averaging 50.66 with the bat

Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers has alleged Australia were ball-tampering from the first match of their controversial 2018 Test series.

Australia captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft received long-term bans for their roles in using sandpaper to alter the ball during the third Test in Cape Town.

Former Australia batter Usman Khawaja, whose new autobiography has re-started scrutiny of the scandal, has previously claimed that sandpaper was also used during the preceding Test at Gqeberha, then known as Port Elizabeth.

Warner and Bancroft have both corroborated Khawaja's claims about that match, but De Villiers has now suggested the ball was altered during the series opener in Durban.

"It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE," De Villiers said on his YouTube channel ABD360. "I'm very happy for people to quote me on that.

"I see everyone is sort of admitting that in Port Elizabeth it also happened. I can very much tell you Durban was no different, in the first Test. Go look at the footage. Absolutely no doubt in my mind.

"We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there.

"So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or (a) nail, I don't care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew. Just stand up and say 'we were wrong'. A lot is at stake now because they lied.

"The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse. It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."

In a 4,000-word article last week, Bancroft said sandpaper wasn't used in Durban, where left-arm paceman Mitchell Starc finished with match figures of 9-109 as he bowled Australia to their one victory in the series.

"Casting forward to the first Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used," he wrote. "There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter-seam picking, this practice became so normal after my first Test."

Australia's bowling attack in the three Tests and Darren Lehmann, their head coach at the time, have consistently denied any knowledge of ball-tampering during the series.

Current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the bowling attack, labelled Khawaja's claims as "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense" at a news conference earlier this month and has received backing from Cricket Australia to continue in his role.

Cricket Australia has launched an independent "forum" for players and staff involved in the scandal to voluntarily share their version of events, but it is not a full investigation and will not involve any new penalties.

"It's become really personal for all the people involved and I do have sympathy for them," added De Villiers, who played in every match in the series and retired from international cricket after its conclusion.

"Obviously not sympathy for what took place on that day and who knows how many games before then.

"I just feel they should have stuck together as a unit. They threw the guys under the bus and forced a situation like this to pop up again eight years later."

De Villiers also acknowledged that he was not an "angel" during his playing career but insisted his side had stayed within the rules of the game when working on the ball.

"I'm not playing all innocent and saying that I'm the perfect person," he said. "We all try and get the ball to reverse. We try and bounce it in. We try and do it in a legal manner and we try and push the boundaries as much as possible.

"We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something, to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object onto the field and blatantly cheating."

Cricket Australia has been contacted for comment.
