What six grazing horses tell us about England's housing crisis

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 06:00:43 GMT

About a five-minute walk from the train station in Middlesbrough, six horses are grazing lazily on a derelict patch of land.

Tethered and friendly, the animals do not attract much attention from residents, despite being so close to the town centre.

But their presence on the land, by the banks of the River Tees, is a symbol of the UK's decades-long failure to build enough houses.

In 2004, the local council announced plans to build 2,400 homes on the grass the horses are eating.

But 22 years later, just 216 homes have been built. The money initially outlined for the project has never been found.

The UK is in a housing crisis with demand for homes continuing to outstrip supply.

To understand why successive governments have failed to build enough houses, BBC News went to this Middlesbrough scheme, and planned developments in York and the Isle of Sheppey, in Kent.

Each has its own story, with finances, infrastructure planning and developers' appetites all playing a major role - issues mirrored at other sites across the country.

Combined, the projects we visited promised to build 7,400 homes. To date, just 326 have been constructed.

Shortfalls like this affect national goals significantly, says Anthony Breach, director of policy and research at the Centre for Cities think tank.

The UK's reliance on "large, complex schemes" to deliver new housing means that "when our larger sites get a bit stuck, that has a disproportionate impact on national housebuilding", he says.

These large-scale projects, increasingly favoured by private developers and often driven by local councils, are key to the Labour government's target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election.

That target will probably be missed.

The 2004 plans for Middlehaven in Middlesbrough, a long-disused industrial site, included not just thousands of homes but also a theatre, restaurants and hotels.

It was billed as a £500m development, but it had one fundamental flaw: the money never existed.

Instead, this figure was simply an estimate of overall cost, Middlesbrough Council told us.

Almost a decade later, in 2013, the development was proposed again. This time, the council bought 185 homes that already existed, so they could be demolished to make space.

Yet only 216 homes have been built to replace them, a net gain of 31.

The council says delivery of the masterplan was curtailed by the 2008 financial crash, "leading to the departure of the council's development partner".

A college campus, business space and housing have been delivered, it says, and a new school is being built.

The price that new homes will sell for is a key factor in large developments progressing, says Breach, as housebuilding firms look for returns on their investments.

In places where house prices are lower, he says, public sector funds may be needed to "bridge the gap between the cost of building [works] and the price at which the houses can be sold for".

In September, Middlesbrough Council announced plans for 462 new homes on the site - the beginning, it hopes, of a development of 3,400 homes in all.

This time, however, the council is far more cautious, acknowledging the money might not be there to achieve everything it would like.

In York, a plan for 3,000 homes was announced in 2001, but a quarter of a century later, not a single house has been built.

Alongside the homes, close to the historic centre of the city, were to be business and hospitality opportunities - just like in Middlesbrough.

Planning consultant Nora Galley was hired by the local council to develop the York Central masterplan.

Her designs, she tells the BBC, combined a realistic vision with a plan to deliver it.

"It wasn't just a beautiful place that looked great in architect's drawings," she says.

But by the time the 2008 crash hit, work had not begun.

In September this year, the project's first phase was finally given the green light, with some 2,500 homes planned to be built by 2040.

Galley is disappointed that construction has taken so long to get under way, and that fewer homes will be built than originally planned.

"There is no fabric in this country to manage the delivery of strategic projects," she tells us - highlighting what she sees as supply chain issues and a lack of construction training.

In June, trade body the Construction Industry Training Board backed Galley's point - citing a need for 206,000 new construction workers across the UK between now and 2030.

York Central is now set to cost £2bn to complete, far more than the hundreds of millions of pounds local papers reported when plans were first set out.

Delays to the project have cost York greatly, says Galley. The city has missed out on "wealth, opportunities, a better-performing economy".

Residents we spoke to were largely in favour of York Central, seeing its potential. But all seemed puzzled by the amount of time it had taken.

Cycle lanes, pristine paths and bus stops surround the site, yet nobody was around to use them. "I had colour in my hair when they first announced it," quips one middle-aged woman who lives in the neighbouring estate.

The main problem has been the site's positioning, surrounded by railway lines, says Labour leader of City of York Council, Claire Douglas.

The project stalled because, for a time, there was no money from government to pay for an access road allowing construction materials on to the site, she says.

But now the access road is nearing completion and the first houses should be built within two years, she says.

Nearly 200 miles (322km) south, on the Isle of Sheppey in Kent, a planned development of up to 2,000 new homes was meant to help regenerate a deprived part of the island.

It is now 23 years since the plan was initially conceived, and 17 years since it was backed by local councils. But only 110 houses have been built.

The project was hailed in a 2009 press release as a "£400m regeneration" of the area, but Swale Borough Council has told the BBC that, as in Middlesbrough, the money never actually existed.

The figure, it said, was an estimation "of the likely investment required to deliver the scheme at that time", and there was no housing developer lined up.

Some 3,000 jobs were also expected to be created, but only some have materialised.

A retail park housing a Morrisons, Burger King and Sports Direct among other outlets has been completed, but plans for a marina have been scrapped.

Where the hundreds of homes should stand is an empty field surrounded by metal railings. Locals say the grass is occasionally mowed.

Meanwhile, the council has 1,800 households waiting for social housing.

"We do need a few more houses [here], but we also need more doctors and things like that as well," says Marie Miller, lifelong resident of the neighbouring village of Rushenden.

The planned "state of the art" healthcare centre on the same site remains unbuilt.

Nothing has happened on the site in a long time, Miller says.

The original 2,000-homes plan was scaled back in 2015 to 1,180, but even this reduced figure is unlikely to be achieved. According to council documents, the project is back at the planning stage.

Homes England, the government's housing and regeneration agency, is now approaching housebuilders for their "early observations" about developing the site.

After the economic downturn of 2008, the planned level of development "proved to be an optimistic forecast", the local council said, adding it was "working closely with Homes England to agree an updated timescale".

These three schemes we have visited are not the only projects to have failed to deliver new housing over long time periods.

In London, where housebuilding has fallen substantially in recent years, not one of the 3,500 homes planned for Convoy's Wharf in Deptford has been built - despite outline planning permission being given in 2005. Planning problems and objections from locals have contributed to the delays.

On the north side of the Thames, a 2008 plan to build 10,800 units at Barking Riverside was stalled for years because of poor transport links. However, since the creation of a new rail line, 3,000 homes now have been built and plans have been approved to almost double the housing development to 20,000 homes.

The glacial speed at which things get done, particularly at the sites we visited in Middlesbrough, York and Kent, offer key insights as to why the UK has not built as many homes as it needs.

Part of the housebuilding challenge, says Anthony Breach from Centre for Cities, is that the UK's planning system is "pretty unusual internationally".

Even if a developer follows all the rules "you can still be denied planning permission by local politicians", he says - meaning developments take much longer, and risk being upended if a new party is elected locally.

To overcome planning delays, mayoral development corporations (MDCs) are increasingly being established by England's regional mayors. These bodies can take planning duties away from a local authority and make compulsory land purchases, enabling large-scale projects to move more quickly.

Breach sees this as a positive step, describing MDCs as a shortcut through the planning system that should see housebuilding increase.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing told the BBC it was "working with Homes England to get stalled schemes moving, with housing starts up 20% on this time last year".

They added: "We've unblocked and accelerated more than 130,000 homes and, through our planning overhaul and £40bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme, we are unlocking development and building the homes our country needs."

The schemes in Middlesbrough, York and Kent may eventually come good - but decades later than promised, their failures all contributing to the UK's chronic lack of housing.

Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain

BBC News Mon, 23 Nov 2026 01:05:07 GMT

Energy prices are forecast to rise by 26% for millions of homes in January, but experts say there are ways to keep a check on rising bills.

Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase.

Energy regulator Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.

So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.

With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.

Research foundation Nesta suggests:

These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.

Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.

Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.

Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.

Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.

Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.

Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.

The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.

Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.

Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.

The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.

There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes.

This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.

Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.

Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.

Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme can help you repay energy debt.

You can get more advice from Ofgem, Citizens Advice, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes.

People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.

But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.

Submarine finds world’s deepest explosive volcanic activity in Mariana trench

New Scientist November 23, 2026

Scientists exploring the Mariana trench with a remotely operated submarine rover have discovered the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic activity to date. Experts say that the nature of the activity is also unusual and ripe for further exploration.

Robert Stern, formerly at the University of Texas at Dallas, and his colleagues were collecting rock samples at the Mariana trench – the deepest valley in the world’s oceans, and home to the deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep – to understand the geology of the unique spot.

The Mariana trench began to form about 52 million years ago when one tectonic plate – the Pacific plate – slid or “subducted” under another called the Philippine Sea plate. At Challenger Deep, the trench is almost 11,000 metres below sea level.

Advertisement

‘Shazam for whales’ uses AI to track sounds heard in Mariana Trench

Focusing on an area about 6100 metres deep, in the vicinity of Challenger Deep, the team found deposits containing volcanic ash and rock – evidence of the deepest volcanic eruptions ever reported. The location was also unusual, occurring in an area where the mantle is generally not thought to be hot enough to melt. The team made the discovery using a remotely operated submersible named Jason.

While the team hasn’t yet identified exactly where the eruptions occurred, only finding evidence of volcanic activity in samples, they believe that it can’t have occurred far above the collection site on the trench wall. This is because the volcanic ash and rock in the samples had welded onto rocks at the sample site, showing it was hot when it was deposited. If the volcanic activity had occurred at a much shallower depth, the volcanic ash would have cooled by the time it reached the site 6000 metres below sea level.

Peter Kokelaar at the University of Liverpool, UK, says that the site sits closer to the meeting point of tectonic plates than would usually be expected. “It’s probably the deepest product of an active volcanic system that’s been recorded,” says Kokelaar. “It’s particularly interesting because it’s a peculiar place for active volcanism, so close to the trench.”

Free newsletter

Peter Rowley at the University of Bristol, UK, says that the site seems to show evidence that the Pacific plate is subducting deeper under the Philippine plate than expected, creating a stretching effect on the upper section of the Philippine Sea plate and thinning it out. This thinning might make it easier for mantle material to punch through the crust to trigger volcanic activity.

“Material that was originally quite deep down, stuff from the upper mantle, is actually quite accessible. So what they’re sampling is material which has some mantle origin to it. And getting to access mantle material is something we’ve been trying to do in various locations for a very long time,” says Rowley. “It’s an unusual tectonic setup.”

“So, certainly, [this is] explosive volcanic activity at greater depths than we’ve seen before,” says Rowley. “Possibly this is the deepest volcanism we’ve seen. Submarine volcanism is something we’ve got quite big knowledge gaps in. It’s that famous thing that we know less about the seafloor than we do about the moon.”

The overlooked longevity nutrients that may add years to your life

New Scientist November 23, 2026

Bruce Ames was remarkable in many ways. A renowned biochemist who continued working into his nineties, he is best known for developing a low-cost screening test for cancer-causing substances. But he devoted the latter stages of his long career to an intriguing idea: that a hitherto-unrecognised class of nutrients plays a key role in promoting healthy ageing. “Many as-yet-unknown longevity vitamins and proteins likely remain to be discovered,” he wrote in one of his last papers, in 2022, just a couple of years before he passed away, aged 95.

But could such nutrients have been hiding in plain sight all along? A number of promising candidates are under investigation, including some found in mushrooms and seaweed. Proving the long-term health impacts of dietary factors in rigorous trials is a huge challenge, and the field of anti-ageing supplements has been plagued by ideas that failed to live up to their promise, but we could still be on the cusp of finding out if Ames was right. If so, what might we one day be dosing up with for the benefit of our future selves?

Rapid bursts of ageing are causing a total rethink of how we grow old

A healthy diet requires various vitamins and minerals for basic metabolic reactions in the human body – that is, to keep us alive in the immediate future. There are around 30 of these essential micronutrients, including the vitamins from A to K, and minerals such as calcium and iron. A deficiency in these can cause conditions such as scurvy, rickets and beriberi.

Advertisement

But Ames had a compelling idea that inadequate intake of micronutrients also causes insidious, long-term damage. Building on his many years of research investigating metabolism and ageing, in 2006 he proposed that when vitamins and minerals are in short supply, our bodies operate a triage system, allocating them to systems involved in immediate survival and sacrificing other functions that are more important for long-term health, such as DNA repair and maintenance of mitochondria. This could explain why moderate deficiencies in vitamin D, for instance, are associated with certain cancers and cardiovascular disease.

His subsequent studies, working with Joyce McCann at the Children’s Hospital Oakland Research Institute in California, demonstrated that when selenium and vitamin K are scarce, they are indeed preferentially allocated to the biological systems that are most important for short-term survival.

This led Ames to the idea that some dietary compounds are particularly adept at supporting long-term health, and that there may be an entire other class of unrecognised nutrients that might be capable of activating various protective pathways in our bodies. If we consume enough of them, he suggested, they can fine-tune our metabolism and help shield us from insidious, long-term damage.

In that 2022 paper, Ames produced a list of around 40 nutrients – key ingredients for thousands of chemical reactions throughout the body – which he believed to be critical for preventing chronic conditions and promoting longevity.

“I propose that many of the known vitamins and minerals have, besides a ‘survival’ function, aging-delaying (‘longevity’) functions as well. I also propose that other dietary biochemicals, not officially recognized as vitamins or as having age-delaying functions, have a positive age-delaying effect,” he wrote.

Perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that some lesser-known substances in our diet may have this impact. There are myriad biochemicals in our food, and we know surprising little about this “nutritional dark matter” or its impacts on the body. But proving the efficacy of any purported longevity nutrients – substances whose effects gradually accumulate over the long term – was always going to be difficult, not least because they would sail under the radar of standard tests for deficiencies.

Free newsletter

A recent academic book, Supplements and Drugs for Healthy Longevity, describes more than 250 chemicals that are listed in various databases as potentially being able to alter the ageing process. However, it notes that the evidence mainly comes from experiments on organisms such as yeasts, worms or other animals. “[Strong evidence] on the human species is absolutely missing,” says Suresh Rattan, a biogerontologist at Aarhus University in Denmark, who co-edited the book.

This could change, however, as the results of robust clinical trials begin to roll in, and with new research efforts under way to identify nutrients that may slow the clock.

One of these is a 2025 analysis of 777 generally healthy and active people aged over 70 who took part in the DO-HEALTH randomised controlled trial to investigate whether vitamin D, omega-3 fatty acids and a simple home exercise programme could prevent disease in older age and thereby prolong healthy life expectancy. This measured the biological age of the participants after three years of the trial and found that omega-3 alone moderately slowed the rate of biological ageing, with extra benefits from the addition of vitamin D or exercise.

Although we don’t yet have data about the ultimate impact this has on healthspan – the number of years that we live in good health – the study’s authors noted that “even small changes in biological aging, if sustained, may have relevant effects on population health”.

Another large-scale clinical trial that reported results earlier this year analysed the anti-ageing effect of a daily supplement of cocoa extract (containing high concentrations of substances called flavanols, thought to assist healthy ageing) and a daily multivitamin in 958 people in the US aged over 60. This found that the cocoa extract had no impact, but the multivitamin resulted in a small but significant reduction in the rate of biological ageing, which might be linked to our micronutrient requirements increasing with age.

The negative flavanol finding is interesting, because Ames, too, thought that certain substances in food that aren’t classed as vitamins could have a positive long-term impact on our health. But rather than flavanols, the candidates he proposed were pigments called carotenoids, as well as certain antioxidants produced by bacteria and fungi. Now, initiatives to investigate some of these are under way, with researchers in Singapore at the forefront of these efforts.

It is projected that, by 2050, a third of Singapore’s population will be over 65, with spiralling rates of conditions such as cancer and dementia too. The urgency of the situation has led to large-scale investment in clinical trials exploring new ways to elongate healthspan – and among the nutrients in the crosshairs of researchers there is one highlighted by Ames called ergothioneine. Produced mainly by fungi and bacteria, the best dietary source of it is mushrooms, particularly oyster and shiitake varieties.

A number of studies from the past few years have already shown that eating mushrooms is associated with a lower risk of various chronic conditions and longer life expectancy. Humans have also evolved adaptations that allow our bodies to absorb and retain ergothioneine. A specific transporter molecule for this nutrient in our intestines and other tissues means that when we eat foods such as mushrooms, it is distributed around the body – suggesting that it is important for us. But why?

New insight into how we age suggests it may be driven by a failure to switch off the forces that build our bodies. If true, it could lead to a deeper understanding of ageing – and the possibility of slowing it

Research from three decades ago revealed that ergothioneine is a particularly powerful antioxidant, a substance that helps negate damage to cells caused by unstable molecules called free radicals, one of the underlying drivers of ageing. It is up to 30 times better at neutralising free radicals than glutathione, one of the body’s innate antioxidants.

Barry Halliwell, a biochemist recruited by the National University of Singapore to lead anti-ageing trials, suspects that an ergothioneine deficiency could be linked to numerous neurodegenerative conditions. “Age-related diseases of the brain, Parkinson’s, vascular dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, cognitive impairment, are all associated with low ergothioneine levels,” says Halliwell. And research on human brain cells and miniature lab-grown organs known as organoids suggests that consuming sufficient ergothioneine might actively protect the brain.

This evidence has convinced Halliwell that maintaining a minimal level of ergothioneine in the bloodstream may be essential for a healthy brain. “Our hypothesis is that it’s actually a vitamin and you need it,” he says. “But it’s different to, say, vitamin C, where you’ll start to have symptoms within a few months if you don’t get enough. We think that the consequences of ergothioneine deficiency take a long time to manifest.”

In an attempt to find out if that is true, he and his colleagues launched a pilot study a few years ago where people aged over 60 with mild cognitive impairment took ergothioneine supplements for a year. Because the study was interrupted by the covid-19 pandemic, they were only able to recruit 19 people, as opposed to the planned 150, but there were still signs that it improved memory and learning abilities and slowed neuron damage. “We just got funding to redo the whole trial,” says Halliwell. “We need to do a full double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial, which we are planning.”

Meanwhile, in the UK, a trial is measuring the impact of ergothioneine, as well as another antioxidant called taxifolin (found in onions and fruits such as apples), on people aged 50 to 65 as a possible way of keeping the immune system more resilient through midlife, when it starts to decline. The aim is to see whether this reduces the prevalence of so-called senescent immune cells, white blood cells that have ceased to function normally and instead contribute to chronic levels of inflammation, and hence the ageing process. The results are due soon.

From dampening inflammation to boosting mental health, the many types of dietary fibre have a surprisingly large impact throughout the body. Here's how to get your fill

But ergothioneine is just one of the possible longevity nutrients in the spotlight. Other candidates have been pinpointed through studies of the foods common in the diets of people who live well for a long time, such as fucoidan, a chemical found in the cell walls of brown seaweed.

A number of large-scale population studies have highlighted an association between consuming more seaweed and lower levels of both cognitive and physical frailty. Fucoidan, which can activate a gene called SIRT6 that promotes DNA repair, is one possible explanation.

Andrea Maier, director of the National University of Singapore’s Academy for Healthy Longevity and the mastermind behind the country’s various approaches to slowing ageing, is now leading a trial giving 2.4 grams of fucoidan per day to 60 Singaporeans aged 50 to 80 with signs of pre-frailty. The aim is to see if it can slow ageing based on inflammatory and immune signals in their blood, as well as their DNA.

In addition, the team will examine body composition, muscle and sleep quality, cognition and skin health. “In roughly four or five months, we will know if you should eat more brown seaweed,” says Maier.

Elsewhere, other researchers are working to identify overlooked compounds in food that might be important to our health. In 2024, for instance, a team led by Sastia Putri at Osaka University in Japan analysed the chemical footprint of tempeh, a food made from fermented soya beans that is reputed to protect against heart disease. This enabled the researchers to pinpoint a substance called meglutol, a cholesterol-lowering chemical found in soya beans that increases in concentration following fermentation. “It works in a similar way to statins,” says Putri.

This is an important step forward in understanding unrecognised nutrients in our food, but there is still a long way to go to discover any impacts that tempeh and meglutol might have on long-term health. And it is important to remember that there have been plenty of red herrings in relation to longevity nutrients.

For instance, Ames enthused about taurine, an amino acid thought to support the brain, muscle and heart. Studies showed that concentrations of taurine in our blood decline with age, suggesting that deficiencies might be a driver of ageing. However, a major analysis last year by a team at the US National Institute on Aging instead found huge variation in the amount of circulating taurine between adults, and no clear association between taurine levels and health status.

Researchers in Singapore faced their own setback when studying another proposed longevity nutrient called alpha-ketoglutarate, or AKG, which plays critical roles within the body in everything from energy production to kidney function. Animal studies have shown that AKG can have a potent impact on lifespan, and AKG supplements are also used by athletes to aid muscle repair and recovery. However, when Maier and her colleagues trialled a daily supplement of AKG in people aged 40 to 60 who were deemed to be ageing rapidly, based on a biological test assessing changes to their DNA, it failed to offer noticeable health improvements.

Maier suspects that AKG could make more difference in a more vulnerable population, and a new trial taking place in Singapore is examining whether it can help prevent the development of post-operative frailty in older adults after heart surgery.

These findings also raise the question of how longevity nutrients might best be utilised. Rather than standalone supplements, Putri, Rattan and many others think they are more likely to offer health benefits when present in whole foods. In light of this, Putri is now developing ways of increasing the meglutol concentration within tempeh by tweaking the fermentation process. “What I find really interesting about food is that there’s rarely just one interesting compound,” she says. “Tempeh contains many that may have useful effects, and some may work together synergistically.”

A new understanding of our relationship with our "friendly" gut microbes shows they actually have a dark side and help cause ageing. Here's how to fight back

More broadly, Rattan isn’t convinced of Ames’s ideas about longevity nutrients, pointing out how the field of ageing has long been dogged by unrealistic claims. He highlights the bursts of hyperbole surrounding the purported benefits of different supplements including NAD+, a substance produced by human cells that helps convert the energy within food into a form that our bodies can use.

Some researchers have described the steady decline of NAD+ levels in our cells through the decades as “the driving force in ageing”, giving rise to a burgeoning industry of companies selling various formulations of NAD+ or nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), its precursor molecule.

But while Rattan suggests that boosting NAD+ may be useful for people with certain conditions, he says there is little evidence that it alters the ageing process, describing the supplements as “gimmicks”. “In people with cardiological or even some eye problems, these things can be useful,” he says. “But when we take them as geroprotectors, it’s mostly hype.”

However, while Rattan still isn’t convinced that a single nutrient can slow ageing and extend life, he does expect the research efforts in Singapore to shed new light on the role that different nutritional deficiencies can play in the loss of physical or mental function with age.

Addressing these shortfalls could allow people to retain their independence for longer, and may eventually enable more of us to maintain our vitality into a ripe old age – just like Ames.

COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus

New Scientist November 23, 2026

A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.

Advertisement

But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.

Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.

Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”

Free newsletter

The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.

Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”

Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.

But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?

The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.

With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.

The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.

There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

Ancient human settlements boosted biomass of today’s Amazon rainforest

New Scientist November 23, 2026

Ancient human civilisations in the Amazon have had a lasting beneficial impact on the rainforest. Places with a history of human occupation have, on average, 2.8 per cent greater biomass than unoccupied areas. This could affect estimates of how much carbon is stored in these rainforests and help spot previously unknown historical human sites.

Past studies have revealed that human societies in the Amazon, before the arrival of Europeans, altered landscapes by domesticating certain plants and boosted crop productivity by piling up biodegradable waste to create particularly fertile soils known as dark earth, or terra preta.

To get a better idea of how historical human occupation of the Amazon – which is estimated to have involved many millions of people – has altered the forests, Chris Doughty at Northern Arizona University and his colleagues began by working much further north at the archaeological site of Xmakabatun, a Maya city in what is now Guatemala, which was occupied from about 400 BC to AD 800.

Advertisement

Lost civilisation in the Amazon may have numbered 3 million people

The site was chosen because there is a wealth of information about past occupation in the region from mapping it with high-resolution airborne laser imaging.

Doughty and his colleagues analysed the present-day forest along 29 transects through the now-overgrown ancient stone city. Each transect was 30 metres long; nine of them incorporated ancient buildings, 11 went through former agricultural terraces, and nine were in regions of forest that have never been modified.

“It is really incredible, because on the lidar you can see these perfectly preserved ruins, but when you’re actually there, you can’t see a thing,” says Doughty. “We couldn’t have done it without the lidar data directing us to these places.”

Free newsletter

Among other factors, the team estimated the total amount of biomass in each transect by measuring the diameter of tree trunks and their height. They also measured leaf mass and identified how many of the trees were five frequently domesticated species, including the breadnut (Brosimum alicastrum), grown for food and timber, and the copal tree (Protium copal), grown for its resinous incense.

“We saw some significant structural differences,” says Doughty. Crucially, they discovered there was greater biomass where ancient human-built structures sat than on former agricultural terraces, or on undisturbed sites. At both the structures and terraced agricultural areas, there were also more of the frequently domesticated tree species. The trees with fruit often grow slowly, but end up bigger and have more biomass, says Doughty.

“Because we know that there are legacies of past soil modifications, fire and cultivation for modern plant communities, it seems logical that those activities have also altered plant trait compositions,” says Crystal McMichael at the University of Amsterdam, who wasn’t involved in the work.

Ancient cities discovered in the Amazon are the largest yet found

To see if the same changes could be seen by remote sensing from above, Doughty and his colleagues looked at data on biomass and leaf traits in the region around Xmakabatun, gleaned via lidar studies and Sentinel-2 satellite observations. This revealed a reduction in leaf mass and higher biomass at more densely settled archaeological sites than at control sites with no evidence of past human modification.

With the pattern corroborated, the team moved on to the Amazon, where it is harder to trace past human habitation because communities there had little access to stone for building permanent structures, instead building with earth. They focused similar remote sensing techniques on 500 areas listed in archaeological data sets as featuring fertile dark earth and almost a thousand additional areas with earthworks known as geoglyphs – both implying past habitation. They compared these with 3000 randomly chosen control sites.

Overall, they found that forests at dark-earth sites were shorter but had about 6 per cent more foliage than control sites, and forests near geoglyphs were taller, so had more biomass overall despite the trees being about 20 per cent less bulky in their middle sections than those in control plots. From this, the team has estimated that ancient human occupation has increased modern Amazonian biomass by, on average, 2.8 per cent, equivalent to 0.8 per cent of the globe’s above-ground stores of carbon.

Archaeological surveys have uncovered earthworks built by pre-Columbian societies across the Amazon, suggesting the rainforest isn’t as pristine as we once thought

This might mean evaluations of the Amazon rainforest’s biomass – and thus how much carbon is stored there – are slightly overestimated, says Doughty, because current figures are based on surveys in accessible places, which are often where people have formerly lived, so may also be areas with higher-than-normal biomass.

Vinicius Peripato at the Tropical Ecosystems and Environmental Sciences Laboratory at Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research, who wasn’t involved in the research, says the work could help us understand inaccessible rainforest areas. “The ability to detect the effects of ancient human occupation on present-day forest structure using remote-sensing products allows us to investigate these patterns even in remote forest areas.”

The findings have another implication, says Doughty: they suggest it might be possible to spot previously unknown areas where humans have lived in the past. “You could say biomass is better explained where you have archaeology, but you could also potentially use biomass to predict archaeology,” he says.

EcoEvoRxiv DOI: 10.32942/X25H6M

The brain benefits of letting children do things on their own

New Scientist November 23, 2026

Recently, I needed to post a letter. The postbox is at the end of my street, across a small T-junction. It occurred to me that I could send my eldest, who is 8, by herself to post it, but anxiety about letting her out of my sight and across a road immediately kicked in.

It reminded me of the widely publicised case of Karyann Parkinson, a mother in Virginia who was convicted in September of a misdemeanour after allowing her 5-year-old son to walk 800 metres to collect feathers near a pond.

The responses to that story in my parent group were mostly of the “I would never” or “He could have drowned” variety. But increasingly, I have been wondering about the other side of this calculation – in keeping my daughter super-safe, am I giving her enough opportunities to build a brain that can cope with adversity? Could my protective instincts be contributing to some of the anxieties I see bubbling away in her?

Advertisement

Exercise may create new neurons by making other brain cells contract

To find out, I spoke to Peter Gray, a psychologist and neurologist at Boston College, whose new book, Restoring Childhood: How to set kids free in the age of anxiety, piqued my interest.

His ideas are provocative. He believes that our preoccupation with smartphones and social media as the main cause of declining mental health in children risks us overlooking another major contributor: their dwindling opportunities to play independently from adults.

Children are born dependent on their parents, Gray points out, but also with a strong drive for independence. “Getting away from your parents, doing things on your own, getting into trouble, figuring out how to get yourself out of trouble. This is how children develop resilience, confidence, the agency, the sense that ‘Yeah, I can handle myself’.”

But we no longer allow them to do that, he says. “They go into their teenage years frightened, anxious, not able to deal with the bumps in the road of life because they haven’t had the ever- gradually increasing experience doing that growing up.”

It is certainly an intriguing idea. Rates of anxiety and depression in school-aged children are at an all-time high in the US, leading three US children’s health organisations to declare children’s mental health a national emergency in 2021. Meanwhile, over a quarter of parents in the UK say their child has struggled with anxiety or experienced a panic attack over the past year.

And while social media and screen time are likely to contribute, analyses of the results from several studies on the effects of screen time suggest the harms are fairly small and highly nuanced. “It’s important to look elsewhere,” says Gray.

Intuitively his arguments make sense. Allowing children to play, roam and engage in independent behaviours without direct oversight from adults offer opportunities to develop the three psychological pillars that support good mental health: autonomy, competence and friendship.

Gray argues that we satisfy all three needs by letting kids play together without adult supervision. “When children play [unrestricted], they’re at the cutting edge of their abilities, they’re becoming good at the things they like to do and can see progress, and they make friends doing it.”

What interests me is whether reduced opportunities to play independently could also shape the developing brain. Animal studies suggest that might be the case. For instance, in a 2022 experiment, researchers prevented young rats from playing with each other and then returned them to normal social housing. As adults, they had atypical neural circuitry involved in decision-making and flexible behaviour. Other animal studies in rodents and marmosets show that a lack of play also affects circuits involved in mood and stress responses.

This suggests that play may help our brain develop a healthy stress response – and it will certainly give me pause for thought when I must next decide whether to push my children to do homework over going to the park. But what about the independence aspect? Should I let them go to the park by themselves?

To understand why independent play matters, we need to think about our internal “locus of control” (LOC), says Gray. This is the tendency to believe we have control over our life and can solve problems when they arise. A low internal LOC is associated with a greater risk of anxiety and depression in children and adults.

To see why this is relevant, consider this experiment. Rats who had some control over an unpleasant experience – an electric shock – saw changes in the medial prefrontal cortex, a brain region involved in suppressing stress-related neural activity. These changes seemed to offer some protection against the effects of later, uncontrollable stressors, compared with rodents that had no control over the initial electric shocks.

Gray reckons that, just like these rats, being given an opportunity to feel in control of your life and its challenges helps form an internal LOC that changes the brain in ways that protect you further down the line. “Children develop [a LOC] by practising controlling their own lives – and we’re not allowing children to have that practice.”

Of course, experiments on lab animals can’t prove that climbing too high on playground equipment before finding your own way down, or resolving disagreements over Pokémon cards without adult intervention can protect us from anxiety and depression. But they do offer an intriguing biological explanation for why discovering we can cope with risky situations or that we have some modicum of control over negative experiences when we are young might influence how we respond to later-life stress and adversity.

And although it comes only from correlations, we see support for this idea in human research, too. Young children who have a greater amount of unstructured play score more highly on emotional control and self-regulation later in life than children who played like this less frequently, for instance. Likewise, elementary schools that have longer recesses tend to have higher pupil wellbeing – and not to the detriment of academic success, either.

Cause and effect remain difficult to disentangle, of course: anxious parents may limit a child’s freedom while also passing on a genetic predisposition to anxiety, say, among other factors.

Banning children from VPNs and social media will erode adults’ privacy

And what about the dangers of letting kids play by themselves? Gray challenges the assumption that the world is more dangerous to kids these days than it used to be. “In fact, crimes against children are way down [in the US],” he says. In terms of non-fatal violent crimes outside the home, that is true. These declined by 85 per cent between 1993 and 2022, according to Bureau of Justice Statistics. Similarly encouraging stats exist in the UK. Road safety is another concern, but the crime statistics alone challenge some of the assumptions that childhood has become universally more dangerous.

So, while I’m not entirely ruling out the effects of social media and other influences on declining mental health in children, I’m certainly persuaded that declining independence could be an integral factor – and unlike social media, it’s something I feel fully in control of.

Starting with that solo trip to the postbox. One errand won’t substantially change my daughter’s developing brain, but it does give her something my reassuring words alone cannot: the experience of doing something that feels a little risky and discovering that she’s able to cope. She returned with a story about a car that stopped to let her cross and how she remembered to say thank you. To her, it was a small adventure. I hope it’s the first step of many that will increase her resilience and protect her brain from the bigger adversities ahead.

Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

New Scientist November 20, 2026

If the past year was the “mathpocalypse”, a claim that AI has helped produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis is its most stunning horseman yet. Levent Alpöge at AI company Anthropic says he has used AI to solve this problem, which has sat at the heart of mathematics for nearly 200 years. This is not just the latest in the series of famed mathematics problems to fall to AI, but could be the biggest mathematical result of the century. Accordingly, mathematicians have received the news with a combination of exhilaration, bewilderment and caution.

“If true, it would, in my opinion be the greatest achievement yet by AI, and one of the greatest proofs in the history of mathematics,” says Thomas Bloom at the University of Manchester in the UK. “The Riemann hypothesis has represented a major barrier in our current understanding of the way numbers behave – if the AI proof has correctly solved it, this would represent a huge leap in what we know.”

Rainer Dietmann at Royal Holloway University of London is similarly in awe. “If it turns out to be correct, this is not only huge, it’s the biggest result in pure mathematics ever… It’s like having found the Holy Grail,” he says.

Advertisement

Dating back to the 1800s, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers. Because they cannot be factored into any smaller whole numbers, primes are like the atoms of numbers – they are the simplest units out of which any other number can be made. However, predicting when a prime will show up in a list of numbers is notoriously difficult. In 1859, Bernhard Reimann hypothesised a formula that would stunningly reduce that difficulty, but didn’t finish a proof before he died. Mathematicians have been trying to wrangle it ever since. After years of approximate results, including an AI-generated proof released by Open AI in October, Alpöge’s work may have finally confirmed Reimann’s centuries’ old intuition.

“It has captured the imagination, presumably because it is about something that we can all understand – the prime numbers – and because it has resisted the efforts of so many for so long. And it is important to mathematicians because it is so useful for other problems: a lot of theorems begin, “assume the Riemann hypothesis…” says Chris Daw at the University of Reading in the UK.

The new proof has not been formally reviewed by other mathematicians, which would be required for publication in an academic journal, and Alpöge hasn’t released the full proof, which he described in a public statement as being over 250,000 pages long. Instead, he has released the version of the proof that has been adapted for verification in the proof-checking software Lean, which is 17 million lines long. Anthropic and Alpöge did not respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

Michael Levitin at the University of Reading says hundreds of thousands of pages of Lean output won’t be easily checked. “In proportion to the magnitude of this claim, we should be appropriately sceptical,” says Bloom. “Even after the Lean formalisation has been independently checked, it remains possible that the AI might be taking advantage of some subtle undiscovered bug in the code. I’d feel more confident once we have a combination of the Lean compiling correctly, with no bugs found, and also human experts [having] had a chance to discuss the ‘big picture’ of the proof and whether it seems plausible.”

“Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean. They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to understand the proof themselves. And that will of course take time, since we only move at biological speeds,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. It is here that this new result, with its prospect of incredible historic significance, exemplifies the trouble mathematicians have had with AI over the past year, as it has been used to check one problem after another off their most coveted list of open questions.

Put simply, AI-assisted work benefits tremendously from prior work by human mathematicians, yet its end result isn’t immediately understandable to them. Coming to terms with the new proof will almost certainly take a long time, and it brings to the fore big questions about the future of mathematics. “Pretty much every mathematician will need time to process this. If AI can do this, what can it not do – in mathematics, at least?” says Daw. Many mathematicians already feel a sense of grief and anguish over how quickly AI tools have been solving problems that would have previously consumed a human mathematician’s whole career, and Dietmann says this new proof could have a similarly negative effect.

“What looked impossible one year ago has become reality. Many other problems in mathematics, computer science and related fields will fall as well, and it will become increasingly difficult for humans even to follow and understand,” he says. “While this progress is tremendous, it will massively amplify the despair by many in the mathematical community.”

Some mathematicians are more optimistic. “This is a very exciting time for pure mathematicians, and we are needed more than ever,” says Alex Bartel at the University of Glasgow in the UK. “AI is capable of spitting out proofs at a much faster pace than we are used to, but our task remains that of properly understanding what is going on… and that work is as fulfilling as ever, but there is now a lot more of it. The announcement of a very long proof of the Riemann hypothesis only reinforces my view.”

Mere hours after Alpöge’s announcement, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, wrote in a blog post that mathematician Alessandro Masullo has also put forward a proof of a generalised version of the Riemann hypothesis. This proof was completed without the use of AI, and it is 940 pages long. It has also not yet been checked by other mathematicians nor confirmed using Lean.

This day will be remembered as a shocking one, and the aftershocks may continue. “I can only compare this achievement to the aliens with a vastly superior intelligence coming to the Earth and explaining to us all the sacred mysteries we ever dreamed of,” says Alexei Skorobogatov at Imperial College London. “Humanity managed to create an amazingly powerful yet completely alien form of intelligence. The only event in history I can compare it to is the discovery of a nuclear bomb. Hopefully, AI will be put to better use!”

Quantum effect could reverse gravity and violate Einstein’s theory of relativity

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Flying in the face of Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity, quantum physics could turn the famous force repulsive instead of attractive – and we could soon test the idea in the lab.

A hallmark of gravity as we know it is that it pulls objects with mass together: gravity explains why the moon orbits Earth, and why an apple falls to the ground after detaching from the tree. While this is well established, there is still no agreement on how gravity works at scales dominated by quantum effects, and what quantum properties it may have.

Now, two research teams have independently found that quantum effects can make gravity act repulsively, pushing objects apart instead of pulling them together.

Advertisement

Could gravity produce quantum entanglement if it’s not fully quantum?

“Gravity is always attractive – this has been the cornerstone of gravity from Newton to Einstein,” says Pablo Saldanha at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Brazil, who worked on one of the studies with Vlatko Vedral and Chiara Marletto, both at the University of Oxford. “Anti-gravity or repulsion: no one has seen that before,” says Sougato Bose at University College London, who co-authored the other study with Lev Vaidman at Tel Aviv University in Israel.

A key concept for both studies was that of a quantum superposition state. Consider a car driving down a city street. When it arrives at an intersection where one road forks into two, it can take either the left or the right branch. But a quantum car would have another option: to enter a superposition of taking the left road and also the right one, assuming a state where it is impossible to tell where the car is exactly without disturbing it.

Another quantum object, called a probe, moving along a path parallel to both the left and right road branches, would be gravitationally attracted to the car. In both new studies, the researchers mathematically modelled an analogous setup and used equations to show that this gravitational interaction would make the car and the probe inextricably connected through the link of quantum entanglement.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The two teams mathematically examined a scenario equivalent to the two roads – left and right – merging some time after they had split apart. At this point, a measurement taken by the probe can reveal how each of the paths shaped the superposed car’s quantum state.

Quantum mechanics is probabilistic. This means that if this experiment were repeated many times, the final state of the car wouldn’t always be the same, but would follow some distribution of states instead, reflecting its capacity to follow a combination of the left and right branches. The researchers in both experiments found that if all but some specific states were then discarded after the measurement – a technique called post-selection, partly pioneered by Vaidman – then the probe should theoretically experience gravitational repulsion and be pushed away from the car in the experiment. “That repulsion, that going away [from the superposed object], is created at the time of the measurement,” says Bose.

Even Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which has for over a century proven to be an incredibly accurate description of gravity, doesn’t predict this kind of gravitational repulsion. “There is a measurement that will somehow conditionally give you repulsive gravitational force,” says Vedral. Confirmation that such a repulsive force occurs would demonstrate the quantum nature of gravity.

If gravity is a truly quantum entity, something as simple as measuring the strength of an object’s gravitational field should change its quantum state

Because this measurement effect is inherently quantum, just like the possibility of a superposition state is, the scenario the two teams explored doesn’t have any non-quantum analogues. But it could still be tested in experiments.

Objects that can stay in a superposition state for the duration of an experiment would have to be very small, says Bose, and yet also still massive enough for gravity to make a difference to their behaviour. Bacterium-sized objects should do the trick. He and Vaidman calculated that the probe object at this scale would experience acceleration roughly smaller than a quadrillionth of gravitational acceleration on Earth. Vedral says that he and his colleagues are already working with experimentalists who specialise in unusually large quantum objects.

Tomasz Paterek at the University of Gdańsk in Poland says that the new idea is “brilliant”. Past studies explored making the force between electrons attractive, even though it is usually repulsive, through post-selection. But this is the first time that the same process has been shown to potentially reverse gravity’s character, too, he says. In Paterek’s view, lab experiments that use gravity to quantum entangle objects could be achievable in the near future – but he cautions that they will be really difficult to perform.

Physical Review A DOI: 10.1103/df22-8kb6

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.22715

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

New Scientist November 20, 2026

The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven, and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions.

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago.

“This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. The proof of the Reimann hypothesis is also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million prize for a solution.

Advertisement

The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers. These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention.

He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. These numbers are complex – so each is actually a pair of numbers, one called real and one called imaginary – and when they are plugged into the Riemann zeta function, the function spits out zero. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called non-trivial zeros. Riemann discovered that summing over a sequence of these complex numbers allowed him to predict the distribution of primes up to a certain high number. Effectively, he came upon a formula that could make sense of primes’ seemingly random appearances among numbers.

But the formula only works if all the zeros always sit on the same vertical line when plotted in a coordinate system where the horizontal axis tracks their real number constituents and the vertical axis their imaginary ones. Riemann calculated some of these zeros, which confirmed his idea, but could not prove the hypothesis more generally. It became the biggest unsolved problem in all of mathematics. “It is a legendary problem, the queen of all the Millennium Problems,” says Scott Armstrong at Sorbonne University in Paris. “For the whole field of mathematics, there could not be a bigger theorem.”

In the intervening years, mathematicians used computers to verify that the first 12 trillion non-trivial zeros line up on Riemann’s vertical line and much work has gone into proving that the zeros at least must lie in a strip of the coordinate systems around this line. In fact, a previous release of AI proofs by OpenAI on 6 October contained the proof of a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, placing the non-trivial zeros in the neighbourhood but not exactly on the line Riemann predicted.

In a statement released to the public, Alpöge wrote that his proof, developed with Anthropic’s Claude AI, is over 250,000 pages long, and it has not yet been fully read, digested or understood by the mathematics community. Even its translation into the language of the proof-checking software Lean is 17,000,000 lines long. That means it will take time to carefully adjudicate. “I have not had a chance to read the 17 million lines of Lean, so cannot speak to their truth,” says Alex Walker at University College London. And the announcement didn’t illuminate the details of the method, he adds.

OpenAI has released hundreds of papers claiming to make progress on the biggest open problems in mathematics – here are some with the most potential

Consequently, it is currently unclear exactly what mathematical tricks the AI leveraged, though early commentators suggest that it drew on a vast swathe of mathematics spanning several fields including number theory and arithmetic geometry. Some have suggested the AI made connections across these fields that don’t already clearly exist in the literature.

The Lean code is in the process of being adapted to efficiently run on a computer that can review it, which will provide a crucial check on the new proof. “While Lean itself has some issues, so far none of the AI results with Lean certificates have had to be retracted,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. Still, it may take years to unravel all the details of the new proof and reap any of its mathematical insights, he says. But the ramifications will certainly be enormous and extensive.

Notably, it resolves the biggest open question of number theory by finally making primes make sense. Numerous results also build on the assumption that Riemann was right and will now stand on firmer ground. And then there are implications for functions similar to the Riemann zeta function, known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis. “An extremely large number of results have previously been proven subject to the generalised Riemann hypothesis,” says John Nicholson at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Germany. He says there are also a number of fast algorithms for computing quantities in algebraic number theory whose correctness depends on the generalised Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis even has ties to theories of chaos in quantum systems in physics.

“The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers,” wrote Enrico Bombieri at Princeton University when outlining the Millenium Problem more than a quarter of a century ago. Now, thanks to a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, that distribution may have been shown to be not that dangerous after all.

US bill aiming to boost clean energy could backfire

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Among the grass, sagebrush and tumbleweeds on a cattle ranch in Rawlins, Wyoming, workers have been building roads and pads for 600 wind turbines. Meanwhile, transmission lines are being strung from the site to a hub in Nevada, where the electricity generated can help power Las Vegas and Los Angeles.

It will be one of the biggest wind farms in the US, a win for the economy and the climate. But it took 18 years to get the approvals to start building. Even less complex projects now typically wait five years to connect to the grid.

These delays are the target of a 400-page permitting reform bill backed by Republicans and US President Donald Trump as well as many Democrats. It has just passed the Senate and will now be taken up by the House of Representatives.

Advertisement

How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it far easier to build renewable energy projects and transmission lines. One of its authors, long-time climate champion Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, says it would be the country’s “biggest implemented climate bill”.

But BAAJA would also speed up permitting for natural gas plants and pipelines, coal mines and data centres, while weakening environmental regulations. The American Petroleum Institute has even sent a BAAJA-branded food truck to hand out free tacos on Capitol Hill. The climate movement is split. Some experts fear the bill would increase greenhouse gas emissions, and former Vice President Al Gore called it a “serious mistake”.

Both sides say BAAJA is a gamble, but supporters say it’s one worth taking. Jigar Shah, who formerly oversaw infrastructure loans at the US Department of Energy, says it would set up a race between clean energy and fossil fuels. “The world’s best energy developers right now are in the clean energy space,” he says. “Why wouldn’t I bet on the world’s best energy developers?”

Free newsletter

Climate policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.6°C of warming by 2100, and greenhouse gas emissions are not yet falling, partly because additional renewable energy supply has been outpaced by additional demand from data centres. Data centre energy demand will double by 2030, and in the US, 60 per cent of that demand will be met by natural gas, according to the International Energy Agency.

The US grid, which is fractured into three separate grid regions and seven electricity markets, needs to speed up the build-out of renewables and transmission lines from the sunny, windy areas in the central US to the population centres near the coasts. But grid operators and regulators are overwhelmed, developers disagree on who should pay for transmission lines and court battles can last years. As a result, more than 2000 gigawatts of electricity generation and storage projects are awaiting grid connection, most of them renewable.

BAAJA would allow the federal government to override states’ objections and force grid regions to plan transmission lines together. But it would also narrow the timelines and reasons for challenging projects under environmental laws like the Clean Water Act, and, in some instances, cut lower district courts out of these cases. It essentially gives up tools to stop fossil fuel projects in exchange for tools to accelerate clean energy ones.

Environmentalists like Bill McKibben have warned that accelerated pipeline construction could lock in fossil fuel demand, and weaker protections would disempower concerned residents.

“Why would we choose now to give the fossil fuel industry what it’s wanted forever?” says David Watkins at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “Compromise will be required; I just think the balance here is off.”

Plug-in solar is coming – how dangerous is it and is it worth it?

Following this month’s election sweep, Democrats will take control of Congress in January and could potentially renegotiate the bill. But Trump would probably veto it, and even when the party controlled both Congress and the White House in 2022, it failed to pass a proposed permitting reform bill.

“You have a lot of newly elected oil-and-gas-state Democrats,” cautions Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh at Columbia University in New York.

Think tanks have projected that although the bill would increase liquefied natural gas exports, it would boost the build-out of renewables more than coal and gas plants. This would eventually reduce electricity prices by 3 to 5 per cent and US annual emissions by 0 to 4 per cent, depending on the future costs of clean tech and fossil fuels, according to Rhodium Group.

But modelling by Kevin Kircher at Purdue University in Indiana found that BAAJA would raise US annual emissions by 2 per cent. While energy demand will increase in any case, he argues the bill would increase demand still further, due in part to the Jevons paradox. This is when a decline in the cost of a resource leads buyers to consume more of it. For instance, if electricity prices did go down under BAAJA, cryptocurrency mining operations might run for longer periods or install more hardware.

“Unless all of that additional new electricity demand is met by clean energy, if even 10 per cent of it is met by fossil fuels, then emissions increase overall,” says Kircher. “People are severely underestimating the amount of new fossil fuel combustion that we will also see as a result of BAAJA.”
