Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis

New Scientist November 20, 2026

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI.

Advertisement

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.”

Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans

Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.”

Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.

He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution.

Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.

Cooney said the alleged offender was found near Thornton Beach but did not stop for police.

The quad bike was found abandoned a short time later on a rural property near Gow Rd in Edgecumbe, where a motorcycle was stolen from a nearby shed, she said.

“The alleged offender was stopped on Gow Rd a short time later and taken into custody.”

A youth has been remanded in custody, charged with multiple offences, including escaping custody, burglary and dangerous driving, and will appear in Youth Court at a later date.

Police also searched properties across Kawerau and Whakatāne after a series of trailer thefts, Cooney said.

Two men, aged 18 and 22, have been charged with burglary and will appear in court at a later date.

Cooney hoped these arrests provided reassurance to victims and the wider community.

“The dedication, professionalism and perseverance of police staff during these incidents were an outstanding demonstration of our work to ensure the safety of our community.

“Police would like to thank members of the public who have helped police in relation to these matters.

“Community information is often critical to solving crime, and we encourage anyone with information about offending to contact us,” Cooney said.

I drove the length of NZ asking doctors about gaps in care. It wasn’t a pretty picture – Dr David Galler

New Zealand Herald November 23, 2026

Dr David Galler (left) and Dr Malcolm Mulholland took a road-trip from Bluff to Cape Rēinga to write a report on the current state of the health system under the coalition Government’s “stewardship”. Photo / Supplied

As we wait for the election result to play out, pundits say it will take weeks for the final shape of a new Government to emerge; in the meantime, life goes on, for better and for worse.

A lot is hanging on the result for those who rely on our public health system for care and for the many who work so hard to provide it.

On our recent road trip from Bluff to Cape Rēinga, Dr Malcolm Mulholland and I heard from them and have used what we learned to create a report on the current state of the health system under the coalition Government’s “stewardship”.

The trip was funded by Kaitiaki Hauora, an advocacy group for public healthcare, and took two weeks spanning 4300km and 28 towns.

As we drove, we joked that what we were shaping was a BOM as well as a BIM – a briefing for an outgoing minister and, in part, a briefing for an incoming one.

The report card takes the form of performance not against targets but instead the expectations of others, users of the health “system” and those who work in it.

The issues we are highlighting here are not new; they have been the subject of much commentary, but they remain until they are addressed.

Instead of having a system of co-ordinated activities to support good care linked to people’s needs, we heard stories of providers working in isolation and without support.

Up and down the country we heard the same thing from community providers; “we don’t know who holds what contract for what round here”.

There is no map to link community-based services in the districts and there is no one co-ordinating what community resources exist to ensure people get the care they need.

The same holds when it comes to the co-ordination of patient care between community and hospital-based services.

All are run off their feet trying to keep up with demand, barely able to manage what’s directly in front of them at the time. As a result, people’s trust in what was once a true system of care has disappeared.

Weirdly, the coalition Government has shown little interest in addressing the social and commercial drivers of ill health that account for 80% of our population’s health status.

I would assert that through their repeal of the smokefree legislation, the gutting of the school lunch programme and reneging on our commitments to reduce greenhouse gases, they have undermined that further.

A new Government will have the opportunity to change tack, to massively improve the value of our investment in healthcare to deliver good outcomes at low cost by introducing evidence-based policies to reduce harm from commercial products like alcohol, tobacco products, unhealthy foods and regulate gambling, as part of a wider approach across government to promote and maintain the good health of our people.

I include a new National-led Government in this hope for change, but have my doubts based on the past term.

I would urge any new Government to see our health workers as an asset and to engage them in all aspects of the design and delivery of the services our communities need.

Sadly, that’s not been the case to date. Instead, and despite the minister’s denials, his officials instituted a hiring freeze for new nurses in order to cut costs.

Also, many health workers feel intimidated and are in fear of retribution from their employer for speaking out, denying them the opportunity to contribute to policy and practice in areas where they have genuine expertise, thereby denying the public the opportunity of improved services.

Minister of Health Simeon Brown also chose to scrap the NZ Health Charter – Te Mauri o Rongo – which was co-created with thousands of health workers as a means for them, managers and decision makers to work more closely together to support good care.

Many of the health professionals we spoke with expressed great concern about the minister’s proposal to change the Health Practitioners’ Competency Assurance Act, tilting the balance of oversight of healthcare professionals away from self-regulation towards a far greater degree of political control.

They say that will undermine the quality of clinical services and make health even more of a political football than it currently is.

We found the morale of the health workforce to be at rock bottom.

There was much talk about how the Crown has reneged on its obligations to Māori, diminishing their ability to achieve equitable health outcomes for themselves.

Clinicians up and down the country who deal with different people every day were scathing of the Government’s one-size-fits-all approach to the governance and provision of health services, seeing that as an indicator of how removed they are from the reality of everyday work.

Primary care was a hot topic raised by everyone on our road trip.

We can confirm what is common knowledge, that this essential foundation of healthcare is in a state of complete chaos. Large areas of the country are without primary care.

In those areas where there is a presence, people struggle to get appointments and often face steep fees.

GPs are struggling to get their patients access to diagnostics and advice from hospital specialists to better manage them in the community. In addition, low pay and the burden of administration is now so enormous their job has become unattractive to new entrants.

Recruitment and retention of staff in rural areas is left to the market and, under current conditions, is becoming near impossible.

Locals know there is no one approach to fit the different contexts that exist across the length and breadth of the country and want more support from Health NZ. In many cases, state-employed general practices may be the solution.

Many pointed out that the percentage of health spending going to primary care is woefully inadequate and way behind OECD averages. Currently around 5% – that should at the very least double and specialist GPs should be paid like hospital specialists.

Primary care has become the wild west, a place where corporates and private equity interests fight it out at high noon to make money out of the very services that are supposed to keep them well.

Everywhere we went we heard calls for any new Government to address these issues and not become a “dumb client”.

Mental health services around the country are frequently non-existent or utterly overwhelmed, leaving many in acute distress because they are unable to access help.

In our small towns we heard stories of high youth unemployment, drug use and high suicide rates.

Up and down the country dentists told us about the appalling state of children’s teeth, the high and increasing numbers of theatre lists devoted entirely to full clearances.

Hours and hours of theatre time.

This is preventable with the right support, care and messaging. There are some solutions here but there seems to be little interest from the minister to pursue them.

The problems continue across our hospitals. Not just in our overcrowded emergency departments but across all services.

This has become a vicious cycle – lack of staff leads to burnout and resignations, which puts more pressure on existing staff.

Because there are so many more people waiting to see hospital specialists to receive care than specialist services can cope with, many referrals made by GPs are declined.

As a result, many GPs have changed their practice to only refer the most serious cases, in effect creating a hidden waiting list behind what is reported.

Faced with this demand, the most recent Minister of Health has chosen not to invest to support and expand the public health system, but instead pumped more and more public money into private services with few strings attached.

Many are without performance measures or accurate measures of costs, making this question who owns our health system one of the most pressing issues facing a new government.

People we spoke with were clear: the agenda to privatise health services is now explicit and it will undermine the future of public healthcare, driving inequity and poor outcomes for most New Zealanders who rely on it.

The picture is a grim one but despite that there is hope. But we need a plan.

Kaitiaki Hauora and its affiliates, along with many other organisations and experts, are ready and willing to contribute to that plan and look forward to working with whatever government finally takes office in New Zealand.

Improving the health of our people helps secure the economic success of our nation.

Dr David Galler is the spokesman for health lobby group Kaitiaki Hauora and is on the board of the Health Coalition Aotearoa. For many years he was an intensive care specialist at Middlemore Hospital and for seven years the principal medical adviser to ministers and directors general of health.

Waipawa District Lions Club raffle wheelbarrow prize stolen from senior citizens’ building

New Zealand Herald November 23, 2026

Waipawa District Lions Club president Kim Walker said the club would have tried to help if it had known someone was in need.

A donated wheelbarrow filled with goodies as a first-place raffle prize has been stolen from a senior citizens’ building in Waipawa.

Waipawa District Lions Club president Kim Walker said the club noticed the wheelbarrow was missing during a meeting at the Waipawa Senior Citizens Hall on Waverley St on Thursday.

It had been seen at a meeting a week before, she said.

“It’s a bit of a kick in the guts.

“We would just like to say something to the individual or individuals that if there was something you actually needed in this life, we probably, if you had come to us, we would have done our best to support you and get you those items.”

She suspected the wheelbarrow and its contents were taken when someone else had been using the hall and the theft had been reported to police.

“While they were in there, someone has gone in another door and into the back room, and just walked out with our wheelbarrow.

“We are certainly not laying any blame on the people that were using the hall.

“It’s just gone.”

She said they were disappointed in the opportunistic behaviour, as money raised in the raffle was to go back into the community.

The proceeds were to help with running costs of the mobility van that transported people to and from Hawke’s Bay Hospital and doctors’ appointments, with 18 trips each month.

“It was meant to be something positive.

“They can take the physical stuff from us, but they are not going to take our community spirit.”

Walker said she didn’t want the “unfortunate incident” to take away from what the club did and the generosity of the community, which had pulled through with a new wheelbarrow and raffle items.

She said the club planned to go ahead with the raffle with a new wheelbarrow donated by Waipukurau Mitre 10.

Tickets for the raffle will be sold outside Waipukurau New World today, from 10am to 6pm, and December 1, from 10am to 6pm.

It will be drawn in December.

The head of one of New Zealand’s most prestigious schools says digital exam platforms can’t be trusted, as pupils look to resit an English exam plagued by tech issues.

The NZ Qualifications Authority has announced a paper-based NCEA Level 2 English exam will be held on December 4, with any student allowed to resit the digitally compromised online test, including those who previously sat the paper exam.

Boys at Auckland Grammar School already did their NCEA and Cambridge exams with pen and paper, as part of a wider school philosophy that avoids devices, headmaster Tim O’Connor told Herald NOW’s Ryan Bridge Today.

Asked if any school should trust digital exams, O’Connor said “not right now – I think that’s proven”.

While his own students would have been disadvantaged in a digital exam as it was unfamiliar, students more broadly appeared to be anxious going into exams knowing they could face tech issues.

“If you’ve got a pen and a spare pen and you’ve got paper in front of you, then you know actually that’s reliable.”

Auckland Grammar was not a BYOD (bring your own device) school because “they’re simply a distraction”, O’Connor said.

“The teacher is the expert in the room; we want young men to be focused on them.”

Research into the cognitive process involved in handwriting also found retention of knowledge was far greater when putting pen to paper.

O’Connor said that as the new curriculum was rolled out, NZQA should look into how exams are run in the Cambridge system, sat by around 60% of AGS students.

Cambridge exams were broken up into chunks, meaning students sat more exams but they were shorter and spread over a longer time.

That meant students potentially had more time to prepare for each test and were less anxious overall.

“In the New Zealand education system right now, I think students are struggling to cope with any form of external assessment system.”

Education officials are giving students the chance to resit the Level 2 English exam after technical problems disrupted multiple English exams across the country on November 12.

The NZQA previously apologised after Level 1 and 2 English exams were hit by technical problems within a week, leaving upset students facing the prospect of relying on derived grades to pass.

NZQA chief executive Christian Hawkesby told the media that students impacted by the Level 2 English exam disruptions would have the option to sit an additional paper-based exam on Friday next week.

Level 1 English exams were also affected, but a repeat exam is not planned as paper copies of the exam were available, students were able to get back into the system, and they were given extra time on the day, Hawkesby said.

Fire crews faced “significant risk” entering a smoke-logged bakery in Auckland’s Onehunga overnight.

Emergency services were called to the fire around 12.20am, initially being told it was at a laundromat. On arrival, they found the fire developing inside the Angkor bakery opposite Onehunga Library.

“When they arrived, the building was heavily smoke-logged and had not yet vented, which posed a significant risk to our crews,” Onehunga senior fire station officer Ivan Millan told the Herald.

“We had to force entry through a roller door at the back, then locate the fire – so they were wearing their breathing apparatus sets to enable them to make entry safely, locate and extinguish the fire.”

A second alarm was transmitted, with six additional trucks, including two aerial, sent to the burning bakery.

“We used both our aerial appliances for observation. They are very valuable in ensuring there is no fire spread to [the] rest of the tenancies,” Millan said.

The fire was extinguished within an hour and the crews waited for the bakery owners to arrive.

“We’ll take them inside and we’ll have a look at the damage and just ensure there has been no further fire spread through any of the other commercial buildings,” Millan said.

The bakery had suffered “moderate” damage. A specialist fire investigator would determine the cause of the blaze.

Meanwhile, about 6.30am, crews were called to a small laundromat fire in Browns Bay.

Half an hour later, Fire and Emergency shift manager Nadine Davies said several fire engines were being used to battle the blaze on Bute Rd.

Gerrit Vryer was walking along Browns Bay Beach when he smelt and saw “thick black smoke”.

He walked around to Bayview Rd and saw smoke “billowing” from the Laundromat roof vents.

Fire engines arrived at the scene and were quickly able to extinguish the blaze, Vryer said.

Locals oppose housing development on flood-prone Christchurch land

New Zealand Herald November 23, 2026

The development would 800 homes built across 170 hectares of land previously intended for a luxury gold course. Photo / Quin Tauetau, RNZ

By RNZ Checkpoint

A local resident says taxpayers could end up bearing the cost if a proposed mega housing development on flood-prone land in Christchurch goes ahead.

Tammy Wells is among residents who opposed the Whisper Creek development in north Christchurch, which would see 800 homes built across 170ha of land previously intended for a luxury golf course.

Wells said she was concerned the risks associated with the site could eventually become a financial burden on home owners and taxpayers.

“Are they going to be able to insure their homes?” she said.

She questioned who would be left responsible if the developer completed the project and walked away, leaving the council and the taxpayers to deal with the consequences.

The development attracted 63 submissions raising concerns about human health and natural hazards, including earthquake liquefaction and flooding from the nearby Styx River and heavy rainfall.

Wells also raised concerns about emergency evacuations.

“If you suddenly then perhaps have 1600 cars all trying to evacuate out of two entrance exits at the one time, I mean, that just sort of spells disaster.”

An independent commissioner who has given the project a green light found the risks could be adequately managed or mitigated.

Wells said she was not opposed to subdivisions but believed developments needed proper controls.

“I’m not anti-subdivision. I’m really not. But I think it’s got to have controls and it doesn’t feel like it does in this situation for us,” she said.

Wells said the council has got this wrong and that she is devastated by the decision.

Napier cafe bystanders intervene as knife allegedly held to worker’s neck by shirtless man

New Zealand Herald November 23, 2026

Bystanders stepped in to help the worker at Ajuna Eatery in Napier. Photos / NZME, 123rf

Bystanders at a Napier cafe intervened to help a worker who allegedly had a knife held to her neck by a shirtless man as she tried to get him to leave the premises, a witness says.

The breakfast incident happened about 8.20am on Sunday at Ajuna Eatery.

Police were on the scene quickly and arrested the 44-year-old man.

He has been charged with injuring with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, and was due in court on Monday.

A Hato Hone St John ambulance attended, and ambulance staff treated and assessed one patient at the scene, who did not require transport to hospital.

A representative at the cafe declined to comment.

A witness, who was at Ajuna cafe at the time and did not want to be named, said the man was shirtless and he appeared to be a rough sleeper.

They said the man was hassling customers before the incident.

“It’s just 8.30am on a blimmin Sunday morning, people are just having coffee; it’s rubbish.”

A group of people eventually wrestled the man away from the worker, the witness said.

The witness said cafes and shops shouldn’t have to deal with that sort of aggressive behaviour.

The witness believed more needed to be done to move on rough sleepers in Napier’s CBD, and to protect workers and customers.

They had noticed police on the beat in Napier CBD in recent weeks, as well as Napier Assist safety workers, which was positive.

Ajuna Eatery closed early after the ordeal. A sign on the door said it would reopen as usual on Tuesday.

Reporoa’s historic Butcher’s Pool gets a $145,000 upgrade, its first in 25 years

New Zealand Herald November 23, 2026

Butcher's Pool, about 2km south of Reporoa, is undergoing improvements to make it safer and more accessible. Photo / Stephen Parker

It’s been described online as looking like “Shrek’s swamp” – now a rural Rotorua thermal swimming spot and “local treasure” is receiving a $145,000 upgrade.

Butcher’s Pool, about 2km south of Reporoa, is undergoing improvements to make it safer and more accessible.

A local landmark, the pool has been a popular spot for residents and visitors since it was gifted to the community by Mr HR Butcher in 1927.

The land became a Rotorua Lakes Council-owned recreation reserve in 1964.

In recent years, the pool has suffered instances of vandalism and its reputation has taken a hit online, with social media criticism of its condition and cleanliness – including the swamp comparison.

Plans to revamp the reserve were deferred in 2021 and council documents said community engagement from 2022 found “divergent” views on the pool’s future.

Discussions continued, including with local iwi and the wider Reporoa community in 2022 and 2023.

Concerns about signage, broken glass and safety at the pool have been raised at several Rotorua Rural Community Board meetings.

The refreshed renewal project includes new pool steps and handrails, improved pathways and seating, repairs to concrete areas, and changes to the pool’s water outlet.

A small changing room and storage cubbies are being installed, with the toilets also getting a refresh.

Rotorua Lakes Council community experience manager Alex Wilson said this was the first significant upgrade to the historic pools in 25 years.

“Work is now underway and on track to be completed before Christmas,” Wilson said.

Community feedback had helped shape the project, with improved access and the changing room addition identified as key priorities, she said.

“These improvements are expected to benefit visitors for the next 15 to 20 years.”

Rural ward councillor Karen Barker said locals, mana whenua and visitors had “long enjoyed the therapeutic and relaxing properties of this natural thermal pool”.

The project’s council budget of about $100,000 had been topped up with a Rural Community Board contribution of $45,000.

Barker said the additional funding was needed to deliver the proposed programme of work.

“Maintaining and upgrading rural recreational facilities is an ongoing challenge for council, with inflation, regulatory costs and cost-of-living pressures all affecting available budgets,” she said.

“But this local treasure is used by locals, visitors, and tourists alike and so has wide value, use and appeal.”

“By using smart collaboration and careful stewardship of resources, we can achieve great outcomes at a lower impact to ratepayers.”

Barker said she would like the pool to be maintained in a “safe manner” for the next 10-20 years and she also saw “potential” future community involvement in its “kaitiaki and stewardship”.

Rural Community Board member Colin Guyton said the upgrade was overdue, with the pool looking “a bit shabby” after more than 20 years without significant work.

Guyton said the board had supported additional funding for the project because it allowed council to improve an existing facility rather than create new assets that would require ongoing maintenance.

“We quite like adding to a council project as opposed to finding a new one that maybe is just going to add assets to the council’s register that they need to maintain in the future,” he said.

The board’s contribution had also helped fund the dedicated changing area, meaning visitors would no longer need to use the toilets or change elsewhere.

Guyton, who lives about 1.5km from the pool and uses it himself, said it was well used by locals and had increasingly become a destination for tourists and visitors.

He said the facility was free to use, but its upkeep came at a cost to local ratepayers.

Guyton encouraged visitors to respect the facility and leave it in good condition for others.

“Just treat it like it’s your own house, because it’s free for people to use, but it’s actually not free,” he said.

“Just remember you’re in someone else’s backyard when you come there.”

Ongoing maintenance of the site post-renovation will be managed through the council’s parks and reserves maintenance budget.

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

Tauranga rates and council spending: Hundreds march demanding accountability

New Zealand Herald November 23, 2026

Hundreds of people marched through Tauranga’s CBD on Sunday to protest city council spending and transparency.

The protest, led by Wayne Farrant, who fronts Wayne’s Worldview on social media, called for the council to improve accountability, transparency and “out-of-control spending”.

The protesters marched from the Devonport Rd carpark to The Strand, chanting and thrusting signs into the air.

Signs read: “Toxic City Council”, “Sack them”, “Tauranga Chaotic Council”, “Stop Tauranga Council money grab”, “You work for us”.

In response, the council said it respected the right of people to express their views, including through peaceful and lawful protest.

“The council is aware of varying views in the community and remains focused on delivering for the people of Tauranga.”

Residents can attend weekly council meetings and speak to the council during public forums.

In videos leading up to the protest, Farrant told his Facebook followers to join him in standing together to make their voices heard.

He had called for the leaders and senior executives of the council to resign, including former chief executive Marty Grenfell, who resigned on September 29.

“We need to start asking some serious questions about how Tauranga ratepayers’ money is being spent,” he said in one video.

Residents have raised questions about excess spending and a lack of transparency related to the recovery of Mauao following January’s severe weather event, the redevelopment of the Memorial Pool, the recently launched place brand TaurangaNZ and the Marine Precinct.

In a recent council meeting, elected members decided to consult the public on deferring the pool project for at least three years so the council could develop a citywide aquatic network plan.

The deferral was one of several cost-saving measures debated as it looked for ways to reduce capital spending by about $200m to prepare for the Government’s proposed rates cap.

The Local Government (Rates Capping) Amendment Bill passed its first reading in September. It would require councils to cap annual rates increases at 4% per capita.

Councils would have to consider the cap in their long-term plans from July, before it becomes mandatory in 2029.

The city council set an average 7.2% increase this year, following a 9.9% increase in 2025.

On Sunday, Farrant used a microphone to address the crowd from a makeshift stage. “The questions haven’t been answered, and the need for accountability hasn’t gone away, so we keep going.

“We keep asking questions, we keep demanding answers, and we keep shining a light on the stupid decisions that affect our city and the people who live here.”

Protester Allyson Wilson told Local Democracy Reporting she was standing up against council spending and “huge” rates.

Her husband, Nick, had lived in Tauranga his whole life and said the current council was “worse than before the commissioners”.

“They just can’t stop spending.”

Penny Henderson, owner of the Pottery Studio, formerly on Devonport Rd, said she was there to “stand up and be heard, otherwise you’re just a keyboard warrior”.

Henderson said she had to move the business away from the city centre because of the cost.

“We were paying $17,000 a year in rates, plus body corporate fees ... How to kill a centre.

She was pleased with the turnout and age range, saying she expected mostly older people.

Henderson said some projects were nice to have, but the budget was not there for them. “Nobody’s done the maths.”

She said there was a lack of respect for the people the council represented.

“People have had enough.”

Lisa Olsen said the council was “out of touch” and high rates were making it unaffordable to live.

Farrant said in a statement afterwards the protest attracted a much larger turnout than anticipated, describing it as “an outstanding success”.

“While we haven’t established an exact attendance figure, the number of people who turned up was extremely encouraging.

“We also received messages from many others who were unable to attend but wanted us to know they were behind us.”

He said the protest demonstrated something the council should take seriously.

He said the council tended to dismiss people who questioned its decisions as “a handful of disgruntled individuals sitting behind keyboards complaining on Facebook”.

“Well, the weekend’s turnout told a very different story.”

Farrant hoped elected members and senior council management would recognise the turnout’s significance.

“People should not have to take to the streets simply to feel that their concerns are being heard.”

Potholes and polling booths: Danny O’Brien’s fight to hold back the orange wave – and fix country roads

Sydney Morning Herald November 24, 2026

Amid the expected electoral carnage of Saturday night, when anywhere between 25 and 40 seats in the Victorian parliament could change hands, one of the more remarkable stories may be that of the party that, against all odds and without much fuss, quietly protected its own.

Nationals leader Danny O’Brien, while prefacing all his remarks with the normal caveats about taking nothing for granted and having to fight for every vote, says there is a real possibility his party will emerge from this election without losing a seat and perhaps with one or two extra in its column.

If this happens, and the Jess Wilson-led Coalition forms the next government with a comfortable parliamentary majority, it will have been the Nats Wot Won It – the party which stopped an orange wave from swamping northern Victoria.

According to O’Brien, such a result would reinforce two truisms in politics. The first is that, as a political outfit which for as long as anyone can remember has been declared at death’s door, the Nats are very hard to kill. The second is that, for voters who live outside our major cities, elections are principally local affairs.

“We’re counting no chickens,” O’Brien tells The Age during a break in campaigning from his home outside Sale. “We’ve got a long way to go yet until all the votes are counted. But we’ve been through this before. In fact, for 110 years, we’ve had people writing off the National Party, saying we won’t exist after the next election or we will be reduced to a rump.

“We have always prevailed. We’ve lost seats, we’ve won them back and we’re still here because I fundamentally believe that people want a party that stands up for rural and regional Victoria.

“All politics is local. We have local champions as MPs who really work their electorates hard, and we pick candidates who are local champions and passionate about their electorates.

“I’ve seen it, time and time again, where pundits will look at the mood across the board or the polling across the state, and extrapolate that to individual seats and say the Nats will be in trouble. It won’t be the case because we’ve got a fantastic local member or a great candidate who’s really picked up on a local issue.”

The Age reported dire statewide seat projections five months ago, showing the Nats could be swept aside by Pauline Hanson’s One Nation in Murray Plains, Shepparton, Gippsland East and Morwell. Not for the first time, the analysis put insufficient weight on the capacity of the National Party to understand its constituents and the issues that matter.

With only days remaining in the Victorian campaign, the Nationals remain in a perilously close contest in Gippsland East and Morwell. But with both Bendigo seats now considered possible pick-ups, the Nats have a good chance of breaking even and perhaps doing better than their 2022 result.

O’Brien says he was worried when early voting opened last week in Sale and a long line of voters pushed past him to grab a One Nation how-to-vote card. The longer the week went on, the more Nationals voters came his way. A similar pattern was reported at other polling places around country Victoria. “We know we’re under stress in a number of areas so we’ll wait until the votes are counted before we get excited. But there’s no doubt that we’re fighting hard and in with a good chance of doing quite well.”

If O’Brien can hold his own seat of Gippsland West and the Coalition wins the election, as all major polls are predicting, two significant jobs await. The first is serving as deputy premier to Wilson. The second is serving as roads minister in a state where potholes, especially on major regional roads, have become a rim-busting emblem of Victoria’s decline.

O’Brien says his greatest frustration from listening to ministers and senior bureaucrats in public accounts and estimates committee hearings, is the emphasis placed on how much money is spent on a problem, rather than whether it is fixed. The Coalition has committed a whopping $5 billion to road maintenance over the next four years, but O’Brien says the challenge is to spend money smarter, rather than more of it.

He says one episode that stuck in his craw was when the departmental secretary previously responsible for roads, Jeroen Weimar, commissioned consulting giant EY to conduct a study into why 40 per cent of the roads budget wasn’t being spent on roads.

“That just astounds me. Firstly, that the secretary of the department can’t find that out himself and secondly, where is it going? I think we can do a hell of a lot better with the money that we’ve got, and that is not just me. I’ve heard that from contractors, from VicRoads people, and people involved in the sector for a long time.”

O’Brien, like any MP who represents a regional constituency, has become something of an expert on roads. Perhaps the only member of the Coalition who knows more is the Liberal candidate for Benambra, Steve Martin, a project manager with a master’s degree in pavement engineering. O’Brien says you don’t need a postgraduate degree to understand the problem with Victoria’s roads.

“It’s really about basic maintenance,” he says. “We haven’t been doing that preventative maintenance properly. I’ve asked engineers and road builders whether I have missed something, whether a change in technology means we shouldn’t be grading the roadside or cleaning table drains. They say no, that is exactly what we should be doing, we have just stopped doing it because the government hasn’t put any money into it.”

A report by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office published in September found that, as of 2024, about half of Victoria’s road network was in a poor or very poor condition and a “substantial and growing road maintenance backlog” had been created by a shortage of funding. Shortly before the report was published, the government announced $352 million would be spent fixing potholes this financial year in addition to the $1 billion already allocated to road maintenance.

O’Brien warns the fix, now that our roads have got to this point, will be slow and cost far more than the maintenance the government chose not to do. Whereas resealing an asphalt road to stop water getting in costs about $10 a square metre, rebuilding costs 10 times that amount.

“It’s not dissimilar to the message that Jess [Wilson] and I have been giving on the budget. It’s going to take a long period of time to fix the roads. The roads are likely to get worse before they get better, simply because there hasn’t been that preventative maintenance. I am asking people to be patient. The roads are our single biggest state asset. As an asset manager, we have treated them appallingly.”

O’Brien says that if the Nationals survive this election with all their seats intact, it won’t mean that the threat from One Nation wasn’t real – only that the Nationals, through the hard work of their MPS and candidates, were able to convince enough voters to stick with them.

He says that, irrespective of the result of this election, the anger that drove people to One Nation will not have disappeared.

“People are angry at the way things are. Broadly, that is because of Labor governments, state and federal, but that has reflected on us. People are saying “we want change”, even though they know it isn’t our fault that we are in this position.

“We need to get into government and turn things around. We need to rebuild trust in politics and in our institutions as well. That’s an important job that we’ve got to do if we do get there and even if we don’t. We need to rebuild that trust for people around this state.”

Metropolitan police seize 893kg of cocaine hidden in boxes of oranges

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 20:41:43 GMT

London force also makes eight arrests in operation centred on New Spitalfields Market in the capital

A tonne of cocaine was found hidden in boxes of oranges as part of one of the biggest drug seizures in the history of the Metropolitan police.

Suspected cocaine weighing 893kg has been seized and eight arrests made as part of the investigation that targeted an organised crime group alleged to have been smuggling class A drugs into the UK. A Met spokesperson said the investigation was continuing.

Officers made arrests at London’s New Spitalfields Market on Sunday evening, the force revealed.

A large quantity of suspected cocaine was found hidden in boxes of oranges and five men, aged 27, 33, 41, 43 and 58, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to supply class A drugs.

Video footage shows officers rifling through the cardboard boxes full of oranges to find black packages, featuring a drawing of a four-leaf clover, buried underneath.

Pictures taken separately on Sunday evening show blocks of suspected class A drugs filling up five empty cardboard boxes. Some blocks feature the number “1100” on their front.

The fruit and vegetable market, which relocated to Leyton in 1991, is the UK’s largest wholesale market, covering an area of about 13 hectares (31 acres).

A sixth man, aged 44, was also arrested nearby with 100kg of suspected class A drugs, the force spokesperson added.

Separately, police searched a property in Cheshunt, Hertfordshire, and arrested a 48-year-old man on suspicion of the same offence. Officers seized an estimated £450,000 in cash.

A lorry was also stopped near Maidstone and taken to Dover to be searched, with officers seizing around 250kg of suspected cocaine. The driver, a 50-year-old man, was also arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to supply class A drugs.

All eight men arrested remain in custody.

Det Spt Lindsey Billany, who is leading the Met’s investigation, said: “The seizure of these drugs, which would have been worth millions of pounds, represents a significant loss to this criminal enterprise and is one of the largest drug seizures we’ve seen.

“This policing operation demonstrates our focus on bringing down the drug traffickers whose trade fuels violence on London’s streets – and should serve as a warning to organised crime groups importing class A drugs.”

Israel seeks to jail Palestinian student activist without trial after dorm arrest

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 19:48:58 GMT

Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations

Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.

Police took Tounsi, 26, a criminology and sociology student from East Jerusalem who is active in Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, from his dorm room on 8 November.

When he appeared by video link at a court hearing on 19 November he had visible bruises on his face, did not have the glasses he needs to see properly, and his hair and beard had been shaved.

Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, in the patrol car and at the police station, Israeli media reported. Interrogators questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.

Both groups called for his immediate release and warned against using security agencies to silence political activity and critical speech.

“[This] could happen to any student and any one of us, especially in a month when the government is persecuting Arab citizens, from [journalist] Abed Abu Shehadeh to the leaders of Arab political parties,” Standing Together said in a statement, calling on the university to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process.

Ir Amim described Tounsi as thoughtful, gentle and a valued partner “in movements bringing Palestinians and Israelis together”, in a statement that also warned of “serious concerns for his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process”.

After losing the election, Netanyahu and his allies weaponised false accusations of mass fraud – Israel’s election commission validated the results – in an attempt to hold on to power by delegitimising the votes of Palestinian citizens of Israel.

The prime minister has also been accused of politicising security institutions in his campaign against Palestinian-led parties, and fostering a rise in racist rhetoric.

When police powers to hold Tounsi under the original arrest warrant expired last week, they submitted an order to hold him without trial in administrative detention, signed by the defence minister, Israel Katz.

The administrative detention law allows Israel to hold individuals for up to six months without charging them or allowing them to see evidence against them, although it has to be presented in a closed court.

Because the Shin Bet security force did not send a representative to the hearing on Tounsi’s detention last week, it was postponed until Tuesday.

Ahead of the court hearing, Jewish and Palestinian students demonstrated at universities across the country, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, with signs including “Free Mahdi” and “Kidnapping Palestinians will not silence justice”.

The university authorities did not inform his family, and his detention only came to light after concerned friends reported him missing.

Hebrew University said in a statement that it was notified about the arrest shortly before police seized Tounsi, that no university representatives were present when he was detained and police afterwards said the arrest took place “without unusual incidents”.

It did not directly address the allegations of police violence, his visible bruising, the shaving of his head and beard, removal of his glasses or the shifting legal framework.

“The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings,” the statement said.

“We are concerned for his wellbeing,” the statement added, saying the university hoped “that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process”.

Israeli police did not respond to requests for comment about Tounsi’s detention.

Tounsi is a resident of East Jerusalem, not a Palestinian citizen of Israel. Palestinians holding that status can move freely inside Israel and Jerusalem but are stateless and can not vote in Israeli national elections.

Burnham says it would be ‘unthinkable’ to rejoin EU without referendum

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 19:26:01 GMT

Prime minister also says former Tory premiers who have criticised revival of Brexit debate are ‘stuck in the past’

UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham has said it would be “unthinkable” for the UK to rejoin the EU without holding another referendum, offering his strongest commitment yet to directly consulting the public if he concludes Britain should go back in.

The prime minister is planning to set out the long-term options for closer ties with the bloc next month, with concrete steps coming after the next general election, as he has pledged to stick to Labour’s manifesto red lines.

Downing Street insiders expect that Burnham would – if he concluded the best route forward for the UK was to rejoin – push for a mandate to start negotiations in the next manifesto, then hold a confirmatory referendum.

In a Commons statement on last week’s Brussels summit, Burnham was asked whether he could give a “clear and unequivocal” statement he would not take the UK back in without one. “Yes, it would be unthinkable,” he replied.

Burnham has criticised former Tory prime ministers for being “stuck in the past”, dismissing the advice of Rishi Sunak, David Cameron and Theresa May, who have said he should not reignite the Brexit debate.

“I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal. They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did,” he told broadcasters.

“I’m not a prime minister that’s going to be stuck in the past. I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills.

“All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union. I believe it will be better for Britain to take this path, and I won’t be listening to those voices who put us here in the first place.”

However, Burnham later told MPs that he would pursue a “pragmatic approach” to the UK’s future relationship with the EU and there was “no fixed opinion” and “no fixed destination” inside No 10, despite publicly revealing that his personal preference would be to rejoin.

“I do think it’s important for me to say again that the world has changed and will continue to change, and we need to test any options against that reality,” he said. “But always, we should be, in my view, pragmatic and choose whatever option secures the best deal for Britain.”

There are some concerns inside government that with four big EU states, including France, heading to the polls in the next year, the rise of rightwing populist parties could change Downing Street’s calculations.

“As we look to the next year, the politics of Europe could change considerably. I think we need to go into the further consideration of options with all of those factors in mind. We’ll have to obviously watch how life changes,” Burnham said.

The prime minister told MPs the deal he signed in Brussels on Friday – covering food and drink checks, emissions trading and youth mobility – was a “landmark moment” that would lower the cost of living.

The government wants to persuade the public that closer ties with the bloc will boost the UK economy, although some insiders acknowledge the difficulty of making that argument when the global economic outlook remains bleak.

Burnham, who will lay legislation next week to implement the food and drink deal, said big supermarkets had confirmed it would “lift the pressure off the weekly shop”.

EU officials have indicated that last week’s deal was contingent on the UK aligning tuition fees so that European students would pay the same amount as domestic students, with a six-month deadline to reach a compromise.

There is expected to be further discussions on the UK joining the EU’s still-to-be-finalised “Made in Europe” scheme, which protects against cheap Chinese imports, as well as the bloc’s electricity market, with other talks on touring artists and illicit migration.

While the bill setting out last week’s “reset” deal will be presented to the Commons this week, the result of the subsequent discussions is unlikely to emerge until the next UK-EU summit, expected next summer at the earliest.

Officials in both the EU and UK have signalled they would like to see those talks with Brussels run in parallel to the “national debate” that Burnham has said he wishes to have with the UK public about what the closer future relationship might look like.

The two sides agreed last week to a “brainstorming” process to look at the options for closer ties, including options of a Swiss-style deal with close sectoral alignment, a single market and customs union deal or a path for Britain to fully rejoin the EU, with an informal summit next year.

“We will say more next month when we publish the plan for Britain about how we move forward. But the initial agreement we have reached … is that it will be an informal exchange of ideas, with the results to be presented around the time of the next UK-EU summit,” Burnham said.

The legal text of the deal, expected in the coming days, is likely to contain a clause which would penalise the UK if it reneged, in order to pay the costs of reinstating customs infrastructure, which opposition parties have called a “Farage clause”, should the Reform UK leader win the next election and reverse the deal.

The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:29:05 GMT

Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action

In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.

Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive.

While the failure to agree Cop31’s “cover decision” dominated the summit’s headlines, other decisions did pass. The work on a just transition will continue for three years, but the mechanism to make it operational is missing. There was progress on how to assess adaptation needs for developing nations, but not on how to pay for it. Such gaps highlight the unresolved political conflicts at the heart of the UN talks.

An agreement to transition away from fossil fuels was made in 2023. A tripling of adaptation finance was promised in 2025. Yet the Australian-Turkish joint presidency diverted attention away from delivering these commitments towards a cover decision promoting controversial technologies and electrification without tying this to renewable energy. The latter has an energy-security rationale: disruption from the US-Israel war on Iran strengthens the case for replacing imported fossil fuels with homegrown electricity. But how that electricity is generated matters – and poorer countries need support to fund the switch.

Wealthy nations don’t have much of a moral pedestal upon which to lecture them. The UK government is spending less on climate finance per year over the next three years than it did over the last five and is expected to give a nod to Rosebank – the biggest undeveloped oilfield in UK waters – by the end of 2026. More egregiously, Sweden’s environment minister, Romina Pourmokhtari, who led the EU’s finance group at Cop31, publicly backed a weakening of the country’s emissions rules that lay behind its 7% greenhouse gas increase in 2024.

The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and an opportunity to shape outcomes. Before the next Cop, in Ethiopia, trust between parties must be repaired through a transparent negotiating process. Strenuous efforts must also be made to avoid last-minute wrangling over a text that displaces the original agreed agenda by making progress on turning finance pledges into action.

This year brought glacier collapses, record European heat and wildfires across Asia. The world must do much more to confront a human-made catastrophe. It is unarguable that fossil fuels are the primary cause of global heating. What is required is a fair and equitable transition on a global scale to cleaner energy. “The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground. Neither can we,” said UN secretary general António Guterres. It is impossible to disagree.

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is the sensible strategy

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:28:47 GMT

On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

Over the weekend, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, made the case for closer ties and a bigger British voice in Europe’s affairs. The country needed, Mr Miliband told the BBC, to move beyond a status quo in which Britain is a passive rule-taker in relation to its largest trading partner, rather than exerting a direct influence inside the decision-making room. As the EU continues to move to protect its industries against Chinese and US competition, to the possible detriment of British interests, that is an argument that will only grow in force.

There is frustration in some Labour quarters that having unexpectedly opened up the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU in the autumn, Mr Burnham shows no sign of moving towards explicitly advocating for it. But the prime minister’s cautious and undogmatic strategy is sensible politics on deeply treacherous terrain. Without committing himself in a way that would worry some “red wall” members of his own cabinet, Mr Burnham’s unequivocally pro‑European stance has positioned Labour at the head of a progressive electoral bloc at a time when the right is bitterly divided.

The national verdict that Brexit has been a disappointment gives space to argue for building on Friday’s direction of travel. Implementing the reset deal will take up the remainder of the current parliament, as the prime minister indicated on Monday in his statement to the House of Commons. But that leaves the way open for the prime minister to make a broader pro-EU case at the next election – whenever that comes. An open‑ended approach also allows necessary room for manoeuvre during what is set to be a febrile and destabilising period in European politics, with the possibility of a far-right French president entering the Élysée in the spring.

In his Commons statement, Mr Burnham made reference to that continental volatility, while at the same time underlining that Friday’s agreement could be followed by further major changes following an election. The contemplation of options and “informal brainstorming” sessions with Brussels cannot go on for ever, particularly as the nascent “stay out” movement revives the kind of false arguments that blighted the 2016 referendum. Eventually, the government will have to nail its colours to the mast and choose a case to make. But it is right to undertake that process of discernment with a sense of caution and an emphasis on building consensus.

Former prince Andrew was paid £750,000 in hope of helping Turkish woman with passport, high court told

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:20:03 GMT

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was paid a £750,000 “bribe” in the hope of helping a Turkish woman with her passport, the high court has been told.

Nebahat Isbilen is suing her former adviser, businessman Selman Turk, over allegations he misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her funds.

She also claims Turk misled her about a £750,000 payment made to the former Duke of York in 2019, dishonestly saying the money was needed as a gift for Mountbatten-Windsor’s help with her Turkish passport. The money was later paid back by Andrew, the court was told.

On Monday Isbilen’s lawyers told the court that Turk instructed separate payments to Mountbatten-Windsor’s former wife Sarah Ferguson, including a £15,000 payment purportedly for her 60th birthday party in 2019. There was also an unquantified wedding gift for the couple’s daughter Beatrice, the court heard.

Turk denies the claims. He argues that Isbilen knew the money was being paid in the hope that Mountbatten-Windsor could help her husband, who is in prison in Turkey.

Turk’s lawyers told the court: “Her own case is that she understood that the payment to the Duke of York was a bribe, either for assistance with her passport or her UK residency.”

Mountbatten-Windsor, who is not accused of any wrongdoing, is due to give evidence on 14 December, after a judge allowed Turk to issue him with a witness summons compelling him to appear.

Simon Colton KC, for Isbilen, said in written submissions that the 81-year-old was part of the Evyap family, which owns a large soap and cosmetics firm in Turkey.

The submission said her husband, a former member of the Turkish parliament, had been imprisoned in the country since 2015 on “politically motivated” terrorism charges and, in 2017, she was facing “political persecution”.

She met Turk in January that year and gave him control of most of her financial assets, but Colton said Turk “persuaded Mrs Isbilen that her assets were at risk and that he was able to transfer them to a safe place”.

Colton said Turk “deliberately and systematically abused” Isbilen’s trust and transferred the money to companies he owned or controlled, for his own benefit, leaving her the victim of a “major, cynical fraud”.

Isbilen left Turkey for Greece in 2017, and moved to London in 2018.

Colton said that documents obtained by Isbilen under disclosure showed that Turk had sent about £2m to a company called Alphabet Capital, some of which was transferred to Mountbatten-Windsor.

He said Isbilen approved the £750,000 payment to Mountbatten-Windsor, but that Turk “lied to her” about its purpose.

One payment was made by a bank on Turk’s instruction to Alphabet Capital of about $275,000 (£210,000), Colton said, most of which was then paid to Ferguson.

The high court was told in 2023 that Isbilen reached a settlement with Mountbatten-Windsor and Ferguson.

Joshua Hitchens, for Turk, said in written submissions that Isbilen’s claim was “a mess” and should be dismissed.

He said that she knew the true purpose of the payment to Mountbatten-Windsor, adding: “Paying public figures for preferential treatment was well within the claimant’s modus operandi.”

Hitchens also said that in December 2019, Isbilen “dined for some five or six hours at Mr Turk’s flat with the Duke and Duchess of York and Mr Turk’s family, seated next to the duchess, having asked for the dinner to be held in private rather than in public, and discussed her husband’s case with the Duke.”

He said in those circumstances: “She cannot have believed that the £750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa.

“The payment was what Mr Turk told the bank it was: a gift, made in the hope of Mr Mountbatten-Windsor taking steps to assist her husband.”

The trial before Mr Justice Adam Johnson is due to conclude in March, with a written judgment at a later date.

Game over? How playing Grand Theft Auto VI is affecting elite athletes’ performances

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:14:03 GMT

Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad

“They miss games, the cheque’s still clearing. And you’re trying to tell me they got this kind of addiction to a video game that they sitting there with their thumbs looking like Donald Trump?” That was EPSN’s Stephen A Smith, one of the US’s most provocative and influential sports pundits, spitting fire and fury last week after hearing that so many NBA and NFL stars were absorbed in Grand Theft Auto VI.

Smith was hardly an outlier. Other pundits, as well as some Manchester United fans, also questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s focus and professionalism after he posted an image of GTA VI and the word “historique” after midnight on Thursday. Meanwhile before last weekend’s Premier League games, the Odd Sport social media account predicted that Chelsea, Brighton and Manchester City would all lose. Why? Because their younger squads might be more focused on Vice City than their opponents, and therefore play with less intensity as a result. By Monday that forecast had been liked tens of thousands of times.

So is there really such a thing as a Grand Theft Auto effect, beyond all the recent hysterics and polemics? The Houston Rockets basketball player Steven Adams certainly thinks so. A couple of months ago he predicted that the launch of GTA VI would cause performances across various leagues to “plummet” in November.

Instinctively, you can see his point. If a basketball star spends hours shooting gangsters, are they really going to be as focused on shooting threes? Then again, players spend their lives around consoles. So are their levels really going to be that affected by the launch of a new game?

Fortunately the area of how video games can affect mental fatigue in elite sports stars is increasingly attracting the attention of sports scientists. And while it is still early days, the findings are certainly intriguing.

One study in 2020 took 25 professional footballers in Brazil, and split them into three groups who were either made to watch adverts, play Fifa 18, or go on social media before playing a 90-minute match. The result? While the groups made a similar overall number of passes, accuracy dropped by 6.5% in the video game group compared with the control group.

Another systematic review of eight studies in 2022, which examined the link between playing video games and mental fatigue, also found that there was a “significant impact” on the technical performance of footballers – including missing more tackles and making more errors. Surprisingly, though, passing skills were unaffected.

What’s more, other studies have found that when athletes are mentally fatigued they often demonstrate longer fixation time on opponents and less on their teammates, which leads to poorer decisions. As you would also expect, mental fatigue often makes physical effort feel harder too.

However, before clubs start banning GTA VI en masse, they should hear the thoughts of John Kiely, an Irish sports scientist who recently studied mental fatigue among Brighton’s first-team players, and has also worked with Egypt’s World Cup squad in 2018, Ireland’s rugby team, and UK Athletics.

Kiely, who also recently co-authored a paper that examined 28 recent academic papers on football and mental fatigue, warns there are several important caveats. Many of the studies have been conducted on small-sided training games, such as five-a-side matches between academy players. They are often small in scope. It means that what happens in the lab may not necessarily translate to the thunder and intensity of the Premier League.

“The studies are way too lab-based at the moment,” he says. “And it’s very hard to extrapolate them to what will happen with a seasoned professional player who’s used to high-stress environments.”

As Kiely also points out, individual players also behave differently to the same stresses – something that he and his fellow researchers found when they monitored Brighton’s players over a season to track their mental fatigue. So playing GTA VI until 3am might affect one player a lot less than another, simply because of how their brains are wired and stimulated.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

But, you might ask, surely playing esports improves reaction times and speedy decision-making? Perhaps for the general population. However, Kiely is sceptical that it transfers over to elite athletes. “The chances that the reflexes you learn on an online game are going to transfer to the field if you’re already elite are nonexistent,” he says.

However Kiely is more enthused about the potential of using eye-tracking to test a player’s reflexes when they are tired. “If you track something, be it a ball or whatever on a screen, are your left and right eyes moving simultaneously, or is there a little bit of a lag?” he asks. “Well, those lags increase with fatigue.”

So what advice would Kiely give clubs about GTA VI? Broadly they should relax – as long as players aren’t settling down for marathon sessions late at night.

“I wouldn’t see anything too much wrong with it, providing it doesn’t stimulate a player so much that they stay awake the night before a game and they lose sleep,” he says. “That’s one of the biggest dangers. Because losing sleep is a clear performance decrement and a clear injury risk promoter.

“ So my advice is play for 40 minutes, get up, take a walk, get some fresh air and do some eye exercises, and you’ll be fine.”

There is a final point worth making here. Burning the midnight oil playing a console game might not be optimal preparation for a professional player. But it certainly beats the old-school way of unwinding, of boozing and living it up out on the town.

So the advice is clear. Place gun in holster, put pedal to floor, and enjoy the next chapter of GTA. Just remember to go for a walk and do your eye exercises afterwards.

Your article (Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit, 20 November) marks a welcome moment of political realism after years of denial about the consequences of Brexit. I wholeheartedly agree with Andy Burnham when he said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe.” For years, the evidence has pointed in the same direction, that the UK economy is worse off as a result of Brexit. Trade barriers have increased, growth has suffered and businesses have been forced to navigate unnecessary bureaucracy.

Many of the industries that Brexit supporters claimed would flourish have instead struggled. Fishing, farming, construction and touring musicians have all faced new obstacles, costs and restrictions. Meanwhile, younger generations have seen opportunities to study, work, travel and collaborate across Europe reduced through no fault of their own. The benefits of closer trade links with the UK’s nearest and largest market cannot be overestimated. Yet Nigel Farage and Conservative Brexit supporters have failed to deliver the economic opportunities and global trade advantages they promised.

Andy Burnham deserves credit for acknowledging that Brexit has failed in many respects and for supporting practical steps to rebuild relations with the EU. The choice is no longer between leave and remain; it is between decline and renewal.

The country deserves leaders willing to put economic reality ahead of ideology, and this agreement is a welcome step in that direction. Stuart Finegan Lewes, East Sussex

The sight and sound of former prime ministers criticising Andy Burnham’s proposal to open a discussion on Britain’s future relationship with the EU is unedifying. It is as though they have learned nothing and forgotten nothing, not least their own responsibility for the toxic mess of Brexit. The point of democracy is surely the right of the people to change their minds. We accept this during the routine electoral cycle. Why can we not do so regarding our relationship with the EU? It is inconsistent to argue that the 2016 referendum was binding for all time whereas the 1975 EEC referendum was not.

Labour’s next manifesto should therefore include a commitment to explore and openly present the options, followed by discussions with the EU on the terms that might be on offer and by a referendum, conducted on the same basis as that of 2016, whether to accept those terms. Yet by anchoring his case in the prospect of stronger GDP growth, he is simply returning to the hard-headed economic logic that has governed Britain’s relationship with Europe for more than half a century.

When Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973, the argument was never built on federalist sentiment. It sought access to a dynamic continental market to revive sluggish growth and boost exports. Two years later, in the 1975 referendum, voters overwhelmingly backed remaining for the exact same bread-and-butter reasons, just as British economic self-interest later drove the creation of the single market.

Seen through this historical lens, 2016 was not the culmination of a longstanding economic critique but a political aberration. In the runup to the Brexit referendum, rational debate over trade and living standards was hijacked by a toxic combination of Boris Johnson’s ruthless personal ambition for the Tory leadership and visceral anxieties over borders – anxieties turbocharged by Angela Merkel’s 2015 decision to open Germany’s doors to about a million Syrian refugees. Steven Spielberg has announced his next project: a western scripted by Paul Thomas Anderson.

According to Deadline, the two Oscar-winning film-makers will collaborate for an adaptation of Kevin Barry’s 2024 novel The Heart in Winter.

The film is set to bring together the Oscar-winning actors Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy and Mark Rylance. It tells the story of two fugitives on the run in the 1890s.

“It’s really the excitement for me to get to work together with my dear friend and colleague Paul Thomas Anderson on a genre, but more particularly, the genre notwithstanding, a story that quite quickly became close to both our hearts and we felt that we could do as a team,” Spielberg told Deadline.

Earlier this year, Spielberg also spoke about the film while at SXSW. “Can’t reveal anything right now, but I have a western in development,” he said, before adding that “it kicks ass” and “there will be no tropes”.

It will be the first time Anderson will have written a complete script for a different director, although he was involved in uncredited rewrites of Martin Scorsese’s Killers of the Flower Moon and Ridley Scott’s Napoleon. He recently won three Oscars for One Battle After Another.

The Guardian’s Sandra Newman called The Heart in Winter one of the best books of 2024, writing that it “effortlessly walks the line between goofy and gothic”.

“This story is about the people who refused to settle for a life that is less than they deserve but maybe more than they can handle,” Spielberg also added. “Jessie and Cillian were the first people to ever come to mind for this and they also have never made a film together.”

Earlier this year, Buckley won the best actress Oscar for her performance in Hamnet, produced by Spielberg, and will next be seen in The Three Incestuous Sisters alongside Saoirse Ronan, Dakota Johnson and Josh O’Connor.

Murphy, who won the best actor Oscar for Oppenheimer, was last seen reprising his role of Jim in 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and in Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man. Next summer will also see him return to the Quiet Place franchise.

The film will follow Spielberg’s sci-fi thriller Disclosure Day which made $247m worldwide upon release this past summer.

A release date is yet to be officially confirmed yet but the film is believed to be scheduled for 2028.
