A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:09:00 GMT

Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction

The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all (UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November).

The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines.

Specialist species have been hit particularly hard. The willow tit, which depends on young wet woodland, is nearing extinction. Its close relative, the marsh tit, has had a catastrophic fall in numbers. As woodlands become increasingly fragmented, their populations are left isolated and vulnerable. We know that creating larger, better-connected habitats can help these species, but too little has been done to create and protect them.

There is, however, reason for hope. The recovery of the Dartford warbler from near extinction in the 1960s shows what is possible when suitable habitat is properly protected. When governments invest in and support nature, species can recover.

We have the evidence. We understand many of the causes of decline and what needs to be done. The government must now respond to this legal failure with long-term investment and action before more of our cherished birds disappear. Emma Phipps Scientific research and impact manager, SongBird Survival

Only six beds for trans victims of domestic abuse in UK, report finds

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:07:04 GMT

Exclusive: Services say supreme court ruling on single-sex spaces has made it ‘almost impossible’ to find refuges for trans people

There are only six beds specifically for trans victims of domestic abuse in the UK, a report has found, with services saying it is “almost impossible” to find refuges for trans people since the supreme court ruling on single-sex spaces.

Galop, an LGBTQ+ anti-abuse charity, called on the government to create an emergency national fund for specialist trans refuges, as many people were being turned away from mainstream services.

Prior to the supreme court ruling on single-sex spaces in 2025, trans people could be placed into some mainstream domestic abuse refuges, Galop said.

However, since that ruling determined same-sex spaces referred strictly to “biological sex”, many refuges that previously accepted trans people are now no longer able to.

Galop said it has been unable to secure non-specialist refuge accommodation for any trans women in the UK in 2026 – it has only been able to find space at specialist LGBTQ+ or trans providers.

Jasmine O’Connor, co-CEO of the charity, said: “Finding housing suitable for trans survivors has been very challenging for a long time, but since the supreme court ruling, that challenge has become absolutely acute. It’s devastating.

“What was a very limited supply of housing has shrunk to virtually zero. For us as a service, it’s desperate to have to turn individuals away, week in, week out, because there is nowhere for them to go.”

Across England and Wales, there are nine LGBTQ+ specialist accommodation services for domestic abuse victims providing a total of 106 bed spaces – of these, only six are specially reserved for trans people and they are all based in one refuge.

Data suggests that demand far outstrips the supply. LGBTQ+ people are twice as likely to experience domestic abuse as heterosexual and cisgender people, and government data showed that 500 trans or non-binary adults were supported in domestic abuse safe accommodation in 2024-25.

Galop said that 40% of its domestic abuse clients were trans+ in 2025/26, and that many were having to make the “unimaginable choice about whether to stay living with their alleged perpetrator or having no home”.

“We’ll never know the amount of people who are making the choice to stay in a really abusive relationship because there is not a safe route out until, sadly, they’re in the headlines,” she said.

In a landmark case last year, the supreme court ruled that the terms woman and sex in the Equality Act referred to a “biological woman” and “biological sex”, which meant that transgender people could be excluded from same-sex spaces. In October, the NHS announced that trans people would no longer to be placed on same-sex wards.

The report says many domestic abuse services only place trans people in dispersed accommodation, self-contained spaces in the community, which are often most in demand and most difficult to access.

Others only place trans people in mixed-gender homelessness accommodation, where they are more likely to experience further abuse.

One trans woman quoted in the report, who has lived as a woman for over 20 years, said she was turned away from a women’s refuge because of the supreme court ruling, and Galop staff said many people were reluctant to approach services because of they fear the humiliation of being rejected.

O’Connor said she hoped the government would speak to them about ringfenced funding for increasing trans services across the country: “We’d like a conversation with the government and a commitment to create this fund so that there is the right money available to commission the right sorts of services.

“We see this very much in line with the government’s commitments on domestic abuse and wanting to ensure that LGBTQ+ survivors are supported within that strategy.”

In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines may be found via www. befrienders. org

Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:04:25 GMT

There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg

Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector (‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation. Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign, initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development. Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech, providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere. At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova, and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl, have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption. Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources. Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies. James White and Nora Söderberg Department of Technology and Society, Lund University

Madness erupts as Sevilla deny Betis in wild end to Spain’s ‘derby of derbies’

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:49:56 GMT

Rivals have been heading in opposite directions in recent years but latest clash showed some things never change

“If we didn’t celebrate a goal, especially in this game, that would be madness,” Kike Salas said. Instead, this was madness, the kind of moment a derby is meant to have, even if it has nothing else. It was late, it was lucky, and there wasn’t even a winner but right there, right then, at 24 minutes past 8pm on Saturday evening in the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium, it felt like there was. Frankly it was a bit rubbish, as bad a goal as you’ll see, but it was also the best, practically Pelé against the Nazis. Suddenly there were arms and legs everywhere, tears too. Cameras confirmed it. Zoom in and there they are: actual, real life tears.

In the 91st minute of the 146th meeting between Sevilla Fútbol Club and Real Betis Balompié – “derby of derbies” according to Luis García, the Sevilla coach for whom it was the first – Salas’s shot from 18 yards went through Marc Bartra’s legs and Álvaro Valles’s hands. The ball dribbled into the Betis net so apologetically it barely touched the net at all and hadn’t got there before Sevilla’s vice-captain was gone. Raised in Morón de la Frontera, to the south of a city divided, Salas joined Sevilla at 11; now, having levelled the game at 1-1, he went tearing towards the terraces, absolutely losing it like they were.

In the six-yard box, Robbie Ure, the Scottish striker who had watched the ball pass and whose own shot barely 100 seconds before was the eighth Betis blocked, resigned to the fact that it just wasn’t going to happen, reacted to the fact that it actually had with his right arm pumping like Animal on the drums. Screaming as he went, Salas thumped at his chest as hard. Around the Sánchez Pizjuán, 42,983 went wild except the 600 Béticos high in the corner. They couldn’t believe this and nor could their players: of all the ways to let go. From the Sevilla bench, everyone ran towards the team.

García went the other way through the crowd in his blue suit, like the final scene of a romcom: a man fighting against the rush-hour tide, bundling into a busy subway station desperate to reach the train before it leaves with her on board. He was in the middle of the pitch when he put the brakes on and returned, alone. He had been through the emotions; frustration, relief, joy, vindication and frustration again. A colleague awaited with a high five that was hard too. They could have won. But they also could have lost – Sevilla had trailed to Antony’s goal, which wasn’t great either, and Odysseas Vlachodimos’s superb save had prevented the Brazilian from getting Betis’s second and ending it – but at least they had salvaged a point.

At the final whistle, the Betis midfielder Dani Ceballos came to console Valles. “You’ve been our best player this season,” he told the goalkeeper, which was true. No one in La Liga has made more saves and none have been more significant either. Valles’s xG avoided is 8.3; the next best is 4.1. At the same time, Salas tried to do the post-game interview but couldn’t hear over the noise. Behind him, his family were waiting for a hug. As Betis’s players made their way, Sevilla’s players stood before supporters at the north end, applauding and applauded back.

“When you go to your greatest rivals’ ground, you deserve to win but they get a draw and on top of that they celebrate it, you know you’re doing things right,” said the Betis captain Bartra, who also claimed that Salas shouldn’t have been on the pitch to score the equaliser after he had trodden on Isco’s ankle. “A bad game from us only allows them to draw at home,” said the Betis president, Ángel Haro. “Fortunately, we’re in a period when a draw feels like sadness to us and a triumph for them.”

And so the debate was served, so the accusations came, the usual nonsense. In Spain? In Seville? Surely not?! Etc and so on. But if the words of Betis’s captain and president prompted that, if those words were a little pointed in a city where they pride themselves on being wind-up merchants and the derby is the most passionate in the country, there is an obvious response: well, yeah. Not least precisely because it’s about putting one over on each other. Every goal is an explosion and Sevilla got theirs in the 91st minute. Against Betis. From the centre-back who’s been at the club half his life. Of course they celebrated it.

If it might have seemed a little odd for Sevilla to stand there before their fans celebrating when they hadn’t won and a run of one win in seven in the league had been confirmed, that too was part of it. Because Bartra and Haro were right, to their credit and to Sevilla’s too. At the start of this derby, a huge banner came down over the north stand; a supporters’ work of art made by hand as ever, it lauded a history of greatness, but maybe history is the word, and that’s the real greatness: it is three years since Sevilla won a trophy or qualified for Europe, those days not just fading fast but long gone, yet here they are anyway, more than 35,000 of them every week.

Sevilla are a club in crisis, where the former president José María del Nido is at war with the former president José María del Nido – and, yes, they are father and son. Where the debt is almost €200m (£167.2m) and the solution, a sale to a consortium led by Sergio Ramos, fell through. Where they have the lowest salary limit in the whole of primera, at €20m (£16.7m), and four second division teams were allowed to spend more. Where this summer they had a net spend of minus €25m (£20.9m). And where they qualified for the Champions League three years running under Julen Lopetegui, sacked him, went through seven managers in three years and finished 12th, 14th and 17th, closer to relegation every season.

In May they finished 13th yet only escaped relegation in the penultimate week, and that was a miracle. The day that García had been presented as coach, arriving on a rescue mission that seemed impossible, the sporting director was overheard saying: “It’s like a funeral in here”.

after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, Betis have been heading in the other direction. Sevilla’s first division league positions since 2006 read: 5, 3, 5, 3, 3, 4, 5, 9, 9, 5, 5, 7, 4, 7, 6, 4, 4, 4, then: 12, 14, 17, 13. Betis’s read: 14, 16, 13, 18 and relegation … then, after two years away, 13, 7, 20 and relegation again, followed by 10, 15, 6, 10, 15. And then, under Manuel Pellegrini: 6, 5, 6, 7, 6, 5. While Sevilla crumbled, Betis consolidated. Under the Chilean they have won a Copa del Rey – one of only three in their history – and this season are back in the Champions League, 20 years on. Defeated just twice, they sit fourth. Their salary limit is seven times Sevilla’s.

The only thing missing, some said, was precisely this: the derby. “I think I’ve always understood the importance for our people,” Pellegrini said, “but if you ask me, I would prefer to finisher higher up than to win the derby.” From 2020-2025 Betis won only one of 10 – although that was in the cup en route to winning it. Then they beat Sevilla 2-1 in March 2025, and again in December; they came into Saturday night without defeat in three, an inescapable superiority imposed. At the end on Saturday night, Antony turned to the Sevilla fans and mouthed: “You’re very bad, you’re terrible.”

Athletic Bilbao 0-1 Espanyol, Alavés 3-1 Deportivo La Coruña, Rayo Vallecano 0-1 Valencia, Sevilla 1-1 Real Betis, Real Madrid 2-1 Celta Vigo, Barcelona 3-2 Villarreal, Racing Santander 3-2 Real Sociedad, Osasuna 1-0 Málaga, Getafe 0-3 Atlético Madrid

It was born of anger but not entirely untrue. These may be the best days of Betis’s lives, possibly even ever. For Sevilla, it’s different, the limitations clear. Yet García has got more from them: the team seemingly destined to fight for their lives again went into this game in a European place. And while it is worth a word of warning here – after four victories in their first six, Sevilla are on a miserable run, reality creeping back in – they came out having competed again, a team. Bad they might be, but Antony and his teammates hadn’t been able to beat them. Only Atlético, Real Madrid, Barcelona and Getafe have.

In fact, Sevilla hadn’t just competed. When Pellegrini described this as the “typical derby” where neither side did much, García suggested he must have been watching a different match, insisting that the draw was bittersweet because his players had deserved more. Still, at least it wasn’t just bitter. When Salas scored and sent everyone wild, it was their 25th shot, something like justice done and something like satisfaction found, something to hold on to and why not? Not least because as well as against their rivals it had been done, the coach said, against a great team: a Champions League side full of talent. In this city of symbiosis, these years of change, Betis’s success was indeed the measure of Sevilla’s and vice versa, just as it always was. And the way it came, tension liberated late in the night that means more to them than any other, was reason to celebrate. That’s what football is for. Anything other than madness then would have been madness.

Kemi is beside herself that Burnham is trying to salvage a Brexit deal. Can’t we all stop talking about it?

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:37:46 GMT

Badenoch ends her anti-EU speech by calling herself ‘the leader of common sense’. Really?

When you’ve got David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak saying you’ve got it wrong on Brexit, then the chances are Andy Burnham must be doing something right. These four are the former prime ministers that are largely responsible for the mess the UK is currently in. Lord Big Dave had never really given the possibility of leaving the EU much thought. The Maybot spent three years saying nothing more intelligent than “Brexit means Brexit”. Boris lied through his teeth to get his deal over the line. And as for Rishi? It’s hard to think of anything he achieved.

All of which makes life tricky for Kemi Badenoch. Because in an ideal world, Kemi would rather we all forgot about Brexit entirely. Not because it is going so well, but because it it isn’t. She would like you to believe that Brexit was nothing to do with her – even though she was a hardline Brexiter – or the Tories. Rather it was some kind of paranormal event that just happened to the country while the Conservatives were in power. Correlation does not imply causality and all that. In KemiWorld we would pretend that everything is more or less OK and that the noblest course of action is to live with the self-inflicted injury.

It goes without saying that this isn’t Labour’s action plan. Nor, as it happens, is it the preferred option for the Confederation of British Industry. They are all for restoring closer ties with the EU. Which made Kemi’s speech to the CBI on Monday morning something of an outlier. For one thing, the CBI is a traditional graveyard for Labour politicians, not Tories. For another, Kemi usually only plays to home crowds where members of her team lead the whoops and cheers for even the most banal insights. Here at the CBI she had a far tougher crowd. If not overtly hostile, then severely Kemisceptic.

There again it would probably have helped if Kemi hadn’t begun her speech with a brazen lie. She had had nothing to do with Brexit, she said. Had been working in the private sector in 2016. This is probably the only time you will ever hear being a Brexit-supporting member of the London Assembly as a career in private business. But Kemi is desperate to distance herself from all things Brexit. She would rather no one mentioned it and is beside herself that Burnham has chosen this moment to try to salvage a better deal from the wreckage of the one the Tories negotiated. Even more inconveniently for Kemi, a third of all Conservatives wouldn’t mind rejoining the EU.

So Kemi now operates in this weird half-life. Where things can be true and untrue at the same time. Spoken and yet unsaid. The worst of all worlds. Because every time she tries to stop talking about the EU, someone spoils it all by mentioning it. And she has no real answers. She knows the Brexit deal was a bad one but can’t bring herself to say how to make it better. Other than if the EU were to become a subsidiary body to the UK. That is the Tory and Reform fantasy.

Nor is Kemi capable of rational judgment on Burnham’s deal. She doesn’t appear to be able to name any Brexit benefits that we would lose out on. All she can say is that everything about the deal just negotiated is hopeless and that if she were in power she would do something completely different. Which for now is too top secret for her to share with the rest of us. We just have to take her word that she has a grand plan. The plan of plans. The Tories have become a niche, pro-Brexit cult.

It was like this, said Kemi. The key to negotiating with the EU is never to tell them what you want or else they will think you’re weak and stupid. There was only one problem with this. Everyone already knows what the UK wants from a trade deal with the EU. It’s not a secret.

The problem is not what’s on the bucket list; it’s getting the EU to agree to it. So it turns out that Kemi’s cunning plan is to ask for things that the EU won’t expect. Like more regulation and red tape. The best way to get what you want from the EU is to ask for things that actively harm the UK. As it happened, it would turn out that Kemi did think there were some times when you have to reveal your plans. In her excitement to leave the ECHR, she did admit that she would leave instructions for Stormont and the Republic of Ireland to be extra nice to one another. Sometimes you have to conclude that Kemi has the Midas touch.

Kemi also reckoned that Burnham was placing far too much emphasis on growth. It really wasn’t worth pursuing a £17bn – 0.4 % – uplift to the UK economy if the price was taking rules from the EU. Everything would have to be on our terms. We would only get along if the EU followed our rules. However, it was definitely worthwhile following the same rules as the Australians to get 0.01% growth. Sometimes, she said, less is more. What matters most is not the amount of growth but who negotiated the deal. Tories, good: Labour, bad.

after newsletter promotion

By now it appeared that the Tory leader was totally off script. Just winging it. This can happen to you when you are talking total bollocks. It used to be remainers who were accused of Brexit derangement syndrome. Now it seems as if the virus has jumped species. Her speech ended with Kemi insisting that she had a five-point plan for business. Point four was to cut red tape. Er, that’s exactly what Burnham’s new deal had done. The one to which she was viscerally opposed. Point five was to champion business. Just none who were members of the CBI and had been hoping she had a more pro-EU message to tell.

The speech ended with the sound of one hand clapping. But Kemi hadn’t finished digging her own grave. In answer to a question from the audience, she declared that being in office had constrained her power to act. Now that she was in opposition, she found it far easier to come up with ideas that no one liked. “I am the leader of common sense,” she said. Really? Is that what you call it?

Sport of kings will be going to the dogs if horse racing is complacent on welfare

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:37:39 GMT

Latest greyhound racing blow is a wake-up call with new five-year plan keeping RSPCA on side for now

Britain’s greyhound racing industry woke up on Monday to the news that the Racing Post, the daily trade newspaper that has carried extensive coverage of the sport since its launch in 1986, will drop both editorial and greyhound racecards in its print edition from 10 December.

In a letter to Racing Post readers, Tom Kerr, its editor, said that it had been an “immensely difficult decision” and blamed “tax rises that have hit betting shops [which] have put pressure on the whole industry,” adding that “like other businesses, we have to make hard choices about where we focus our resources.” Five members of staff are expected to lose their jobs as a result of the decision.

While the Post will maintain a greyhound section on its website, Monday’s news was greeted with anger and dismay by greyhound racing’s fans and professionals alike.

“This undoubtedly will have come as a shock to those who have followed the sport for decades and relied on the paper as a trusted source of news, results and insight,” Mark Bird, the chief executive of the Greyhound Board of Great Britain (GBGB) said in response.

“It is deeply disappointing news, particularly at a time when it feels more important than ever for horse racing and greyhound racing to stand together in the face of the challenges confronting both sports.”

Bird added that the GBGB is “already exploring what opportunities may exist with other national publications to increase the visibility of the sport. We hope those discussions will prove productive, and we will keep stakeholders updated as and when there is meaningful news to share.”

There are currently 15 active greyhound tracks in England and Wales, although Valley Greyhounds near Ystrad Mynach, Caerphilly, currently the only greyhound track in Wales, will close by April 2030 after the Senedd (Welsh parliament) voted to ban greyhound racing earlier this year.

Scotland, which has not had a GBGB-licensed track since March 2020, also voted to outlaw the sport earlier this year, and Monday’s news will be seen as another significant setback for a sport that has had little to celebrate in recent years.

As recently as 2004, there were 12,000 new registrations of racing greyhounds in the UK, and a total of 51 tracks – including 20 “independent” venues – staging racing, generating a total of around £3bn in betting turnover annually.

The sport has since suffered steep declines in attendance and turnover, however, following the closure of many tracks including the high-profile London venues of Walthamstow and Wimbledon, the former home of the Greyhound Derby. It generated estimated off-course turnover of approximately £1.2bn in 2025 according to the Gambling Commission, with around half that total coming via betting shops.

Unlike horse racing, meanwhile, which has the benefit of a statutory levy to return income to the sport from betting in addition to its significant media rights deals, greyhound racing has only ever had a “voluntary” levy paid by gambling firms. That too has dwindled steadily in recent years.

All in all, it has been one thing after another for the dogs, and in addition to falling crowds and revenues, since September 2023 the sport has also faced a concerted and well-funded campaign for its phased abolition.

That campaign has been co-ordinated by a grouping called Cut The Chase, a coalition of animal welfare charities including Blue Cross and, most significantly, the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA).

The RSPCA’s involvement with Cut The Chase marked a major departure from the organisation’s previous stance of working with the greyhound racing industry on its welfare issues, most obviously the injury rates while racing and the uncertain future for competitors post-retirement.

At the organisation’s launch, the RSPCA signed a joint statement declaring that greyhound racing is “inherently dangerous”, and that “significant welfare issues for racing greyhounds have not been resolved and cannot be resolved.”

Fans of both greyhound and horse racing may see an immediate parallel here, as the RSPCA’s current policy with regards to horse racing is to “engage” with the industry to encourage the highest possible welfare and safety standards.

There have been moments, though, in recent years when the organisation’s language has veered more towards confrontation than conversation. After this year’s Cheltenham festival, for instance, when the deaths of four horses at the meeting – from 475 runners – prompted the RSPCA to issue a statement that suggested “these incidents are clearly at odds with the UK’s status as a nation of animal lovers”.

Racing launched its latest five-year welfare plan at the House of Commons earlier this month, focusing on safety, quality of life and lifetime responsibility for all Britain’s racehorses. It should be required reading for anyone with the sport’s future prosperity at heart, as it sets out in detail what racing has done, and will continue to do, to maintain the highest possible welfare standards.

The day when the RSPCA calls for a ban on horse racing still feels some distance away. Greyhound racing’s many struggles, though, of which the loss of Racing Post coverage is only the most recent, are a sharp reminder that there is no room at all for complacency.

Nvidia’s humiliated board should resign out of embarrassment

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:37:10 GMT

Jensen Huang’s return as CEO comes despite fact board hasn’t completed investigation into reports of affair with alleged Chinese spy

Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO

Business live – latest updates

What was it that Nvidia’s board was saying about there being no chance of Jensen Huang coming back?

The position – a mere six days ago – was supposed to be definitive. The exit of the co-founder came after “disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”, said Harvey Jones, who had been rapidly installed as chair of the chipmaker. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” after he “voluntarily resigned”, added Jones.

The contribution of the US treasury secretary was equally forceful. Scott Bessent was already focused on the need for a new-broom external hire to replace Huang amid the scrutiny over Nvidia’s compliance with US export controls. “They need to go outside the company,” he said, calling for “a dramatic shake-up”.

Those statements are now inoperative, in the famous phrase of Ron Ziegler. The board says it has “every confidence in Jensen” and his “candor and ability to lead Nvidia”.

What prompted this humiliating U-turn? At least Jones and his fellow directors didn’t bother to disguise the fact they’d been lent on. There was “input from senior levels of the United States government”, which can only mean somebody above Bessent. Sure enough, Donald Trump said he convinced the board to reinstate Huang, calling him “a great patriot and national treasure” and adding that the US government had no reason to think his return posed a threat to national security.

The most jaw-dropping detail is that Nvidia’s board hasn’t even completed its investigation into reports that Huang was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”, the only formal reference to his alleged affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former boss of a Singapore-based company suspected by US officials of smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

Why even bother continuing the inquiry when we can safely guess that it will conclude that the boss did nothing seriously wrong? As for Huang’s two alleged affairs with Nvidia subordinates – relationships that would usually be a sackable offence at a US company – the board will probably never reference them again.

Huang, with his big tech petition-signing crew shouting their support, has proved too big to fire. At Open AI in 2023 Sam Altman was fired and reinstated four days later. The process has taken only slightly longer at Nvidia.

The clinching factor, one can speculate, was the fall in AI share prices after Huang’s resignation. From Trump’s standpoint, a bursting of the AI valuation bubble represented a danger to the last two years of his presidency, so best to give investors (or most of them) what they wanted and get the “godfather of AI” back at the wheel of the circular financing carousel. After the hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off Nvidia’s valuation in recent days, $1tn was instantly wiped back on.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

The gamble won’t necessarily work for ever, of course. Bessent, before starting his own U-turn on Huang’s position in recent days, was asking the right questions. Congressional scrutiny of Nvidia’s export controls won’t stop just because the company has belatedly formed a committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. One trusts Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, will still be pressed for details of the famous intelligence memo he reportedly circulated in the spring identifying Alice Huang as a Chinese spy. Huang himself can no longer be taken seriously on the subject of export controls.

But it is Nvidia’s board that emerges looking idiotic. The directors have reversed the biggest decision they had to make. They have done so under political pressure, forfeiting any claim to independence. And, even as Huang returned, there was no real signal that his powers will be checked to create a semblance of conventional governance. The patsy directors should resign out of pure embarrassment.

The best Black Friday deals The best Black Friday deals on winter essentials

Few of us may be able to justify the cost of a big-ticket TV this Black Friday, but beauty is one area where we can usually afford a treat or two. Thank you, lipstick effect. It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower.

But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups that cause our typically rational brains to short circuit. Add a high-pressure countdown, and before you know it, you’ve been enticed into buying countless products you didn’t set out to buy. Impulse beauty buys are easy to regret later when you snap back into consciousness – not only because of the money you’ve spent, but also because of the waste they create.

To avoid getting caught up in the frenzy, always write a wishlist before you shop. Consider yourself and the people you’re buying gifts for, and then stick to researching the products you actually need. And if a new product catches your eye but you’re uncertain about it, remember that the Boxing Day sales aren’t far away.

That said, if you’ve landed on this page because you’re hoping to upgrade your beauty routine for less, or because you’re searching for a gift for a loved one, I’ve dug out a selection of genuinely good savings on beauty products we’ve tested and love at the Filter.

We’ve tested our way through hundreds of beauty products, from eye creams to hot brushes and LED masks. Our team of expert beauty journalists have decades of experience between them, so they truly know how to sort the wheat from the chaff. These deals are hand-picked from the most effective products in skincare, makeup and hair care.

Not all Black Friday discounts are what they seem. Some retailers have inflated their prices over the past few weeks, only to drop them to normal under the guise of a Black Friday discount. This happens every year, so to avoid misleading deals, we always check the price history of every discount we recommend.

To do this, we use the free Camelizer browser extension, which unveils the price history of any Amazon listing. I recommend using this any time you shop on Amazon; I’ve been covering Black Friday for half a decade and have found thousands of dud deals using this tool.

The deals below are legitimate savings on products our beauty experts recommend and actually use in their beauty routines. Focker In-Law review – triangle of sadness as Ariana Grande joins Stiller and De Niro in the circle of trust

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:32:54 GMT

Even Grande’s talent can’t save the fourth outing of this 90s-style grossout cringe comedy from a depressing sense of overfamiliarity

So to the fourth film in the most consistently moderate but undeniably lucrative comedy franchise in modern Hollywood history, often featuring heavyweight actors (Dustin Hoffman, Barbra Streisand, Harvey Keitel) who don’t appear to be completely sure about what they’re supposed to be doing.

Even now, even after all this time, I’m still not convinced that the great Robert De Niro is 100% on top of it. He sometimes gives the impression – the same impression he’s given in the previous three movies – that he’s thinking about something else.

This started more than a quarter of a century ago, when gags about beta-males employed as nurses and called Gaylord Focker were cooler than they are today and this film is possibly the last surviving example of old-school grossout cringe comedy from the 90s era of There’s Something About Mary.

Ben Stiller was Focker himself, the nervy, prickly guy engaged to Pam (Teri Polo); he had to meet his future father-in-law, former CIA agent Jack Byrnes (De Niro) who put Gaylord through an excruciating process of assessment over a mortifying weekend, in the course of which Focker met Teri’s impossibly charismatic ex, Kevin (Owen Wilson).

Now, in a movie written and directed by John Hamburg, who has script credits on this franchise and Zoolander, we’re a generation further on. This latest iteration features the formidable comedy talent Ariana Grande who does, in fact, show every sign of having mastered the material. But she’s given so little material to work with.

Focker is now the age that Jack was when they first met – and Stiller plays him as a lean, drawn, glassy-eyed figure. He is very close to his son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) and wary and suspicious of meeting Henry’s serious new girlfriend Olivia, played by Grande, with whom he has an embarrassing meet-uncute on a plane.

A family gathering for Jack’s 80th looms: also present will be Gaylord’s daughter Samantha, gamely played by Beanie Feldstein, and her goofy boyfriend Eduardo (Eduardo Franco). Does Focker now get to be the glowering, disapproving patriarch alpha … just as Jack was (and still is)?

Not really. Olivia is a supercool former FBI agent who instantly gains Jack’s respect. For her, membership of the “circle of trust” is a mere formality and poor, maladroit Focker is humiliated by his father-in-law and future daughter-in-law.

The movie rattles along with one or two gags here and there – there’s some funny stuff about Jack’s aggressive new dog, a German shepherd to whom Jack speaks in rasping German. There is a wince-making scene in which Focker sings John Legend’s All of Me in a horribly inappropriate context. But the film always has a weird ingredient of bland to counteract the vinegar of comedy and the Fockers and their eternally recurring crises have become overfamiliar.

You Can See Everything tells us nothing about Elizabeth Holmes. I guess that’s what the courts are for

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:16:40 GMT

The Theranos founder talks in frustrating riddles – but was she lying to us, or to herself? Or could she be a cog in a larger, more sinister, lie-machine?

I went to see You Can See Everything with a friend who had never heard of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos. She knew that she was a convicted fraudster, because as the film opens, Holmes is 34 days from commencing her prison sentence for defrauding investors. But she was completely open-minded as to whether this was definitely fraud or a miscarriage of justice, whether Holmes was the puppeteer or the puppet (of her previous business and romantic partner, Sunny Balwani, who was also convicted of fraud), and whether Holmes’s central claim, of huge diagnostic capabilities from putting a drop of blood into a tiny box, had any scientific foundation. My friend was probably the co-director Nathan Fielder’s perfect viewer, someone who had no preconceptions about what was true: what would she learn, from three hours with a camera so close to the subject’s face that you could count her eyelashes? “Well … She seems nice?” she said after the film had finished.

I veer towards the old-fashioned and deeply held view that the courts, having soberly examined many documents, must have got it right. The whistleblowers and bystanders, giving their testimony not only to lawyers but also to podcasts, which turned into TV documentaries and dramas, as well as investigative print journalism, which begat yet more journalism – that all seemed pretty convincing as well. I definitely did not go into the cinema with my true-crime head on, which is fortunate, because I’m a sucker for a faulty conviction and I’d have probably found her innocent within 15 minutes.

My question was rather: is she a pathological liar, a dark triad personality, a psychopath? Or is she so naive, so peculiar, so childlike, that she believed all her claims as she was making them, and therefore is, never mind the harm she caused, philosophically speaking, innocent? That question is completely unanswerable, and it becomes clear as the film unfolds that Fielder never intended to answer it.

Holmes doesn’t answer direct questions directly. It’s all procedural deflection, shunting you from the issue to the fact that there is an issue. Ask her if she knows a thing, she’ll say she didn’t know whether or not she knew. What is the thing? What is knowledge? Why do people keep asking about the thing? All the while fixing Fielder with her unblinking gaze, supposedly the hallmark of sincerity and veracity – nobody could lie this close to your face. Except people who don’t mind lying. Trying to distinguish between honesty and brazenness is more than difficult; if you stare too long, you feel a little seasick. It’s impossible to say whether that’s disorientation or disgust.

I escaped this discomfort by wondering about side issues: what the hell is going on with her partner Billy Evans’s face? Why did he like Charlie Kirk so much? Why does he keep sniffing? He has said it’s allergies, but I can’t be satisfied until I have some of his blood in a tiny box. If only someone would invent one that worked. The cute paradox of You Can See Everything is that Holmes’s founding fantasy was that you could discover everything from one drop of blood; Fielder, by contrast, summoned three hours of blood, sweat and tears, to discover nothing at all.

This same weekend, I was listening to Jon Ronson read his new book, The Castle, again with this giant imponderable in the middle: a very rich man trying to do something no one had ever done before – create a fairy princess castle, which young women would willingly, nay joyfully, live in, just to dress up as princesses. Was this man an eccentric visionary, or a fantasist? (Charges of sexual assault, in Argentina, were dropped; the Department of Homeland Security has an investigation open – he denies any wrongdoing.) The story, again, resisted clarity or certainty, and again, those things weren’t really the point.

In both cases, it’s all about the fable. In the case of Holmes and Balwani, were they lying to you or to themselves, and if it’s the latter, do they know they’re lying, or are they just cogs in a larger lie-machine? If you want to know which bits are true, it’s safest to assume none of it, and it’s also a little pedestrian of you to ask. Both the book and the film were completely engrossing, and both left me feeling a little bleak, as if they had signalled a mass cultural surrender.

But that, on mature consideration, cannot be true: post-truth doesn’t work for anyone. The grifters often end up in prison, which is about as real as reality gets. I’m taking these instead as epilogues to the era of bullshit, readying for the phase that comes after post-truth – post-gullibility.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Words are not enough after the Myanmar genocide ruling. The world can do better – but it must take these steps

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 17:07:17 GMT

Atrocities happen again and again. We need a comprehensive framework that would allow us to predict, prevent or respond to them

For the first time a state, Myanmar, has been found directly responsible for the crime of genocide. On the instructions of the country’s Tatmadaw regime, at least 10,000 Rohingya men, women and children were murdered, and thousands more were subjected to sexual violence and torture in a 2017 military campaign.

While the international court of justice ruled a decade after the crimes that they amounted to genocide, it is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will ever be brought to justice, whether any of the more than 1 million Rohingya refugees will be able to return home or whether the country’s government will even have to pay reparations for its crimes.

We say “never again” when atrocities such as these are exposed. But “never again” risks becoming not a promise, but a ritual. We say it with sincerity. But sincerity is not a strategy. Sympathy is not prevention. Condemnation is not policy.

In fact, atrocities happen again and again. And just like the crimes against humanity happening in Sudan, which are rarely in the headlines, the likelihood of atrocities being committed against the Rohingyas was known in advance and could have been prevented. And so a new report from the Standing Group on Atrocity Crimes, co-authored by Aarif Abraham and colleagues, poses a question for countries: can we build a system not just to punish atrocities when they happen but to predict and prevent them, and respond to them lawfully, consistently and in time?

There are a staggering 130 active armed conflicts raging across the globe, a level not seen since 1946. In 2024, people in more than half of the world’s countries said they had experienced some form of atrocity in the past year. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s annual Democracy Index says there are now only 26 full democracies in the world, the rising number of autocracies given comfort in the past few days by the US president’s willingness to extend the hand of friendship to Vladimir Putin and to join him in attacking the international criminal court now examining Russia’s atrocities. This is not turbulence at the margins of the international system; it is a warning that the foundations of that system are under sustained assault.

Instance after instance of past atrocities were raised in July’s House of Lords debate on the genocide determination bill, which proposes allowing UK courts to make preliminary determinations of genocide or the serious risk of genocide. Lord Hermer described genocide as the “apex crime”, the crime above all crimes, and yet our ability to prevent a descent into genocide appears limited – even when in the case of Sudan, there were at least two dozen credible reports that the Rapid Support Forces were preparing an assault on the city of El Fasher and that mass atrocities were highly likely.

For too long, most countries have treated atrocities as a moral emergency, a humanitarian concern or an unfortunate consequence of conflict. They are all of those things. But they are also a distinct strategic threat. Atrocities drive armed conflict. They fuel mass displacement. They destabilise regions. They fracture societies. They embolden authoritarianism. They damage trade, security, energy markets and public trust. They do not stay “over there”.

In an interconnected world, the screams of victims have an echo in the politics, streets and conscience of Britain. That is why this is not a call for sentimentality but for statecraft. Countries are under legal obligations in international law to prohibit, prevent and punish atrocity crimes such as genocide. Each has moral responsibilities born of history. But each country also has a national interest in ensuring a world governed by law rather than force.

The world can do so much better. Most countries, including the UK, have as yet no comprehensive framework that would allow us to predict, prevent or respond to atrocities. Important initiatives exist upon which we can build a clearer structure for responding: from early warning preventive work and training for diplomats to sanctions, parliamentary inquiries and civil society-led campaigns. But they are too often piecemeal, reactive and dependent on the commitment of individuals rather than the discipline of institutions. This can change.

First, we need to deploy the power of prediction. Atrocity crimes are not confined to traditional battlefields. Genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes can grow inside states and societies long before any tank crosses a border. As the ICJ has confirmed in the case of Myanmar, they emerge where discrimination is systematised, law hollowed out, minorities dehumanised, impunity rewarded and where powerful states conclude that rules are for others.

Every country concerned about the prevalence of atrocities should adopt clear criteria for measuring their risk, rooted in international law and operational evidence, and apply them consistently across intelligence assessments, development programming, trade policy, arms licensing and ministerial decision-making. If officials can identify the early signs of possible financial crisis, terrorism or military escalation, they can and must also be equipped to identify the early signs of mass killing, persecution and extermination.

Second, prevention is not a slogan; it is a set of choices that have to be made before the cameras arrive. It means supporting local peacebuilders and human rights defenders. It means strengthening accountable institutions. It means using diplomacy early, not only after catastrophe. It means ensuring that trade, security cooperation and arms exports do not assist serious violations of international law. It means treating the risk of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression as matters for national security, not simply crisis management.

Third, we need responses that go beyond mere statements of disapproval and are powerful enough to deter the next set of perpetrators. For instance, the ICJ’s advisory opinions on the withdrawal of aid to Gaza and the discrimination and unlawful expansion of settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem have been taken on board by the UK, but for the most part remain unimplemented elsewhere.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

When atrocities occur, the UK and our allies must act with consistency, legality and courage. That means supporting the collection of evidence and insisting on domestic accountability as well as on the role of international courts. It means sanctions that are targeted and principled. It means diplomatic coalitions that do not collapse when the perpetrator has influence or is commercially useful. It means listening to victims and survivors not as mere symbols, but as holders of truth, memory and legal rights.

Some will say this is unrealistic. But the unrealistic course is the one we are already on which has served the Rohingya people and others so badly: waiting for atrocities to mature, then spending far more in humanitarian relief, military stabilisation, refugee protection, emergency diplomacy and moral repair. Prevention is not only better than cure; it is cheaper, wiser and more humane. If we can speak of a “defence dividend”, we should also speak of a “peace dividend”: the savings, security and stability that come from stopping the worst crimes before they consume whole societies.

There is reason for hope. Not the hope that denies evil. But the hope that comes from knowing atrocities are made by human choices and can therefore be disrupted by human choices. We have access to better early warning tools than ever before. We have investigators, lawyers, diplomats, journalists, analysts, survivors and activists who understand how atrocity risks develop. And we have allies abroad who want principled leadership, and citizens here in the UK who, when told the truth, do not want their country to be passive in the face of mass suffering.

Opening the Nuremberg tribunal, Robert H Jackson, the chief prosecutor, warned that the Nazi crimes before the court were so calculated, so malignant and so devastating that civilisation could not tolerate their being ignored, because it could not survive their being repeated. Yet they have been repeated, as the harrowing stories of Myanmar recount. Not because we lacked grief. Not because we lacked words. But because we too often lacked systems strong enough to turn warning into action.

The Myanmar judgment is a critical reminder that we must give meaning to “never again” by making it not a lament after failure, but a discipline of government before catastrophe. Britain cannot prevent every atrocity. No country can. But the choice is between watching history repeat itself and having the courage to attempt to change it.

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

How freaked out should we be? After mass outages, experts tell us how close we are to ‘doomsday’

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:58:17 GMT

As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night

Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly.

Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure.

For their part, politicians and the spokespeople of affected companies have denied such master plots. And while many presumed that the nationwide airline ground stoppage on 13 November resulted from the Federal Aviation Administration’s rollout of new AI-assisted administration software (called, perhaps aspirationally, the Smart System), the FAA themselves laid the blame on a downed router in Arkansas. Microsoft has chalked the recent outage to Outlook not to malicious intrusions, but some buggy code that has been laying dormant for months. Some people will buy such explanations. Others, naturally, may remain skeptical.

Just how worried should we be? Are these disruptions just a new, extremely annoying part of daily life?

The Guardian spoke to experts across fields to understand how AI and other threats are jeopardizing critical infrastructure, and how exactly we’re mitigating worst-case scenarios.

Bob W Mann Jr, former airline executive and airline industry analyst

Did the FAA’s nationwide ground stoppage in November surprise you at all?

The extent of this outage was surprising. And to be honest, the excuses about what caused it are not credible. The FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure is fully duplicated, fully redundant; every link, every node. There are tens of thousands of nodes and pieces of hardware. The idea that one router in Arkansas could take down an entire network is not credible.

Can you give me a sense of how in need of upgrades the FAA’s systems are?

Well, they’re held together with rubber bands and chewing gum and paperclips. But paperclips are conducting! They’re actually good conductors! But they’re 50-year-old systems. A lot of the basic architecture is old, and analog, and it’s being replaced over time.

There was some speculation that the outage had to do with the FAA rolling out this new AI-system, the Smart System. Do you give any credence to that?

That happens to be my theory on the outage. I work in this area, and we have deployed what you can call “AI” if you want, but I would call computer-based operations research techniques. But it’s designed to reduce airspace congestion and complexity. This Smart System has some AI, which is to say it involves computers talking to pilots. It’s designed to help flight-tracking, and reduce delays and it’s been tested on a carrier-level, with individual airlines. There’s been no issues. What happened, I believe, was that the FAA tried to roll it out simultaneously, for all flights across the nation, which has a bigger risk.

Can you explain what that risk is?

The network gets overwhelmed with these administrative messages, saying, basically, “instead of flying this trajectory, fly an alternate trajectory.” If you have a large number of these messages, it will cause quality problems with radar data, radio data and, to some degree, voice data. When you overwhelm the network with administrative crap, you can cause the quality of radar data to deteriorate. That’s when people working air-traffic control get understandably concerned. And they respond to that by cutting the volume in the system, and just shutting it down.

What are the things you are worried about, as the airlines and FAA try to modernize their infrastructure?

It’s understandable that we want everything to be up to date. Since I’ve been looking at this problem, we’ve spent close to $150bn over four generations of system upgrades. And we basically have the same system. And it doesn’t address the issue of delays. It’s an own goal. They’re not using their institutional knowledge of what is the likely outcome, and not testing it adequately. They tested it on 180 flights over 60 days, in Washington, and then said: “We’re good to go. We’re just going to do all nationwide fights.”

So the worst-case scenario is people implementing things at scale, without adequate testing, and understanding what could happen. You can overwhelm that telecommunications infrastructure. Don’t be concerned about flight safety. Pilots, and their dispatchers, and FAA, they’re professionals. They ensure the system is safe. That’s what gets us to a vanishingly low accident rate.

In your view, what motivation does the FAA have to cover up the cause of the outage?

They don’t have much invested in a single router. But they do have a lot of investment in their new AI system. And I’m not alone in thinking this. A lot of air traffic controllers have been speaking out about it. They don’t buy the router theory either.

William Wetherill, chief information security officer at DefenseStorm, a cyber-attack risk management agency servicing banks, credit unions and financial institutions

A recent report on the state of the banking industry showed that 81% of financial institutions surveyed reported unauthorized access and other cyber-security intrusions in the past year. That seems like a lot.

The amount of attacks that you see is kind of incredible. Banks have always been juicy targets for attacks. And that doesn’t change today. AI has made attacks cheaper. When you’re in this world, and see what’s happening, well, everyone is getting attacked all the time.

What do these hackers want, exactly? To drain out bank accounts?

If they could just steal money, they’d do it. But that money is all insured. And it’s traceable. The FBI can track them down in 24 hours. Sometimes they’ll try moving money: hack a business email and get into the middle of the transaction and change the routing number. But it’s usually more about extortion. They’ll steal data from banks and credit unions, which we call “target rich”. Then they threaten to release it, unless they’re paid however many million dollars. It’s more about the ransom. They’re looking for the institutions to pay crypto, so it’s not traceable. The damage you can do is pretty high. You could shut down a credit union, if they get ransomed too much and consumers lose confidence.

What is the closest a financial institution has come to a total breakdown?

What we just witnessed with multiple banks going down was a major event. For those of us whose money is stored in online bank accounts, and whose livelihoods are stored by credit unions, we don’t have access to our funds, that’s about as critical as you can get. That’s devastating, on a smaller scale.

The biggest thing that can happen is attacking our backbone: infrastructure like Swift payments that are the underlying fabric of financial transactions across the globe. If those come down, that would be our doomsday. But that hasn’t happened, yet.

The majority of cybercrime is financially motivated. [Financial criminals] don’t have the motivation to kill the one thing that’s helping them. You destroy banking, you destroy this technology, and you destroy the entire world.

So how worried should people be about losing all their money?

The first thing to understand, and I’ll say this loud and clear, is that nothing has fundamentally changed. The speed and breadth of attacks has changed. But it’s all things we’ve already dealt with. There’s a lot of paranoia. And people really, really suffer for it. When you have your identity stolen, it’s really exposing, and mental health comes into play. You have to understand that these are blanket attacks, you’re not being targeted, personally. When I deal with individuals, I want them to understand that in this case, you aren’t special. And that should make you feel better. An individual shouldn’t have a mindset where they’re prepping for the end of the world constantly.

Dr Scott J White, director of the cyber-security program and cyber academy at George Washington University, former officer with the Canadian Security Intelligence Service

How much does AI increase the threat of a major cyber-attack?

Anyone with a laptop computer and connectivity can now be an asymmetrical threat against the west. A lot of minor actors, who never had the capability, now AI makes them active players. AI is a threat multiplier. Who are these threat actors?

We have what we call our advanced persistent threats, or APTs. There are four major ones: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. But every time America moves in the world, we’re going to get a proxy. For example, with the American incursion into Venezuela, you’re going to see people who support Venezuela, or Venezuelans, start to attack the United States. As the US continues its conflict with Iran, we have Iranian proxies globally that will be launching attacks against us globally. Now you’re adding a very low-level, low-skilled individual with AI, and we have to start using AI as a defensive structure as well. We’re asking AI to try and find these threat vectors, as they’re coming in. It doesn’t surprise me at all that these attacks are coming in. You have to remember that every new piece of software that comes out, our adversaries are also getting that same piece of software. They’re reverse-engineering it.

In the event that these defenses aren’t sufficient, or aren’t implemented swiftly enough, what’s the worst thing that can happen?

The worst case-scenario, globally, would be incursions into water treatment facilities, hospitals, and so on. Imagine launching a cyber-attack against a country: take its communication, and water treatment facilities, and energy distribution nodes offline. Make the country blind. Then follow with a kinetic attack. How successful would that be? It would be extremely successful. Leave the country blind, and unarmed. Then follow with a traditional attack. That’s a formula for success.

The probability of such a scenario remains relatively low. The Russians are well aware that an attack of this nature could trigger a rapid and significant escalation, potentially extending to the use of nuclear weapons. The consequences would be extraordinarily severe and the risks of triggering a broader global conflict would be difficult for any party to control or predict. That said, a low probability does not mean the scenario can be dismissed or overlooked.

It seems like cyber-security can only play catchup to advanced attacks from AI hackers.

Absolutely we’re playing catchup. That’s exactly the problem. We have something called “security by design”, sometimes called the “zero trust” security approach. This is when you build out a system from the beginning, accounting for threat vectors. But not all systems are built like this. And it’s very difficult to retrofit those kinds of systems. We continue to layer security and try to create a smaller attack surface and limit the attacker, and how they can get to us. That’s the world we are in. Is it a dystopian world? I wouldn’t go that far. But it’s going to require us to do a lot more upgrading on our security. These responses have been condensed and edited for clarity

Barbados town’s three-year deal with Bristol ‘part of the reparative process’

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:53:13 GMT

Island’s labour minister, Tony Dyer, says agreement acknowledges links between Speightstown and UK city are rooted in slave trade

A town in Barbados known as “Little Bristol” has signed a “twinning’” agreement with the UK city, marking a new chapter in a centuries-long relationship rooted in the transatlantic slave trade.

Barbados says the new partnership between Speightstown and Bristol is part of its wider push for reparatory justice, built in small steps rather than around a multi-trillion-pound claim.

Colin Jordan, the island’s labour minister, signed a three-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Bristol city council leader, Tony Dyer, at City Hall on Friday.

Speightstown is the second-largest town in Barbados. In the 17th and 18th centuries its port shipped sugar, produced by enslaved African people, to Bristol. A bar bearing the name is still a popular venue within the island, Jordan said.

In an interview after the ceremony, Jordan said the agreement sat firmly within the island nation’s wider push for reparations, led by the prime minister, Mia Mottley.

“I see the MOU as part of the reparative process,” he said. “It is doing it in a complementary way because it is focused on the relationships between two towns, two cities, two peoples.”

He was careful with his language. “People get emotive about reparations,” said the politician, who is also MP for St Peter, the parish where Speightstown sits. “The word reparations comes from the word repair.”

Defensiveness, he continued, had threatened progress around the conversation. “The walls go up, and then it’s difficult for the message to get through.”

The agreement has no money attached to it and Bristol city council confirmed there was no dedicated funding for major projects involved.

However, it does set out a framework for cooperation on heritage, education, tourism, culture and the creative economy. The exact terms are to be determined through a series of discussions.

Jordan said the money question was settled. “There is not going to be some grand $4tn something somewhere,” he said. “It’s going to be building block by building block.”

He offered a Barbadian proverb to make the point that steady progress was better than extravagant windfalls: “A sheep head a day is better than a cow head a year.”

The MOU recognises that the relationship began in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. “Acknowledging that, we believe, is probably half of the repair,” he said.

He described a relationship that ran one way for roughly two centuries. “Bristol and the UK benefited from the extraction of wealth from Barbados and Speightstown,” he said. The aim now was one that was “mutually beneficial, inclusive”.

Jordan expected exchanges between schools and universities, and between cricket and football bodies – and also pointed to trade.

Repair, he argued, was not only financial. “Value is not just currency,” he said. He gave the example of a Speightstown schoolchild whose parents might be unable to afford a school bag, who could be helped through a link with a Bristol school. He also suggested the relationship could offer “psychological repair” to Bristolians uneasy about their ancestors’ part in slavery.

The MOU runs to November 2029. Jordan has said it “will not become a ‘shelf’ document” but will serve as “a roadmap, as well as our motivation”. He was already looking to 2030, the 400th anniversary of Speightstown’s founding, for a successor agreement.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

Dyer said the deal was “firmly about the future” but should be honest about the past. At the ceremony, he said much of the work lay ahead and warned against signing the agreement and “putting it in the cupboard”.

“Bristol and Speightstown have a long and complex shared history, and signing this agreement is an important opportunity both to recognise that past and to decide together how we can build on our relationship.

“Our connections were shaped by the transatlantic trafficking and enslavement of African people and the sugar trade. It is important that we are open and honest about that history, while working with communities in Bristol and Barbados to deepen our understanding of it.”

Bristol is pursuing the same model elsewhere. A parallel MOU with Odesa, in Ukraine, covers the same period.

Edmund Hinkson, Barbados’s high commissioner to the UK, who witnessed the signing, placed the deal within a longer history. Barbados’s 1650 slave code, he noted, defined Black people as chattel, and was later copied across the Caribbean and the Americas.

Hinkson said Barbados was not looking for the trillions of pounds that economists, including the Brattle Group, have estimated is owed for two centuries of unpaid labour.

“We know that the UK is not going to pay that,” he said, although he noted that British taxpayers, including Caribbean ones, serviced the debt used to compensate 46,000 enslavers in 1834, until 2015.

The high commissioner commended Bristol’s “maturity” in recognising the historical link between Barbados and the city’s role in the transatlantic trafficking of Africans into the Caribbean, including Barbados.

He said he believed that the Black Lives Matter’ protests in 2020, which included the toppling of the statue of enslaver Edward Colston, had propelled that recognition and education of Bristolians.

When asked to expand on the point afterwards, Hinkson said the Black Lives Matter movement did not drive Barbados’s reparations stance, but reiterated his belief that it had shaped the UK response. He pointed to the recent Commonwealth summit in Antigua where, he said, a British prime minister recognised the need for “structured and respectful dialogue” over a formal apology for Britain’s role in enslavement.

Speightstown also has a twinning-style MOU with Reading, formally signed in 2003, and Charleston, South Carolina, part of the Gullah Geechee corridor, in the US.

The signing with Bristol comes days before Barbados marks 60 years of independence on 30 November, and five years as a republic.

Will the Jilly Cooper plagiarism allegations taint our love of Rivals? I doubt it

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:34:29 GMT

The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one

“Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own.

Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”.

Beyond the issue of plagiarism itself, the controversy raises a bigger question: when does creative borrowing become outright theft? And should it change how we feel about the work of writers and artists we love?

It isn’t the first time Cooper’s work has faced such accusations. More than 40 years ago, similarities were identified between her novels Emily and Bella and Elaine Dundy’s The Dud Avocado. Cooper said she was mortified, and that her notes had somehow become confused with her own thoughts.

While there is an obvious difference between borrowing and simply copying, I think her explanation speaks to the sometimes blurry line between influence and appropriation. After all, the history of culture is, in many ways, a history of artists borrowing from one another.

Shakespeare borrowed plots; filmmakers revisit familiar ideas; musicians sample and rework earlier songs. Hitchcock’s Rear Window, for instance, established a template for the voyeuristic thriller that has been deployed countless times. When AJ Finn’s The Woman in the Window appeared in 2018, readers noticed striking similarities with Sarah A Denzil’s earlier novel Saving April. Both featured an isolated woman watching a family across the street, convinced something terrible was happening. Yet both could also be understood as descendants of Hitchcock’s film.

When Leon Arden sued the makers of Groundhog Day, claiming the film had stolen the idea of a man trapped in an endlessly repeated day from his novel One Fine Day, a judge dismissed the case, describing the film as “substantially different from [Arden’s] expression of his idea”. More recently, Ed Sheeran successfully defended himself against claims that Thinking Out Loud had copied Marvin Gaye’s Let’s Get It On.

This month, after accusations that Olivia Rodrigo’s new Christmas single appeared to borrow from his 2012 hit Candy, Robbie Williams published a lengthy response saying he “couldn’t care less” and “we all stand on the shoulders of people who came before us”.

But one thing that stands out in the Cooper controversy is the power imbalance at play. When John Lennon borrowed the opening line of Chuck Berry’s You Can’t Catch Me, he was quoting an already successful rock star. But while Cooper sold more than 11m books in the UK alone and was awarded a damehood in 2024, McFadden struggled financially in her early career while raising her daughter and working to establish herself as a writer. Was Cooper able to get away with using near-identical dialogue because the writers she was seemingly lifting from were far less well known?

The fact that Cooper wrote popular commercial fiction surely played a role, too. She produced more than 40 books, and the bonkbuster was never going to be afforded the same critical scrutiny as literary fiction. We read her novels for their sex, glamour, outrageous characters and aspirational escapism, not their originality of prose.

Nor would she be the first prolific novelist to face plagiarism accusations. Barbara Cartland was accused by Georgette Heyer of lifting characters and plot details. Even Charles Dickens faced claims of stealing a ghost-story plot. There is something almost fitting about the idea that a writer who churned out so much popular fiction might have magpied a few words along the way. It’s hard to imagine Cooper’s light literary fingers would have evaded detection for so long had she been more critically revered.

Sign up to Opinion UK

See things from another point of view with our daily selection of opinion pieces. You might even change your mind

after newsletter promotion

Will many be worrying about Cooper’s corner-cutting as they root for Danny Dyer’s Freddie Jones to get his happy ending with Lizzie Vereker in the TV adaptation of Rivals? I doubt it. And 35 near-identical passages, however striking, should be seen in the context of an entire novel. But the industry has a duty to ensure less successful writers don’t lose out if bigger names profit from their work. Popular fiction may be written to entertain, but that doesn’t mean anything goes.

There is some irony in allegations of literary cut-and-paste coming to light as the creative industries struggle with the AI avalanche – and whether machines should be allowed to learn from, and reproduce, writers’ work. These days, generative AI can easily synthesise a multitude of authors’ material without crossing a legal line. By contrast, Cooper’s alleged direct copying belongs to a distinctly analogue age.

But the underlying question is much the same, whether the borrower is a machine or a human – and the real distinction Eliot was getting at. The best artists can take something that already exists and make it their own. The trick is to steal the inspiration, not the words.

Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian
