Ian Huntley killer felt ‘sick of him’ and that he had nothing to lose, court told

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:34:15 GMT

Jurors hear inmate Anthony Russell bludgeoned Soham murderer with metal bar after being bullied by him

A prisoner thought he had nothing to lose when he killed the Soham murderer, Ian Huntley, by repeatedly striking him over the head with a 4kg iron bar, a court has heard.

Anthony Russell, 44, who is serving a whole-life term at HMP Frankland in Durham, told prison staff Huntley had been bullying him and that he had had enough.

He denied murder at a trial that opened at Newcastle crown court on Monday. The court will hear that he claims the crime was committed as a result of diminished responsibility.

Jurors heard that Russell said he had killed Huntley because he was sick of him “getting in my face”. He told the prison governor: “I ain’t putting up with it any more, I’m not getting out and I’m a natural lifer, so I thought ‘fuck it’.”

The prosecutor, Matthew Bean KC, told jurors that Huntley’s name “will be known to many, if not all of you. He had been convicted of the murder of two girls, Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman, that took place in the village of Soham in Cambridgeshire in August 2002.”

He said Huntley’s crimes aroused feelings of disgust and anger, and jurors might not have sympathy for what happened to him.

“More than that, the prosecution do not ask for sympathy,” Bean said. “Ultimately, this case is not about the appalling actions of Ian Huntley during his life, but the manner of his death.”

He said it was the crown’s case that Russell was responsible for a “cold-blooded murder that had been planned weeks in advance of its execution”.

The court heard that he was in jail for the murder of three people in 2020. He and Huntley were serving their sentences on Frankland’s A wing.

On 26 February, the two men were working in the prison’s recycling workshop, a large room which had a conveyor belt in its centre where the prisoners would sort waste.

Bean said they had made threats against each other over a number of months. In January, Russell had a black eye he said had been the result of falling over. The jury would hear that Huntley may have caused the black eye, Bean said.

On the day of the incident, there were no raised voices or any suggestion of tension, he said. There was then a commotion “caused by the defendant, Anthony Russell, repeatedly striking Ian Huntley to the head with a long orange metal bar”.

The jury heard that there were four orange metal bars kept in the workshop, each weighing 4kg and 1.2 metres (4ft) in length, that were used as stillage posts for stacking items on pallets.

One witness would give evidence that he had seen Russell hit Huntley on the head six times, describing the blows as brutal, Bean said.

Russell later told a prison officer that Huntley had been “pushing my buttons for months” and was “winding us up”.

Huntley was bleeding heavily and unconscious when he was taken to the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle where treatment included removing a section of his skull to reduce pressure on his brain.

He did not regain consciousness and medical staff concluded he could not survive the serious brain injury he had suffered, the court heard. After a week a decision was taken to withdraw treatment and he died on 7 March.

Bean said jurors would see footage of Russell telling the prison governor: “I’m sick of Ian Huntley ... He put it on me. I’ve been in this jail nearly five years … He put it on me about six months ago but I walked away, but …

“When he sees weakness in people he tries to bully them and he’s been getting in my face the last few weeks and my head just thought ‘fuck it’ … I ain’t putting up with it any more. I’m not getting out and I’m a natural lifer, so I thought ‘fuck it’.

Bean said the “natural lifer” phrase was because Russell “would never be able to seek parole and would never be released from prison”.

The court heard that when Russell was asked what his intention had been in the workshop that morning, he replied: “To kill him … that’s why I caved his head in about six, seven times with a metal bar.”

In a police interview Russell described an incident in March in which Huntley had threatened him, he said, and “got in my face”.

“Since that time I walked away from him, cos I wasn’t going to lose it all for him, he’s been getting really arrogant, cocky, in my face, winding me up. Just little smiles as if to say ‘yeah’ sort of thing, and I’d had enough of it.

“I thought ‘fuck you, you’re getting away with it’, ‘I’ve got nothing to lose, I’m never getting out’.”

Bean said Russell did not deny causing Huntley’s death with an iron bar but “in this trial, the defendant maintains that he is not guilty of the murder charge on the basis of diminished responsibility”.

The trial continues.

‘The brains of a pea and the mouth of diarrhoea!’ It’s the wildest I’m a Celebrity spats

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:29:02 GMT

Mariella Frostrup is facing a backlash after blowing up in the camp. It’s not the first time a stranded star’s tongue has caused a row – and some of them have been truly pathetic

The unique selling point of I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! is that it is currently the only show on television where you get to watch animal abuse and reputation-destroying arguments at the same time. The former is an ongoing affair, with petitions and boycotts rumbling on as always. But the latter has just exploded, thanks to Mariella Frostrup and all her microaggressions.

If you haven’t been watching, and in this day and age why would you, here’s a brief precis. Last Thursday, latecomer AJ Odudu offered to help Frostrup cook a meal, which Frostrup took as unwelcome criticism of her skills. But when they cooked together the following night, things went badly, Frostrup snapped and Odudu cried. But last night, during an attempt to clear the air, Frostrup said she had actually been glad to have had help. Odudu’s’s reply was essentially that she had a funny way of showing it, to which Frostrup replied: “You see, that’s just aggressive and that’s what keeps happening.” Odudu’s response was to sigh: “Please don’t use those words towards me.” Nevertheless, the altercation was enough for Frostrup to be called to the Bush Telegraph so producers could “discuss why what was said might make someone uncomfortable, how to address it, and how to move forward.”

The spat has caused something of a backlash against Frostrup. Fellow campmate Leomie Anderson has said that, “Black women are always painted to be aggressive when we’re just expressing ourselves,” while Judi Love posted on social media: “For most of us black women who have been through this in all scenarios, workplace, the shop, schools, wherever, we know what AJ’s feeling in that moment.” Good Morning Britain host Narinder Kaur wrote on X that, “Reality TV has never been a safe space for any person of colour,” while Alesha Dixon wrote: “Mariella in the bin.” On the other hand, Nigel Farage has defended Frostrup, so there’s that.

But if you’ve watched I’m a Celebrity for any length of time, you’ll know that flare-ups – when they happen – tend to be slightly more pathetic than this. Here are some of the more notable instances.

Quite honestly, you could make a whole list from this series. The biggest, and easily the most entertaining, blow-up came when Lady Colin Campbell picked a live beetle and threw it on to a campfire. Tony Hadley from Spandau Ballet reacted badly to this, informing Campbell of her cruelty. It is not an exaggeration to say that Campbell took this particularly badly. In the ensuing melee, she called Hadley a “bully”, a “liar”, a “gutless creep”, a “total zilch”, a “greedyguts”, a “dumbo”, a “hypocrite”, a “pretentious arsehole”, “the lowest of the low” and a “chippy oik”, while adding that he had “the brains of a pea and the mouth of diarrhoea”.

Oh fine, let’s have another. This time, despite her best efforts, Lady Colin Campbell ended up being outheckled. The context is that her team had just won a banquet, while the opposing side were left to go hungry. Campbell had previously purchased a can of soup from a jungle vending machine, and proposed that the best way to end the suffering of the other team would be to give them a quarter of her can of soup between them. Duncan Bannatyne objected, saying it might be fairer if they had the whole can. Campbell took this particularly badly, calling Bannatyne a “mouse” and a “little pussy”. But Bannatyne fought back, calling Campbell a “nasty woman” and “the most selfish person I have ever met”.

After winning the camp a reward of strawberries and cream, Iain Lee and Amir Khan decided to eat the whole thing themselves then tell the other campmates there had been no reward. A long and tense stalemate followed before Lee eventually relented. This enraged Dennis Wise, who informed them both that they were banned from eating any other future treats. It is also worth pointing out that Amir Khan was dressed as a cat when he apologised.

The wildest blow-up to ever happen during I’m a Celebrity happened relatively early on in its run. John Fashanu had won a reward for the camp. However, due to either a mix-up or a genuinely dark social experiment, this reward came in the form of one sausage each. At this point, Antony Worrall Thompson became so outraged that he effectively unionised the entire camp, urging them to tear off their microphones in protest. The campmates bundled into the Bush Telegraph and watched in awe as Worrall Thompson exclaimed: “What if we all walk out tomorrow? You’re fucking screwed”, citing the show’s own title as a precedent for their simultaneous departure. According to contemporaneous reports, producers backed down and gave him what he wanted, which was presumably two sausages.

Teenage boy stabbed 14-year-old girl 55 times in park in south Wales, jury told

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:19:06 GMT

Defendant and Lilly Jones had been messaging for months and arranged to meet on evening she was killed, court hears

A teenage boy stabbed a 14-year-old girl 55 times after the pair met up in a park near her home, a jury has heard.

The body of Lilly Jones was found two days later in a wooded area about 500 metres from her home in south Wales, the court was told.

Lilly and the boy, also 14, had been messaging each other for several months having developed “some kind of relationship” and arranged to meet on the evening she was killed, the court heard.

Lilly learned the boy was also “in a relationship” with another girl and the two teenage girls had planned to confront him, the jury heard.

Anna Pope KC, prosecuting, said: “This case is about the tragic death of Lilly Jones who in June this year had just turned 14. At around 6.30pm on Saturday 20 June she went out, telling her dad she was popping out for a bit. She never came home.”

The police were contacted and a missing person investigation began. Lilly was found dead two days after meeting up with the boy, the jury heard, with stab wounds on her neck, back and chest.

“The missing person inquiry turned into a murder inquiry,” Pope said.

The boy and Lilly were seen on CCTV together at about 6.50pm on the evening she went missing, Newport crown court heard.

Pope said: “Police quickly identified that the last person to see Lilly alive was the boy.”

When he was first approached by police, the defendant told them he had been due to meet up with Lilly but she did not turn up. After being shown the CCTV footage, he said he had been with her for 15 minutes before he left her, the court heard.

Pope said: “We say Lilly did not meet up with anyone else that night. We say that the boy was the last person to see her alive. We say that he was the person who murdered Lilly and then left her in the woods, either dying or already dead.”

The court heard the boy and Lilly began to “take an interest” in each other in March when Lilly was 13.

Pope said Lilly later learned the boy was also “in some sort of relationship” with another girl. Jurors were told Lilly and the other girl formed a friendship and had planned to confront the boy.

The court was told the boy’s DNA was found under Lilly’s nails, from where she had scratched him. A camping knife was recovered from the boy’s bedroom that could be scientifically linked to Lilly, jurors heard. Her phone was never discovered.

Forensic examination of the knife also found matches to Lily’s DNA, and small areas of blood staining were identified once the blade was taken apart, the jury was told.

Pope said: “The prosecution says that this was the weapon which [the defendant] used to kill her and that whilst he had made some attempts to clean the knife, we say he was not able to remove traces of her DNA which had ended up down inside the handle of the knife.”

The trial heard that examination of a phone belonging to the defendant showed he had searched for Gwent police and similar terms about 30 times the morning after Lilly disappeared.

Pope said Lilly, from the town of Blaina, enjoyed cosplay, Pokémon and was in regular contact with her friends in school. The prosecutor said Lilly had been shopping with her father for Pokémon cards on the day she was attacked.

In opening remarks to the jury, Mrs Justice Stacey said: “The boy says it was not him who did it but it was someone else she met after he left her in the park. The death of a teenage girl, especially in these circumstances, is very distressing, and the fact a 14-year-old boy has been accused of her murder is also very distressing.”

The defendant, who cannot be named, denies murder. The trial continues.

Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:00:51 GMT

Exclusive: Figures from cache of 11m death certificates reveal suicides account for about a regiment of Russia’s war dead

Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict

In late October 2024, Alexei Bolgov, a sergeant guarding a military headquarters in the occupied Donetsk region, told his wife, Natalya, over the phone: “It’s horrific, what’s going on here. I’ll tell you when I get back.”

He never made it home. Five weeks later, shortly after turning 29, Bolgov walked about 300 metres from his unit’s command post near the village of Stepove into woodland and shot himself, according to a written account by his commander seen by the Guardian.

“On the day of his death, Bolgov was in a withdrawn state,” his commander wrote.

Bolgov is one of more than 1,000 Russian soldiers recorded as having died by suicide since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to confidential data from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, analysed by the Guardian.

The deaths of a further 885 soldiers in or near Ukraine were recorded as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”, a classification that experts say can conceal suicides and that was used in several cases independently identified by the Guardian as suicides.

Taken together, the suicides amount to approximately a Russian regiment of dead.

The data, which analysts say almost certainly underestimates the true number of suicides, offers a rare, previously unreported glimpse of the strain on Russia’s armed forces nearly five years into a war in which heavy losses and harsh discipline have sapped morale.

Suicides among soldiers are a feature of most wars. A New York Times investigation found that at least 158 active-duty US army soldiers died by suicide in 2023.

But in Russia’s army, military analysts say, the problem is compounded by intense pressure from fellow soldiers and commanders, as well as fear of being sent on extremely dangerous combat missions. Contracts that in effect leave soldiers with no way out of the war add to the sense of desperation.

“There’s clearly a lot of coercion used by the Russian military to force people to go forward. In some cases, they will abuse them, torture them, use different types of physical abuse,” said Rob Lee, a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute. “So it’s not surprising that some guys commit suicide,” he added.

The figures come from a cache of more than 11m death certificates obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacking group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow.

The Kremlin does not publish data on suicides in the military and treats casualty figures as a state secret.

Of the 1,087 suicides by military personnel identified by the Guardian, at least 614 took place in occupied areas of Ukraine or Russian regions bordering it, mainly Belgorod and Bryansk. A further 113 records did not specify a location of death.

More than half of suicides involved firearms – particularly those near the frontlines. The deaths occurred at military camps, combat positions, training grounds and private homes.

Of those suicides that took place in the war zone, 43 were young soldiers aged 18 or 19.

The figures also include 108 men under 25 who died by suicide elsewhere in Russia away from the front. Some are likely to have been conscripts, who are not formally sent to fight in Ukraine but have often been pressed to sign contracts that allow them to be deployed.

Recorded military suicides have risen as the war has gone on, from more than 50 in 2022 to more than 200 in 2024, peaking at 365 in 2025 – mirroring Russia’s overall death toll. In 2026 – despite records being incomplete and lagging behind the battlefield reality – the database already records almost 300 suicides, the second highest total for any year of the war so far.

Activists and lawyers who work with Russian deserters believe the real number is higher.

“I would say it is a low estimate,” said Ivan Chuvilyaev, a spokesperson for Idite Lesom, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert. “Obviously, it is a lot more.”

He described the frontline as “a tin can” from which little information escapes. “Any Rosstat statistic, like any statistic relating to the war, is just reports passed up the chain.

“A man can kill himself, and on paper he is a hero. His parents might even be sent some medal,” Chuvilyaev said.

Officials, he added, had little interest in an accurate count, as the figures would be scrutinised further up the chain of command.

after newsletter promotion

Chuvilyaev and Lee also suggested that most cases in which Russian soldiers took their own lives on the battlefield, often after being wounded or as a Ukrainian drone approached, would probably be recorded as combat deaths rather than suicides. Such incidents have been documented in numerous grim videos from the front.

The gaps are visible in the Rosstat data.

Sergei Savenok, a 62-year-old lieutenant colonel from the Irkutsk region, volunteered in September 2022. Before leaving for the front, he is seen in a video clip taking to the stage of his local community centre to address the men heading off with him. “I’m from Donbas myself. Let’s fucking smash them, lads! That’s all!” he shouted, to applause.

He was found shot dead in occupied Luhansk region in July 2023. His wife, Yelena was informed by officials that his death was suicide, but he does not appear among the suicides in the Rosstat records.

A certificate matching his date of birth instead records a death from injury resulting from the discharge of a handheld firearm, with undetermined intent.

The Guardian was able to identify 1,038 military related deaths with similar causes – 885 of which took place in Ukraine or a bordering region of Russia.

Nor does Alexander Lazor, a 21-year-old private who died near the village of Solodke in Donetsk region in the summer of 2022, appear among the suicides in the records.

His family was told he was killed in combat, and in Rosstat data he is listed to have succumbed to “injuries due to warfare caused by firearms”.

But two soldiers who served alongside Lazor told the Guardian that members of their unit had been informed he had taken his own life.

“Our whole unit was told he killed himself. Perhaps, they decided to cover it up so that our unit doesn’t look bad,” said one of the soldiers, who spoke on condition of anonymity, speculating about why his comrade’s death had not been officially recorded as a suicide.

The suicides are just one sign of an army under strain.

By the end of May 2025, Russian military courts had received cases against 20,662 men for refusing to serve, most for going absent without leave, according to the independent outlet Mediazona. IStories verified this data and found at least 49,000 servicemen of the Russian armed forces had been declared deserters or Awol.

Thoughts of suicide were common among the soldiers Idite Lesom helped to desert, Chuvilyaev said.

“Of course they appear,” he said. “It’s the next stop, after a man realises where he has ended up.”

In the UK, Combat Stress is a charity offering mental health support for military veterans. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline. org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders. org

Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:00:50 GMT

Exclusive: Analysis gives most detailed picture yet of the nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022

Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war

Alexander Korepanov signed up to fight in August 2023. He was wounded twice and twice sent back to the front. On 11 May 2025, after 20 months at war, he was killed in the village of Uspenovka, near the eastern Ukrainian city of Pokrovsk, aged 52.

More than 5,000 died with him that week.

The Russian army was losing a staggering 720 men every 24 hours, the highest rate of the war, and at least a third of them were killed around Pokrovsk, where Moscow had thrown tens of thousands of troops into its spring offensive.

The figure comes from a cache of more than 11m death certificates obtained by the hacking group Cyber Partisans, which is linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow.

Analysed in depth by the Guardian, they give the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Among them, the Guardian identified more than 460,000 deaths linked to the war between the start of the invasion in February 2022 and September 2026. War became the leading cause of death in Russian men under 65 last year.

“There was always sort of an unknown X factor: how many Russian deaths are we missing? And that turned out to be much much more,” said Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, who has closely tracked military deaths.

Militaries typically expect about three wounded for every soldier killed. But Kluge said the data suggested Russia could have more soldiers killed in action than severely wounded.

“This tells you something about this war and the way that it’s fought,” Kluge said.

For all those losses, the frontline has barely moved. Since the start of 2023, Russia has gained about 8,000 sq km, less than 1.5% of Ukraine’s territory, according to data from the Ukrainian monitoring group DeepState.

Stuck on the frontline, Russia has this year turned to destroying Ukraine’s economy and making life in its cities unlivable, in an attempt to force Kyiv into accepting its terms for peace.

Russia’s defence ministry has not updated its official death toll since September 2022, when it said 5,937 servicemen had been killed, and Moscow treats its casualty numbers as a military secret.

The records analysed by the Guardian, compiled by Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, from civil registry offices across the country, show a war that grew steadily more lethal, peaking dramatically in 2025, with little territorial gain for Moscow.

Almost 20,000 deaths were recorded during the first year of the invasion and 50,000 in 2023. In 2024 the toll more than doubled, to more than 134,000 and it rose a further 52% a year later, to close to 200,000, the deadliest year of the war: about 548 men a day, against an average of about 277 since the invasion began.

The scale dwarfs anything suffered by Russia or the Soviet Union since the second world war. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers were killed over the nine years of the Soviet war in Afghanistan, according to official figures; in the worst year, 1984, the toll was about 2,300.

In Ukraine in 2025, Russia was losing that many men roughly every four days.

The comparison with recent western wars is starker still. In the single week that began on 5 May 2025, the Russian army lost more men than the US did in eight years in Iraq, where roughly 4,500 American troops died. About 2,400 US service members perished in two decades in Afghanistan.

The real toll is likely to be higher. The deaths of missing soldiers are often registered months or years later, when bodies are recovered or courts declare men dead, and the records thin out sharply in 2026, even though the fighting has remained exceptionally deadly. Nor does the database capture every death, with some never registered or soldiers missing.

The analysis includes death certificates classified as war-related or where conflict is mentioned as a cause of death – a count which may include some civilians. It also includes all deaths where the employment was marked as military – but excludes any certificates from non-combat age people.

The losses are deepening a demographic crisis the Kremlin has struggled for years to reverse, with consequences likely to be felt for generations.

In 2025, war became the leading cause of death for men under the age of 65. Of the death certificates with recorded cause, 29% mentioned war, followed by 26% of deaths due to circulatory diseases and 12% from external causes, such as accidents, assaults or medical complications. More than half a million Russians have also left the country since the invasion.

“We’ve been predicting demographic doom for Russia for a few decades, and somehow the catastrophe never materialised,” said Judyth Twigg, a professor of global health at Virginia Commonwealth University in the US.

“But the current situation really does look qualitatively different … Today’s losses are a direct consequence of regime policy: combat deaths, political emigration, foregone births, healthcare budgets raided to fund [military] signing bonuses and death payouts.”

The certificates record where most soldiers died, down to the village, from mid-2023 onwards.

The records show how much Russia has paid for every kilometre gained on a handful of narrow fronts, above all in the slow advance through the fortified mining towns north-west of Donetsk.

Almost 116,000 of the deaths – over a quarter of the total with a known recorded location – occurred in Pokrovsk district, which takes in both Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, scenes of two of the longest and bloodiest battles of the war.

Pokrovsk itself, a coalmining town of 60,000 people before the war, covers less than 30 sq km. More Russian soldiers have died in the district around it than Ukrainians lived in the city itself.

After neighbouring Avdiivka fell in February 2024, Russian troops took 21 months to cover 39km (24 miles) to the edge of Pokrovsk, according to the Institute for the Study of War.

In that time, about 88,700 Russian soldiers were recorded as dying in the district, more than 2,200 for every kilometre gained.

By September 2024, Russia’s gains formed a bulge of fields, slag heaps and mining villages about 30km long and 20km wide.

The rest of the front is traceable through the data too. Recorded deaths in Russia’s Kursk region rose from 12 in July 2024 to close to 1,200 in August, when Ukraine launched its cross-border incursion into the area, and reached more than 2,400 in December as Moscow fought to retake the territory.

The losses are eroding Russia’s ability to mount new offensives, and help explain why its army looks set to fail to carry out Putin’s order to capture the whole of the Donbas region by the end of the year.

“If we compare the death data with Russia’s official recruitment rates, it becomes clear that Russia’s military has a manpower problem,” said Kluge. “The absolutely horrible losses combined with slower recruitment rates apparently forced Russia to slow down its attacks in 2026 already,” he added.

In 2018, Putin spoke of Russians looking forward to a “well-deserved retirement”, when they could devote more time to their families, children and grandchildren. Eight years later, more and more older Russian men are dying on the battlefields of Ukraine.

The average age at death has risen from 34 in 2022 to close to 40 this year.

Almost a fifth of the soldiers killed in 2026 whose age is recorded were over 50, against 6% in the first year of the war. Across the war, men aged 35 to 44 make up a third of the dead.

The shift reflects how Russia has filled its military ranks. Rather than order a second mobilisation – the first, seven months after the start of the full-scale invasion, in September 2022, was deeply unpopular – the Kremlin has relied on cash bonuses to attract volunteers, and the money has often appealed most to older men such as Korepanov.

From the start of the war, the Kremlin has sought to keep the cost out of sight in Moscow and St Petersburg, where discontent poses the greatest political risk.

The losses fall hardest on Russia’s poor, far-flung regions, many of them home to large ethnic minority populations. The eight Russian regions with the most poverty recorded a military death rate four times higher than those with the least, recording more than 10 deaths per 1,000 men aged 18-69, compared with fewer than three per 1,000.

In at least 19 Russian regions, most of them in the far east, more than half of deaths of men under 50 in 2025 were due to the war. The figures are based on place of birth, using records where a cause of death was given.

In the Jewish autonomous oblast, a region in eastern Russia bordering China where about a fifth of the population lived in poverty in 2022, which despite its Soviet-era name is less than 1% Jewish, war was listed as the cause of more than three-quarters of recorded deaths of men under 50 last year.

The highest death rate was recorded in Zabaykalsky Krai, another region bordering China thousands of miles from the front, where about one in six people live below the poverty line. Since the beginning of the war, 32 men aged 18 to 69 born in the region have died per 1,000 population, compared with one per 1,000 in St Petersburg and Moscow, where less than 5% live in poverty.

As losses have mounted, Moscow has cast its net even wider. Alongside the cash bonuses offered at home, Russia has recruited heavily among central Asian migrant workers inside the country and, through networks of murky middlemen abroad, from as far afield as Nepal, India, Cuba and Kenya.

Many recruits were lured by promises of high pay, Russian citizenship or civilian jobs, only to find themselves at the front.

The Guardian identified more than 7,300 probable foreign soldiers among the dead, not counting Ukrainians. That includes 2,700 who were born abroad but have no recorded citizenship.

Many come from the large central Asian migrant workforce Russia has courted with fast-track citizenship in exchange for service, with more than three-quarters coming from former Soviet republics, mainly from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Belarus.

But the analysis identified foreign fighters from 78 other countries beyond the former USSR, including 440 whose citizenship was from an African country – such as Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt, and about 200 from South America, most of them from Colombia and Cuba.

The records miss what is likely to be the deadliest foreign contingent of all. North Korea sent more than 10,000 troops to help Russia drive Ukrainian forces out of the Kursk region in late 2024 and 2025. South Korea’s national intelligence service estimates about 2,000 of them have been killed, and about 6,000 killed or wounded in total.

The foreign soldiers arrived late. Of those whose date of death is recorded, three-quarters were killed in 2025 or later. Every Colombian death with a recorded date falls within that period, as recruiters turned to Latin America to make up for losses at home.

What the scale of the losses will mean for Russians’ attitudes to the war in the long run remains unclear.

In interviews, many relatives of the dead said their grief had only hardened their support for the war. Several insisted that Russia must fight on, so that the sacrifice would not have been in vain.

State propaganda has cast the fallen as heroes, holding up their deaths as a reason for Russians to stand united behind Putin and the army.

The few who once spoke out against the war have mostly been jailed or forced to leave the country. The last group publicly protesting against the war, Put Domoi (Way Home), a movement of wives and mothers of mobilised men, was criminalised in 2024.

One woman who was once among its most outspoken members said she now feared for her life.

“I don’t have emotions any more; I am numb at this point. Just a question,” she asked rhetorically. “Is it worth it?”

The husband is not being named in order to protect the identity of his victim, who is entitled to lifelong anonymity. He has pleaded guilty to more than 60 offences committed against his wife over a period of more than 20 years.

Separately, during an ongoing trial at Minshull Street crown court, Robert Stewart, 70, pleaded guilty on Monday to two counts of rape, and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent. He denies a fourth charge of conspiracy to rape.

Several men have also pleaded guilty to offences against the same woman. Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, a former technician at the city’s university, admitted a number of offences, while Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport, pleaded guilty to assault by penetration, and Graham Brougham, 74, from Cheshire, pleaded guilty to rape.

Karl Lindsay, 56, from Somerset, a former chief executive of the non-league football club Taunton Town, also pleaded guilty to “non-contact” offences against the same woman; conspiracy to rape and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

Lindsay has also admitted three offences of making indecent images of children between February 2024 and November 2025, which came to light after his arrest, and which he was prosecuted for separately.

Nine men, including Stewart, are on trial at Minshull Street crown court accused of being involved in the abuse of the woman, who was drugged, raped and sexually assaulted by her husband while he “lived a double life masked in respectability”.

Two of the men, Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable in Kent and David Graves, 59, from Ilkeston in Derbyshire, are on trial for “non-contact offences”, in which they are alleged to have encouraged the abuse online.

The other seven are alleged to have visited the couple’s home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, and participated in the abuse of the victim.

Mauricio Pochettino can now see just how desperate Manchester United are

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:45:50 GMT

The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided

Sign up for our free newsletter here

In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter.

Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0. Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023. Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered.

And when you’ve conceded more goals in all competitions this season than anybody else in Europe’s top five leagues, and when you’ve let in more in the league than anybody other than Crystal Palace, it’s pretty obvious that the defence is a major problem. There are serious reasons for concern; a switch of manager alone will not magically save United.

Perhaps Yoro was unfortunate to be sent off. Senne Lammens may have got to the ball ahead of Alexander Isak. But the opposite is also true. Had Yoro not been sent off, it would only have been because Isak’s first touch was heavy. By far the bigger issue as Pochettino prepares for Wednesday’s Champions League game at Sporting and Saturday’s Premier League match at home to Brentford is how easily United were undone by a simple ball over the top. First Matthijs de Ligt, who was much deeper than the rest of the defensive line, inexcusably left it, and then Yoro, in scrambling back, made an appallingly clumsy foul.

De Ligt, who has only been back in training for six weeks as he recovers from a back injury, had not started a league game since November last year. He looked way off the pace, as he had in the defeat to Como, and his selection, in retrospect, was an error by Pochettino. Yoro, who had looked one of United’s better recent signings in his first year after signing from Lille, had become a case study in the damage being part of a dysfunctional team can do to a player: his confidence is shot and he now lurches around like a sad horse, a player who seems always to be at the centre of unfortunate events – such as that header against his own bar against Aston Villa.

There are manifold problems at United, from the leadership to the recruitment to the stadium, but if there is to be an improvement in form, the first thing Pochettino needs to do is to change the mood. This is nothing like a great squad. It is a mess of ideas and strategies, put together over six different managers with no consistent goal in sight. But it is not a squad made up of terrible players. It is a squad made up of players who have lost their way, who had been dragged down into the morass. It’s obvious that United should be better than this, but even this United should be better than this.

United have won only one of 11 games in the league this season, and that was against newly-promoted Ipswich in August. To put that in context, Burnley are the only other side of all 92 in the league not to have won at least twice; when United were relegated in 1973-74, they won three of their first 11 games. Bruno Fernandes has now played in four defeats to Liverpool by four goals or more, a record.

It remains, still, almost inconceivable that United will be relegated, or even that they will find themselves in a proper battle. It’s almost a category error; this cannot happen. But there are no terrible sides in the Premier League this season. Perhaps Manchester City’s appeal will fail and their punishment means they will obligingly occupy one of the relegation slots. But the three promoted sides are all showing signs of fight. Crystal Palace will probably improve under Thomas Frank, Sunderland have started keeping clean sheets and are a very different side if Brian Brobbey is fit, Nottingham Forest are far better than their league positions suggests and Fulham are five league games unbeaten.

The opening night of the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend on Friday is poised to be played in front of around 40,000 empty seats, with the top tier of the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham to be closed.

The Guardian has learned that more than 50% of tickets at the 82,000-capacity venue for the Ireland v Australia/Italy v Fiji double-header remained available on Monday. That figure could grow after tournament organisers opened a ticket swap exchange for fans wanting to watch their team.

Ticket sales for Saturday and Sunday are stronger, at 70% of capacity, with Nations Championship officials hoping to sell out Saturday’s England v New Zealand/Wales v Japan double-header and Sunday, when France and South Africa will contest the final after Scotland play Argentina.

Supporters had to wait for the final round of group games to be completed on Saturday to learn which of the six fixture slots each country would play in.

Selling out three successive rugby events was always likely to be challenging, particularly the Friday, with Fiji v Italy kicking off the opening match at 4.40pm GMT.

Tickets have been competitively priced, starting at £60 (£20 for juniors) for Friday, rising to £100 on Saturday (£50 for juniors) and £125 for Sunday (£50 for juniors).

Despite the difficulties of selling tickets at the last minute the Nations Championship is committed to the finals weekend concept, although Qatar have pulled out of hosting in 2028 due to the Middle East conflict, as the Guardian revealed earlier this month.

TV viewing figures have been far more positive, with ITV averaging audiences of 3m across all fixtures and Wales’ shock win over New Zealand gaining more than 4m.

Inside Fifa and US Soccer’s plan for 2031 World Cup: ‘the largest women’s sporting event in history’

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:16:29 GMT

The US-led four-country bid was confirmed in Zurich on Monday, projecting record-setting total revenues of $4bn

The biggest and most lucrative event in the history of women’s sport was confirmed at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress in Zurich on Monday, with a joint bid from the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031’s Women’s World Cup formally ratified by a vote of Fifa’s 211 member associations.

In the bid book submitted to Fifa last year the prospective hosts pledged to generate total revenues of $4bn if awarded hosting rights, which would represent a staggering increase on the $570m earnings from the last World Cup held in Australia and New Zealand three years ago, the first women’s tournament to break even.

“We have the stadiums, the infrastructure and the expertise to set a new standard for the Women’s Word Cup. Commercially, it will be the most successful Women’s World Cup ever,” US Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone said Monday. “That’s the scale of our ambition and we have a plan to deliver it.”

While Fifa is forecasting an almost doubling of tournament revenues to $1bn for next year’s competition in Brazil, achieving a further fourfold growth by 2031 would appear to be challenging.

The United Kingdom’s bid for the 2035 tournament, which was also ratified Monday, does not include a revenue target. So how do the US and their co-hosts plan to generate $4bn, and what will be the impact on fans?

Fifa has yet to publish its financial accounts relating to last summer’s men’s World Cup, but it was undoubtedly a huge success. Gianni Infantino told the national associations on the eve of the final in New Jersey last July that Fifa’s revenue projection for the 2023-2026 cycle had increased from $11bn to $15bn, the majority of which was the product of the World Cup itself.

Emboldened by that success, the US Soccer Federation is confident $4bn is a realistic target for 2031, a projection largely based on bringing in $1.4bn from commercial deals, $1.25bn in matchday revenue and $1bn in broadcast income.

“It is a very significant increase from 2023, but I expect [the] 2027 [Women’s World Cup] to continue to be a step forward, and in 2031 to really blow this out of the park because of the maturity of our market here and the excitement that we see,” Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy who presented the bid to Fifa in Zurich, told the Guardian.

“The market here in the US is unlike anywhere else. The 2026 World Cup will be well north of $10bn in revenue, and we’re looking at a tournament with the same number of teams involved. We do have a high level of confidence in that revenue number. We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history.”

The most likely driver of growth is the sheer size of the would-be hosts’ plans for the tournament, which will be the first women’s World Cup to feature 48 teams, increasing the number of matches from 64 to 104.

Just as significantly, most games will be played at large NFL stadiums, with the 13 of the provisional shortlist of 20 venues in the official bid – 14 in the US, four in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica – having capacities of more than 60,000.

To further illustrate the scale of the tournament’s ambitions, seven of these US-based stadiums hosted matches at the 2026 World Cup, with three others having staged games at the 2025 Fifa Club World Cup.

While some smaller stadiums will be used in the group stages, the hosts are targeting a total 4.5 million tickets sold, which would bring average crowds of 43,000 per match, enough to generate ticket revenue of $550m, more than 10 times the $43m made from ticket sales of 1.8 million in 2023.

The bid also projects hospitality sales of $300m, plus $400m in other match day income such as merchandising, parking and transport.

The bid actually contains 50 potential stadiums across 35 different cities, and the initial shortlist is largely theoretical at this stage, with the final decision on venues to be taken by Fifa by the end of 2028.

All of the US venues are in operation other than the proposed redevelopment of the Washington Commanders’ RFK Stadium, which is due to be completed in 2030 but is under consideration.

Mercedes-Benz Stadium (Atlanta), AT&T Stadium (Dallas), SoFi Stadium (Los Angeles) and MetLife Stadium (New Jersey) have been identified as the most likely candidates to host the final, although that decision will not be taken until 2030.

“We think every knockout round can be in a 60,000-plus seat stadium,” Cosler said. “We’ve got the infrastructure to do that, and I have a high level of confidence that every knockout round game can be a sellout. The success of our women’s national team and the NWSL has proven that we’ve got the demand for that.”

Fifa’s Evaluation Report published earlier this month is even more bullish than the bid in terms of the potential value of ticket sales, claiming that the widespread use of NFL stadiums should mean that ticketing and hospitality revenues “significantly exceed” the $550m forecast, which is described as “a very conservative position with significant upside potential”.

Given that the bid is forecasting a tenfold increase in revenue from the 2023 tournament based on selling two-and-a-half times more tickets, it is clear that the prices will also increase significantly from that tournament. However, lead bidders US Soccer are determined to make the event more accessible than last summer’s men’s World Cup.

after newsletter promotion

“We propose a pricing table that balances what the women deserve in terms of the revenue generated from this tournament, but also access in a way that will continue to grow the game,” Cosler said. “I think there are some really good initiatives that US Soccer has done with our own national team games. We’ve partnered with local universities. We’ve offered $25 tickets that have resulted in filling stadiums and success. This isn’t a charity, but at the same time, we want this game to be accessible to fandom everywhere.”

In comparison to the men’s World Cup and other premium events in the US the pricing structure proposed in the bid looks affordable, with tickets ranging from $35 to $120 in the group stage, and $120 to $600 for the final.

Fifa will make the final decisions though, and after making almost $5bn from ticket sales last summer may choose to demand more from fans, many of whom will be concerned by one paragraph in the Evaluation Report.

“Based on the performance of other recent tournaments hosted in the region, most notably the Fifa World Cup 2026, gate revenues may far exceed initial projections,” it states.

The 2023 World Cup was the first time Fifa sold sponsorship deals separately from the men’s event, with 30 new partnerships bringing in $110m. This program has been scaled up significantly ahead of Brazil next year.

The projection for 2031 is $1.4bn in commercial revenue due to the size of the US market and the prospect of bespoke deals for individual cities, although that proved a source of tension last summer.

US Soccer and the other host federations are pushing for greater local control this time around, and crucially the prospective host cities have not signed binding contracts just to enter the contest, which should give them greater freedom to negotiate their own commercial deals.

“I think the end state we ultimately arrived at in 2026 resulted in a really successful tournament,” Cosler said. “Fortunately we can start there from a negotiation perspective, rather than where we maybe were six or seven years ago. Contracts were signed eight years beforehand in a way that didn’t reflect the nuances of the business model.”

After banking $270m from the first separate sale of Women’s World Cup rights in 2023, with many of the deals coming in at the last minute, Fifa have sold $424m worth of rights for Brazil with the 2031 bidders projecting to break through the $1bn barrier, which would value the competition’s media rights as the same as the men’s 2025 World Cup.

Independent analysis conducted by Nielsen Sports has predicted that global TV viewers will increase by 58% from Brazil due to the expansion to 104 matches, and more favorable time zones for the large North American audience.

The bid book is forecasting an additional $400m in “ancillary gameday revenue”, which will come from merchandising, fan fests, parking and transport charges, many of which were sources of long-running disputes involving the local authorities, venues and Fifa in the build up to this year’s World Cup.

After belatedly reaching agreements, which often involved state and local government subsidising the cost of transport and parking in particular, US Soccer is hopeful that preparations for 2031 will be more harmonious.

Having backed down from their initial demand for fan fests in every city last summer which proved undeliverable due to escalating costs, Fifa has already agreed to adopt a hybrid approach based on local provision.

“Each city ultimately had a slightly different fan fest strategy,” Cosler said. “There’s been a willingness and openness from Fifa to continue to have flexibility in that. So you might see an instance in which a city has one fan fest, like Atlanta right next to the stadium, but other cities could go down a route where there’s a couple of smaller fan fests around different neighborhoods of the cities.”

Despite inevitable difficult conversations looming over Fifa’s extensive tax demands, there is also optimism among the organizers that some of the major disputes around transport costs that plagued World Cup preparations in New Jersey and Boston in particular last summer can be avoided.

“We also have a greater understanding around the importance of funding, and the prices of public transit and security,” Cosler added. “So that will all act as the starting point. I expect a lot less friction.

“We’re starting in a slightly different position this time around. Of course, cities will still have to contribute. We’re not saying that Fifa is going to cut the check for everything, but I think it will be a more equitable type model.”

‘Celebrate, inspire, unite’: UK confirmed as host of 2035 Women’s World Cup

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:09:18 GMT

Country’s first World Cup since men’s 1966 edition in England

Bid lists 22 stadiums as potential venues

The UK has been confirmed as hosts of the 2035 Women’s World Cup, the first global competition to be staged in the country since England won the men’s World Cup in 1966.

A joint bid from the Football Associations of England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales was approved by acclamation at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress conducted virtually, with another uncontested bid from the United States, Mexico, ⁠Costa Rica and Jamaica being awarded the 2031 tournament.

In a surprise move the UK bid was not presented by the FA or any of the home nations’ chief executives despite them all travelling to Zurich, with the presentation instead led by the Sky Sports News presenter Jess Creighton and four schoolchildren, one from each country.

FA sources rejected suggestions this was a deliberate attempt to distance themselves from Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, who presided over the congress. All four associations called on him to resign in the summer.

After the tournament had been formally awarded, the FA chair, Debbie Hewitt, took the floor and hugged Infantino before promising the UK would “celebrate the power of women’s football” and deliver an “exceptional” World Cup.

The UK pledged to deliver the biggest single-sport event ever held in the country, setting targets for 4.5m ticket sales and a projected TV audience of 3.5bn. With 63m people living within two hours of at least one proposed venue the bid team also claimed it would be the most accessible tournament ever staged in the UK.

“The world is coming to the United Kingdom,” Andy Burnham said. “In 2035 the biggest tournament in women’s sport will be played in cities across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, bringing visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country.

“Our players have inspired a generation of girls. In 2035 that generation will watch the best in the world play on their doorstep – and some of them will be on the pitch. But the impact of this World Cup will go much further. It will reach into communities across the country, bring more people into the game and leave a legacy that lasts long after the final whistle.”

The UK bid lists 22 stadiums as potential venues: 16 in England, three in Wales, two in Scotland and one in Northern Ireland. 15 host cities are in the running (the bid officially lists 16, counting Trafford as distinct from Manchester).

Wembley has been proposed for the final, having hosted it at the 2022 Women’s European Championship, which was won by England.

Fifa has evaluated 19 stadiums, assessing them as being of “high quality”. All were awarded a score of at least four out of five, except for Elland Road in Leeds (3.9), Easter Road in Edinburgh, Windsor Park in Belfast and Nottingham’s City Ground (all 3.6). Old Trafford has been assessed by Fifa but the proposed new Manchester United stadium could play a significant role instead if built in time.

The three listed stadiums not assessed by Fifa are Birmingham City’s proposed 62,000-seat Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham’s stadium – which is due two stages of redevelopment – and Chelsea’s stadium because only a redeveloped Stamford Bridge or a new club stadium would come into the picture.

The 22 stadiums will be whittled down to between 14 and 16. The tournament is scheduled to involve 104 matches played by 48 teams over 39 days. The dates are yet to be confirmed but indicative dates of 21 June to 29 July have been informally used as a template during the bidding process.

England, Scotland and Wales are also due to co-host – along with the Republic of Ireland – the men’s European Championship in 2028.

‘Most of the video budget went on Steve Strange’s makeup’: Midge Ure on how Visage made Fade to Grey

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:08:47 GMT

‘I was really into pre-Raphaelite paintings – Millais’ drowning Ophelia and the like – so I wrote a romantic study that eventually became this’

Visage were an amalgamation of three bands: Rich Kids, Magazine and Ultravox. Since all three were touring, getting everybody in the studio at the same time was nigh on impossible. Still, we were making our debut album and were a track short, when along came this gift from God.

We had no money so I’d been moonlighting with Thin Lizzy, and keyboardist Billy Currie had been playing with Gary Numan. Fade to Grey started life as an instrumental that Billy had been jamming with Chris Payne from the Numan band in soundchecks. They’d tried to release it but nobody was interested. I thought it was wonderful and suggested writing lyrics so we could use it on the Visage album.

The instrumental created this brilliant atmosphere – mysterious, melancholy, dark, dystopian, film noir – which put pictures in my head. I imagined a guy sitting on a train station with a suitcase, trying to escape his life, hence: “One man on a lonely platform, one case sitting by his side …” There’s a term in video-making, “fade to black”, but I changed it for the song because it gave the impression of a transition to something else. I imagined the man getting on a train not knowing where he’d end up.

The music was already recorded so we didn’t do a huge amount to it. I think Rusty Egan played some electronic drums. Steve Strange was the frontman but wasn’t a natural singer. So I put down a vocal, then he sang while listening to my vocal in headphones – what came out of his mouth was the same melody, but in his voice. You can hear me on the “aahs”, the “fade to greys” and some of the harmony parts. Rusty had a Belgian girlfriend, Brigitte Arendt, so someone – probably Rusty – suggested she read the title in French along with a translation of the lyrics. It was the icing on the cake.

Godley and Creme wanted to showcase themselves as video-makers so they made one for us for just £1,500: most of that went on makeup artists for Steve. The song and the video just seemed to capture a moment: the Blitz club, New Romantics, synthesisers. Then suddenly it was in the charts all over Europe.

Fade to Grey started off in 1976 or 77 when I was a music student at Chichester and we had to compose something. I was really into pre-Raphaelite paintings – Millais’ Ophelia and the like – so I wrote a romantic study with the chords that eventually became Fade to Grey, but played on piano in a different manner. After I joined the Gary Numan band, I used to mess around playing the chords on a Polymoog synth and a bassline on a Minimoog. One day Billy and drummer Cedric Sharpley joined in. As the tour progressed, we developed it in soundchecks.

After the tour, Billy was due to go back to Ultravox, so we wanted to record it as a keepsake. We used producer Martin Rushent’s studio in London, but when we set up the gear the Minimoog wasn’t there, just the Polymoog. However, the brass setting gave the bassline the distinctive attack on Fade to Grey. Cedric started the song with a CR-78 drum machine and put the drums down. Billy sprinkled synth over it and that was it. The arrangement was created on the fly. Then Billy called asking: “Do you mind if it goes on the Visage album?”

And the rest is history. The next thing I knew my publisher called me to say it was at No 45. Then my neighbour came in going: “It’s on Top of the Pops! And there’s this most amazing video.” Then it was in the Top 10 – and No 1 in some countries.

I’m really happy with its success. On YouTube, there are loads of people doing different takes. I’ve just done a version for Midge’s new album, and my wife sang the French bit. It’s come full circle.

Midge Ure’s Chapters: The Best Of is out now on CD, 2LP and a 3CD deluxe version including Chris Payne’s remix. A new version of Fade to Grey is available digitally and on 7” vinyl from midgeure. tmstor. es. Midge Ure is on tour this month

How many more ‘landmark’ reforms of benefits for disabled people are we expected to take?

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:07:03 GMT

The Timms review will be yet another trial for Pip claimants – where fixing welfare costs is brutally framed as a means of reducing stress on taxpayers

When Stephen Timms announces his long-awaited recommendations regarding personal independence payments (Pip) on Tuesday, it will be the third time in 16 months that the government has trailed “landmark” reforms to the key disability benefit. First seen last year when Keir Starmer’s proposed Pip cuts were stifled by a Labour backbench rebellion, it was only last week that the Milburn review pitched pulling the benefit entirely from under-25s. Or perhaps I’ll put it another way: it was only a few days ago that disabled people on social media were last sharing their fear they will lose the money they need to live on. What exactly Timms – a New Labour stalwart who is now minister for social security – will propose is still unknown, but leaks suggest his will be a “much softer” approach than Milburn’s £3.6bn a year of proposed cuts, in part because it has been co-produced with disabled people’s organisations. It is likely that Timms will recommend the assessment process for Pip should be made simpler and easier to complete, particularly for people with fluctuating conditions – something that will be welcomed by the many people who have become accustomed to being wrongly rejected for the support they need. The review is also expected to say that all ages should keep the benefit – putting Timms at direct odds with Milburn’s call last week for many young people with health conditions to lose their monthly cash and instead apply for one-off payments for specific goods, such as therapy or a mobility aid. No matter where you fall on the political spectrum, that will sound like a colossally inefficient way to reform a system. Why did we spend last week discussing Milburn’s proposals if Timms was going to make different ones, days later? Will disabled people aged 25 and over have a separate assessment and entitlement from that for younger people or not? Why did Milburn even have Pip – a benefit that pays for the extra costs of disability and is for those in work too – as part of his brief on unemployment? That a source has told the Times that the two reports will “converge” and form part of yet another government policy paper early next year does suggest that Labour might be doing all this as some sort of an elaborate bit. As the political class wrestles with how to tackle the benefits bill and a sicker population, it feels as if the nation is doomed to ride a perpetual cycle of ideas. The government presents a plan for reforming the benefits system. Rightwing parties cry it doesn’t go far enough. Charities and disabled people’s organisations express concern. Then we go again. “Welfare reform” in 2026 is effectively stuck in Groundhog Day, except in the film Bill Murray at least learns something. The irony, of course, is that Pip is in desperate need of overhaul. Since 2013, when the coalition government brought in the benefit as part of its wider austerity agenda, Pip has, by any measure, been a disastrous piece of public policy: pushing disabled people to food banks, physical and mental decline, and, in extreme cases, death. Meanwhile, public resentment grows at the mounting cost, while private companies are given multimillion-pound contracts for running inaccurate assessments (currently, nearly two-thirds of appeals over Pip decisions are successful at tribunal). We will soon see whether Timms’s recommendations finally buck the trend and offer some genuinely useful solutions for what is a deeply complex issue. And yet there comes a point where we have to ask whether another government review into disability benefits is actually about doing something to help those who rely on those benefits – or about being seen to be doing something by those who don’t. Few things demonstrate this more than the way snippets of the two benefit reviews have been leaked to the press in the days before publication. That this is standard practice doesn’t mean feeding frenzied media speculation doesn’t have a very real impact on what are often vulnerable communities. The priority is apparently to reassure Labour MPs and middle England, as disabled claimants anxiously refresh news pages to learn their fate, drip by drip. The lens through which we see “welfare reform” has for a long time been distorted in this way, with fixing the benefits system framed as a means to reduce stress on the taxpayer, rather than the disabled people relying on it (two groups that aren’t actually separate). It is a particularly brutal type of dehumanisation, in which it becomes possible for non-disabled people to discuss removing the money someone needs to charge their electric wheelchair to leave the house without ever really thinking of them at all. It is not simply that large sections of the political and media class see prospective benefit cuts as abstract – a Westminster game in which to score points – but the same applies to the millions of people who would be affected. In this debate, disability benefits claimants are rarely fully fledged human beings, they are a statistic or a problem. When disabled people look at the news this week, they will yet again have to hear pundits discussing their lives in terms of cost: what their economic value is, how much of a burden they are, and whether they are really trying hard enough. It should be possible to talk about public spending on disability with maturity and nuance, of course, but it would be generous to claim many of the key players in British politics manage that. Or, as the Tory party leader Kemi Badenoch recently put it, when proposing £36bn of cuts to social security: “double amputees run marathons”. Because that’s the thing about “reform”. A disabled person can do all the right things – send the Department for Work and Pensions their wad of medical evidence, tell the assessor how they put their bra on, go through a lengthy appeal if they’re wrongly rejected, and then do it again in a few years – and they know that at any given time, the money they rely on to function can still be pulled away. That sort of knowledge is a weight on someone’s back; something that tugs at the joints and squeezes the breath on a cold night as you doubt whether you can afford to put the heating on, or will have to go to bed early in pain. Timms will make his recommendations. Columnists such as me will debate them. The Treasury will do the maths. But behind closed doors, disabled and sick people will be wondering whether this time, the headlines might just become reality. On and on it goes.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

Wild stock market swings: will I lose money, and is there anything I can do?

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 14:51:44 GMT

Shares are volatile amid jitters over tech and AI – but think carefully before you decide to ditch investments too

Business live – latest updates

It has been a volatile time on global stock markets, with rapid rallies and punishing sell-offs. There have been signs in recent weeks that investors are getting cold feet over the outlook for AI companies and selling off technology stocks.

Last week, the AI company Anthropic launched on to the market and had a record-breaking first day, but on Friday stock markets around the world tumbled and the US Nasdaq closed 5% below its mark on 1 January.

On Monday, the dramatic return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia sent its shares soaring and contributed to a jump in US stock markets.

Investors seem to be losing faith in AI – or rather in the valuations of companies that are involved in the industry. This month, several events have led to sell-offs – the surprise scale of the Democrats’ win in the US midterms was swiftly followed by Huang’s exit over an relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The rapid offloading of tech stocks after these events suggests a jitteriness among investors.

Lots of people own shares that are falling in value, either through their pension or other type of investment account. Many of the shares that are experiencing the biggest falls are companies that have dominated indices and, as a result, the passive funds that track them.

Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell, says two of the most popular passive investments among investors are global equity funds and funds tracking the S&P 500 US stock market index. “Both have exposure to the giants of tech in a large way,” he says. And, as a result, both have fallen in recent days.

Coatsworth says that, while 15 years ago US shares represented half of the MSCI World index – a benchmark for the global stock market – it is now 73%. Tech is the dominant sector and officially represents 30% of the index. However, Google’s parent Alphabet and Facebook’s owner Meta are classed as communication services stocks – adding them bumps up tech to about 35% of the index.

Investors who think they have diversified by being in a global fund may be having a nasty surprise.

The investment platform interactive investor (ii) reports on the top holdings of its customers every quarter. Its most recent report shows global tracker funds are well-represented in their portfolios, as is Scottish Mortgage – an actively managed investment trust that holds shares in SpaceX, Nvidia and Anthropic, among others.

However, an important thing to remember about falling share prices is that you do not lose money until you sell. Only at that point do you crystallise your loss.

And you may not even have losses on paper, depending on when you invested. In recent years stock markets have been climbing. The FTSE 100 is still higher than it was last year. Scottish Mortgage has been falling since mid-October, but its shares are still well up on this time last year.

Resist panicking. Holly Mackay, the chief executive of the consumer website Boring Money, says: “Humans are programmed to fight or take flight when something goes wrong. However, this instinct to take action is often the worst response to falling markets when doing nothing is the most sensible response.”

Coatsworth says recent sell-offs “may seem unpleasant, but it isn’t out of the ordinary. History shows that markets go through cycles and what’s unfolding in front of our eyes is par for the course.”

He points out that markets bounce back, including after recent falls such as in April 2025 after Donald Trump’s tariffs announcement, and earlier drops fuelled by inflation and the Covid pandemic.

Camilla Esmund, the head of investor campaigns at ii, says this is a timely reminder to review your investment strategy and check the level of risk you are taking and whether you are sufficiently diversified.

“It is wise to diversify your portfolio across sectors, regions, and asset classes, so no single shock derails your progress,” she says. “By doing this, you are spreading your risk and ensuring that you are not overexposed to one area of the market.”

Coatsworth says if you are approaching retirement, “the key is to review your investments to make sure they are still aligned with how you plan to take an income from your pot.”

Coatsworth says there are a few paths to consider.

“One way to dial down tech exposure is to switch into a global equity fund that excludes the US,” he says. “For example, iShares MSCI World ex-US ETF invests in a basket of companies from around the world excluding the US.”

Tech stocks outside the US account for 10.9% of the portfolio, but the main holdings include banks, healthcare companies, oil producers and miners. “That would provide more sector balance and less dependence on tech, but it would mean some of the key names that have led the US market rally in recent years like Nvidia no longer being in the driving seat,” he says. However, if those stocks recover, you will be missing out on any potential gains.

He says a possible “middle ground” is the Invesco MSCI World Equal Weight ETF. At the end of September, the US represented 40.6% of the investment – less than with a traditional global equity fund. “The investor still has their toe in the pond for US tech exposure, but they wouldn’t be up to their neck in the water,” he says.

Some people see falling prices as an opportunity. Earlier this month, the investment platform Hargreaves Lansdown reported that its clients had been buying overseas tech shares after the post-midterm falls.

Mackay says there are many great tech companies which make a lot of money and have huge growth potential.

“I expect some pain but I’m sitting tight and will actually look to buy into any quality companies which are unfairly punished as some rattled investors rush for any exit,” she says.
