AI conquered chess. What happened next should give us hope

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 13:00:31 GMT

As two 20-year-old prodigies prepare to battle in the world chess championship, the game offers a surprising lesson about AI and what it cannot replicate

The upcoming world chess championship between Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov and India’s Gukesh Dommaraju in Geneva has all the makings of a barnburner.

Earlier this year, Sindarov, 20, won the Candidates Tournament as an outside longshot with a magnificent attacking style that overwhelmed the competition, locking up his title shot with a string of dazzling early wins.

His opponent Dommaraju, also 20, is the reigning champ. He’s hugely resilient under pressure, facing complications and crises with astonishing equanimity. Sindarov can blow people away and Gukesh is extremely hard to blow away. It’s a classic set-up: irresistible force meets immovable object.

Play over the board will be only one aspect of the significance of the struggle in Geneva. A world chess championship is a kind of status report on intelligence itself, and human intelligence is in a state of radical flux. If you want to understand AI, what it changes and what it doesn’t, chess is the first place to look.

The world championship is also an opportunity for tens of millions of ordinary chess lovers, like myself, to realize, once again, just how much we suck at chess.

My current rating on Chess. com hovers around 1,800. For some, that number might seem impressive – it puts me somewhere around the top 80,000 players on a site with 174 million members. For real chess players, that number is laughable. A master rating typically starts at about 2,300. I’m nothing.

What makes that rating a tad shameful is how much work has gone into it. I was a teenage chess club kid in the 1990s, when it was literally the definition of geekiness, the late-to-puberty crowd disputing fianchetto fortresses and knight posts on the sixth rank. I have played chess almost every day since without serious interruption. I have read many, many books, living in hope. I have gone through the drudgery of memorizing endgames, although I forget them all a month after studying, which is probably the root of my problem.

Put it this way: If I had spent the time I had spent playing and studying chess on, say, learning Mandarin, I would be one of those white guys you see on Chinese TV doing the equivalent of “Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.” And I’m at 1,800.

Every other skill I have tried to improve at, I have. I wanted to get better at cooking. I can now, if you give me a Sunday, make gâteau de crêpes à la Florentine or an (admittedly crooked) croquembouche. I started doing crosswords a decade ago. I finish them more often and faster. It’s the same with almost anything. Except chess.

Why do I suck at chess? I think, by now, I have expended enough energy to know the answer: my brain simply isn’t built for it. It’s just not that good at the spatial, logic problems that are the essence of the game. The question then shifts: why am I obsessed with something my brain can’t do very well?

Perhaps the answer is in the question. Obviously, part of the appeal for me is that it’s a break from the monstrous, unending struggle with words and their meanings which is my profession. That, and the gift of sucking at chess is the same as its curse. The blessing is the agony. I can see the beauty in what I cannot master, although I admit it troubles me that, in India, there is a six-year-old kid who would not lose a game to me if we played 100 times and there’s nothing I can do about it.

Chess is, more than anything, a game for people who love to think, which is why it has always served as a harbinger of intellectual currents, always ahead of its time. The first world chess championship, in 1886, was a conflict between the nostalgic Romanticism of Johannes Zukertort and the modern positional play of Wilhelm Steinitz, between chess as gusts of sudden drastic insights into tactics and chess as the revelation of the power of systematic, accretive advantage – the efflorescence of nature against the incipient power of industrialization.

The hypermodern school that emerged in the 1930s reflected both modernism and postmodernism. Its proponents rejected traditional play towards the centre in favour of the margins on the board. Traditional structures contained weaknesses which could be exploited. Chess, as much as literature or architecture, bears the imprint of the zeitgeist.

Occasionally, politics infuse the game. The most famous world championship match, between the American Bobby Fischer and the Russian Boris Spassky in 1972, stood in for the cold war as a whole because it posed a test of whether idiosyncratic genius could compete against the power of the state. The 1985 Kasparov-Karpov match, contrasting Anatoly Karpov’s cold precision with Garry Kasparov’s wild, effervescent creativity, represented the triumph of a reformist younger generation over an entrenched bureaucratic elite. Gorbachev first used the term glasnost, the policy of opening up the Soviet state, while the match was under way. Today, India’s newfound prominence as a chess superpower is evidence of the rise of the global south.

But when Sindarov and Gukesh sit down to play, the question hanging over the board will be bigger than politics. It will be a question of the nature of the mind itself: what is the place of human intelligence in a world increasingly dominated by machines?

You probably started thinking about artificial intelligence as something that might affect your life in or around 2023, when ChatGPT launched. Chess has been grappling with the implications of AI since 1996.

The dream of building a machine that could outthink humans at chess is centuries old. The Mechanical Turk, a chess-playing automaton which wowed imperial courts in the 1770s, was the first “thinking machine”. It turned out to be a little person tucked inside the machinery. Alan Turing himself wrote the first chess algorithm in 1948. And the moment Deep Blue beat Kasparov in the late 1990s was the first clear triumph of the technology, the first sign that the machines were coming for the brain.

Chess today is what an intellectual activity looks like after AI has gone through it.

In the past, if you lost a game, you would play it over with a friend or coach, to see where it all started to go wrong. No need to spend days examining your every move any more. The machine tells you. Throughout the 70s and 80s, in the pages of Chess Informant, theoretical debates raged over opening lines. Debates unfolded over years sometimes, and often not to any definite conclusion.

World championships, and the candidates tournaments that led up to them, used to involve teams thrashing out new strategies, searching for exciting imbalances their opponents had not encountered. Tournaments sometimes became laboratories of individual openings, and preparations were research into the nature of the game itself. Now you plug in a line and the computer tells you if it’s right. There’s no debate.

Positions have right and wrong answers now. The competition between styles and schools that defined chess since its beginning is no longer meaningful.

All that grand intellectual tradition … right in the bin.

Here’s the thing: you might think that computers would end chess. If a phone can beat the best player in the world, why bother?

But AI didn’t end chess at all. The opposite. Chess has never been more popular.

The world used to have room for one, maybe two, chess celebrities. You probably knew who Bobby Fischer was, and you might have known Spassky, but probably not his first name. Kasparov was the chess guy for about two decades. Now you don’t need to be world champion, or even to be close to being world champion, to be a chess celebrity.

There are numbers of fans devoted to the dazzling calculative ability of Hikaru Nakamura, the absurdly dynamic daring of Alireza Firouzja, the elegance of Fabiano Caruana (my favourite player), and even the somewhat villainous, psychologically intimidating Hans Niemann.

In my neighbourhood in Toronto, any given week, I can play on Monday nights at the local Japanese listening bar, where a room full of glamorous 25-year-olds, some of them on dates, lounge in the dark over boards, sipping $20 yuzu cocktails. There’s also a Wednesday night meetup at what can only be described as a frat boy pub; they literally call themselves chess bros. There’s also the official club in the Zen Buddhist temple on the corner. And that’s just within walking distance of my house.

The sheer quantity of online chess is overwhelming. The Botez sisters, who combine master-level play with the charming dramas of their sisterly intimacy, have more than 3 million followers. GothamChess, with over 10 million, is one of the world’s top influencers, period.

The lesson of chess, for anyone trying to understand what artificial intelligence does, is that it removes the sense of human superiority from an activity and it reinscribes that activity as sport.

And chess is an amazing, if bizarre, sport. In 2024, I attended the candidates tournament in Toronto. In the hall itself, there was a smell of violence, intoxicating, hormonal. The smell of confrontation. A bit like a boxing match. Even though they were just sitting in front of each other, there was a sense of men having their brains beaten out.

In a basement under the hall, away from the players, I and a couple of hundred other fans thrashed out the variations of the games under way. Again, the engines had altered the experience completely. Even lowly players like myself, with access to the technology, know the correct next move, so we sit around watching the superstars make mistakes.

Patzers like me clutch our hair and shout, “How could you blunder like that, Fabi?” exactly like football fans who couldn’t run a mile screaming at the world’s greatest athletes: “I could have scored from there.”

There are other essential lessons about AI that chess can teach the world. The first is that artificial intelligence has serious limits. One of the reasons the current champion Gukesh is so strong is that his coach, the grandmaster Vishnu Prasanna, banned him from using AI until he was a strong player. The AI, he knew, would be a crutch, a way of unlearning. The old-fashioned analysis was essential for the growth of the mind. AI is easy to master after you’ve figured out how to think.

The deeper lesson is that the game people play when they play chess is not the game “chess”. It is the game “human chess”. Occasionally, GothamChess analyzes games between different AI bots. These matches are totally fascinating insofar as they are utterly distinct from human play. Endgame subtleties work themselves out over 30 or 40 moves – totally beyond comprehension. Engines are willing to put up with the stress of keeping their kings in the open in a way that no human could accept simply because of the mental effort required to consider its dangers.

Sometimes GothamChess, which once achieved a rating higher than 2,300, can’t explain the reasoning behind the moves at all. They’re beyond people.

But games between engines are curiosities, fascinating in their own right but of limited interest to the game as it is played. It turns out that what is of interest to humans is what humans find of interest, what they can grasp.

Sindarov-Gukesh 2026 will be a very human affair. The question will be: who is tougher? Who can take the punishment? Who can dole it out? “Chess is war over the board,” Fischer once said. “The object is to crush the opponent’s mind.”

The Chinese player Ding Liren beat Russian Ian Nepomniachtchi in 2024 to become world champion, but the effort seems to have crushed him. He retreated from the game altogether for nine months. “I was exhausted but still couldn’t sleep well. This led to depression. I was treated in a clinic twice,” he told a German newspaper. Reading Louise Glück and Albert Camus offered him some comfort.

When he returned to the board, Carlsen bemoaned that Ding seemed “permanently broken”. He is, now, by some accounts, recovering. But the championship did something to him, like fighting Sonny Liston did something to Muhammad Ali. As in all truly great sports events, there’s an ugliness at the heart of the beauty. Everything intoxicating has its dollop of poison.

AI humbles human ability. “We have discovered that humans are not that good at playing chess,” Magnus Carlsen told a Spanish newspaper recently. That remark is some comfort to patzers like me. Everybody sucks at chess. Some suck more than others. More importantly, it’s a clarification of the state of the human mind itself, and the future of the mind. Humanity lives in a permanent state of misunderstanding.

AI is now coming for everything. Chess was just first. The state of the game is a sign of great hope and despair at once for the future of thinking. It demonstrates the limited connection of the mind to the reality at hand, but damn is it fascinating. Chess, and everything else, is going to remain a mystery impenetrable by our little ape brains. We are never given more than a fragment of the significance of anything, even in games of our own construction. Our role is to appreciate and to marvel at the beauties and the terror of the glimpses we can gather. Our role is to play.

Even in the company of glamorous machines, all we have is each other, and the boards and pieces we put between us.

Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:42:51 GMT

Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

Europe live – latest updates

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”

Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped over for several days, under a cooperation agreement, to refuel and resupply as it escorted Russian cargo ships that could carry military supplies en route to Russia.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.

Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts to use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The confirmation that Ukraine was behind the attacks was condemned by the UN-recognised government in Tripoli. It said Libya rejected ⁠any foreign ⁠military ​operations on its territory or in its waters.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said Ukraine’s strikes in the Mediterranean “were exceptionally brazen and provocative”.

He added: “The question now is how Russia will retaliate,. Perhaps even more pressing is how the [Hafter] family will respond, given how traumatic the scale of the destruction has been for eastern Libyan authorities.”

Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:34:42 GMT

Management team were in line for huge payouts

Fifa denies Infantino would have profited from plan

Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.

Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. They outline a plan, produced days before July’s final of the 2026 World Cup, to profit from the sport’s burgeoning commercial revenues for almost a century.

Infantino hopes to be re-elected for a fourth term as president in March and is the favourite to win that contest.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

An internal Fifa risk assessment dated 17 July, designed as one of the final steps before concluding the FFE agreement, spells out the scheme’s extraordinary scope. “This deal provides for Fifa to create a for-profit subsidiary which would have all the commercial rights for Fifa events transferred to it for commercial exploitation for the next 96 years,” one section reads.

Another internal Fifa document written the following day, outlining the proposed agreement with Thrive, says the deal’s contract period “would be for rolling 12-year license periods to a sum maximum total of 96 years” and goes further in stating Fifa would assume 51% ownership “in perpetuity”.

The existence of a lucrative “management incentive plan” for unnamed individuals helming the scheme casts into stark light the extent to which its architects could have profited. The plan is first mentioned in a term sheet and “backstop letter” drawn up by Thrive on 17 July, which refers to FFE as “Project Box”, and sets aside up to 5% of FFE’s stock as a bonus pool for the new firm’s management. In theory it could have paid out up to $50m (£38.2m) for each $1bn added to the scheme’s value above $20bn, which was its initial valuation.

The term sheet says the plan “will permit the issuance of profits interests representing up to 5% of the fully diluted capitalisation of FFE, which will dilute all unitholders on a pro rata basis”. According to the Fifa memo the pool’s existence aimed to “ensure sufficient motivation to perform well”.

A further clause states that, if Fifa breached its agreement with Thrive or completed an agreement with a rival party, Thrive would have been entitled to a break fee totalling 1.25% – $250m – of FFE’s worth. Fifa would not have been permitted to engage in talks with other potential lead buyers for a year, or until the FFE deal closed.

Fifa’s memo of 18 July confirms there was no tender process “owing to the specific and unique nature of the proposed investment”. The risk assessment document confirms its own finance department was “not directly privy to the terms of the transaction”, casting further doubt about the processes followed in pursuing the deal.

Fifa has consistently denied that Infantino stood to profit personally from FFE, which will raise questions as to who would have benefited from the management incentive plan.

The documents make clear that the issuance of so-called MIP units would be managed by the board of FFE, which Infantino was due to chair.

“For the avoidance of doubt, any potential management incentive plan was exclusively for members of FFE management, of which Fifa officials could not have been part. This is customary for proposed structures of this nature. Fifa’s leadership would only have had leading roles in the board, which would not have led to any additional remuneration. The one change that worked: At 21, I was terrified of seeming ‘cringe’. Then I rediscovered my inner child

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:00:55 GMT

Four-year-old me had never worried about fashion fails or making a fool of myself. It was time to ditch this grown-up obsession with getting everything right

I’ve always been a perfectionist. As a student, I have spent months worrying about assignments long after submitting them, and criticised myself over tiny things such as making spelling mistakes in birthday cards. When I speak to friends or strangers, I’m so focused on not saying the “wrong” thing that I forget to enjoy chatting with them.

As part of gen Z, I know there is a wider culture of fear among my generation: I’m not the only one worried about doing or saying something that is embarrassing or, God forbid, cringe.

In avoiding mistakes, it struck me that I had become afraid of doing anything at all. I’ve abandoned hobbies I used to enjoy, such as writing poetry, because I worried it might be seen as “naff”. I stopped playing the violin because I didn’t want to make a fool of myself when practising in student halls.

As I turned 21, I realised that I didn’t want to carry this mindset with me for the rest of my life. The solution came to me unexpectedly one night over dinner with friends, when we began scrolling through photos and videos of our childhood. After the initial hilarity about our poor fashion choices and bad camera angles, I noticed something I had forgotten: my younger self had a remarkable sense of freedom.

Four-year-old me wore bright green socks with pink sandals without worrying about making a fashion “fail”. When, at the age of seven, I wrote songs with my brother and cousin, we didn’t aspire to write a hit single, but just enjoyed the process of creating something together. I began to wonder whether the best antidote for perfectionism in adulthood was to revisit the time before it existed.

Soon, whenever I caught myself being critical or avoiding things out of fear of making a mistake, I began to think about what my younger self would make of the situation.

When I moved to Copenhagen for a year abroad in 2025 as part of my university degree, cycling everywhere – as Danish people do – felt like a terrifying, insurmountable hurdle. Despite familiarising myself with the rules, I was worried about navigating busy traffic, and almost gave up on it altogether. Then I remembered how I’d learned to ride a bike much later than most of my classmates. When I was 10, cycling didn’t come naturally to me, but I kept trying because making mistakes never felt like a reason to give up.

I realised that if this version of me knew that I was even considering cycling abroad, she would be so excited. I started on quiet streets near my accommodation, before gradually exploring the whole city. Instead of expecting myself to be perfect, I just enjoyed the experience.

A similar shift happened with my friends. Because they are all so smart, I often overthought things I said in conversations with them. But remembering the 10-year-old version of me, who always felt slightly out of place but hoped for a group of friends that would feel like my family, suddenly made just being with them feel like enough.

I also began to use music to connect with my childhood self, rediscovering songs that my dad used to play in the car when I was young. The Sun Always Shines on TV by a-ha became the soundtrack to my life during the cold Danish winter, and when I played it to my friend in Amsterdam a few months later, she told me it was also one of her childhood favourites.

We can both sometimes feel self-conscious when we go out clubbing, but with a-ha playing through the speaker, we could dance on her balcony without worrying about looking silly. In that moment, letting go of perfectionism felt easy.

The more I let my younger self back into my life, the less power perfectionism seems to have over me. Realising that I am not just achieving but surpassing the small dreams she once had has reminded me to stop measuring every moment against my impossible standards. As a teenager, I thought that becoming an adult meant leaving my childhood self behind – but now I can’t wait to bring her along for the ride.

The ruling against Myanmar makes proving genocide more feasible

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:00:54 GMT

The international court of justice has settled questions over the issue of intent, with powerful implications for Israel

The international court of justice (ICJ) decision last Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya recognizes the plight of one of the world’s most persecuted minorities. It also resonates in Gaza, where the same court is now more likely to find that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians.

That possibility has incensed the Donald Trump administration, but it should think twice before attacking another international tribunal.

The case stems from the Myanmar military’s brutal “clearance operations” in 2017 when it used murder, torture, rape and arson to kill at least 10,000 Rohingya and to send more than 700,000 fleeing to neighboring Bangladesh. The Rohingya are a Muslim minority that has long faced severe discrimination in Myanmar, whose dominant Bamar ethnic group tends to be Buddhist and have lighter skin.

Myanmar has 135 recognized ethnic groups but refuses to accept the Rohingya as the 136th. A 1982 law denied most Rohingya citizenship despite their deep roots in the country.

Even Aung San Suu Kyi, awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1991 as an icon of her country’s quest for democracy, refused to call them Rohingya. She preferred the disparaging appellation “Bengali” to suggest they were foreigners who immigrated from Bangladesh. In 2019, she traveled to the Hague to defend the Myanmar military from the genocide charge.

Her actions reflected her fellow citizens’ vilification of the Rohingya. She also evidently hoped that by ingratiating herself with the military, it might allow her to become president despite a constitutional ban because her husband and two sons are British.

Instead, the military overthrew the country’s fledgling democracy in 2021 and has detained her ever since.

Genocide is defined in a widely ratified treaty. The Myanmar case, like many others, hinged on whether certain atrocities were committed with genocidal intent – that is, the intent to destroy a protected group, in this case a religious and ethnic minority, “in whole or in part”.

There was ample proof that the Myanmar army committed systematic murder, torture, rape, and arson against the Rohingya, but did it have the requisite intent?

In theory, genocidal intent can be proved by the statements of senior officials, but most are smart enough to use less incendiary language. As a result, intent usually must be inferred from conduct.

In rulings on genocide cases brought by Bosnia and Croatia against Serbia, the ICJ held in 2007 and 2015 that such a deduction could be made if “the only reasonable inference to be drawn from that conduct is one of genocidal intent”. That suggested to some that genocidal intent could not be found to coexist with another intent.

That view seemed built on genocides designed to kill a group “in whole”. For example, after a certain point during the Holocaust and the genocide in Rwanda, the aim was to kill every possible Jew or Tutsi.

But what about a genocide aimed at killing a group “in part”? That might arise when genocide is not the sole goal of mass atrocities but a means to another end, such as ethnic cleansing.

According to this interpretation, the ICJ’s Serbia rulings would perversely suggest that the commission of the crime against humanity of mass forced displacement might serve as a defense to allegations of genocidal intent. That made no sense.

In the Myanmar case, the court, by a vote of nine to six, interpreted this standard more sensibly. Citing general principles of criminal law, it ruled that dual intents were possible. “Genocidal intent may exist alongside other intentions, provided that such intentions are not incompatible with the existence of genocidal intent,” it explained.

In other words, its earlier ruling that genocidal intent must be shown to be the “only reasonable inference” from a course of conduct should not be read to mean that genocide is the sole intent. Rather, it meant there should be no reasonable understanding of the evidence that disproves genocidal intent, even if there was also a parallel intent.

The Myanmar government claimed its intent was not to commit genocide but to mount a counterinsurgency operation against a rebel group in the part of western Myanmar where most Rohingya lived. The court discounted that explanation because the army committed atrocities even in places where there was no insurgency and engaged in gratuitous atrocities such as raping women, killing children, burning villages and attacking fleeing civilians.

Myanmar also asked the court to consider the possibility, never admitted, that its aim was forced displacement, not genocide. That paralleled the ICJ’s finding from the evidence against Serbia that it did not have genocidal intent.

But in the latest case, the court held that so long as the only reasonable inference from the evidence was that Myanmar intended to commit genocide, it didn’t matter that the evidence reasonably supported the conclusion that Myanmar also sought to forcibly displace the Rohingya or to fight an insurgency. Genocide can be a means to an end, not just an end in itself.

That ruling must have sent shivers down the spines of Israeli officials. Anticipating it, Trump’s ambassador to the United Nations last month threatened the ICJ judges with sanctions akin to those already imposed on international criminal court judges if they “were to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide”. (The ICJ mainly resolves civil disputes between states, including on how to apply the Genocide Convention, while the ICC prosecutes individuals.)

But the ICJ didn’t lower the standard. It interpreted the standard in the most sensible way possible to ensure that the commission of parallel mass atrocities does not become a defense to genocide.

Moreover, as Trump toys with sanctions against yet another international court, does he really want to be seen as defending the brutal Myanmar military, which today is terrorizing people across Myanmar while ruthlessly quashing their hopes for democracy?

The administration of Joe Biden already found Myanmar to have committed genocide against the Rohingya. The Trump administration, having never repudiated that conclusion, says it is “examining” the ICJ ruling.

Like the Myanmar case, the genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel before the ICJ is likely to turn on the question of intent.

Similar to its Myanmar counterpart, the Israeli army gratuitously killed and harmed Palestinian civilians – indiscriminately bombing neighborhoods, attacking Hamas fighters knowing that there would be disproportionate civilian dead and wounded, shooting hungry Palestinians as they ran for food, bombing housing blocks knowing many civilians remained inside, and creating conditions of starvation and deprivation that were incompatible with sustaining life.

The Israeli government didn’t attempt to kill all 2 million Palestinians in Gaza, just enough to persuade the rest to accept “voluntary emigration”, as an Israeli minister put it.

Might that attempted crime of mass forced deportation undermine an inference from these atrocities of genocidal intent? Similarly, might Israel’s military campaign against Hamas, however ruthless and indifferent to the requirements of international humanitarian law to spare civilians, serve a comparable role in negating genocidal intent?

The original ICJ language in the Serbia cases left open the possibility that this perverse “defense” might work. The Myanmar judgment makes clear it will not. The intent to commit genocide can coexist with the intent to forcibly displace or to fight an insurgency.

If the only reasonable conclusion from the totality of the evidence is that Israel possessed genocidal intent, which I suspect is true, the ICJ will find that Israel, like Myanmar, committed genocide.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to take various remedial steps for the Rohingya, such as reparations, restoration of citizenship, the possibility of safe return to the country, and prosecution of offenders. But the court has no power to enforce its ruling. That task falls to the UN security council, which is likely to be stymied by China’s and Russia’s veto, and other governments, whose pressure so far has been ineffective.

But we should not minimize the importance to the Rohingya of the court’s acknowledgment of their plight. There was cheering among Rohingya in their refugee camps in Bangladesh. The odds now increase that the Palestinians of Gaza, too, will have their moment of recognition.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

This article was amended on 23 November 2026. The Israeli army shot hungry Palestinians as they ran for food – not Israelis, as previously stated.

‘One area of the tent was known as fart corner’: what it’s really like to be on The Great British Bake Off

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 10:00:53 GMT

As we come to the end of another series, former contestants including Kim-Joy, Syabira Yusoff and Christiaan de Vries reminisce on their time in the tent – and the aftermath

The Great British Bake Off is just about to finish its best season in years. Like a cloud of Swiss meringue buttercream on a slightly sunken cake, Nigella Lawson has added glamour and indulgence to a format that needed saving. But this year’s contestants have brought the joy, too: talented, charismatic individuals who have interrupted their lives to spend three months with bits of dough stuck to their elbows and indigestion from all the recipe testing.

We spoke to five previous contestants to find out why they put themselves through it, and what they feel they achieved in the process. The scale runs from “a very nice level of X-list celebrity” to “a better version of me”, with a lot of life lessons (and a fart corner) along the way.

Syabira Yusoff – Series 13, winner

A couple of years after I moved to the UK [from Malaysia] I watched an episode of Bake Off where they were making brownies for the technical challenge. I thought: “I can make brownies, I can be on the show.” That’s it! I didn’t know how intense it is and how crazy it was going to be. No expectation, nothing.

[After I won] people started asking me: “Could you be like Nadiya Hussain with her TV show?” and I was thinking: “Yeah, maybe I’ll give it a shot.” I did try getting more involved on social media and putting myself out there, but the more I did it, the more I missed my job [in genetic research]. I decided to go back to work and maybe one day open a bakery or something. But for now I need stability and sanity! I like to dream really big, but being a researcher suits me better than being in the spotlight.

I enjoy doing food festivals – a full tent with everybody watching you baking gives you an adrenaline rush. I got invited to Buckingham Palace to see the queen and the king – I still have the invitation with my handwritten name on it in my drawer. I didn’t bake for them, but I did make a cake for Jimmy Choo, the shoe designer, for his birthday last year. It was a black forest pandan cake. He paid well!

I now understand when people say “believe in yourself”, because if I hadn’t trusted myself in the middle [of the series] when I hit rock bottom, I don’t think I would have come out as a winner. Not only did I get flowers and a cake stand, I came out as a better me.

Abbi Lawson – Series 14, 10th place

I have always entered various baking categories in our village show, and the theme one year was its 70th anniversary. I made a cake of the village show marquee with all the entries inside and sheep outside and it won best in show. That’s what gave me the confidence to apply for Bake Off.

There were a lot of tears when I was practising. I’d given myself the extra challenge of using seasonal, foraged ingredients, so I was having to practise with substitutes. It’s a lot of work! It’s really fun, but you’re trying to fit that in around everything else in your life, and you can’t tell anyone.

After I went out on bread week, I made a different type of bread every week for a year. It was really hard to not feel as if I’d let myself down. It’s a really stressful environment, and there’s so much going on. I learned a lot about my passions and my creativity; my career path is much more food-focused than I ever thought it would be.

I’m now a local celebrity. I live in a rural area, so there’s not loads going on, but I do Women’s Institute talks, I do stuff at the county show. I’m really happy. I didn’t want to leave my veg box delivery job behind, I didn’t want to be going down to London every week to do TV appearances. It’s a very nice level of X-list celebrity.

Kim-Joy – Series nine, runner-up

Because I grew up with selective mutism, I always felt as if I needed to get to my future self. I felt very trapped in my head, so every single thing I did was about challenging that. Bake Off was almost like exposure therapy, like if you’re scared of snakes and you put yourself in a tank of snakes. Although Bake Off is much better than a tank of snakes.

I was terrified the first week. I cried the whole time during the showstopper challenge, for no reason. They kept asking me why I was crying, and I was like: “No reason really, just leave me to it.” They didn’t put it in the edit, which I’m glad about. Last year I got an autism diagnosis, which possibly tied into it: the unfamiliarity was particularly difficult, and one of the things I found hardest was how bright and how hot it was.

Bake Off is the best thing I’ve ever done. I’m writing graphic novels now, working on another baking book, going to comic conventions. I’ve managed to get into interior design, decorating my house like a giant cake. That’s not to say everything is perfect. I have anxiety and depression so it’s hard. But I’m very grateful for all the opportunities, and I try to just embrace that and do as much as possible.

Christiaan de Vries – Series 15, runner-up

My boyfriend and I started watching Bake Off on Sundays when we were a bit tired and hungover. I worked as a fashion designer at Alexander McQueen, but when my whole team was made redundant I started baking. I watched Matty win series 14 and then on the screen it said: “Do you want to be in the tent?” I was like: “You know what? I’ve got nothing to lose. For lols, let’s just sign up.” I didn’t even think I was going to get through to the second round.

In fashion you would always hear, “This is not good enough, scrap this, redo that,” and that’s what I was expecting with Bake Off too. I was bracing for impact all the time, but it’s not like that at all. Everyone is really supportive and it has done a great deal for my self confidence.

But in the moment I was just really stressed! Sometimes Prue and Paul would be like, “I don’t like this,” when I really loved it, and my mother-in-law, my boyfriend, and my friends had tasted it and said it was great. That was such a big life lesson for me. I don’t care any more, basically.

Everything that’s happened since has been a rollercoaster. When the show was on, I remember getting off the train at Victoria in London and one person recognised me, and then another person came to stand with them for a photo, and then another one, and all of a sudden there were 20 people around me. It was insane. I mean, I enjoyed it. I’m not gonna lie. But it was crazy.

Howard Middleton – Series four, seventh place

As a child I was bullied – the enamel never formed on my teeth so they were discoloured. When I’d been working for a while I could afford to have them done, and that gave me a lot of confidence. Bake Off was a way of challenging myself; I didn’t need to keep my mouth closed any more. Although some awful person did review our year as being the year that had the worst teeth generally …

Within 20 minutes of being in the tent, I managed to cut my thumb quite badly. Off screen I went to A&E. Then, in week two, Sue Perkins accidentally put her elbow in my muffin during a technical challenge, and then week three was Custardgate ... just my luck, really. But I was thinking: “It’s good TV.”

Part of the reason people do TV is to get the behind-the-scenes experience, and I heard the full uncensored version of Mel and Sue. The rudeness of them! Swearing at Paul and things like that. Sue is openly rude, Mel is a bit more subtle.

There was an area of the tent which was affectionately known as fart corner. Mel had a vegetarian diet or something like that, so they created a little area where she could go and fart. At one point, when the judging was taking place, she wandered off to the corner and wandered back and Mary Berry’s face was just … [grimaces].

I now do some food writing and host online classes with a company called Bake With a Legend – we get so many people from America. The first demo I did I was so nervous, but then I realised people aren’t that bothered about what you’re doing, they just want a bit of humour and a bit of engagement. That was a revelation. People love it when things go wrong and I very rarely disappoint them. I’ve found a niche.

Dapper Liam and Noel, experimental Björk, and Bowie ‘cuddling himself’: Rankin reveals his never-before-seen shots of the stars

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:00:50 GMT

After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says

“I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.”

His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.”

That culminated in nine months of work for his scathing AI conceptual art project and magazine Faik (thefaik. com), made up of artificially generated images, from a skateboarding granny to Rankin-style magazine covers of the likes of Elvis, Frida Kahlo, Nelson Mandela and even God, as well as billboards with bleak warnings: “The people who control AI will control history itself”; “When anyone can generate art in seconds, who will pay for it?”

Rather than falling head-over-heels for the alluring new tech’s “limitless” possibilities, Rankin’s exploration of AI sent him running back into the arms of his first love – photography, as made by real humans in an actual time and place – and inspired his new book, Contact. “Trying to figure out what this new technology means for the craft and the thing I love reaffirmed how important the exchange between people is,” he says.

The hefty 500-plus-word page tome contains an ocean-size collection of images (bands, actors, writers, models) that Rankin took between 1987 and 2006: Oasis, Blur, Tony Blair, Kylie, Kate Moss, André 3000, Hugh Grant … Rather than presenting just the standout shot selected for a magazine cover or lead, Rankin presents contact sheets of thumbnail images, which bring to life the encounter between photographer and subject – the double meaning of the book title’s referencing the importance of human contact. “It’s about how much you kind of fall in love with people each time – platonically, of course, unless it’s my wife,” Rankin says. “I’m always going for connection. You rarely see a picture of mine where the person isn’t looking in through the camera. I tell them: ‘Forget about me – connect through the lens.’”

Born in Glasgow in 1966, Rankin, or John Rankin Waddell, grew up in St Albans, initially training in accountancy before photography consumed him. In 1991, he and Jefferson Hack co-founded the influential arts, culture and fashion magazine Dazed & Confused, Rankin’s exuberant images dominating the covers. He went on to photograph everyone from the Rolling Stones to Queen Elizabeth II. In 2011, he also founded Hunger magazine.

His next major project will be a sequel to his 2006 book Tuulitastic, dedicated to the model Tuuli Shipster, his wife of 17 years. He’s also planning to immerse himself in wet-plate photography, a slow 19th-century process that also feels like an antidote to AI.

Rankin doesn’t believe AI will replace people wanting to take or have “proper photos” taken. But he does expect it to transform the medium and devastate the industry, predicting it will be replacing jobs within less than a year, from image-retouching agencies to hair, makeup and styling. “AI is like Photoshop on crack,” he says.

While he’s not working on any AI-focused projects currently, he hasn’t finished with it entirely. “I’m quite sick of it,” he says. “But I do feel I’ve got more to explore. I’m looking at what you can create with it that you’ve never created before. People really hate it and I can’t stand it. But I’m still inquisitive about what it will become.”

Contact by Rankin is published by Hunger (£30), with a Contact exhibition also at Rankin’s Annroy Gallery, London, 2 December to3 February.

Liam and Noel Gallagher, 2002, Q, issue 190 (main image) “I always loved photographing Liam and Noel. Liam was like a panther – you never knew if he’d scratch you or purr. And Noel had brilliant one-liners. I’d set up a studio. Keith Drummond, the art director, and I were obsessed with David Bailey’s Lennon and McCartney shoot, so that inspired us. They looked so dapper, like real rock stars, and they played up the sibling rivalry for us.”

Björk, 1994, Dazed & Confused, issue 9 “Björk is the best person in the world to photograph; she’s so experimental. I was trying to do a version of another photographer’s image. She knew the photo and said: ‘Don’t do that – be yourself.’ I must’ve taken 200 rolls of film with her.”

David Bowie, 1995, Dazed & Confused, issue 14 “I expected to meet the dude from The Man Who Fell to Earth film: a spaceman who was cold, serious and unemotional. Instead, I met Tigger,” says Rankin. “Bowie was so excited. I sometimes say to people: ‘Cuddle yourself’ – it’s a self-love thing. David Bowie was one of the first people I tried it on. You can see he’s cuddling himself, but then there’s a performance there.”

Vivienne Westwood, 2002, POP magazine “Vivienne was so funny – no ego. She was such a laugh to shoot. The editor who commissioned me for this hated editing my shoots, but you can see her mark on this one. Most people would think they look ugly in that picture but Vivienne loved it so much that picture ended up being her poster for her V&A exhibition.”

Goldie, 1999, Dazed & Confused and INCredible Supplement “What’s great about Goldie is that he always performs to the camera. You never fail to get a good picture with Goldie. I like this one, as it’s a bit less like Goldie – it’s more subtle. He’s often in-your-face, which is lovely, but I feel that there’s a bit more of the softer Goldie in this photo.”

Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can’t see Andy Burnham pulling it off

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 05:00:47 GMT

Brussels rolled out a warm welcome for the PM but toxic UK politics around rejoining have not gone away

Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave.

To be sure, Brussels laid on a warm welcome. Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce.

There was positive progress on food and drink trade, youth mobility and aligning carbon markets. Yet there was also an inability to resolve relatively simple issues such as the fees young Europeans will pay to study at British universities from 2030, and whether the UK will apply the same tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as the EU. That is a taste of what lies ahead if a future government, backed by a groundswell of public opinion, decides to apply to rejoin.

The fundamental problems of being outside the EU were laid bare: you have to pay for market access and align with rules on which you no longer have a vote. But the issues around seeking renewed membership were also highlighted: the EU always has the upper hand in accession negotiations and the candidate country must adopt its rulebook wholesale – including the free movement of people – and pay into the common budget.

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, was right to say the door is always open but at a price. Burnham is right to argue that Brexit has not benefited the economy, ordinary people or the UK’s standing in the world. However you do the counterfactual economics, Britain has lost substantial investment, export markets and potential growth, while citizens have faced increasing hassle travelling and living on both sides of the Channel. Young people have also been robbed of opportunities to study and work abroad. As the EU’s divorce negotiator, Michel Barnier, accurately forecast, Brexit has been a lose-lose equation for both sides.

However, the summit also illustrated that the toxic British politics around any move to rejoin have not gone away. Once again, the issue would dominate the agenda if the choice were put to a referendum or made the centrepiece of the next general election.

Burnham is correct to reopen a national debate on the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU and to put the option of membership back on the table. As ever, there is a domestic political calculation in his gamble. It helps Labour win back voters lost to the Greens and the Liberal Democrats in this year’s local elections and to mobilise pro-European youth support. He may also reckon that working-class voters lost to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK care more about cost of living issues than they do about Europe.

Farage, who built his career on stoking English nationalism and conflating EU membership with uncontrolled immigration, was quick to warn of a betrayal of the British people’s democratic 2016 vote by political elites. The line of the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, that Burnham had been made to accept an unfair deal, in which the UK will have to pay too much for too little return, was a telling indicator of the epic battles over money that lie ahead.

Signals from Brussels before the summit suggested the EU would probably not insist that the UK join the euro or the Schengen area of passport-free travel. But it was equally clear that Margaret Thatcher’s EU budget rebate, won after an epic battle in 1984, would not be returning.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

It’s not clear that the UK’s political class or its powerful Treasury mandarins have accepted the fundamental pay-to-play logic of either partial access to the EU market or full membership. The widely held denial that Britain needs to pay for market access led to the collapse of negotiations last year to join the EU’s Security Action for Europe programme of soft loans for joint defence projects. Brussels shares responsibility for that failure by pitching an unrealistically high entry fee.

While many EU countries would welcome the UK back for geopolitical as well as economic reasons, especially in northern and central Europe, it is less clear that France, which since the presidency of Charles de Gaulle has seen Britain as aligned with US interests, would be so keen. If the hard-right nationalist Marine Le Pen, who applauded Brexit, wins next year’s French presidential election, she has vowed to reduce Paris’s contribution to EU coffers and may want to charge London a high price.

The prospect of an EU in which hard-right national populists, less supportive of Ukraine and more friendly in some cases towards Russia, enjoy growing influence may also make rejoining less politically attractive to a UK that is trying to shake off a decade of its own national populism.

I would love to see the UK back in the EU, where it always belonged as a European nation. But I’m not sure I will see it in my lifetime.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

Our 30 Easiest Thanksgiving Recipes for Busy People

The New York Times September 28, 2026

These simple recipes for roast turkey, stuffing, pie crust and more will set you up for a spectacular meal.

By Margaux Laskey and Sharon Attia

Published Nov. 6, 2020 Updated Sept. 28, 2026

Between work deadlines and family obligations, holiday travel or hosting relatives, spending hours cooking Thanksgiving dinner can feel impossible. But there’s no need to panic. Plan ahead, keep it simple and delegate when necessary. Below are 30 foolproof recipes to guarantee a memorable meal for you and your guests.

Depending on the size of your crowd, serve this succulent turkey breast from Sarah DiGregorio as a simple substitute for a whole roast turkey. The herby dry brine helps ensure moistness and flavor, so don’t skip it. The recipe tester called results “really, really good. So juicy, tender and not at all dry.”

Recipe: Slow-Cooker Turkey Breast

Is it stuffing, or is it dressing? Whatever you call it, it’s arguably the best part of the Thanksgiving table. This simple version from Lidey Heuck works with almost any kind of bread, even the store-bought stuffing cubes. (Just make sure you get the plain, unseasoned kind.)

Recipe: Easy Herb Stuffing

More than the sum of their parts, these potatoes from David Tanis are extremely simple to make, but deeply satisfying. Boiling the potatoes with eight garlic cloves and then mashing them with olive oil, some cooking liquid and plenty of salt results in the “lightest and fluffiest mashed potatoes ever made.”

Recipe: Olive Oil Mashed Potatoes

According to Melissa Clark, brussels sprouts are one of the best vegetables you can make in an air fryer because the little leaves turn brittle and delightfully crunchy. In this recipe, you get the bonus addition of garlic slivers, which turn into flavorful chips. Dress everything with balsamic vinegar simmered until thick and then spiked with lime juice and soy sauce for freshness and umami.

Recipe: Air-Fryer Brussels Sprouts With Garlic, Balsamic and Soy

Store-bought pizza dough infused with loads of softened butter makes these rolls from Melissa Clark both fast and flavorful. The trick to a fluffy, pillowy texture is to cover the pan with foil straight out of the oven, allowing the batch to steam as it cools.

Recipe: Easy Parker House Rolls

Gather your cranberries, orange juice, orange zest and sugar. Simmer until the berries burst. That’s it. If you’d like, Sam Sifton said you could add an allspice clove or two, a little freshly grated ginger or a handful of chopped nuts.

Recipe: Cranberry Sauce

For a lovely sweet-and-sour side dish to serve as a lively counterpart to the rest of the brown foods on the table, try this Priya Krishna recipe for butternut squash gently stewed with spices, tomatoes and brown sugar.

Recipe: Kaddu (Sweet and Sour Butternut Squash)

Save yourself the stress of trying to make gravy under the hungry eyes of your waiting guests. This one from Mark Bittman can be made ahead, so all you have to do is heat it over low heat and add some drippings from the turkey before transferring it to Grandma’s gravy boat.

Recipe: Make-Ahead Gravy

In the category of bright and snappy, serve up a big bowl of green beans like these from Kia Damon. Skip the big pots of boiling water, and cook the beans in a little butter and olive oil, so the beans will release their natural water content in a smart combination of steaming and sautéing.

Recipe: Sautéed Green Beans

Julia Moskin’s brilliant recipe has over 15,000 ratings and is easy as can be. Whiz together some cottage cheese, milk and seasonings in a blender, combine with uncooked pasta and grated Cheddar, and then bake until golden and bubbly.

Recipe: Creamy Macaroni and Cheese

“This was a bright and crunchy alternative to all usual heavy dishes and it was great in turkey leftover sandwiches the next day!” one reader wrote about Hetty Lui McKinnon’s autumnal salad. The 20-minute recipe features shaved brussels sprouts, apples, shallots, pecorino cheese and slivered almonds in a sweet-tart maple-mustard dressing.

Recipe: Crunchy Brussels Sprouts and Apple Slaw

“This pie got rave reviews at our Thanksgiving!” one happy reader wrote about Melissa Clark’s much-praised pumpkin pie. Yes, you can roast and purée your own butternut squash, but the canned pumpkin purée (not pumpkin pie filling) will do just fine. The spice combination and two tablespoons of brandy (budget tip: buy an airplane bottle) are what make it really special.

Recipe: Brandied Pumpkin Pie

Ina Garten’s festive holiday drink can be made quickly: Throw dried cranberries, cranberry juice cocktail, good vodka, Triple Sec and some ice into a large shaker and shake when guests arrive. It’s the perfect accompaniment to the annual “going around the table and sharing what you’re thankful for.”

Recipe: Cranberry Martinis

For a foolproof, 45-minute (really!) roast turkey, try Mark Bittman’s spatchcock version. Cut out the backbone — or ask your butcher to do it for you — and spread the bird out flat before roasting. If you want an organic, farm-raised bird, be sure to place your order a few weeks in advance, and invest in both oven and meat thermometers. (Accurate oven temperature is a key to success here.)

Recipe: Roast Spatchcock Turkey

“This dish was a big hit at our traditional Thanksgiving dinner, loved by adults and toddlers alike!” one reader wrote about Yossy Arefi’s sheet-pan side. Carrots get a head start in the oven, to make sure they get all nice and caramelized, and the kale is sliced thinly and massaged with oil and salt before cooking.

Recipe: Easy Roasted Carrots and Crispy Kale

In Puerto Rico, yuca is one of the most popular viandas, a regional word for starchy fruits and vegetables, such as plantain and taro. It has a subtly sweet and somewhat nutty flavor that’s complemented nicely by a garlicky citrus mojo dressing in this recipe from Von Diaz.

Recipe: Yuca con Mojo

Swirl cranberry sauce into a light and tangy mixture of whipped cream and Greek yogurt, and you’ve got yourself an easy, cooling dessert to finish off the big meal. For a little crunch, Ali Slagle recommends pairing it with gingersnaps, or adding a dollop atop slices of pie.

Recipe: Cranberries and Cream

Naz Deravian’s buttermilk biscuits come together quickly in one bowl — no rolling required. The batter is spread over a pool of melted butter in a baking pan, which is where the name comes from. While the biscuits bake, they absorb all the buttery goodness and crisp up around the edges.

Recipe: Butter Swim Biscuits

An artfully arranged platter of deviled eggs is always a welcome — maybe a little nostalgic? — addition to the holiday table. This recipe, which was adapted from “U. S. A. Cookbook,” by Sheila Lukins, an author of the Silver Palate cookbooks that were popular in the 1980s and ’90s, is pretty much perfect.

Recipe: Classic Deviled Eggs

You could go to all the trouble of mashing a bunch of sweet potatoes and covering them with a blanket of marshmallows, but it’s not necessary. In this simple recipe from Lidey Heuck, cubed (peeled or not) sweet potatoes are roasted on a sheet pan until crisp-edged and soft-centered.

Recipe: Roasted Sweet Potatoes

When you’re cooking what feels like a zillion homemade things for Thanksgiving dinner, a bag of frozen hash browns is your best friend. Also known as funeral potatoes, this creamy, cheesy casserole from Naz Deravian is made by combining the hash browns with cheese, sour cream and homemade cream of chicken soup, and then baking until brown-edged and bubbly.

Recipe: Hash Brown Casserole

Broccoli roasts beautifully in the air fryer, and frees up precious oven space. Eleanore Park’s five-ingredient, 15-minute recipe gives the veg a hit of umami from soy sauce, which is bolstered in the high heat, resulting in nutty, salty and deeply caramelized flavor.

Recipe: Air-Fryer Broccoli

Do not fear making your own pie crust. Melissa Clark’s recipe is hard to mess up and works with practically whatever kind of pie you like on your Thanksgiving table.

Recipe: Pie Crust

For perfectly moist and tender meat, brine your turkey first. This recipe is for a classic wet brine, which was adapted from an old Yankee Magazine recipe for a traditional New England roast turkey. (We also have a dry-brined turkey recipe.)

Recipe: Turkey Brine

Like a fresher, deconstructed version of classic green bean casserole, this dish from Kay Chun features green beans simmered in a classic flour-butter-broth gravy swirled through with miso, sour cream and lemon juice. Top with the classic French fried onions, of course.

Recipe: Miso Gravy-Smothered Green Beans

Salty, crispy and cheesy, these petite appetizers from Melissa Knific are precisely what you’ll want to nibble on while you sip an Old Fashioned as the turkey rests. They’re not at all sophisticated, and that’s part of the charm: Squares of white bread are spread with a savory combination of butter, Cheddar, egg, heavy cream, Worcestershire sauce, garlic powder and dry mustard, and then baked until warm and browned on top.

Recipe: Cheese Dreams

Real talk: Samantha Seneviratne’s apple crumble tastes just as good as pie, and it’s so much easier to make. When shopping for apples, select a combination of tart and sweet, like Granny Smith and McIntosh. They’ll cook and soften at slightly different rates, which will make the filling jammy and pleasantly firm all at once.

Recipe: Apple Crumble

If you love pecan pie, but the thought of eating an entire piece after the feast seems impossible, serve these treats, adapted from Hannah Kaminsky, a columnist at VegNews Magazine, for an adorable and slightly boozy finish to the meal. Combine pecans, graham cracker crumbs, brown sugar, maple syrup, bourbon and vanilla, shape them into balls, and then dip them into dark chocolate. Brown the butter first, as some readers do, for a nuttier, toastier flavor.

Recipe: Pecan Pie Truffles

Hungry guests are not happy guests. While you put the finishing touches on the meal, set out a platter of something that isn’t too filling and that tastes completely different from the rest of the menu, like Alexa Weibel’s bright, spicy marinated feta with herbs and peppercorns. (It takes just a few minutes to set up the night before.)

Recipe: Marinated Feta With Herbs and Peppercorns

Alexa Weibel took baked Brie and brilliantly made it into a vegetarian Thanksgiving centerpiece packed with roasted butternut squash, seared mushrooms, herbed brussels sprouts and tangy red onions. Cook the individual components in the days leading up to the holiday to make assembly and baking a breeze.

Recipe: Baked Brie and Caramelized Vegetable Pie

25 Easy, Five-Ingredient Thanksgiving Recipes

Washington Memo

In a new memoir, the most celebrated journalist of his era finally tells his own story. It was “liberating,” he said in an interview. “Nothing is hidden here.”

Credit... Jared Soares for The New York Times

Supported by

By Peter Baker

Like many Washington reporters, Peter Baker has both worked with and competed against Bob Woodward. The former was easier.

He has interviewed presidents and kings and spies and generals. Along the way, he has extracted some of the most revelatory and enduring stories of the past half-century about the power players who run Washington. So what would Bob Woodward ask if he were interviewing Bob Woodward?

He was sitting in the sunroom of his Georgetown house on a bright autumn day when the question was put to him. He paused a moment before answering. “What is the internal turmoil?” he suggested. Which sounds like a good question. But what would his answer be? Mr. Woodward has long been more comfortable asking the questions than answering.

Perhaps the most renowned journalist of the modern age, Mr. Woodward has turned the lens on himself after 55 years of examining others, with a new memoir called “Secrets” recounting the story of his celebrated career. It may not exactly be a tell-all, but it is a tell-much and has already set Washington buzzing about the revelations it promises when it is published on Tuesday.

For the first time, he names names, disclosing the identities of many sources he has spent a career guarding, either because they have since died or because he obtained their permission. During Watergate, he reveals, some of his sources were President Richard M. Nixon’s own lawyers, who did not think much of their client. He divulges the names of five Supreme Court justices who talked for a book on the court. He identifies cabinet secretaries, White House aides and other officials who whispered secrets over the years.

For Mr. Woodward, the 83-year-old chronicler of modern Washington, this has all turned out to be a “liberating” experience. Not just because at long last he shows his homework, but because he has confronted, not always that willingly, his own story as well: how a boy from Wheaton, Ill., ended up at The Washington Post, found himself in an underground parking garage with a source nicknamed Deep Throat and changed history.

“I can tell the story. I don’t have to leave anything out,” Mr. Woodward said in a lengthy interview at the four-story, 19th-century home where he has hosted the prominent and powerful princelings of the nation’s capital. “Nothing is hidden here. Nothing is hidden. There’s not some story about some information I got from somebody. It’s all laid out there.”

Some of the most illuminating parts of the book hint at that “internal turmoil” he mentions. He writes about how at age 8 he began noticing troubles in his parents’ marriage and how at age 11 he discovered his mother kissing his father’s best friend. He learned that his parents were getting divorced by rifling through his father’s sock drawer where he found a letter mentioning it.

He writes about the fire that gutted the family home when he was a teenager and left him so frightened that to this day he keeps fire extinguishers stashed throughout his house — “at least a dozen,” according to his researcher Claire McMullen. He writes about how unnerved he was as a young Navy officer aboard a nuclear-armed ship with access to codes that could unleash Armageddon.

All of which taught him to be “a snoop” and “a catastrophic thinker,” as he puts it, to assume that there are always secrets and that the worst can happen. “I have lived since age 8 with suspicion about everything,” he said. And so a career was built. He would ferret out official secrets. He would explore worst-case scenarios. “In a way, it’s finding the sock drawer of history,” he said.

The process of writing a memoir after all these years had a predictably teeth-pulling quality to it for a man reluctant to talk about himself. The people closest to him kept pushing him to open up, including his wife, Elsa Walsh, herself an accomplished journalist; Carl Bernstein, the other half of the famed Watergate duo; and Scott Armstrong, his lifelong friend and former reporting partner.

“I said: ‘You’ve got to go deep. This is really the time to do it,’” Mr. Bernstein recalled. “‘The fabric of your life is incomplete unless you marry up both the deeply personal and the professional.’”

Ms. McMullen, a writer who has worked with Mr. Woodward on three previous books, made a point of recording their lunchtime conversations to try to get beyond all the interview memos he kept. The first time they sat down to talk about the memoir, she asked him a question he used to ask others: What was his first childhood memory?

She pored through many of the 500 boxes he has kept over the years containing not just memos of practically every interview of importance going back to the 1970s but other memorabilia and arcana collected over time. Nothing, it seems, was not saved. “Was this a historical sock,” she recalled asking of one discovery, “or just a sock?”

She took to relying on her own sources. “When I couldn’t get through to Bob on getting him to talk about something personal,” she said, “I’d call Carl and get him to tell me.”

Among the personal episodes recounted in the book is the rift between Mr. Woodward and Mr. Bernstein. When they followed up their book “All the President’s Men” with “The Final Days,” about the end of Nixon’s presidency, Mr. Woodward felt that Mr. Bernstein was not carrying his weight. (“It’s true,” Mr. Bernstein says now.) For a while, they stopped speaking.

When they finally made up, they concocted a “boy’s fairy tale” of an idea in which Mr. Woodward would take over as The Post’s Metro editor and Mr. Bernstein would become the Style editor. Then, when Benjamin C. Bradlee retired as executive editor, the two would run the newsroom together. When the idea made its way to the publisher, Katharine Graham, she is said to have quickly shot it down. “Are you out of your mind?” she reportedly exclaimed, adding that the two needed management, not the other way around.

Even so, there are limits to how much Mr. Woodward reveals. He is not by nature an introspective man, and some will undoubtedly finish the book wanting more. At some point, it becomes a recitation of all the important interviews he conducted with presidents and potentates, drawn often in great detail from the memos he kept. This is a record that historians will draw from for years to come, but it is not soul baring.

Mr. Woodward knows the criticism. He has heard it all before. He depends too much on anonymous sources. He has grown too close to power. He treats those who talk with him better than those who do not. He is not a particularly lyrical or analytical writer and does not put his inside-the-room reporting into context. A “stenographer to the rich and powerful,” as the writer Christopher Hitchens once acerbically put it.

To all of this now comes the latest criticism that in “Secrets” he finally identifies sources who have since died. While that has been his practice in the past, it has prompted a new debate about whether the promise of confidentiality survives death in the way that, say, attorney-client privilege does.

Donald E. Graham, the former publisher of The Post and Mrs. Graham’s son, came to Mr. Woodward’s defense recently against the negative reviews his books have received over the years. “They were being reviewed by journalists much less successful than Woodward and they reek of jealousy,” Mr. Graham wrote online.

“In the old days, they typically said, ‘How does Woodward dare to tell us all this astonishing stuff and not name his sources?’” Mr. Graham went on. “In this book, Bob DOES name several now-deceased people who were his sources over a lifetime. His reward is a review and many social-media comments asking how he can dare to name dead sources! Can’t win, I guess.”

Mr. Woodward, once played on the big screen by Robert Redford, concedes that he travels in more rarefied circles today than when he was a 20-something rookie investigating a rogue president. He has written about 11 presidents, interviewed 16 defense secretaries, runs into Supreme Court justices at parties and lives around the corner from cabinet officers.

He is, it is true, now part of the world he covers. But he argues that he uses that access to unearth information that would otherwise remain unknown. “Part of that world does not mean they set the terms,” he said. “I set the terms. And the terms are, I want to know what happened.”

Mr. Bernstein said Mr. Woodward had pulled secrets “out of the black hole of the modern presidency” that no one else could obtain and that have set a foundation for history. “People can argue over it, what the truth and the context is,” he said. “But it’s out there as information that never would have gotten out. And there is nothing comparable in the history of the country.”

That’s not to say Mr. Woodward has no regrets. With hindsight, he believes he missed the mark in “The Agenda,” his first book on President Bill Clinton, by overemphasizing the chaos of a White House that ultimately produced peace and prosperity. He acknowledges that he, like other reporters, was not skeptical enough about claims that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction before President George W. Bush’s invasion. He believes he did not take Covid-19 seriously enough at first.

But perhaps most of all, Mr. Woodward said, he wishes he had recognized the danger that he now believes President Trump poses and had done more before his first election in 2016 to explore what kind of president he would be. “I should have dropped everything and focused on Trump completely,” Mr. Woodward said.

The Trump presidency has been so extreme that it has propelled Mr. Woodward out of his traditional journalistic neutrality. In a new foreword to the 50th anniversary edition of “All the President’s Men” in 2022, he and Mr. Bernstein portrayed Mr. Trump as a greater threat to democracy than Nixon had been.

In the interview this month, Mr. Woodward, who has published five books about Mr. Trump, said the war against Iran demonstrated the danger. “Who starts wars?” he asked. “Tyrants start wars. It’s absolutely mind boggling, and it is a danger to the country.”

He traced his concerns about Mr. Trump to his own Navy days aboard a nuclear-armed ship. “I’m haunted by the danger we are in, having somebody in the presidency with that authority, unchecked, unmonitored,” he said. “It’s frightening. And I go back to that time as a 22-year-old seeing exactly how nuclear war can be started by a president.”

Mr. Woodward, the catastrophic thinker, added: “It keeps me up at night.” And he further added: “The impact of Trump is danger, danger, danger.”

All of which could lead to a little internal turmoil.

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.
