Trump Orders Army to Pause Planned Ammunition Explosion in Iowa

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump said on Monday that the Army should wait to detonate a cache of dangerous explosives until a legal challenge is decided. His comments added to a confusing situation.

By Quinn Glabicki and Hiroko Tabuchi

Quinn Glabicki reported from southeastern Iowa near the blast site and Hiroko Tabuchi from New York City.

President Trump on Monday ordered the Army to pause its plan to detonate a stockpile of unstable explosives at an Iowa facility, throwing uncertainty into a situation that has caused confusion and alarm in the surrounding communities.

The Army maintains that it needs to blow up five tons of lead azide, a dangerous material that has been stored for decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa but has deteriorated so much, it risks spontaneous explosion.

The planned detonation threatens to send a plume of toxic lead dust over local communities, livestock and farmland, forcing some residents to either evacuate or try to seal themselves in their homes.

The Army first planned to detonate the stockpile on Friday, giving much of the public just a few days’ notice. After an uproar and a court challenge, officials pushed the controlled blast to Monday, then to Tuesday and again to Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving.

But on Monday afternoon, President Trump mixed it up further, saying he has instructed the Army to wait until the legal challenge is decided.

The president also wrote on his social media site that he would not allow the detonation unless Rob Sand, the incoming Iowa governor, also approved. And, Mr. Trump wrote, “If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and long term situation.”

Mr. Sand, the first Democrat to be elected governor in Iowa in 20 years, could not be immediately reached for comment. He has said the health of Iowa residents should be protected and has been critical of the way the Army has handled the matter.

“The situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been,” Mr. Sand wrote on X on Sunday evening. He asked why the Army had rejected alternatives and delayed action, and was now rushing to detonation. “Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” Mr. Sand wrote.

The American Lung Association is advising people to stay indoors for 24 to 48 hours after the blast, at one of the year’s busiest travel times. Local residents are studying weather forecasts to figure out where the toxic plume of lead dust may fall. Scientists have been taking soil samples ahead of the blast, in order to establish a base line for lead levels. Farmers are trying to figure out how to shield their livestock.

“We’re feeling less confident that anybody knows what they’re doing,” said Jim Plate, a retired teacher who lives with his wife about two miles south of the Army facility’s fence line. “We’re getting very frustrated by whatever the heck is going on.”

Some elected leaders are calling for investigations into how a seemingly avoidable crisis developed.

Iowa’s senator-elect Josh Turek, a Democrat, also said on X that the public deserved answers as to “why the U. S. Army’s communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning.”

In a statement, an Army spokesman said planning a controlled detonation had allowed it “to communicate and work with local, state, and federal leaders to implement public safety measures to the greatest extent possible.” The government had also taken “deliberate steps to minimize and contain the blast and airborne dust, including carefully evaluating weather conditions for the safest possible conditions,” and had adopted safety measures to minimize dust and debris, the spokesman said.

Impending colder weather in Iowa adds to the urgency, the Army said, because freezing temperatures could fracture the unstable crystals inside the barrels, potentially triggering an uncontrolled explosion, which could be far more dangerous than a planned detonation.

But even a controlled detonation is expected to produce a plume of lead dust stretching as far as 60 miles, over communities, farms and the Mississippi River watershed.

Lead is a neurotoxin and there are no safe levels for exposure. It poses a particular danger to children and pregnant women. Lead can interfere with fetal brain development, cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm and increase the risk of premature births or miscarriage.

On Sunday, a team of scientists fanned out across the rural farmland south of the Army’s facility. Equipped with sensitive air monitors, plexiglass and filters that capture airborne particles, they set up their gear in backyards and placed soil samples in plastic bags with gloved fingers.

“We’ve never done anything like this before,” said David Cwiertny, director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination at the University of Iowa. “The only other place where you can get data like this is the middle of a war,” said Ezazul Haque, an environmental toxicologist from John Jay College, who arrived from New York City last week to study the plume.

Dr. Cwiertny said there is potential for “significantly high concentrations” closer to the blast, and that any lead dispersal would be dictated by the amount of lead spread by the detonation and the size of the particles.

“I don’t know that we have a good sense. I would hope that the Army does,” Dr. Cwiertny said. With the delay to Wednesday, the scientists are once again repositioning their equipment, he said.

The path the plume will take depends on the wind, Dr. Cwiertny said, standing over an array of sensors and instruments near fields of harvested corn south of the Army facility. And without word from the Army on the timing of the detonation, he said, the scientists were left needing to account for different scenarios. “We’re flying blind,” he said.

The Army has said that it would clean up any soil contamination that exceeds federal thresholds and that residents can file claims for resulting damage. The Iowa Farm Bureau has been advising its members to take soil samples before and after the blast for liability purposes. In a message to members, Patrick Wall, a beef specialist, urged farmers to also remove cattle from grazing areas and from ponds and other drinking-water sources, and if possible, move them to indoor shelter.

Last year, the Trump administration tripled the threshold of lead that triggers urgent government soil excavation at contaminated residential sites. The Environmental Protection Agency also raised the level of lead in children’s blood used to set cleanup goals. The changes could make it harder for nearby residents and farmers to secure government-led cleanup or pursue contamination claims.

The E. P. A. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

About two miles south of the Army’s fence line, Jim and Krys Plate thought they’d be in the clear when the Army planned the explosion of lead azide for Friday, when the winds were blowing northward. Then the blast was delayed, and they found the home they share with their two teenage daughters potentially at the center of a plume of lead dust.

“I’m terrified,” said Ms. Plate, a retired second grade teacher, during an interview on Sunday. “Everybody knows that the acceptable level of lead is zero.”

“We didn’t have any communication from anybody officially,” Mr. Plate said. “This could have been done way better.”

He said that social media has been a swirl of unreliable information, and on Sunday evening the couple was unsure whether or not the blast would come the next day.

“I’m really angry about this. I feel like we’re guinea pigs,” Ms. Plate said.

The family is planning to seal their doors with towels and stay inside for at least 24 hours after the blast and into Thanksgiving, which they plan to celebrate at home.

While agriculture officials were telling farmers to move their livestock indoors, “That’s literally not possible,” said Steve Lucie, a fifth-generation cattle rancher in Hancock County Ill., across the state border from the Iowa blast site. Regarding the potential for a plume of lead dust overhead, he said, “We’re just going to have to weather it if it happens to come over our farm.”

“We don’t trust the government much anymore,” Mr. Lucie said. “Maybe this is why.”

Murray McBride, an emeritus professor at the Cornell College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, said lead dust could settle on leafy crops such as lettuce, making them hazardous to eat. Some of the residue might wash off, he said, but not all of it.

He added, however, that if lead settled on soybean or corn plants, he did not expect it to reach the edible seeds or grains. And while cattle could be harmed if they ingested enough lead-contaminated dust from forage, animals showing acute poisoning symptoms would be an extreme case. Lead, which is relatively immobile and insoluble, was also unlikely to get into the meat or milk, he said.

Still, lead deposited on soil would likely remain near the surface, and if testing showed elevated levels afterward, the surface soil would need to be removed or covered with clean soil. But there were many uncertainties, he said. “There’s no way for me to predict how many grams of this lead would be deposited. So we just don’t know the extent of it.”

A local pastor, Chad Savage, planned to open his church for people who wished to shelter during the blast, whenever it came. “Communication was lacking, and that causes panic,” he said.

Over the weekend, local officials said they had remained in the dark.

“We’re asking the Army, what is going on?” said Laura Liegois, the city manager in Fort Madison, Iowa, a city south of the facility where about 10,000 people live. “What does that plume look like? Will it hit us?” she said.

Quinn Glabicki is a climate reporter for The New York Times and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

Jensen Huang’s Return Shows the Lengths Trump Will Go to Keep A. I. Booming

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

President Trump intervened on behalf of the returning Nvidia chief in a bid to boost a key company driving the stock market.

By Tony RommSydney Ember and Colby Smith

Tony Romm reported from Washington. Sydney Ember and Colby Smith reported from New York.

For President Trump, the stock market has long been a favored barometer for his economic agenda, one that he frequently promotes to showcase how artificial intelligence is booming on his watch.

So when scandal began to consume the chip-making giant Nvidia — toppling its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and sending financial markets into a tailspin — Mr. Trump quickly intervened. He rose to Mr. Huang’s defense and leveraged the muscle of the Oval Office to push for the embattled leader’s reinstatement.

Mr. Trump succeeded. He helped to secure Mr. Huang’s return by Monday, sending Nvidia’s stock price soaring while putting an end to a days-long market rout. In the process, the president demonstrated the lengths he was willing to go — and the risks he was ready to take — to keep both A. I. and a dependent stock market humming.

As Mr. Trump would later explain on social media, Nvidia needed Mr. Huang, and the United States needed Nvidia, to “ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” The missteps of an embattled executive appeared to matter less to Mr. Trump than the economic losses that he saw on the horizon if Nvidia remained in peril.

Nvidia has a unique role in the A. I. ecosystem. It is both a pre-eminent chipmaker and a key financier for technological development, using its deep pockets and powerful semiconductors to backstop a wave of coming A. I. investment.

So the return of Mr. Huang seemed to renew a sense of exuberance on Wall Street, which may have carried a direct benefit for the president, who has previously reported holding millions of dollars in Nvidia investments. Still, Mr. Trump’s advocacy for Mr. Huang nonetheless reignited fears about his growth-at-all-costs mentality, and the extent to which his actions reflect an economy that hinges too much on the performance of a single industry.

“There is real concern about how much everyone is resting on Nvidia,” said Nidhi Hegde, the executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project, a left-leaning group. The company had become “too big to fail” in the eyes of the administration, she said.

Even Mr. Trump appeared to acknowledge the extent to which the markets had factored into his vigorous and unorthodox defense of Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia earlier this month after allegations surfaced of multiple affairs, including one with a woman who U. S. intelligence believes is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Asked if the stock market influenced his decision, Mr. Trump told CNBC: “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term.”

For Mr. Trump, the extraordinary lobbying campaign on behalf of Mr. Huang underscored the extent to which he has staked the economy on A. I. Even as many Americans are uneasy about the technology, Mr. Trump remains one of its fiercest defenders, and he has consistently portrayed the race to develop the technology as an existential struggle between superpowers for economic and military supremacy.

As a result, the president has largely adopted a hands-off approach to A. I., as staggering sums pour into its development. Investors and major technology giants could plow as much as $10.3 trillion into A. I. between 2025 and 2032, some estimates show, helping to buoy a U. S. economy that is tempered by high prices, sluggish hiring and geopolitical discord.

Among the big spenders is Nvidia, whose efforts have earned praise from Mr. Trump. The president has cheered on Nvidia’s stock price, and helped secure Mr. Huang a frequent spot at the White House and on Capitol Hill.

When Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia earlier this month, Mr. Trump praised his leadership and recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple executive, take over the embattled chipmaker. As markets soured over the turnover in Nvidia’s ranks — eventually dragging down major indexes with it — the president then ratcheted up his calls on the company to reinstate its old chief.

“It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U. S. A.,” the president said at one point on social media.

It fit a pattern for Mr. Trump, who has staged some of his most aggressive policy interventions in response to moments of unrest in financial markets. That included revising his punishing global tariffs, as investors grew spooked over a damaging, endless trade war, and claiming progress in talks with Iran whenever the war pummeled Wall Street.

But Mr. Trump’s successful lobbying on behalf of Mr. Huang proved especially troublesome for lawmakers, including some Republicans. While the president declared that “the U. S. government does not possess any evidence that he engaged in any unlawful conduct,” some members of Congress still cited national security risks in Mr. Huang’s return. Skeptics of A. I. also saw the move as a sign that the White House had become too cozy with the tech industry.

“This looks like a decision to protect the wallets of Wall Street fat cats while putting profits ahead of our national security,” added Amy Kremer, a former leader of the Tea Party movement who is now chairwoman of Humans First, which has called for limits on data center development, in a statement.

Some economists also saw signs of a troubling dependency that would warp markets, as investors came to see Nvidia as a business that had won the favor of the president. The concerns echoed the complaints that greeted efforts by the Trump administration to take ownership stakes in private companies, including Intel.

“We want capital flowing to companies for commercial reasons,” said Scott Lincicome, the vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, a libertarian-leaning think tank. He said that investment should not follow “because they have the government’s backing or a politician’s backing, who might be making decisions not based on the commercial interests or even the national interest, but political ones.”

Mr. Trump’s intervention also arrived at a moment when policymakers across Washington were beginning to grapple openly with the extent to which the U. S. economy had become overly reliant on A. I. investment.

The concern was evident at the last meeting of the Federal Reserve. Nearly every one of the 19 officials there in October mentioned the potential fallout if A. I. investments ended up disappointing investors, who have poured billions of dollars into funding the build out, according to recently released minutes of the gathering.

Policymakers homed in on the risks stemming from the “complex and opaque financing structures” that A. I. companies are increasingly relying upon to fuel their growth, the October record showed. Raising the stakes, the Fed’s latest financial stability report, which was released earlier this month, overwhelmingly cited A. I. as the biggest threat in the eyes of market participants the central bank surveyed.

Those concerns predate the tumult facing Nvidia, reflecting investors’ continued uncertainty that they will be able to monetize their eye-popping investments into A. I. infrastructure. Against that backdrop, Shivaram Rajgopal, an accounting professor at the Columbia Business School, described Nvidia as “almost like a state-influenced enterprise,” one in which the government under Mr. Trump had established itself as a large stakeholder.

“The perception is that it’s too big to fail, and Jensen Huang is too important to fire,” he said.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Sydney Ember covers the U. S. economy for The Times.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump decided he wanted to do whatever he could to help Jensen Huang get his old job back, two people familiar with the matter said.

By Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan

White House reporters

Jensen Huang was reappointed as chief executive of Nvidia after President Trump set in motion several days of maneuvering to provide the company’s board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Late last week, Mr. Trump decided he wanted to do whatever he could to help Mr. Huang get his old job back, the people said, despite concerns from his own national security agencies about Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman they believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset and who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations.

On Sunday night, Nvidia’s board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.

In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang’s biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump’s key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.

Representatives for Mr. Huang and Mr. Vance declined to comment. A spokesman for Nvidia did not respond to an email seeking comment.

On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia’s action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company “made the correct and proper decision.” The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U. S. economy.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Mr. Trump wrote.

Mr. Trump has sought to separate Mr. Huang from the investigations into chip smuggling that his government is pursuing. As The New York Times has previously reported, the U. S. intelligence community has collected evidence that a Chinese woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was having a secret affair with the Nvidia chief executive. But the Trump administration did not give Mr. Huang a so-called defensive briefing, a heads up that he was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

The Singapore-based company that Ms. Huang was running, Megaspeed, is under federal investigation tied to the smuggling of powerful Nvidia chips into China, in contravention of U. S. export laws.

Mr. Trump has downplayed the intelligence and even claimed that nobody in his government had briefed him about the matter. In fact, advisers to Mr. Trump, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, briefed him at least twice about the national security concerns surrounding Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang.

Mr. Huang admitted earlier this month to infidelities after initially casting his dealings with Ms. Huang as a business relationship. He also had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, The Times reported shortly before he resigned.

“The United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security,” Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Monday, soon after Nvidia announced Mr. Huang’s return. “The attorney general of the United States has confirmed that the U. S. government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

In a brief telephone interview on Monday morning, Mr. Trump exulted in the decision by the board. “Did I do a good job last night?” he asked.

“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” the president said. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it actually. The stock is up.”

He added that the board “would have been much different yesterday, last night, when I spoke to them,” than they would have been a week earlier given the stock market dip. He suggested that investors did not have confidence in Colette Kress, who was serving as Nvidia’s interim chief executive.

The president remarked that Ms. Kress “gave a rough interview” with Jim Cramer of CNBC.

Mr. Trump declined to answer questions about whether he believes that Ms. Huang was working with Chinese intelligence agencies. He also declined to discuss what he himself had been told by Mr. Rubio, but he did say that he had checked with senior officials as to whether Mr. Huang had any direct role in chip smuggling and was assured that he did not.

“All those guys knew about it,” Mr. Trump said, specifically citing Attorney General Todd Blanche and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence. “I had to go to them before I recommended this. Look, I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted for, for whatever.”

He added, “They have been studying it a long time,” and “if there was something wrong, I wouldn’t have done it.”

He emphasized that Mr. Huang, in his view, made a mistake by stepping down.

“I wouldn’t have handled it the way he handled it,” Mr. Trump told The Times of Mr. Huang, referring to his decision to step down. “The Peyton Place part,” the president said, a reference to the 1960s-era soap opera based on a novel about a town roiled in constant sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier because that got the attention,” he said. “You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.”

Mr. Trump also said that Mr. Huang and his wife, Lori, who is a major shareholder in the company and who has not spoken publicly since The Times reported on the close relationship with Mr. Huang and Alice Huang, have “worked it out.”

“He’s got a very, very, very good wife, and they’ve worked it out,” Mr. Trump said. “She’s a fantastic woman.”

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Jonathan Swan is a White House reporter for The Times, covering the administration of Donald J. Trump. Contact him securely on Signal: @jonathan.941

The MAHA Moms Are Disillusioned

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Julia Belluz

Ms. Belluz is a contributing Opinion writer covering health, nutrition and chronic illness.

On Aug. 23, 2024, when Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced he would suspend his presidential campaign and endorsed President Trump, he vowed that within two years, “we will watch chronic disease burden lift dramatically.” His Make America Healthy Again initiative would clean toxic chemicals from the environment and food supply and battle the corporations “mass-poisoning all of our children and our adults.”

These promises, from an environmental lawyer turned vaccine skeptic, became the glue that bound a motley coalition of thousands of concerned Americans — farmers, food activists, Covid contrarians, wellness influencers and moms — under the MAHA tent.

Two years later, Mr. Kennedy has accomplished little of what he set out to do. One self-described “MAHA mom” and former volunteer Kennedy campaign adviser, Tiffany Cianci, tracked 42 key Trump administration MAHA promises and found that thirty-seven were broken. People noticed. Americans were twice as likely to say the Trump administration’s actions made the country’s health worse than to say they made it better, according to a recent poll by Ipsos. By Oct. 14, the movement’s main political action committee had raised little more than $3 million of its $100 million target for Republican candidates. The midterm elections wiped out many MAHA-backed Republican contenders and champions in Congress.

And yet it would be a mistake to count MAHA out. Instead, it’s time for the Democrats to do what Mr. Kennedy has so far failed to: make America healthier.

The Trump administration, with Mr. Kennedy as health secretary, has relaxed or eliminated regulations and funding for clean air and water, canceled subsidies for healthy food in schools and food banks and spread misinformation that likely contributed to vaccine-preventable outbreaks (the United States just lost its measles elimination status), all the while taking a wrecking ball to federal health agencies and the American science enterprise.

The health secretary’s failure is an opportunity for the Democrats who just took Congress. They should not dismiss MAHA as the anti-vaccine fever dream of one man. The movement Mr. Kennedy brought together may be fractured, and the brand may be tainted in the minds of left-wing voters, but the grass-roots energy is real. That energy goes far beyond opposition to vaccines.

Poll after poll shows Americans value vaccines, including many MAHA supporters (three-quarters of whom say their own children are up-to-date on their shots). Other key issues that have animated the base are still incredibly potent. Think food, pollution and corporate maleficence. Seventy-five percent of Americans say there’s not enough regulation of chemicals in food, and 64 percent say the regulation of agricultural pesticides is inadequate, according to polling by the nonpartisan health policy organization KFF. Fifteen years ago, Michelle Obama was accused of “nanny state” overreach for encouraging healthy eating and more nutritious school meals; today, a majority of Americans support ridding school lunches of ultraprocessed foods.

There’s another reason not to count out MAHA. When Mr. Trump appointed Stephen Miller this month to serve as his White House chief of staff, Mr. Kennedy wrote on X, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” The White House shake-up is already having effects. Some believe it’s the reason the White House last week abruptly pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration. The health news site Stat reported that she was “generally seen as a cautious force” who could hinder MAHA initiatives. As a Trump aide, she was involved in an executive order that supported the production of glyphosate, a herbicide that has been tied to cancer. The move caused many MAHA activists to break with the administration.

Democrats can take advantage of the schism. Their control of Congress, combined with a potentially more MAHA-friendly White House, may present opportunities to pass legislation that could improve nutrition and reduce pollution. Such engagement will require a tricky balancing act. Making headway hinges on bipartisan cooperation and coalition building, according to Jerold Mande, a former senior Food and Drug Administration official who oversaw federal nutrition policy. “Lose Republicans and you lose action for the next two years,” he said.

At the same time, Democrats will need to hold Mr. Kennedy to account for public health harms and alleged ethics violations. Mr. Kennedy delivered mixed messages about vaccine safety amid the growing measles outbreak. There’s speculation his anti-vaccine crusade could be further fueled by Mr. Miller. When Mr. Trump signed the executive order that recommended reducing the childhood pediatric vaccine schedule, Mr. Miller aired his own vaccine skepticism, calling the existing recommendations “a medical travesty.”

Making tangible progress on issues they share with MAHA won’t be easy, but Democrats have a few things going for them. MAHA supporters have recently been outspoken about their willingness to back members of any party who fight for their health. Ms. Cianci, the creator of the MAHA Scorecard, told me, “Republicans rented MAHA voters. They never bought them.” It’s policy over partisanship now, she added. “No moms are going back to feeding their kids poison. No mother is going to be like, ‘Well, the Democrats won. I want Lunchables again.’”

People are fed up with unfettered corporations preying on them. These concerns existed before they were branded MAHA, and they’re not going away. Some of that energy is already having an impact in both red and blue states. Texas passed a law requiring warning labels on food that contains any of 44 additives deemed unsafe by regulatory bodies in other countries. California is phasing out ultraprocessed foods in schools. Several states acted last year to limit chemicals known as PFAS — or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances — in drinking water. Even the backlash to artificial intelligence data centers, a popular rallying point within the MAHA movement, reflects this groundswell of anti-corporate sentiment. “If we can go up against Big Tech, I don’t know why we can’t go up against Big Food,” said Brinda Adhikari, a host of the “Why Should I Trust You?” public health podcast.

Some Democrats already see the opportunities in pursuing MAHA ideas and voters. Abdul El-Sayed, the senator-elect of Michigan and an epidemiologist, promised to fight corporate polluters with his Building a Healthier America policy agenda, and he has signaled he’s willing to work with Mr. Kennedy, so long as he’s “evidence driven.” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York spent months this year courting MAHA voters. Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey and Representative (and organic farmer) Chellie Pingree of Maine are among the Democrats collaborating with MAHA activists on policy papers and bills.

These MAHA-curious Democrats can build on the food and nutrition work Mr. Kennedy started. He has rightly singled out unhealthy ultraprocessed foods as a driver of chronic disease in dietary guidelines. Now we need the long-awaited federal definition of ultraprocessed foods that can serve as the basis for further regulation, including front-of-package food warning labels, as well as lawsuits against food companies. Lawmakers should also make school meals and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program healthier and close an F. D. A. loophole that has allowed food companies to declare dubious ingredients safe.

Such projects will have to be done in parallel with shoring up protections for vaccines and repairing damage done to the health and research infrastructure. It’s a lofty to-do list, but spending the next two years wrapped up entirely in investigations and impeachment trials, without addressing the health issues that are making people’s lives worse, risks sowing more disillusionment.

The Democratic leadership has talked a lot about health care in recent years, but it needs to spend more time tackling the corporate interests, foods, and environmental toxins causing millions of Americans to need health care in the first place. Mr. Kennedy, for all his many faults, has forced us into a more expansive conversation about the causes of rampant chronic disease. Democrats will need to engage in that conversation if they hope to address the frustration and powerlessness so many Americans are feeling.

MAHA under Trump was always the carrot. But there's nothing MAHA about blowing up tons of toxic munitions in Iowa, allowing the toxic cloud to spread across America's most fertile farmland. There's nothing MAHA about higher greenhouse gas emissions, lax clean water rules, and deregulating toxic industries across the country. The only thing RFK Jr. did was encourage Big Food to voluntarily cut back on artificial food dyes and preservatives -- a completely meaningless exercise because if one cares about such things, there are already a wealth of products on the market that are additive-free. The MAHA lie was exposed 2 weeks after the 2024 election when Trump and RFK Jr. posed for pictures with an array of McDonald's burgers and sandwiches. The meaning of that photo op was clear: Trump was telegraphing his dominance. Trump would never embrace MAHA principles. Instead, RFK Jr. would be subservient to Trump.

“People are fed up with unfettered corporations preying on them.”Corporations that make us sick, not just with ultraprocessed foods, but with rampent pollution, pervasive chemicals and the callous withholding of healthcare once we get sick, have overreached in this administration. Profits over people has gone beyond its tipping point and now is the time to hold them accountable too.

Much of the science done in Food and Agriculture colleges is funded by corporations and falls far short of finding the truth. A trip down a drug store aisle of supplements, elixirs and many other snake oils is evidence that the American public is lead by charlatans, Kennedy is just one of many.

Julia Belluz is a contributing Opinion writer and an author of the book “Food Intelligence.”

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

OpinionGuest Essay

Credit... Emmanuel Polanco

Supported by

By Jesse Wegman

Mr. Wegman, a contributing Opinion writer, is a senior fellow at the Brennan Center for Justice.

Beneath the surface of the upheaval in American politics that took place on Nov. 3, there were tremors of what could ultimately be an even bigger political earthquake: the end of the Electoral College as we know it.

Voters in Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Arizona and Nevada elected Democratic governors and secured Democratic majorities in their legislatures. The trifectas — control of the governor’s office and the state legislature — open the door to the imminent adoption of the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

The compact is an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the nationwide popular vote winner. It goes into effect only when states representing at least 270 electoral votes join it. The effort began more than two decades ago and has been quietly pushing toward a major transformation of American politics and government.

If these five states, which together represent 61 electoral votes, sign the compact, then as early as November 2028 we could experience something no one has ever seen — a presidential election in which all Americans’ votes count equally and the candidate who gets the most votes wins.

Created in 2006 in response to the 2000 election, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact aims to award electoral votes to the national popular vote winner. Enactment requires 270 electoral votes. Maryland was the first to join in 2007.

By 2013, eight more states and the District of Columbia joined, reaching half of the votes needed for the compact to go into effect.

As of April 2026, 18 states — predominantly Democratic — have signed on, bringing the total to 222 electoral votes.

As a result of the midterms this month, these five states shifted to Democratic trifectas, placing them in a strong position to adopt the compact.

If the compact hits 270 in time, the 2028 election will be decided by popular vote, rendering the Electoral College as we know it dead.

Note: Figures use 2024 electoral vote apportionment. Source: NationalPopularVote. com

Just imagine: The nation’s leader being elected by a majority (or at least a plurality) of the nation’s voters. Candidates campaigning all across the country because all votes matter. No more red states or blue states, just Americans everywhere casting ballots that actually count. It sounds almost magical, doesn’t it?

Every other election in the country already runs this way, and the majority of Americans have for decades said they want the presidential election to run this way, too. We say this because it is the natural expectation of citizens living in a modern representative democracy.

The arc of the American story has been, in slow and sometimes halting fashion, the vindication of democratic principles through the expansion of voting rights and of popular participation in government. Most of the original barriers to that participation have fallen — from the denial of voting rights to women, Black people and young adults to the selection of senators by state legislatures. The Electoral College, as it operates today, is the last major barrier.

So why not just amend it out of the Constitution, the way those other barriers were toppled? At the moment, that is a nonstarter. There have been more than 700 proposed amendments to change or abolish the Electoral College over the nation’s history, far more than for any other single provision of the Constitution. Yet it survives, a testament to the power of partisan politics, which have derailed so many reform efforts.

Critics of the compact argue that an amendment is the only acceptable way to enact such a sweeping change to American government. “The valid methods for amending the Constitution are specified” in the document itself, the Cato Institute argued, “and an agreement among a minority of states is not one of them.” They see the compact as an end run around the Constitution and fear, among other things, that a popular vote would result in big cities dominating every election. That latter claim, like so many about the Electoral College and the popular vote, is not true. (If “big cities,” which is usually code for liberal areas, actually dominate, how did Donald Trump win the popular vote in 2024?)

States that join the compact agree to use the constitutional power they possess to change how they award their electoral votes. Rather than awarding them all to the candidate who wins the most votes within the state, as 48 of 50 states currently do, states in the compact (there are 18 so far, plus Washington, D. C.) legally bind themselves to award their electoral votes to the popular-vote winner of the entire country.

While there is no “official” national popular vote total, it’s not hard to come up with one. All 50 states and D. C. are already required by federal law to certify the electors they are appointing no later than six days before the Electoral College meets and those electors cast their ballots, which happens in mid-December. That certification must include final popular-vote totals. From there, it’s just adding together the state totals — arithmetic a grade-school pupil could do.

In short, the vote-counting process would run exactly the same as it does today; the difference would be in how the states award their electoral votes.

Once states representing a majority of electoral votes — 270 — join the compact, it turns the Electoral College into the vehicle for an election in which, by definition, the popular-vote winner prevails every time. It doesn’t matter what other states do with their electors, because candidates will know that to win a majority of electoral votes, they have to win the most popular votes in the country, and they will campaign that way. It is an ingenious design, and one that does not touch the Constitution.

The inventor of the compact is one of the more dogged and precise men I’ve ever met. John Koza is an 83-year-old computer scientist who lives in Silicon Valley. After the 2000 election, when George W. Bush won the presidency despite trailing his opponent, Al Gore, by half a million popular votes, Mr. Koza started the compact, which he called National Popular Vote.

He has since devoted most of his waking hours to changing how Americans elect their president. We first met in 2019, when I was writing a book about the Electoral College and the compact, and we have corresponded regularly since. A few days after the election I called to ask him whether he had been prepared for what happened on election night.

“Well, yeah,” he said matter-of-factly. “We’ve talked to almost every legislator in the five states; we targeted them 18 months ago.” He then went down the list and told me exactly where each state stood in terms of its likelihood of passing the compact.

I have learned over the years not to underestimate Mr. Koza’s attention to detail. He is the lead author of a book (revised at least four times and now 1,200 pages) that lays out the Electoral College’s history and the compact’s function, and that rebuts seemingly every defense of the College and every challenge to a national popular vote that you could imagine.

At the same time I have been a skeptic about how likely the compact is to pass: Following an initial burst of states joining it, by the mid-2010s it seemed to be languishing. Except for Hawaii, whose Republican governor’s veto had been overridden, all member states were led by Democratic governors when they joined, and there seemed to be little prospect of Republican buy-in.

That was, by itself, a big stumbling block. If the compact looked like a Democratic plot to win all presidential elections (Democrats won the popular vote in seven of the eight elections before 2024), it would be hard to convince Americans that this was being done for politically neutral reasons.

But the politics turn out to be not so simple. There was a time, before Donald Trump, when some Republican lawmakers were very interested in the compact. Republican-led legislative chambers in Arizona, Oklahoma and New York all passed it, and it enjoyed significant Republican support in Georgia, Utah and Michigan. Yet after Mr. Trump won the White House in 2016 while losing the popular vote, that interest evaporated.

Even some Democratic leaders got cold feet. In May 2019, after the Nevada Legislature voted to join the compact, the state’s Democratic governor, Steve Sisolak, vetoed it. Since then, a few more states have joined, bringing the total number of electoral votes represented in the compact to 222 — 48 short of 270. But it was hard to identify enough states left on the map to clear the bar.

Now, with those five states newly controlled by Democrats, it’s not hard at all. “I’m a little stunned,” Chris Pearson, an executive director at National Popular Vote, told me after Election Day. “But it felt well within the realm of possibility for months now.”

In Michigan, the compact had been co-sponsored by the incoming State House speaker and senate majority leader; in Arizona, it previously passed one legislative chamber with bipartisan support. All five states have now either elected an incoming governor or legislative leaders who have supported the compact. As soon as the next legislative session begins in 2027, those states could join the compact and push it past 270 electoral votes.

It’s difficult to overstate what a big deal this would be. The election of the president by popular vote would vindicate the fundamental democratic principles of political equality and majority rule in the most important election of all. It would also reverberate across the American political system, said Maria Collett, Pennsylvania’s incoming State Senate majority leader, who introduced popular-vote compact legislation this year and plans to do so again next year.

Right now, “if you’re a Democratic voter in a deep-red state, what difference does it make” if you vote, Ms. Collett asked. The same goes for Republican voters in deep-blue states. “When people sit out elections, it hurts down-ballot candidates, people are less engaged, and we have fewer opportunities to make sure people feel heard,” she said. That, in turn, has a corrosive effect on the people’s sense of their own power to choose their leaders. In contrast, “when we say every single vote counts, I think that adds to people feeling empowered,” Ms. Collett explained.

But it’s not only the good things a popular vote promotes; it’s the bad things it prevents.

Consider the Stop the Steal movement in 2020 and 2021, which culminated in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. An effort to stop Congress’s certification of the vote that day was, in President Trump and his supporters’ minds, justified by razor-thin vote margins in key battleground states, which they baselessly attributed to fraud and other irregularities. In contrast, the average margin in the national popular vote over the last half century has been almost seven million ballots — far too big to credibly dispute. “The country is clear,” Pearson told me. “Right now the system does not honor that and leaves us quite vulnerable.”

Narrow state vote margins are dangerous in other ways too: they incentivize lawmakers to pass countless laws making it harder for certain people to vote, and they make it easier for any person (or foreign power) who really does intend to meddle in an election to identify specific states, counties or even precincts where they can get the most bang for their buck.

What happens if the compact reaches 270 electoral votes? Nothing this significant in American politics happens without a fight. So let’s consider some obstacles.

One is political. Should such a profound shift in American politics take place without a constitutional amendment? As I mentioned, critics of the compact have long charged that it is an end run around the Constitution, a sneaky way for about half of the states to achieve something that has an impact on the entire country.

But the compact’s ingenuity lies precisely in its reliance on the Constitution, of which Article II gives the states total control over how they award their electoral votes. The Supreme Court has reaffirmed that multiple times, most recently in 2020, when it ruled unanimously in Chiafalo v. Washington that Article II conveys to states “the broadest power of determination” over electors.

Today, most states use that power to employ the statewide winner-take-all method. (Only Maine and Nebraska use a different allocation method, partly based on congressional districts.) That winner-take-all method is the root cause of so many people’s dislike of the Electoral College, because it awards all a state’s electors to one candidate, regardless of how close the popular-vote margin is.

The most glaring example of this was Florida in 2000, when George W. Bush’s 537-vote popular-vote win netted him all 25 of the state’s electoral votes, and thus the presidency. The key to the compact is the understanding that whatever method a state chooses, it is only that — a choice — and one that a state’s legislature can change as it pleases.

There are legal obstacles too. In Michigan, voters in 2022 approved a series of amendments to the State Constitution, including: “The outcome of every election in this state shall be determined solely by the vote of electors casting ballots in the election.” That language may not have been targeting the compact, but might appear to block it.

Mr. Koza told me he doesn’t agree, because the outcome of the Michigan election — that is, the total popular vote in the state — is still determined by Michigan voters. The choice of how to award Michigan’s electors is a separate process determined by the State Legislature.

Even if the compact survives in Michigan, there is no question it will face multiple legal challenges the moment it takes effect, and could ultimately reach the Supreme Court. If a nonmember state were to sue the members of the compact, that case would go directly to the Supreme Court. In other words, this could all come to a head quickly.

The court would almost certainly weigh at least one straightforward constitutional question: Does the compact need the consent of Congress? The Constitution says consent is required for interstate compacts, but the Supreme Court has for more than a century interpreted that requirement to refer only to compacts that encroach on federal power.

As the court reiterated in 2020, the choice of how to award electors belongs exclusively to the states. The federal government has no role in the process. Consent of Congress should thus not be necessary, although with this Supreme Court nothing should be taken for granted.

Finally there is that knotty partisan issue: If states led by Democratic governors have almost exclusively passed the compact, doesn’t it look like a plot to ensure that only Democrats win the White House? This framing has always mystified me. First, the most recent popular-vote winner was a Republican. Second, the whole purpose of the compact is to benefit all voters in every corner of the country — Republicans no less than Democrats.

In addition, assumptions of broad Republican opposition to the popular vote may be oversold. From years of working with state lawmakers, Mr. Koza has found that many Republicans support the compact’s principles but have self-protective reasons for not saying so — starting with the man in the Oval Office. “If you’re voting against Trump, you’re attacking the way he was elected,” Mr. Koza told me, speaking of the 2016 election. “Frankly, it is fatal in a Republican primary. At least it has been.”

Pat Rosenstiel, a member of the compact team and longtime Republican consultant, noted that polls showed increasing Republican support even before Mr. Trump’s win in 2024. After the 2016 election, only 27 percent of Republicans said they were on board with switching to popular election. A few weeks before the 2024 election, Pew found that number had jumped to 46 percent; it’s almost certainly higher today, after Mr. Trump won 2.3 million more votes than Kamala Harris.

Mr. Rosenstiel pointed out that there has been little resistance by those who oppose the compact in any of the 18 states that have joined it. The one exception is Colorado, where in 2020, opponents managed to get a referendum on the ballot in an attempt to reverse the state’s passing legislation the year before to join the compact. It didn’t work.

The future of the Electoral College may have been altered on election night this month for a second reason. Whenever people ask me what it would take to get more Republicans over the hump to support a popular vote for president, I say that it will happen when Texas turns blue. With 40 electoral votes, Texas is a bigger prize than any state but California, and it’s been solidly red for decades. This year, Democrats didn’t just do well in Texas; they dominated, winning every statewide race on the ballot.

If the Democratic candidate in 2028 were to win the most popular votes in Texas, suddenly a very plausible scenario, Republicans would lose all 40 of those electoral votes. The millions of Texans who vote for the Republican candidate would effectively disappear, just like the millions of Texas Democrats who have not cast a meaningful vote for president in nearly half a century.

Republicans are well aware of how much their electoral fortunes hinge on Texas. “Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America,” Don Huffines, the state’s comptroller, wrote on X late last month. “When the foundation breaks, it ALL falls apart.”

That is true … in an Electoral College world. Under a popular vote, those Texas Republicans’ votes would count just as much as everyone else’s all across America. I don’t know about you, but I find that a thrilling idea.

Right now, tens of millions of Americans’ ballots for president are effectively erased because they voted for the candidate who didn’t win in their state. And if you think you can predict how a popular-vote election would turn out, don’t be so sure; battleground-state turnout data have long supported the claim that when people know their vote matters, more people vote.

Given all the evidence that the Electoral College today serves no one’s interests — except those of the swing states, several of which are now on the cusp of adopting the compact — I struggle to understand the remaining resistance to a national popular vote. The states’ interests are already well protected by their own governments, not to mention their two senators and their representatives in Washington.

The presidency is the only office whose occupant represents all Americans equally, wherever they live and whatever their politics. That’s the way anyone who wants the job should have to earn it, too.

Couldn't a future state legislature and governor from one of the states in the compact vote to withdraw from it and thus invalidate it? Conceivably, it could be in effect for some Presidential elections and then not subsequently, then back again as states change. Explain what I'm overlooking.

You're correct, a state can withdraw as long as it's not during the six-month blackout period (July 20 of election year to Jan. 20 of the following). The larger idea is that once Americans experience an election in which all their votes matter, they will ask why it wasn't done this way all along. That political pressure will make it harder for member states to withdraw, and may ultimately create positive conditions for an amendment.

Amy Nelson, a champion of women in the “girlboss” era, found her family in Amazon’s cross hairs and found herself in a new role as anti-corporate crusader.

Amy Nelson founded the Riveter in 2017, and in three years she raised $30 million in venture capital, hired more than 100 employees and opened 10 co-working spaces. Now the company is just her. Credit... Madeleine Hordinski for The New York Times

Supported by

By Amanda Hess

Reporting from Columbus, Ohio

The girlboss era ended for Amy Nelson at sunrise on April 2, 2020, when two F. B. I. agents pounded on the door of her Seattle home. Nelson was a co-founder and the chief executive of the Riveter, a network for working women, and also the mother of four young girls, so when the knock came at 6:45 a. m., she had been awake since 5, making preparations for a daylong Zoom event as her children played in a mini bounce house she had set up when schools closed for the pandemic.

Nelson opened the door with her diapered baby on her hip. The agents produced a letter naming her husband, Carleton Nelson, as the target of a federal criminal investigation into what it called “kickback schemes” in real estate deals he had facilitated for his former employer, Amazon. The letter advised that if he wished to negotiate a plea on several felony charges, his lawyer ought to give them a call.

Ninety minutes after the agents had left her house, Nelson appeared bright-eyed on a recorded Zoom to introduce the Riveter Community Day Presented by eBay, a marathon digital event Nelson had organized in the wake of a canceled South by Southwest festival. Nelson slipped coolly into her C. E. O. role. Here was the optimistic avatar of women’s ambition, empathetically leading her membership into a “super impactful” day of action in response to a pandemic that would ultimately ravage women’s work force participation, imperil teachers, nurses and child care workers, and set the mood for the demise of the progressive-corporate consensus — and the toppling of a whole set of female founders.

Over Zoom, Nelson invoked her company’s inspiration, Rosie the Riveter, the character representing women who took on men’s jobs during wartime. “They built the planes, the ships, the guns, everything, because the government asked them to — because we needed women to show up,” she said. When she stopped talking, the light in her eyes seemed to die, and she sat there, blinking.

Nelson founded the Riveter in 2017 as “a modern union for working women,” and in three years she raised $30 million in venture capital, hired more than 100 employees and opened 10 co-working spaces across the United States. After Community Day, she would spend the next six years fighting to keep her husband out of prison — and battling Amazon, the multinational conglomerate that had once sprinkled her feminist start-up with attention but that had now filed a civil suit against her husband accusing him of fraud.

After years of federal investigation, Carleton Nelson was never charged with a crime. When asked for comment, Amazon referred to a joint statement negotiated as part of a civil settlement last month, which said that he “violated Amazon’s Code of Conduct & Ethics, broke the trust Amazon places in its employees, and put Amazon’s reputation at risk in the communities it serves.”

The Riveter still exists, though it has shrunk to the size of Nelson herself, who has remade her career as a consultant to women who wish to fling themselves off the corporate ladder and go it alone. And she has become an anti-oligarchy TikTok influencer, one who has spoken out against Amazon executives, Amazon lawyers, the F. B. I., the Justice Department, Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos for her audience of 250,000 as she offers commentary on trending crime stories and makes common cause with some people on the right.

Nelson has emerged as a post-2020 figure, one who represents a skepticism around the female empowerment industry, a chaotic political realignment and a broad distrust of corporate and government power.

I met Nelson in July in her hometown, Columbus, Ohio, where she had relocated with her family after selling her Seattle home to pay her husband’s lawyers. Nelson, who is 46, has the energy of a camp counselor turned loose in adult life, though her enthusiasm is now cut with a discerning cynicism, and she arranged a packed schedule for us — a conference and a podcast recording and meals with collaborators and friends. She was in the process of starting two podcasts, organizing events with the AARP, working for a white-collar criminal defense firm and preparing for trial in the civil case Amazon had brought against her husband, which was finally scheduled for November in Virginia.

She was also guiding her daughters in their first start-up — a towel pants company for other competitive child swimmers — and raising a new puppy, which was not yet housebroken. When we stopped by her home, we found that the dog had peed in the dining room before retreating to a scuffed couch, where he watched soothing drone videos of unspoiled tropical islands. Carleton, pink-skinned in a polo shirt and rubber slides, emerged from a home office and mopped up the puddle. He has the start of a Sun Tzu line on his right arm, inked amid the Amazon fight: “Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night.” Amy has the end of the quote on her left arm, advising how to execute those plans: “fall like a thunderbolt.”

Nelson and I had come from lunch with her childhood friend Lauren Norelli, who has held executive roles and led two IPOs. The Atlantic had just published a story titled “The Girlboss Is Dead,” and it had landed in all of our feeds. “I thought about you,” Norelli told Nelson. The piece concerned the appeal of successful women who disguise their own ambition in a feminine “soft life” routine of the kind represented by the TikTok influencer Alix Earle, who recently gave an interview where she said that she had not read a book since “maybe Dr. Seuss.”

Said Norelli, “It’s this idea that you don’t want to appear to be trying hard at anything, and your beautiful life will manifest itself just because of who you are. That’s the worst thing I can imagine telling a teenage girl.”

Nelson never used the word “girlboss” at the Riveter, “for the simple reason that we don’t call men boybosses,” she said, but the term was soon applied to every female entrepreneur in the business of uplifting women. Nelson now looks back on the peak female founder era, and its celebratory summits and ranked lists, as a kind of fever dream. “The lights were bright, it was fancy, but it all felt very precarious,” she said. The Riveter styled itself as a mission-based for-profit business, which Nelson now sees as a contradiction in terms. “Corporations exist to maximize shareholder value — everything else is performative,” she said.

In this performance, the founders were made to be stars. Nelson was cast as the woman who could raise money and babies at the same time. When an investment bank commissioned a mini documentary in 2020, one meant to reassure male investors that female founders would not slack when they had children, it chose Nelson as its lead. “People thought that because I was nursing in my office, I would be nice and soft,” she said. In fact, she is nice and tough, and despite her confident exterior, she said she felt judged. “It probably goes back to my childhood, and being teased for being chubby,” she said. There was “a cool-girl hierarchy to it,” she continued, and as a mother in Seattle, she was not at the top. “My purse is a Hunter purse,” she explained. “My purse is made by a raincoat company.”

Start-ups like the Riveter were supported by membership dues and ticket sales but also by corporate partners, who benefited from their proximity to a women’s empowerment movement rooted in business success. Being in Seattle, Amazon was the Riveter’s white whale. Nelson had moved to Seattle with Carleton in 2012, before they were married, after he was offered a job at Amazon Web Services developing data center infrastructure. As she founded the Riveter, she emailed jeff@amazon. com, Bezos’ public email address, and asked if he would mentor her. (An aide declined on his behalf.) “I don’t know whether to mock my younger self, cry at this, or throw up,” she said as she forwarded me the exchange.

Nelson spent years courting the company’s many executives, offering her company as a work space partner for Amazon and raising the company’s logos at her various events, in exchange for what she said were a few thousand dollars in sponsorship fees. She rendezvoused with Amazon leaders at Fortune’s Most Powerful Women conference and brought them to her own signature gathering, the 2019 Riveter Summit, which featured Stacey Abrams and Lindy West. And she had scored a visit to the Riveter’s headquarters from Melinda Lewison, then the managing director of Bezos Expeditions — Jeff Bezos’ personal investment fund.

In December 2019, another enterprising business person also emailed jeff@amazon. com, calling himself a “whistleblower” and alleging a “kickback” scheme on a real-estate deal involving Carleton Nelson. The emailer noted that he “wouldn’t turn away compensation” for the information.

Two months later, lawyers for Amazon were presenting a 42-slide PowerPoint presentation to prosecutors at the Department of Justice, accusing Carleton of steering Amazon contracts to a developer in exchange for millions in kickbacks. (The slides were later produced during discovery in a civil case.) Carleton said that he had just joined with several of his active real estate partners to start their own business, which was above-the-table and lawyer-approved.

In 2023, two of Carleton’s business associates negotiated guilty pleas related to the real estate deals. But in 2024, the Justice Department vacated the pleas, deeming them “not in the interest of justice,” and indicated it had dropped its plans to prosecute anyone else.

Nelson herself was never a subject of investigation, but she said she had found her own career trampled beneath the weight of the allegations. A month after the F. B. I. knocked, Nelson was on Zoom with her cohort from the Young Presidents’ Organization — a club for people who have founded or led impressively sized companies before the age of 45 — when she got an overdraft alert from her bank. The F. B. I. had seized all of her husband’s accounts, and Nelson’s personal accounts, too, liquidating the savings she had earned as the Riveter’s C. E. O.

Two weeks later, the F. B. I. paid her family another visit, this time with guns drawn, to execute a search of the house. Nelson started waking her daughters before dawn and taking them on outdoor adventures every morning, so that if federal agents returned to arrest Carleton, they would not be there to see it. “You think you’re going to be really strong when something like this happens, and I completely fell apart,” she said. “I went from extremely high functioning to shaking uncontrollably and hiding in my bathroom.”

By February 2021, however, she had secured a job to provide for her family and pay its exorbitant legal fees — an executive position at a tech company, with compensation that she said totaled a million a year. A week in, the company learned of her husband’s case and fired her. When I asked Carleton about the allegations blunting his wife’s career, he shook his head. “That was probably the worst part for me,” he said. “That didn’t seem fair.”

And still, Carleton’s threatened arrest never came. “I realized that no matter what I did, I was going to be associated with this, and it wasn’t going to end,” Nelson said. She had told her close friends and her board about the case, but not her public. Now she started posting about it on Instagram, and then TikTok.

When she built the Riveter, “I just did it and didn’t stop,” she said. From that moment on, “I directed all of that energy to fighting against Amazon.”

The female founder is the ultimate outsider-insider, the disruptive heroine battling for a place in the establishment. Now Nelson marshaled her entrepreneurial skills to defend her husband — the stamina, the networking, the near-delusional confidence. She went girlboss mode on Amazon.

Nelson told me that she had a hunch that Amazon lawyers were working off the wrong employment contract for her husband — he had joined AWS in 2012 with wide latitude to pursue outside work — and she asked an Amazon employee to search the company directory, where she discovered a different Carl Nelson whom Amazon had confused him with. (An Amazon spokesman confirmed the mix-up but said it had “no bearing on how the case played out.”)

After the judge in Carleton’s case made a string of decisions favorable to Amazon, Nelson messaged a Wall Street Journal reporter on Twitter and asked him to look into whether the judge had Amazon stock; when the paper reported that his wife held a $22,000 investment in the company, he called the idea of a conflict of interest “almost insane” but reluctantly stepped down. And she spent more than two years scouring a Seattle court docket, searching for a case where Amazon had argued that it couldn’t be sued for breaking its own code of conduct. She found one on spring break in 2023, as her children slept, which wound up challenging Amazon’s basis for suing Carleton over its claims of code violations.

“It really bothers me how dumb these people thought we were,” she said.

Along the way, she posted about what she was up to, and soon her social accounts were a never-ending scroll of selfie videos of her steely gaze under captions like “Surviving Jeff Bezos” and “Hot Take: American Billionaires Can Do Anything To Anyone.” Nelson’s posts got media attention, but not the kind that used to fawn over her nursing in a conference room. In 2022, the libertarian magazine Reason covered the civil forfeiture of the Nelson family’s assets, which led to interviews with Glenn Beck and Tucker Carlson. Alex Jones discussed the case sympathetically on Infowars. She took to Facebook with frustration, asking why progressive journalists hadn’t taken up her cause. “I feel so adrift politically,” she wrote. “Like the people and causes I’ve spent my life working on are turning away from me.”

Nelson told me that she spoke out to give her girls a record of how her family had fought. But the new media spotlight cast a long shadow over the Riveter’s business. Nelson had once considered acquiring theLi. St, a private network of high-powered women; instead, she quit after a fellow member called and advised her to stop speaking publicly about her husband’s case. A start-up C. E. O. emailed Nelson to condemn her appearance on Fox, and a venture capitalist told her she was withdrawing her advertising and making a statement with her wallet.

In time, Nelson would connect her story to the Epstein files, the Met Gala, those accused of attacking the U. S. Capitol on Jan. 6 and the Lindsay Clancy trial, leveraging viral events to ensure that a growing crowd of skeptics and truthers would know her family’s story. When Carleton’s onetime pursuer, the U. S. attorney Jessica Aber, died in her sleep at the age of 43, Nelson mixed it up in the comments with people who questioned Aber’s official cause of death. In June, Nelson’s advocacy for people accused of white-collar crimes brought her to a fund-raiser attended by the former Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio.

Meanwhile, Amazon’s lawyers began quoting her TikToks in legal filings and complained that “defendant Nelson’s wife, Amy, has peddled conspiracy theories widely on social media” and “falsely accused Amazon of ‘hunting’ her family.”

“I’m not a conspiracy theorist,” Nelson said. “I am a graduate of a top-five law school, a venture-backed entrepreneur and a former Forbes columnist.” She plucked the worst allegations about herself from Amazon’s docket and posted a carousel of them superimposed over photographs of herself smiling with Jane Fonda and Kamala Harris.

On my second day in Ohio, Nelson took me along to RTRX, a business conference engaged in “priming optimists for action” that featured a longevity testing station and a keynote speech on shame by Monica Lewinsky. We gathered mini quiches and pastries onto little plates and sat in a front row. Though she is from Columbus and has an impressive social reach, “I wouldn’t be asked to speak at something like this,” Nelson told me. “I don’t care about those things anymore,” she added, though there was just the slightest edge to her voice.

She never imagined herself living back in Columbus, where she now sees herself as deemed unfit for even the blandest of conference stages. She’s remaking herself as a consultant and a media expert for people in crisis, while Carleton has built the independent data center real estate business he had planned all along. The pair reached a settlement with the government to recover most of their seized funds. But she wonders what she could have done over the past six years if she had focused on building her own career instead of keeping her husband out of prison.

Nelson’s experience is sui generis, but it is representative of the entropy of the female founder class. She has watched as the other feminist-styled businesses have imploded or shape-shifted as a new political order took hold. Now Mark Zuckerberg speaks of bringing “masculine energy” to corporate America while President Trump’s Equal Employment Opportunity Commission sues a Coca-Cola distributor over a female employee retreat.

The girlboss era evokes some nostalgia now, but it also appears terminally quaint. How easily its stages were dismantled, its progress reversed. “All the stuff that we thought we could do, we can’t do, and so we don’t talk about it anymore,” Nelson said. Carleton spent the summer making a podcast studio in their basement where Nelson could speak on her various interests, which now include oligarchy and white-collar criminal defendants. It’s stocked with a mug that says “I need new conspiracy theories, all my old ones came true.”

Just before the Amazon trial was slated to begin, Nelson posted a TikTok of herself behind the mic, holding a paper that said “All disputes with my husband’s former employer have been resolved.” As a part of a settlement agreement with Amazon, Carleton publicly apologized. Nelson’s old TikToks have begun to disappear, and when her followers question what happened, she always says the same thing: “I refer back to my statement.” But before these disputes were resolved, she made sure to tell me, “I have always imagined that if Amazon settles this case, the price will be my silence.”

Amanda Hess is a writer at large for The Times.

I started following Amy Nelson online in 2019, when she was part of a rising class of female-empowerment founders. She posted about her feminist-styled coworking space, The Riveter, and teaming up with Stacey Abrams and Sheryl Sandberg to support women at work. Earlier this year, I noticed her online persona had changed: She had become a one-woman crusader against Amazon.

High tides reaching two or more feet above normal may cause flooding this week, forecasters warned.

By Nazaneen Ghaffar

Nazaneen Ghaffar is a reporter on The Times’s weather team.

A sprawling storm system is expected to bring strong winds, heavy rain and large waves to the West Coast this week. Meteorologists and emergency officials were bracing for the possibility that the storm could coincide with exceptionally high tides that were already forecast to lead to flooding during a busy period of holiday travel.

Forecasters have warned for weeks that the tides, known informally as king tides, could reach record levels in some places on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. In far Northern California, evacuation warnings were issued in the coastal communities of King Salmon and Fields Landing in Humboldt County. Elsewhere, local authorities shored up vulnerable areas with sandbags and temporary fences, hoping to keep the water at bay.
