The storm system is expected to remain nearly stationary offshore, sending repeated rounds of rain from Washington to Northern California through the week, “one after another,” said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist at the Weather Prediction Center, an arm of the National Weather Service. It will also send persistent winds to the coast, which will constantly “push the ocean waters onshore, which makes everything, all the water levels, higher,” he said.

The wind and rain coinciding with the highest tides could exacerbate the tidal flooding. But whether it will remained uncertain on Monday, Mr. Wegman said. Still, the storm system is also expected to generate waves approaching 30 feet along parts of the coast.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, which last week experienced record rain that overwhelmed the city’s sewage system, the concern is again the combination of high tides and storm-driven water. Forecasters said high tide was forecast to reach around eight and a half feet on Tuesday and Wednesday, more than two and a half feet above normal, while storm surge could add as much as 1.6 feet. Large waves will also raise the risk along exposed beaches, with breaking waves of 18 to 24 feet possible on Wednesday.

The latest forecast on Monday placed the heaviest rain north of San Francisco stretching up the coast toward Oregon. Still forecasters said there was “additional wiggle room” in the projected totals depending on whether the weather pattern shifts north or south.

A northward shift would bring less rain to the city, while a southern shift could push totals higher. For now, San Francisco is expected to see half an inch to an inch of rain, though an outlier scenario — if the storm sets up farther south — could bring an inch and a half or more.

Amid earlier uncertainty about the storm’s timing, San Francisco’s mayor, Daniel Lurie, urged people to avoid traveling this week.

The risk of coastal flooding and beach erosion will extend farther south. While little to no rain is expected for Southern California, forecasters at the Los Angeles office of the National Weather Service said the high tides were expected to reach eight feet along parts of the coast, while large waves could cause moderate to major coastal flooding from the central coast through Los Angeles and Ventura Counties.

In San Diego, forecasters said tides just over eight feet were expected Tuesday through Thursday, and could break current records, while west-facing beaches could see waves topping 10 feet.

Some of the greatest concerns, however, are farther north. In Northern California, the Eureka office of the National Weather Service warned of potentially “record breaking coastal flooding.” The greatest risk is expected on Tuesday and Wednesday when the highest tides could combine with storm surge and large waves.

During Monday morning’s high tides, more than a dozen stations along the California and Oregon coasts had already crept higher than normal.

At least one station, in Humboldt Bay in Northern California, nudged into moderate flood stage, though it still fell short of the site’s top 10 historical flood levels.

The Los Angeles gauge registered 2.3 feet above average on Monday. That ranked among the location’s top 10 historical readings, though it remained well short of the record-setting surge on Oct. 27, which reached 2.70 feet above that benchmark.

At the mouth of San Francisco Bay, the gauge reached 2.1 feet above average. Water levels there were higher earlier this year on Jan. 3, when a strong storm system combined with king tides pushed the gauge to 2.56 feet.

Later this week, water levels around Humboldt Bay could reach about 10 feet, with storm surge potentially pushing them even higher, above the current record of 10.37 feet set in January. Breaking waves could also reach up to 25 feet.

The threat is also significant along the Oregon coast. In southern Oregon, the Medford office of the Weather Service was forecasting up to around three feet of inundation above ground level in low-lying coastal areas on Tuesday and Wednesday, when breaking waves could reach 23 to 28 feet. This could cause flooding of roads, including Highway 101, and especially around Coos Bay, and beaches could become inundated, the office said.

Later in the week, the focus will shift toward Washington. Heavy rain is already drenching the Olympic Peninsula, with two to four inches possible in the mountains, and enough runoff that could impact the Skokomish River. By Wednesday and Thursday, another storm system is expected to increase the risk of coastal flooding around Grays Harbor, where forecasters said moderate to major flooding was possible.

Judson Jones contributed reporting.

Nazaneen Ghaffar is a Times reporter on the Weather team.

Over 700,000 Russian Soldiers Have Died in Ukraine, Analysis Indicates

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Hacked government data underscores the immense human cost of President Vladimir V. Putin’s war of attrition.

By Paul Sonne

Reporting from Berlin

More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine, according to a new estimate released on Monday, underscoring the extraordinary level of suffering that President Vladimir V. Putin has been willing to accept to pursue his war aims.

The updated estimate was calculated by the exiled Russian publications Meduza and Mediazona, making use of a trove of new data that two groups of pro-Ukraine hackers obtained from the Russian state statistics service, Rosstat. The groups, the Cyber Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, released the data to media outlets in recent weeks.

The estimate represents a significant increase from prior assessments of how many soldiers Russia has lost in the war. The Kremlin has concealed that information from the Russian public, leaving many Russians with only a cursory understanding of the scale of the death at the front.

Mr. Putin has been waging a full-scale war against Ukraine for nearly five years and does not appear ready to end it anytime soon. Armed with a powerful combination of repression, censorship and propaganda, the Russian leader has kept a lid on critical information about the war at home and dampened societal discontent about its high cost.

For years, Meduza and Mediazona have been tracking Russian war deaths, primarily by analyzing Russian probate records and death notices. The hack added significant new sources to their analysis, including data from Russia’s civil registry and government-run data exchange system, which feed anonymized information to Rosstat to inform national statistics.

Based on that new information, the publications identified at least 490,000 soldier deaths recorded by the Russian state as of September. But deaths regularly show up in the Russian government system with a huge time lag. The data, for instance, does not account for most of the deaths in 2026 and many from 2025.

Drawing on scientific projection methods, the publications came up with an estimate for what the death toll would be if the registrations were entirely up-to-date and included people who were listed as missing but were most likely dead.

The projection found that Russia had likely lost more than 700,000 soldiers, a significant increase from death estimates that the publications released earlier this year. The projection did not address how many soldiers had been wounded.

The New York Times did not independently confirm the data or the analysis. Exact death counts during wars are very difficult to ascertain, with historians often disagreeing about casualty numbers for years after a conflict.

Michael Kofman, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that while Russia was losing more soldiers than it was recruiting, Moscow was still on track to recruit about 409,000 soldiers in 2026. The Russian authorities continue to offer significant pay incentives for recruits.

The pace of recruiting allows Russia to sustain losses and keep fighting, but probably not to improve its position on the battlefield, Mr. Kofman said. Eventually, the Kremlin could find itself without sufficient assault infantry.

Mr. Kofman said that if Russia did not change how its force was employed, it would continue to face “diminishing returns, with no prospect for improvement.”

There is relatively little reliable information in the public domain about Ukrainian losses. It is generally accepted that Russia has lost far more soldiers than Ukraine has, because armies attempting to advance almost always suffer significantly greater casualties. Russia has also employed tactics that military experts say have increased its battlefield toll.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington estimated that 150,000 Ukrainian combatants had died in the war through June. Two opaque websites that track public information about Ukrainian deaths, Lostarmour. info and UALosses. org, put the number of Ukrainian soldiers lost and missing at well over 200,000.

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.

Netanyahu Wants to Attack Iran. Does That Serve Israel or Him?

The New York Times November 23, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, calls renewing strikes a matter of national security. Military analysts and opposition leaders say he’s prioritizing his own interests.

By David M. Halbfinger and Ronen Bergman

Reporting from Jerusalem and Tel Aviv

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s all-out push for a new Israeli military strike against Iran is being called into question by critics who say that it cannot be disentangled from his efforts to maintain his grip on power.

The embattled Israeli leader, now serving in a caretaker role, has personally lobbied President Trump and sent emissaries to make the case to White House, C. I. A. and U. S. Central Command officials for a new attack on Iran, officials briefed on the discussions have said. But Mr. Netanyahu has yet to tell his own citizens why that would be necessary now, what it would achieve or how it could be contained without escalating into a regional conflagration.

Even analysts who tend to trust the warnings emanating from the Israeli intelligence and military establishment say that it is unclear whether a fresh round of attacks would serve Israel’s interests — or Mr. Netanyahu’s.

“It’s very difficult to make a distinction between the political considerations and the urgency of the threats,” said Raz Zimmt, head of Iran research at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv. The chatter among Israeli security officials, he said, suggested a growing consensus that pre-emptive military action would become necessary before long, as Iran’s offensive capabilities grow into greater threats. But there was no such consensus about when.

“Whether it really requires an immediate action? I doubt it,” Mr. Zimmt said.

The belief that Mr. Netanyahu would stop at almost nothing to stay in power has made it difficult for many Israelis to take his word about the necessity of an attack, let alone about the need to execute one immediately.

“For the sake of his political survival, Netanyahu is pushing Israel into another war,” said Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party and a former deputy chief of staff of the Israeli military. “A government responsible for the gravest security failure in the country’s history, and for a string of strategic security failures, has no legitimacy whatsoever to launch another military campaign.”

Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form a new government, said Monday that he saw “no direct and immediate threat that requires action in Iran in the coming weeks or before a government is formed.”

Mr. Netanyahu retorted, in a statement, that “anyone who downplays the immediate threats is doing so for political reasons.”

In a social media post on Friday, Mr. Eisenkot had accused Mr. Netanyahu of conflating “political interests and agendas” with “operational interests and timetables, and called that unacceptable, adding: “It is madness and a source of danger.”

A spokesman for the prime minister, Doron Spielman, insisted that Mr. Netanyahu’s decisions on Iran were “guided by one consideration: the security of Israel and its citizens.”

It is unclear whether Israel would be willing to attack Iran on its own, or if it would do so provided it had U. S. approval and assurances of support in the event of an Iranian counterstrike.

Three Israeli security officials said that the Israeli military’s position — as presented in internal discussions, including with the prime minister — was that if the opportunity arose to strike alongside the United States, Israel should take it. Israeli officials are aware that the opportunity could close in January, when Democrats take control of the U. S. Congress.

However, the three officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said that the view among many senior Israeli commanders was that Israel must not, in the near term, launch an attack on its own. That would risk squandering the opportunity of a joint strike. And the officials said that the consensus was that there was no urgency and no reason for Israel to attack alone.

Any immediate action could benefit Mr. Netanyahu politically — by disrupting Mr. Eisenkot’s efforts to form a government before a Dec. 6 deadline, and by creating public pressure for a national unity government that included Mr. Netanyahu.

A joint U. S.-Israel attack on Iran might even prompt Mr. Trump to throw his weight behind a potential unity government, some Israeli analysts have speculated.

Even before the Oct. 27 election, as polls predicted defeat for the prime minister, The New York Times reported that Mr. Netanyahu hoped to renew fighting with Iran to generate pressure on Mr. Eisenkot to enter an emergency unity government.

Now, after flatly ruling out a unity government during his campaign, Mr. Netanyahu has been seeding the airwaves with talk of a unity government for nearly two weeks.

Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition had a poor showing in the election. Opposition parties won 67 seats in the 120-seat Parliament. In the days that followed, the prime minister first tried to cast doubt on the integrity of the vote, then sought to deter the opposition from forming a government that relied on the support of predominantly Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats.

But on Nov. 7, he and his allies abruptly began beating the drum for a unity government, arguing that Israel’s Jewish political parties should come together — centrist and left-wing factions joining his right-wing bloc — to “remove the nuclear threat from Iran, preserve Israel as a Jewish state and bring unity among us,” as Mr. Netanyahu put it.

Two days later, he added a key point: “The one who should lead this government, naturally, is the largest party,” he said.

That would be his party, Likud, which won 27 seats in Parliament.

Not surprisingly, there were no takers among the opposition parties, led by Mr. Eisenkot, whose Yashar party won 21 seats. The most adamant of all Mr. Eisenkot’s campaign promises was that Mr. Netanyahu would be dislodged from the premiership.

Resuming the fighting with Iran, however, could amount to the kind of national emergency that tests the resolve of Mr. Eisenkot and his allies to refuse Mr. Netanyahu’s overtures. There is a recent precedent: Mr. Eisenkot entered a unity government led by Mr. Netanyahu after the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023.

Already on Wednesday and Thursday, Mr. Netanyahu arranged briefings on the security situation for two of Mr. Eisenkot’s key allies, Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who leads the Beyachad (Together) party, and Avigdor Liberman of the Yisrael Beiteinu (Our Home) party.

Mr. Bennett has said he favors a unity government, but one led by Mr. Eisenkot, at least to start. Mr. Liberman has rejected any unity government with Mr. Netanyahu, calling it a “trap” and saying that “even if the world turns upside down, I won’t sit with Netanyahu.”

Analysts point to those differences as evidence that Mr. Netanyahu’s unity gambit is working, by stoking friction within Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc. If Mr. Eisenkot and his allies fail to form a government, the likely result would be new elections, in which Mr. Netanyahu would be expected to fare better than in last month’s vote.

Suspicions about Mr. Netanyahu’s motives in national-security matters have clouded his current four-year term as prime minister, and were a factor again when he began pushing to attack Iran before the election.

He met resistance at the time from within the armed forces, including from the military chief of staff, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, who objected to a strike during the run-up to the vote because of the political sensitivities and the difficulty of explaining to the public why an attack had to occur then.

Israel’s goals in a possible strike against Iran have not been detailed publicly by Mr. Netanyahu, but security officials and analysts point to a few potential objectives.

Israel’s military considers intelligence about Iran’s chemical weapons program most concerning in the short term, according to two Israeli security officials, though it is unclear whether such weapons could be deployed soon.

Other possible justifications include further attempts to damage Iran’s nuclear program or its ballistic missile and drone arsenal, which experts say Iran has been replenishing.

An attack on Iran’s energy infrastructure is another possibility, security officials say, should the United States and Israel choose to make a new attempt at precipitating regime change in Tehran.

At the height of the war, the United States and Israel struck civilian infrastructure in Iran that the Iranian authorities said included roads, bridges, rail lines and schools. Israel also attacked Iranian petrochemical and storage sites.

Iran retaliated by attacking U. S. allies in the Gulf. Those countries said they were hit by thousands of missiles and drones targeting energy facilities, airports and water and power plants. Iranian missiles struck apartment buildings and at least one railway station in Israel, the authorities there said.

But Israel planned a wider strike — against Iranian oil production, refining and global export infrastructure, as well as other critical infrastructure in the country — as part of a plan to topple the regime. Mr. Trump put a halt to it.

Later on, however, Mr. Trump threatened similar strikes, saying they would lead to the “destruction of Iranian civilization.”

Destroying such civilian infrastructure would cause widespread suffering in a country of 93 million people and in most cases would be considered a war crime under international law.

Now, those plans are back on the table, according to the three Israeli security officials.

Iran has vowed to respond to such a strike by retaliating against oil facilities, water desalination plants, data centers and other civilian infrastructure across the region, defying hopes of containing a renewed conflict.

Adam Rasgon and Natan Odenheimer contributed reporting from Tel Aviv.

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

Ronen Bergman is a staff writer for The New York Times Magazine, based in Tel Aviv.

The World’s Tech Capital Can’t Keep Sewage Off the Streets in a Deluge

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A downpour once again sent wastewater into San Francisco streets. It could become a frequent occurrence in this El Niño year.

By Heather Knight

Reporting from San Francisco

San Francisco may be best known as the cradle of cutting-edge technology, but during torrential rain storms, the city looks more like a backwater — with a decidedly putrid stench.

During last week’s record-breaking rainfall, flooding dislodged manhole covers, geysers containing wastewater spewed into low-lying streets, and The San Francisco Chronicle issued an alert warning residents of “poop water.”

The ick factor could grow with El Niño threatening to pack a punch over the next few months, and with the city’s sewer system, through which rainwater and sewage move together, unable to handle the onslaught. Another storm is expected to arrive on Tuesday, though the biggest concern may be coastal flooding from king tides.

Donna Marie Ponferrada, 46, was working at her home on Wednesday in San Francisco’s Mission Terrace neighborhood when her aunt, who lives one block over, called her in a panic. The flooding, which had swamped the low-lying neighborhood during previous storms, was back.

Ms. Ponferrada said she pulled on her rain boots, opened her front door and looked down to see murky water climbing up her steps. The smell, she said, was “foul.”

“If that’s not poop water, I don’t know what else to call it,” she said.

Most cities in the United States have one network of pipes to transport wastewater to a treatment plant and another one that sends storm water to a nearby stream or body of water.

But San Francisco has a combined sewer system, with the same underground pipes carrying storm water and wastewater together. And during particularly intense storms, the pipes can get overwhelmed, causing water to collect on streets and spray up though manholes.

San Francisco has one of about 700 such systems in the country; most are in the Northeast and around the Great Lakes region. San Francisco is the only one directly on the Pacific Ocean.

On rainy days that don’t break records, the San Francisco system is a benefit. It captures and cleans rainwater that has been mixed with pollutants such as oil, grease and fertilizer, which all go to a treatment plant before heading out to sea. But on days with deluges, the system overflows, and wastewater that has not yet been cleaned can spew into the streets.

Last week, manhole covers in the Mission Terrace neighborhood popped open, creating geysers in the middle of the streets. Ms. Ponferrada said she tried to walk to her aunt’s house but had to turn back when the water rose past her knees.

She said that during previous storms, she lost two cars and neighbors’ pets had drowned or been electrocuted. This time, she said, several neighbors, including her aunt, had their basements wrecked and were left with “black sewage debris that smells.”

She and other neighbors, as well as residents in other flood-prone parts of the city, are part of a citizens group called Solutions Not Sandbags, which advocates better management of the city’s sewer system.

Sejal Choksi-Chugh, the executive director of San Francisco Baykeeper, an environmental nonprofit, has urged the city to upgrade its infrastructure.

“At least 10 percent of the water that’s spilling into the street and popping out of manhole covers is untreated sewage,” she said. “It’s not good for human exposure, so you don’t want people to walk in those floodwaters and then eat a sandwich.”

Baykeeper recommends not swimming in the Pacific Ocean or the San Francisco Bay for two to three days after a rainstorm because of these issues. Ms. Choksi-Chugh said that people should also avoid contact with floodwater in the city streets.

Nancy Crowley, a spokeswoman for the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, said last week’s storm would have been a challenge for any urban sewer system. On Nov. 18, San Francisco officially recorded 2.64 inches of rain, a record for that date and, in only one day, more than the city’s average rainfall for the entire month of November.

“San Francisco was hit by a historic storm that brought an average of three inches of rain across the city, with half of that downpour coming in one three-hour period,” she said in a statement. “We saw local flooding at several different low-lying spots around the city, as did cities across the Bay Area.”

She said more than 95 percent of the floodwater was rain but acknowledged the rest was wastewater.

The city has three treatment facilities, two dating back to the 1950s and one built in 1994, that can clean a combined 570 million gallons of rainwater and wastewater every day. That is the equivalent of roughly 860 Olympic-size swimming pools.

San Francisco also has 22 miles of underground storm water storage structures that can hold 200 million gallons. But in downpours, that system can reach capacity, and there can be nowhere for the extra water to flow but into the streets.

Homes and businesses in the low-lying areas have been flooded and contaminated in San Francisco for decades. Jan Null, a Bay Area meteorologist, said he had seen it occur again and again in the city’s low-lying areas throughout the 52 years he has been watching the region’s weather.

“It happens along old creek beds and in lowlands and where the soil is getting compacted down and receding,” he said. “It’s been a front-page issue for years.”

Ms. Crowley said the city was investing billions into its sewage system, including modernizing its biggest treatment plant to withstand a three-foot rise in sea level and a 7.8 magnitude earthquake. Smaller projects in the city’s low-lying areas should help with the system’s capacity and reduce the risk of flooding, she said.

But the work may not be enough to withstand storms that are expected to get even fiercer with climate change. Ms. Choksi-Chugh of Baykeeper found it interesting that in a fast-moving city dominated by technology — where Anthropic had a record $1.7 trillion initial public offering on Thursday — focusing on modernizing the sewage treatment system has never been a political priority.

“A. I. is sexy. Data centers are the issue du jour,” she said. “Nobody wants to talk about outdated sewage systems and storm water pipes.”

Amy Graff contributed reporting.

Heather Knight is a reporter in San Francisco, leading The Times’s coverage of the Bay Area and Northern California.

Measles Is a Growing Risk for Adults in the United States

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

The danger is greatest for those who are unvaccinated, but vaccinated people born before 1989 may no longer be sufficiently protected, medical experts said.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

Millions of American adults may be at greater risk of measles than they realize as the virus marches through the country at levels not reached in decades.

Since the United States lost its official measles-elimination designation last week, most of the concern has focused on babies, who are too young to be vaccinated. But even vaccinated adults born before 1989 may no longer be sufficiently protected, infectious disease experts said.

Getting a booster shot could be the best option for many of those adults, seven infectious disease physicians said in interviews.

“Just getting another dose is a very easy and safe thing to do,” said Dr. Cameron Wolfe, who helps investigate outbreaks for Duke University.

In 1989, the measles vaccine went to a two-dose regimen, which is 97 percent effective. People born before then had one dose, which was thought to provide 93 percent protection. But the potency of that dose may have waned over the years because of medical conditions, medication or simple aging, experts said.

People born before 1968 may be even less protected. Those born between 1963 and 1967 received a less effective version of the vaccine. Those born before 1963, when the vaccine first became available, may never have had a measles shot. (People born before 1957 are presumed to be protected through exposure to the disease itself, as is anyone who has had measles.)

These differences did not matter in a country where overall vaccination rates were about 95 percent and outbreaks were sporadic. Until recently, experts advised that one dose was enough protection for most adults. But the risk of exposure to measles has changed sharply in the United States, especially now that the virus is considered a persistent threat in the country. More than 5,800 cases and 12 deaths have been reported this year, numbers widely considered to be an underestimate. More than 40 percent of those reported cases were in adults.

“I think it’s a different ballgame now,” said Dr. Brenda Tesini, an infectious disease physician at the University of Rochester who has spent much of the past few weeks trying to establish whether adults exposed to the virus in New York state’s outbreak are protected.

The vaccine contains a weakened live virus, so it is not safe for pregnant women or for people who have moderate to severe immunosuppression. That makes it all the more important for others to bolster their protection, experts said.

Dr. Wolfe, who has treated a half-dozen adults with measles, said that even a single case can create havoc, both for the hospital and the patient.

When Rita, 63, arrived at an emergency room in Seattle in March, racked with fever, gasping for breath and one rib broken from relentless coughing, measles was on no one’s list of possible causes.

She was otherwise healthy and fit, had received one dose of the vaccine as a child and did not yet have the characteristic measles rash. (She asked to be identified by her first name to protect her privacy.)

Doctors at the University of Washington Medical Center did not isolate her, said Dr. Seth Cohen, the center’s medical director for infection prevention. It took nearly 48 hours for them to diagnose her with measles, and even then, it was only because her 60-year-old vaccinated brother, who was similarly struggling in a hospital across town, tested positive for the virus.

By that point, about 150 patients in the hospital, including some with cancer, had potentially become exposed to the virus. Fortunately, none became ill, Dr. Cohen said: “The silver lining is she was likely much less infectious than she would have been had she not been vaccinated.”

Rita was discharged from the hospital after three days and a $40,000 tab, including $8,000 that her health plan required her to pay out of pocket. She remained sick and exhausted for weeks after returning home.

The measles virus destroys important immune cells, making the body vulnerable even to pathogens it has already fought. Rita lost about half her thick head of hair and has to stay away from her grandchildren whenever they are sick. She constantly picks up respiratory infections. She was sniffly with yet another cold on Friday.

Some measles patients, particularly those who are unvaccinated, end up with severe neurological complications. Measles can cause encephalitis, or an infection of the brain, during or even weeks after the illness, as well as tingling, numbness, deafness or blindness. A small percentage of patients die.

“The prognosis for all of these is actually pretty nasty,” said Dr. Pushpa Narayanaswami, a neurologist at Harvard Medical School and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who treated about a dozen adults with measles while practicing in India.

“The only way to prevent any of these complications is vaccination,” she said.

About 96 percent of measles cases in the United States are in people who were unvaccinated or have an unknown vaccination status, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Public health officials classify anyone who cannot find proof of vaccination as being of unknown status.

Rita could not locate her immunization records when she was admitted but told doctors she had received one dose as a child. Still, the public service announcement to warn patients who may have been exposed to measles during her time at the hospital referred to her vaccination status as unknown, prompting some people in the community to label her “an anti-vaxxer Trump person,” she said.

It may also have led some adults who had been vaccinated to underestimate their risk, mistakenly believing only unvaccinated people to be vulnerable, she added.

“That to me is the most important part of my whole story,” she said.

Dr. Tesini said Rita’s experience was not uncommon and suggests there may be more breakthrough infections in vaccinated adults who may have had only one shot than the C. D. C. estimates.

“Many or most of us adults would fall into ‘vaccination unknown’ — as in, you can’t produce a piece of paper that says you got these vaccines,” she said.

The C. D. C. continues to monitor measles cases and clinical outcomes across all age groups, including adults, according to a spokeswoman for the agency. It has also expanded its Surveillance for Emerging Threats to Mothers and Babies Network to include measles.

The agency recommends measles vaccination for people who have no documented evidence of immunity but maintains its previous stance that a single dose is enough for adults born before 1989. (A committee that advises the C. D. C. on vaccines has not met since last December because of a federal court ruling suspending its work.)

Infectious disease specialists say that may be an outdated recommendation. “It’s a good time to boost for anybody who’s not sure” of their risk, said Dr. Camille Kotton, an infectious diseases physician at Massachusetts General Hospital and a prior member of the vaccine advisory committee. She said she recommends against commercial antibody tests to determine protection because they measure a single component of a complex immune system.

The pharmaceutical companies Merck and GSK, which make the measles-mumps-rubella combination shots available in the United States, said they would monitor demand for the vaccine in case they needed to increase the supply.

Dr. Kotton said she was particularly concerned for her immunocompromised patients and those with underlying conditions. Conditions like H. I. V. infection or a prior blood cancer that devastated the person’s immune system would also increase risk.

More people are now alive thanks to new and powerful immune therapies for conditions that were once fatal. “But it often means dampening down your own immune system as the therapy,” Dr. Wolfe said. Nearly 7 percent of Americans met the criteria for immunosuppression in 2024 compared with less than 3 percent a decade earlier.

The immune system’s strength also declines with age, particularly after age 50. “The protection afforded by the one dose at 30 years is not likely to be the same protection affected by the one dose at 63 or 73 or 83 years,” Dr. Narayanaswami said.

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukrainian drones had sunk a corvette and hit a dry cargo vessel, in attacks that involved special operations forces.

By Maria Varenikova and Carlotta Gall

Maria Varenikova reported from Kyiv, Ukraine, and Carlotta Gall from Lviv, Ukraine.

For years, North Africa and the Middle East have been an unlikely distant front in the Russia-Ukraine war. Ukrainian special operations forces have gone after Russian military and mercenary assets in Sudan, Mali and Syria. Now, for the first time, Ukraine has claimed credit for an attack on Russian ships off the coast of Libya — using drones launched into the Mediterranean Sea.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Monday that Ukrainian forces had been responsible for strikes on two Russian ships the previous day. One, a corvette, sank, and a Russian combat helicopter was destroyed along with it, according to Mr. Zelensky. Ukraine also hit a Russian dry cargo vessel that he said was being used to transport weapons.

Seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were deployed in the strikes, Mr. Zelensky said in a post on social media. He did not say how Ukraine had got the drones — essentially exploding remote-controlled speedboats — into the Mediterranean. But Mr. Zelensky said that the Security Service of Ukraine, known as the S. B. U., was involved in the attacks, an indication that covert work had gone into the operation.

During the war, the S. B. U. has been transformed from a conventional domestic counterintelligence service into a specialized deep-strike and sabotage force. It has been involved in some of the war’s most brazen operations, including strikes last week that destroyed a large part of the only bridge connecting occupied Crimea to Russia.

The S. B. U. said the drones used in the strikes on Sunday, near the port of Benghazi in eastern Libya, were launched from a maritime carrier. The agency did not reveal where the drones were loaded onto the carrier. Suspicion fell on western Libya, where Ukrainian operators have been present for years, analysts say. Libya is ruled by two rival governments, one based in the country’s east and the other in its west. The government in the east is more closely aligned with Russia.

The Benghazi strikes were the latest attack in an intensifying Ukrainian campaign against Russian ships that had largely relied on aerial drones. They demonstrated that Ukraine’s reach extends even to distant seas. Kyiv has long said that it will attack Russian military assets anywhere in the world.

Ukraine’s long-range strikes are a response to Russia’s own campaign of attacks on Ukrainian cities. On Monday afternoon, Russian drones again struck the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, sending pillars of smoke rising from a city-center site a few yards from the presidential office.

“We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” Mr. Zelensky said in his post online, before the attack near his office. “We are developing Ukrainian weapons.”

The drone attacks near Libya came a day after a Russian cargo ship, the Sparta II, was struck in the Gulf of Finland, in the eastern Baltic Sea. Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for that strike, but is believed to have been behind it. The Finnish prime minister also said his country supported Kyiv’s right to conduct such strikes.

A handful of Russian ships have been attacked, with both aerial and sea drones, in the Mediterranean over the past year or so. Ukraine has not acknowledged those strikes but is believed to have been behind at least some, or perhaps all, of them.

In March, Moscow accused Ukraine of attacking the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the central Mediterranean. The tanker, part of the so-called shadow fleet that Moscow uses to bypass sanctions, was carrying liquefied natural gas to Egypt when it was hit by explosions.

The U. N. mission in Libya condemned the latest strikes and warned “against escalatory actions or rhetoric that could fuel tensions within Libya or draw the country into wider regional or international confrontations.”

“Libya cannot afford, and must not become, a battleground for foreign conflicts,” the mission said in a statement on Sunday.

Russian officials echoed this warning, accusing Ukraine of dragging Libya into the war.

Benghazi, in the east of Libya, is controlled by the forces of Gen. Khalifa Hifter. Russia has been cultivating its relations with General Hifter since it lost its base of operations in Syria after the fall of the dictator Bashar al-Assad in 2024. The government in western Libya is backed by Western nations.

The Ukrainian attacks reflected an evolution in Ukraine’s battle with Russia over dominance of waterways. When Russia invaded in 2022, Moscow held sway. Russia had seized most of Ukraine’s navy in its illegal annexation of Crimea eight years earlier.

Lacking a traditional naval force, Kyiv turned to drones. Ukraine scaled up its arsenal and eventually sank about a third of Russia’s once-vaunted Black Sea Fleet. Ukraine has since expanded its operations into the Baltic, Caspian and Mediterranean Seas, analysts say.

The Mediterranean is crowded with civilian vessels, and strikes in that sea could jeopardize Ukraine’s relations with allies. Earlier this year, an explosives-laden maritime drone washed up in Greece, prompting Ukraine to issue an apology.

Such operations suggest that Ukraine has a strong intelligence network in the Mediterranean, said Andrii Klymenko, an editor at Black Sea News, an online outlet focused on naval affairs.

Benghazi is a relatively new port of call for Russian military vessels, which historically preferred Tobruk. That means Ukraine must have had exceptionally good intelligence or highly reactive planning and logistical capabilities to execute an attack on short notice, said Aliona Hlivko, a security analyst and chief executive of the St. James’s Foreign Policy Group in London.

“This points to Ukraine’s growing ability to project maritime power beyond the Black Sea and will almost certainly have broader geopolitical implications,” she said.

Abed Thalji, a trade analyst in Sweden who focuses on energy and shipping, said the attacks on Russian vessels were aimed at damaging Russia’s oil and gas supply chain, which is an economic lifeline for its war effort.

“These navy ships are usually there to accompany the oil and gas tankers that transport Russian oil from the Arctic or the Black Sea to North Africa, and they tend to concentrate around Egypt, Algeria and Libya,” he said.

Mr. Thalji said the attacks were a blow to the power of General Hifter and would warn off other countries from using eastern Libyan ports.

“Ukraine is signaling not just to Russia but to other countries that docking in Libya is not safe,” he said.

Hussam Hammoud contributed reporting from Damascus, Syria, and Oleksandr Chubko and Nataliia Novosolova from Kyiv.

An earlier version of this article misidentified the country where Abed Thalji, a trade analyst, was based. He is in Sweden, not Germany.

Drone Attack Hits Colombian City as Unmanned Explosives Transform Conflict

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

At least three people were injured. The United Nations has reported a 445 percent increase in drone bombings in the country.

By Julie Turkewitz

Drones launched explosives that destroyed a home in a major Colombian city on Monday morning in the first such attack inside a major population hub, as the cheap devices reshape a conflict between the country’s armed groups and the military.

The drones injured three people in the city of Cúcuta, according to George Quintero, a retired colonel who now works as a security adviser to the regional government. He added that they were most likely launched by one of two armed groups battling for control of illicit economies.

The Colombian military, with financial and technical help from the United States, has long fought armed insurgencies and criminal groups. In the last two years, readily accessible commercial drones fitted with explosives have given armed groups new ways to attack government forces and terrorize the population.

Until now, those strikes have happened in relatively rural areas.

The attack on Monday occurred at about 3 a. m., Colonel Quintero said in an interview with the Colombian radio station Blu Radio. The worst-damaged home is half a block away from a police station, which may have been the target of the attack. More than 60 homes and businesses were affected by the explosives, the colonel said, which shattered windows and left shrapnel in walls.

The United Nations reported that drone bombings have risen to 333 instances in 2025 from 61 in 2024, a 445 percent increase.

Cúcuta is on the border with Venezuela, in a region of vast fields of coca, a base ingredient in cocaine. For the last two years, two armed groups — the National Liberation Army, or ELN, and the 33rd Front, a splinter group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia — have been battling for control of the territory. Thousands of people have been displaced by the violence, and many others have been killed.

The area and the two groups have been major military targets for Colombia’s new right-wing president, Abelardo De La Espriella, as well as for the Trump administration, which has been focused on armed groups and illicit economies across Latin America. Last month, in a region on the Colombia-Venezuela border to the south of Cúcuta, the United States assisted the Venezuelan government in an attack on the ELN.

Asked on Blu Radio whether the Colombian government had the right technology to fight the drone attacks, Colonel Quintero said that “there is currently no magic wand anywhere in the world that can effectively counter it.”

“The current national government has provided some tools — such as anti-drone guns and other specialized equipment — and additional procurement is underway,” he added.

But several strikes had taken place in rural areas just as the assault in Cúcuta was underway.

“There were another five this morning,” he said. “It is extremely complex to achieve full coverage against this type of drone-based attack.”

On Monday morning in Cúcuta, explosives had destroyed one home and damaged others. Glass from blown-out windows littered the street.

“The bomb fell right on top of the house,” said Orlando Roa, who said he had escaped the attack with his wife and 17-month-old son. He had shrapnel lodged in his leg, he said. His wife and son seemed to be all right but were being examined at a hospital.

“Thank God they were protected,” he said.

Federico Rios contributed reporting from Cúcuta, Colombia.

Julie Turkewitz is the Andes Bureau Chief for The Times, based in Bogotá, Colombia, covering Colombia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

Elon Musk Faces an A. I. Dilemma at SpaceX

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Mr. Musk’s SpaceX is renting out computing power from its data centers to competitors, including Anthropic. That’s making it harder for his own A. I. effort.

A data center in Southaven, Miss. Elon Musk has spent billions building data centers to catch up with rivals. Credit... Kevin Wurm/Reuters

Supported by

By Grace Kay and Ryan Mac

Grace Kay, who covers Elon Musk’s A. I. ambitions, reported from New York, and Ryan Mac, who covers corporate accountability, reported from London.

Anthropic is one of Elon Musk’s biggest competitors in artificial intelligence. It is also one of his biggest customers.

Since May, Mr. Musk’s SpaceX has made billions of dollars a month leasing computing power from its data centers to companies like Anthropic and Google. At the same time, SpaceX is developing its own A. I. products, like its chatbot Grok and A. I. agent Grok Bot.

Mr. Musk has told employees that SpaceX is falling behind in A. I. development, making it more lucrative to rent the company’s computing power out to rivals than use it to improve its own products, according to three people with knowledge of his comments.

But Mr. Musk is frustrated by the situation, the people said. In a group chat with hundreds of engineers at SpaceX’s A. I. unit, he shared data showing the company lagged competitors. And once a week, he has asked some group members to list their work in the chat to justify the use of specialized computer chips, or graphics processing units, which train A. I. systems, the people said.

In August, Mr. Musk temporarily changed the group chat name to “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” according to communications viewed by The New York Times. He added a warning to employees who were not using the company’s computing resources wisely: “Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team.”

The tension highlights a central conflict in Mr. Musk’s A. I. push. He started an A. I. company, xAI, a year after OpenAI’s blockbuster release of ChatGPT in 2022, and has spent billions building data centers to catch up. Now, with SpaceX newly public and under pressure to show investors it can turn a profit, Mr. Musk is stuck renting much of that firepower out to the same companies he’s chasing.

That has set off a monthslong scramble for resources that has pitted the company’s ambitions — and at times even Mr. Musk’s pet projects — against its balance sheet.

The unit, renamed SpaceXSI, now generates more than half of all revenue for SpaceX, which once relied on money from government contracts to send rockets to space. SpaceX highlighted the risks of selling computing power to competitors in a prospectus before going public in June, saying the company’s data center leasing business could “create operational complexity.”

Anthropic and Google have each forged deals to lease computing power from SpaceX, with Anthropic’s valued at about $3.1 billion a month and Google’s $800 million a month. These deals could run through 2029, but could also be terminated by either party with 90 days’ notice.

Over the past few months, Anthropic has become SpaceXSI’s largest customer. Anthropic, which went public last week, has so much demand for computing power that by October, SpaceXSI needed to finish new data centers to fulfill the A. I. company’s orders, according to two people with knowledge of the work, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not permitted to speak publicly on the company’s behalf.

Representatives for SpaceX and Mr. Musk did not respond to a request for comment. Anthropic referred The Times to a portion of the company’s prospectus for its initial public offering that detailed its agreement with SpaceX.

While SpaceX has lagged rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic, Mr. Musk found an advantage in building data centers quickly. The more computing power a company has, the more powerful it can make its A. I. systems.

In 2024, Mr. Musk’s A. I. company built a data center in Memphis, one of the largest in the industry, in just 122 days. Since then, Mr. Musk has said the company has added more than one million of the specialized A. I. chips to power the technology. This month, SpaceX announced plans to invest $74 billion in data centers in Arizona and Texas.

“SpaceX makes way more money right now renting out compute than from Grok,” said Nicolas Owens, an analyst who covers SpaceX for Morningstar Research. “Grok is not the premier model in town, so I think it’s more doubtful that they would be able to tip the scale to where serving up A. I. off of their own servers is more lucrative than branching it out to Anthropic.”

Last year, xAI used less than half of the capacity of its first data center, Colossus, according to one person familiar with the project and internal documentation viewed by The Times.

While several xAI executives encouraged Mr. Musk at the time to rent out computing power to help recoup costs, he was adamant he would not do so, two people with knowledge of the conversations said.

Mr. Musk changed his mind by April, when he told xAI engineers that Anthropic had approached the company about leasing computing power, according to two people who attended the meeting. Shortly after, the company announced the deals with Anthropic and Google.

After SpaceX went public, the pressure ramped up in the company’s A. I. unit. Mr. Musk has used weekly meetings to press engineers to justify how much computing power they use, two people familiar with the conversations said. He has also become more focused on finding ways to charge those who use its A. I. products like Grok, the people said.

“At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks,” Mr. Musk wrote in August in the group chat with engineers that was viewed by The Times. “If you can’t pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental company. Move the needle on revenue.”

As it builds out data centers for rivals, SpaceX has quietly trimmed back its own A. I. ambitions.

In September, the company shut down a pet project of Mr. Musk’s, A. I. companions. The animated avatars could do real-time voice chats and included Ani, who would undress on command.

This fall, the company shifted resources away from another one of Mr. Musk’s top initiatives. SpaceX’s A. I. unit had been working with Tesla on a project to teach Grok how to work as an A. I. white-collar worker, called Digital Optimus.

A first step in the project was teaching the A. I. system how to play video games like Diablo and League of Legends autonomously, according to three people with knowledge of the project. After the team failed to meet Mr. Musk’s expectations, Tesla engineers were moved off the project this fall to work on the main Grok A. I. model, including its coding capabilities, two of the people said. Despite this, Mr. Musk wrote on X on Friday that the product could now reach a higher level in Diablo.

This month, Mike Nicolls, the president of the A. I. unit, announced the disbanding of the 60-member team behind Grok Imagine, an image and video-generation tool that was once a top priority, according to four people with knowledge of the cuts. Already the team’s share of computing power had shrunk, according to three people with knowledge of the project.

The cuts would “better align our structure and resources with critical business priorities,” according to an internal memo from Mr. Nicolls viewed by The Times. The Information, a tech news site, earlier reported that some members of the Grok Imagine team had been laid off.

At an employee meeting this month, Mr. Nicolls, who has overseen SpaceX’s successful satellite internet service, Starlink, repeatedly emphasized that SpaceXSI was falling behind Anthropic, said two people who attended the meeting.

Still, Mr. Musk praised SpaceX’s relationship with Anthropic last Wednesday.

“When I’ve talked to Anthropic, they tell me it is extremely likely that they will continue to rent compute from SpaceX,” he said at The Times’s DealBook conference. “And in fact that they want significantly more.”

Grace Kay is a Times reporter covering Elon Musk’s companies, with a focus on A. I. and emerging technology.

Ryan Mac is a Times reporter who covers corporate accountability across the global technology industry.

D. N. C. Plans 12 Debates for the 2028 Presidential Primary, Starting in June

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The national party also revealed some initial criteria for participating, including a pledge to denounce spending from supportive groups that do not disclose their donors.

By Reid J. Epstein and Shane Goldmacher

Reid J. Epstein and Shane Goldmacher covered all of the 2020 primary debates and they are getting ready to cover them all again for 2028.

The Democratic National Committee announced on Monday that it was planning 12 presidential debates for the 2028 primaries, scheduling the first for next June in what could be a wide open race.

The party also revealed some initial criteria for participating in the debates, including a pledge that, if enforced, would require candidates to denounce spending on their behalf from outside groups that do not disclose their donors.

Additionally, the candidates will have to agree to not participate in any other event in which two or more candidates appear at the same time, and meet polling and fund-raising thresholds that have not yet been specified. The D. N. C. has enlisted longtime party operatives to oversee the process.

“The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee and put Democrats in position to take back the White House,” Ken Martin, the party’s chairman, said in a statement. He declined to be interviewed about the process.

The announcement comes as the jockeying for 2028 is ramping up in both parties after a midterm election in which Democrats had sweeping victories. While no major candidates have formally entered the race, plenty of behind-the-scenes maneuvering is underway. Some would-be candidates gathered this month at events in Washington and Denver, and a conclave of potential campaign managers and other senior aides is to take place in New York in December.

The 2028 Democratic field could be as open and expansive as any in a generation. Just like in the 2020 cycle when 28 Democrats ran for the party’s presidential nomination, the crop of potential candidates ranges from well-known governors and senators to who’s-that politicians and media figures aiming to make names for themselves.

The D. N. C. said it was prepared to split debate fields into two groups and hold sessions on back-to-back nights if enough candidates qualify, though it said it would limit the number of participants to 20. The party said it would reveal requirements for polling and fund-raising thresholds to participate in debates in January, when it also plans to announce locations and media partners.

The party said it would also involve content creators and influencers in the debate process.

The so-called dark money pledge is the most significant change to the D. N. C.’s debate rules from the campaign for 2020. Then, most of the primary candidates — though not Joseph R. Biden Jr. — adhered to an informal agreement to forswear super PAC spending on their behalf. That arrangement eventually collapsed and even Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who was among the most vocal opponents of super PAC spending, accepted support from one.

Now the D. N. C.’s debate planning committee — which is to be led by Minyon Moore, a veteran party official, and Roger Lau, the party’s executive director — will seek to enforce a “Fair Campaign Practices” pledge that prohibits candidates from having the sort of cloak-and-dagger cooperation with super PACs that have become routine in federal campaigns.

The debate calendar is set to run through March 2028, though the party could add more dates. The party said it would hold all of its early state debates — the first six that start the nominating process — in the 2028 calendar year.

In April, Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent of Vermont, called on Mr. Martin and the D. N. C. to require candidates up and down the ballot to reject super PAC and dark money support. Mr. Martin at the time said he agreed, but argued that it would take commitments from across the party to ban such practices from primaries.

Still, it is widely expected that most major presidential candidates will have authorized supportive super PACs. How the D. N. C.’s pledge affects those organizations remains to be seen.

The D. N. C.’s prohibitions on super PAC and dark money support do not apply to the general election, the party said.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

U. S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

U. S. intelligence is said to show that the woman at the heart of the A. I. chip scandal was in touch with China’s Ministry of State Security during the period when she was in a relationship with Jensen Huang.

By Jonathan SwanJulian E. Barnes and Maggie Haberman

The reporters have been covering the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia and accusations of Chinese chip smuggling.

The board of directors of Nvidia announced on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. Follow live updates here.

The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of U. S. intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said. That period overlaps with at least a portion of the time she was in a relationship with Mr. Huang, then the head of the world’s leading maker of advanced artificial intelligence chips.

U. S. intelligence agencies have also gathered evidence that Ms. Huang’s business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency, the people said.

The extent and specific timing of Ms. Huang’s contacts with the spy agency — and Mr. Kang’s work for the same intelligence service — have not been previously reported.

Ms. Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency last year and up through recent months help to flesh out how U. S. officials came to believe that Mr. Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive earlier this month, was the target of an intelligence operation.

They correspond not just to the time when he was conducting the affair but also to at least part of the period when Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips, some of which went to data centers in Southeast Asia serving Chinese technology companies like Alibaba and some of which are suspected of being smuggled to China.

Allies of Mr. Huang, including President Trump, have sought to minimize the scandal and questioned whether Ms. Huang was spying for Chinese intelligence. But the newly revealed information underscores the continuous contacts that she had with the Ministry of State Security, even as she was in a romantic relationship with Mr. Huang.

It also helps to flesh out why some American officials have been worried that Ms. Huang’s role is just one element of a much broader push by China in that technological battle. The Ministry of State Security has prioritized focusing on acquiring high-end chips and advancing China’s A. I. ambitions.

U. S. officials are investigating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in a network of Southeast Asian companies, including Megaspeed, that have been linked to the possible smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, to evade U. S. export control laws. U. S. officials are still working to determine the full extent and duration of their work with Chinese intelligence.

The intelligence gathered by the U. S. contains evidence — including shipping records — demonstrating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in that network of companies, people with knowledge of the intelligence reports said. The New York Times has previously reported that Ms. Huang and her family have a web of connections to Chinese defense contractors.

Mr. Huang initially described his relationship with Ms. Huang as normal interactions with a business customer. He acknowledged an affair only after The Times revealed last month that Ms. Huang had been identified by the United States as a Chinese intelligence asset and that the Nvidia chief had been picked up on electronic surveillance targeting her.

He stepped down this month after The Times subsequently reported that he had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Administration officials never provided him with a so-called defensive briefing about Ms. Huang, a heads-up that the woman he was in a relationship with had been linked to Chinese intelligence.

The White House and a spokesman for Mr. Huang declined to comment. The State Department, the Chinese Embassy in Washington, Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang did not respond to requests for comment on Sunday.

Before the scandal broke into public view, advisers to Mr. Trump told him on at least two occasions that U. S. intelligence had uncovered Ms. Huang’s links to the Chinese spy agency and that she was in a close relationship with Mr. Huang while he was still running Nvidia, according to U. S. officials with direct knowledge of the briefings.

Both times, including when his national security adviser discussed it with him, the president downplayed the concerns and made clear he did not want to intervene in the matter. The officials said Mr. Trump regarded Mr. Huang as a valuable ally and Nvidia as essential to the health of the American economy and stock market. Mr. Trump has recently suggested that Nvidia should consider bringing Mr. Huang back as chief executive, a possibility the company’s board has rejected.

“We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them,” the president said at a White House news conference on Friday. “I think the company if they were smart they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work.”

Mr. Trump has claimed that no one in his government told him of any intelligence indicating that Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.

“I don’t know that she is a spy,” he said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”

In fact, his administration has been monitoring Ms. Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency for more than a year, a period when the Ministry of State Security has been intensifying its new role in seeking to give China an advantage in artificial intelligence.

“This network of companies working to procure and smuggle Nvidia chips lines up precisely with the M. S. S.’s recently stated core mission of circumventing and undermining U. S. export controls on semiconductors and other key technologies,” said Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Mr. Trump’s first term, and who is chief executive of the open-source research firm Garnaut Global.

The Ministry of State Security has for decades declared that its mission is to combat espionage and to eliminate political threats to Communist Party rule in China. The minister of state security, Chen Yixin, gave a similar five-point statement as recently as late last year. Then in April, he unveiled a new, sixth mission — overcoming the “blockades” choking China’s access to key technologies like artificial intelligence.

“Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development and applications,” Mr. Chen wrote in a party journal. “Focus on tackling the ‘choke holds’ of critical technologies.”

“To assume the M. S. S. wasn’t at the center of this operation would be to assume that they are incompetent,” Mr. Pottinger added. “That’s not an assumption I would make.”

American spy agencies are still working to understand the role played by Mr. Kang, the business partner of Ms. Huang, whom she would introduce to associates as her husband. Multiple people with knowledge of the intelligence said the United States had collected evidence that Mr. Kang worked with the Ministry of State Security.

Ms. Huang also appears to have met with officials of China’s Ministry of Public Security, the nation’s main law enforcement agency, according to multiple people with knowledge of the U. S. intelligence reports.

Ms. Huang, Mr. Kang, Ms. Huang’s sister and companies associated with them have emerged as a significant branch of the Chinese effort to build data centers and acquire access to Nvidia chips to train powerful A. I. models. Ms. Huang’s network has been linked to efforts to supply the powerful chips to Chinese-state owned military contractors doing work for the People’s Liberation Army.

Little of the intelligence about Ms. Huang and her network has been provided to Capitol Hill, but lawmakers from both parties are demanding briefings.

A briefing this month for top lawmakers by John Ratcliffe, the C. I. A. director, and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, was originally scheduled to discuss Iran, but The Times’s reporting on Nvidia led the lawmakers to ask questions about Mr. Huang and Alice Huang. Their answers raised more questions and left some lawmakers puzzled.

Trump administration officials postponed a follow-up briefing for top national security staffers scheduled for last Wednesday, in which senior officials were set to share details of the intelligence collected on Ms. Huang.

The intelligence about Ms. Huang was closely held inside the government until The Times reported the existence of the information in late October. Behind the scenes, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also the national security adviser, had written a confidential memo, dated March 30 this year, laying out Ms. Huang’s ties to Chinese intelligence.

Jonathan Swan is a White House reporter for The Times, covering the administration of Donald J. Trump. Contact him securely on Signal: @jonathan.941

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

They Were Too Old to Enlist, but Not to Fight. Meet the Steppe Wolves of Ukraine.

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

When the military refused to let them sign up, a band of aging men found their own way to wage war against Russia.

When the military refused to let them sign up, a band of aging men found their own way to wage war against Russia.

Members of the Steppe Wolves military unit working on a missile in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, earlier this year. Credit...

Supported by

By Alla DidurCassandra Vinograd and Oleksandr Chubko

Photographs by Laetitia Vançon

Reporting from the Zaporizhzhia region of Ukraine

They called themselves pioneers, which they thought sounded better than pensioners. It was age, after all, that had gotten them rejected by the Ukrainian military and forced to find another way to join the fight for survival against Russia.

“No one can forbid me, at any age, from defending my country, my land, and my family,” said one of the men, whose call sign — naturally enough — is Grandpa. “If they won’t accept us officially, we’ll do it unofficially.”

Grandpa, who got his call sign before he actually had any grandchildren, was 65 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. At the time, Ukraine’s army was accepting only soldiers age 60 and under, so he formed a group of partisans known as the Steppe Wolves.

The outfit fought near Melitopol, then Vasylivka and later Kamianske. These days, they number about a dozen and are primarily based in the Zaporizhzhia region.

That is where, on a visit one early spring afternoon, we saw camouflage pants hanging on a clothesline outside the nondescript building that served as their base. Inside, dozens of rockets were stacked on the floor, many in various states of disrepair.

Ukrainian military units from all over have brought faulty rockets to the Steppe Wolves, who repair them in exchange for being able to keep some for their own use. They have also refurbished abandoned rockets they found to use against Russian positions. Ukrainian soldiers send them coordinates and targets for those strikes, and in some cases even provide additional ammunition.

One artillery commander in a Ukrainian military special operations unit said that he had worked with the Steppe Wolves since 2022 and that they were far more than just enthusiasts.

“They don’t just help with moral support or kind words,” the commander, whose call sign is Bush, said in a phone interview. The older soldiers carry out missions, he said, describing them as “very mobile” as well as “fast and effective.”

Bush, who like the other soldiers interviewed asked to be identified only by his call sign, in keeping with military protocol, said he would gladly bring the Steppe Wolves into his unit officially.

“Judging by age isn’t right,” he said. “It’s about motivation.” And the Steppe Wolves, he said, “just want to work.”

At the Steppe Wolves base one cold morning, a soldier who goes by the name Dnipro, 64, was repairing a detonator in a cramped workshop that smelled like gunpowder. He needs glasses to drive but otherwise has no physical limitations, he said.

“We don’t feel old,” Dnipro said. “Not young, of course — but not old either.”

Like many of his comrades, Dnipro argued that his age made him an asset. “With age everyone gains experience,” he said, pointing to his years of mechanical work and ability to work in teams.

Arsen, 66, used to work as a welder making boilers in Kharkiv. After Russia invaded in 2022, he said, he went to a recruitment office but was told he was “not needed.”

When his son joined the military in January 2024, Arsen said, he was worried, but also proud to see his child “defending the Motherland, not hiding behind his wife’s skirt.”

Six months later, his son was dead.

Arsen spent half a year in deep grief, avoiding life and people, he said, until he realized he “had to do something.” That “something” was serving his country, which led to the Steppe Wolves.

His wife was not pleased, at least initially. Her position later softened, he said, recalling how she told him “go — I understand.”

“My son fought for me. Now I fight for him,” Arsen said. “There was no other decision.”

He said he planned to stay with the Steppe Wolves as long as his health allowed. He has no limitations yet, he said, aside from needing reading glasses.

“Here I found my brothers,” he said that chilly spring afternoon. “And here I feel that I am in my place.”

Petro, 68, insisted that he was “still young.” A former professional weight lifter and coach, he walked with arms held out from his sides like a man who pumps serious iron.

“Now it is especially important to keep my physical condition, because the rockets are heavy,” he explained one morning after lifting weights at a nearby gym.

The only difference between him and a regular soldier, Petro said, was that “we don’t get paid.”

“If, for example, I die, my family won’t receive anything,” he said. “No social protection. Nothing. That’s just the reality.”

He spoke without bitterness, saying he fought not for money but out of duty. But a bit of recognition, he conceded, would be nice.

A month earlier, with Ukraine stricken by troop shortages, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine had signed a decree that would allow anyone over 60 to serve with a one-year contract in the military, with the possibility to extend. But it was taking time for that to trickle down, and in the meantime the Steppe Wolves were in limbo.

“Deep down, it’s a bit hurtful that we’ve put in so much effort and they still can’t organize us properly,” Petro said, as an air-raid warning started to wail. “But the most important thing is to drive the enemy out of here.”

Eventually, he and the other men got their wish: one-year contracts with Ukraine’s military.

The men of the Steppe Wolves were now official.

Oregon and Virginia Sue SpaceX Over A. I.-Generated Sexualized Images

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The states accused Elon Musk’s company of violating consumer protection laws with its Grok Imagine artificial intelligence tool, which created the images.

By Kate Conger and Grace Kay

Oregon and Virginia on Monday sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, accusing the company of violating state consumer protection laws by providing an artificial intelligence tool that allowed users to create sexualized images of women and children.

Mr. Musk last year introduced Grok Imagine, which uses A. I. to generate images and videos. It included a “spicy mode” to create sexualized content.

In just a few days, Grok Imagine was used to generate at least 1.8 million sexualized images of women and at least 65 sexualized images of children that appeared on the X platform, which is owned by SpaceX. Child sexual abuse imagery is illegal in most of the world, and U. S. law prohibits the publication of intimate images of adults without their consent.

Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode” “specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images,” said Virginia’s attorney general, Jay Jones, in a release. The company’s promotion of the product came as Grok trailed A. I. models created by firms like OpenAI and Anthropic and SpaceX did not prevent its tool from being used to create the material, according to the states.

Tools like Grok Imagine are “what made their A. I. model relevant. It was what was going to make them dollars and cents down the road,” Dan Rayfield, the attorney general of Oregon, said of SpaceX. “What we don’t want our technology doing is creating nonconsensual images, specifically of our children.”

Both lawsuits seek financial damages.

In a statement on Monday, X said that people who used its products to generate sexual images of minors or nonconsensual explicit images of real people had deliberately violated its terms of service. The company said it has since tightened its protections and reports offenders to law enforcement.

X users prompted Grok Imagine to create a flood of sexualized images in December and January. After a public outcry and investigations from regulators, X said it would no longer allow users to publicly post sexualized images.

In a regulatory filing in May, SpaceX said Grok’s ability to generate sexual content posed a risk to investors. This year, xAI, the A. I. company owned by SpaceX, sued several Grok users who created child sexual abuse material with the chatbot, saying they misused the technology.

Mr. Rayfield and Mr. Jones likened their lawsuits to recent state litigation against Meta, which accused the social media company of endangering children with addictive platforms. In August, Meta agreed to a $17.1 billion settlement with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U. S. territories over the claims, and said it would make major changes to its products.

“We are going to put all of our resources and energy and time and power behind holding these big companies accountable,” Mr. Jones said in an interview. “People’s safety depends on this, and no longer are we going to let these companies run roughshod over people.”

Ryan Mac contributed reporting.

Kate Conger is a technology reporter based in San Francisco. She can be reached at kate. conger@nytimes. com.

Grace Kay is a Times reporter covering Elon Musk’s companies, with a focus on A. I. and emerging technology.
