The Americas’ Longest War, and 10 Years of an Unfinished Peace

The New York Times November 23, 2026

A decade ago, the largest guerrilla group in Latin America laid down its arms, ending the longest-running war in the hemisphere.

Nearly half a million people had died. The violence had touched almost every aspect of society. The world’s eyes turned to Colombia as an example that peace was possible.

Today, the legacy of the accord is decidedly mixed.

The country’s main rebel group disbanded. But Colombia’s conflicts and criminal economies have only multiplied, fueling new cycles of violence.

Supported by

in photos

The conflict between Colombia’s government and a leftist rebel group ended in a historic 2016 accord. But Colombia is still waiting for true peace.

Photographs by Federico Rios

Written by Federico Rios and Julie Turkewitz

Julie Turkewitz has covered Colombia for the last seven years as the Andes bureau chief, and Federico Rios for the last 15, as a photographer.

The president called it “a common hunger” — peace.

On Nov. 24, 2016, the world watched as Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signed an accord with the country’s largest insurgency, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. The agreement with the FARC ended a war that had lasted generations, dominated the regional security agenda and left millions of victims of kidnapping, disappearance and other abuse.

“Our dear Colombia,” Mr. Santos said, would no longer be “trapped in this labyrinth of violence.”

Thirteen thousand FARC fighters laid down their arms and the government pledged to address the root causes of the war, expand social programs, eliminate the illicit drug industry and establish a framework for truth and reconciliation.

Now, as Colombia marks the 10th anniversary of that deal, there is neither complete victory to celebrate nor absolute failure to mourn. Instead, Colombia has learned to live with a peace that is partial and uneven, a mix of real achievements and half-kept promises.

1960s

FARC fighters training at a camp in the jungle. The group’s origins trace back to the 1940s, when rural workers formed self-defense communities to resist state-backed violence, which morphed into a Communist insurgency by the mid-1960s.

1998

The bodies of Colombian soldiers killed during clashes with FARC rebels in the southern region of El Caguán.

2003

The FARC bombed El Nogal, an upscale social and business club in Bogotá. At least 32 people were killed in one of the deadliest urban attacks in the country’s history, solidifying public support for the military campaign of the conservative president Álvaro Uribe.

The deal led to one of the largest reductions in violence in modern Colombian history, measured in lives affected by displacement, massacres and homicides. But today, domestic support for the accord is at its lowest level since the signing. The country’s newly elected right-wing president, Abelardo De La Espriella, has criticized the deal and promised to dismantle it, and the country’s conflicts and criminal economies have only multiplied, fueling new cycles of violence.

Some Colombians see the country’s security problems as evidence of the deal’s failure; others say the violence is precisely why it must be kept in place — it is the hard-won framework needed to tackle deeply entrenched problems.

“We have a serious and comprehensive road map to close the gaps that fuel violence,” said Mr. Santos, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for his role in the deal. “That is why Colombia must continue moving forward with the implementation.”

2007

Íngrid Betancourt, a Colombian senator, was kidnapped by the FARC in 2002, while campaigning for the presidency, and held for over six years. Her rescue by the Colombian army marked the beginning of the FARC’s military decline ahead of the 2016 peace talks.

2010

A soldier wounded by a FARC land mine being airlifted by a helicopter from the jungle.

2012

A child soldier from the FARC’s Sixth Front with fellow guerrillas after an army ambush in the western mountains of Jambaló. Human rights groups have documented that thousands of minors, some as young as 9, were forcibly recruited into the FARC’s ranks.

As journalists working for The New York Times, we have documented this rocky path between peace and war, repeatedly visiting the nation’s most remote corners.

Colombia has long been an unequal country; in the 1960s the FARC sought to resolve that with guns, creating a Marxist revolutionary army that would redistribute wealth. Eventually, fighters used kidnapping, killing and the drug trade to fuel the insurgency, and the conflict became a war among leftist guerrillas, right-wing paramilitaries and a government backed by billions of dollars from Washington.

At the heart of the 2016 deal was a promise by FARC fighters to lay down their arms, and by the government to build institutions and fund programs that would eliminate the structural inequalities that caused the war.

It was an extremely ambitious promise: An oft-cited statistic from one international development organization is that it takes 11 generations for a Colombian family to rise out of poverty.

2016

FARC guerrillas at a camp deep in the Colombian jungle, months before the peace deal was finally ratified.

Daniela, a young FARC fighter, during a formation.

A FARC fighter known as El Primo riding a mule across the Quiparadó River in a remote stretch of jungle between the departments of Chocó and Antioquia.

A decade in, many changes are tangible: The vast majority of FARC fighters have not returned to arms — 85 percent remain in a program meant to reintegrate them into society, according to the United Nations. People traveling the highways outside Bogotá or Medellín generally do not fear kidnapping or bombs. Tourism flourishes in places once torn by conflict.

The government, at least in some places, has arrived in long-ignored towns with roads, schools and hospitals. The country has seen the opening of a vast new political space to debate something other than security, including social and economic issues, enriching public debate in a way that many feel is irreversible.

For decades the Colombian left struggled to distance itself from the violent guerrilla insurgency; distanced from that stigma, it won the presidency for the first time in 2022.

But Colombia’s violence did not disappear. Instead, it rearranged itself. The map of armed actors, each often competing to take over the criminal economies left by the FARC, is more dizzying than ever, and is supercharged by new technologies. TikTok and Facebook are used to recruit child soldiers. Hobby drones fitted with grenades are increasingly a weapon of choice.

Rebel fighters gathered for the last time before the peace agreement ending their 52-year insurgency.

President Juan Manuel Santos, left, speaking after the signing of the peace deal. FARC leaders sit on the opposite side of the stage and two, Iván Márquez and Jesús Santrich, later returned to arms.

FARC rebels in a camp before the deal was ratified.

FARC members who never signed the deal, or rearmed, have splintered into dissident factions. The National Liberation Army, or ELN, a Marxist group that never signed an accord, persists. One of the most powerful groups, known as the Clan del Golfo, is present in almost half of the country’s municipalities, according to Colombia’s ombudsman’s office, while FARC dissidents have a presence in more than a third.

The illicit economies that fed the war have been inherited, franchised and expanded. Production of the coca leaf, a key ingredient in cocaine, is up 80 percent since the accord was signed, according to the United Nations, and Colombia continues to be the world’s largest cocaine producer. For criminal groups, illegally mined gold is a growing part of the financial portfolio.

Some who remain in arms say they are still fighting for social justice.

“Colombia’s problem will be resolved when we resolve need and inequality,” said Andrey Avendaño, a FARC dissident commander, during an interview in a remote palm grove this year.

2018

Some FARC fighters resisted the deal, while others rearmed. Here, dissident guerrillas taught a member how to use his rifle at their camp, hidden among mountains north of Medellín.

The government, which had promised to sweep into lands once held by the FARC and bring health, education and potable water, was still largely absent in many places in 2018.

A group of fighters who didn’t sign the peace deal having breakfast by a mountain creek in Colombia.

But increasingly, fighting has become a profession, with ideology as window dressing. The FARC never paid a salary; when we visited a new armed group, the Comandos de la Frontera, in 2022, it paid twice the minimum wage — and offered vacation time.

Since taking office in August, Mr. De La Espriella has called the accord a failure, saying the agreement amounted to impunity for perpetrators. He has ended peace negotiations with remaining groups, intensified a military approach to the conflict, and proposed an antiterror law that would expand his powers to target enemies.

The United States, long one of the peace deal’s chief backers, has shifted its focus to this militarized, anti-narcotics approach, part of a larger strategy across the region.

Representatives for Mr. De La Espriella declined to comment for this article.

Scholars and everyday Colombians say his election reflects impatience with the pace of change.

2022

Members of the Comandos de la Frontera, a militia group that formed after the peace deal. Colombian officials said that by 2022 the number of armed groups in the country had grown to more than 30.

A militia member bathing in the Putumayo River.

Militia members on a patrol along the Putumayo river.

A comprehensive land reform meant to address a main driver of the conflict — unequal access to land — set a goal of distributing 3 million hectares to Colombians in need. About a tenth of that has been distributed, according to a United Nations Verification Mission.

Development programs in violence-affected areas were supposed to drive economic change. While 65 percent of programs are on an implementation track, only 5 to 10 percent of them were actually in place in areas recently studied by the ombudsman’s office.

A new court established by the deal, called the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, was one of the accord’s most symbolic and controversial aspects. Charged with investigating wrongdoing, it would mete out non-prison sentences, like hard labor, to those who admitted their crimes.

The court has uncovered the scope of many systematic crimes — establishing that the FARC kidnapped over 21,000 people and recruited nearly 19,000 children. And nearly 8,000 civilians were killed by the military and passed off as rebels in a scheme called the False Positives scandal.

Members of the Comandos de la Frontera militia pay cash for locally produced coca paste, a substance that is a midpoint in the production of cocaine.

A group of Comandos fighters packed and sealed their weapons before leaving camp for vacation, labeling them with their aliases: “Mincho,” “Max,” “Escorpión.”

2023

A member of a FARC dissident faction taking photos of a helicopter carrying United Nations personnel. Women made up an estimated 30 to 40 percent of the FARC’s fighters before the peace agreement.

But it has taken years to issue sentences, heightening a sense of impunity.

Just 27 percent of Colombians trust the court today, according to a study from the University of the Andes, down 10 percent from two years before.

Overall support for the agreement was just above 40 percent in 2016, and fell to about 37 percent last year.

A decade in, the nation debates the reasons violence persists.

Iván Duque, a conservative who opposed the deal, oversaw its early implementation. Critics accuse him of slow-walking the rollout of social programs and other measures, creating an institutional vacuum in rural areas in the first critical years.

Others fault the policies of his successor, leftist President Gustavo Petro, who favored negotiation with remaining groups over military operations, but failed to close any meaningful new deals.

Mr. Duque has blamed the end of a program that killed coca crops by dropping chemicals from planes, saying it allowed drugs to flourish. Mr. Petro has said he fast-tracked land reform after the country lost time under Mr. Duque.

2025

A gathering of dissident FARC fighters and community members in the Llanos del Yarí, a remote region of south central Colombia. In 2016, FARC fighters voted here to lay down their arms. Since then, those who rejected the peace deal have returned to this place again and again.

This gathering took place under President Petro, who tried unsuccessfully to strike peace deals with remaining armed groups.

Members of the post-2016 FARC patrol a rural area in the department of Caquetá.

In the territories most affected by violence, some remain skeptical of the deal, while others insist that a decade is not enough to judge a process devised to last generations.

And pain persists.

Deisy Dorelly Guanaro was 10 when FARC fighters took her from her mother’s home. She was sexually abused by commanders for years, she said, and rescued by the military after a battle in which she was the only survivor of 15 young fighters.

She criticized the accord’s truth and reconciliation process, saying perpetrators had not fully admitted their crimes and had received light punishments and even positions in Congress. The deal gave former FARC leaders seats in the legislature for two terms.

“I do not feel compensated for my pain,” Ms. Dorelly said, “or what they did to me when I was a child.”

2026

A guerrilla fighter, part of a dissident FARC unit, launching a drone at one of the rebels’ strategic positions in Catatumbo, on the border with Venezuela. Access to relatively cheap and easily modifiable drones is upending the country’s decades-long war against insurgent groups.

Locals riding through a town in Catatumbo, on the border with Venezuela, earlier this year. Graffiti celebrates the FARC and a poster calls for “armed rebellion.”

Andrey Avendaño, commander of the 33rd Front, a FARC dissident group that rejects the 2016 peace deal.

Perhaps the most Colombian feature of this anniversary is the sense that every peace agreement opens a new chapter of negotiation rather than closing one.

“One thing this agreement did was create this very broad political consensus that this violence doesn’t come from nowhere,” said Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at International Crisis Group who is based in Colombia. “The fundamental conclusion is: You have to fix the lack of state presence, you have to provide services to people, you have to govern in these spaces, because otherwise someone else will.”

The 33rd Front has been fighting the ELN, a Colombian group that has grown significantly in recent years, in part because it has found refuge in neighboring Venezuela.

Members of the 33rd Front sleeping in their tent in a clandestine camp in the jungle.

A member of the 33rd Front.

The pact with the FARC did not resolve Colombia’s war. It resolved one war, the oldest and the most symbolic, and left on the table a map of lesser conflicts and illegal economies that the state still does not know how to confront, much less dismantle.

Colombia’s peace was never an endpoint but an unfinished process, subject to the shifting winds of each new government. The current president has inherited that ambiguity: an agreement that has survived against all odds, but that is still waiting, in the hardest-hit corners of the country, to accomplish the peace it promised on paper.

The ELN and dissident FARC groups cast themselves as protectors of the poor and refuse to lay down arms.

Julie Turkewitz is the Andes Bureau Chief for The Times, based in Bogotá, Colombia, covering Colombia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

The Benefits of Eating Purely for Pleasure

The New York Times November 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Savoring delicious food is not only enjoyable in the moment, it may even enhance long-term well-being.

By Alice Callahan

For most of the year, Paul Rozin, a psychology professor at the University of Pennsylvania, follows a pescatarian diet. But every once in a while, including on Thanksgiving, he allows himself to indulge in a few bites of meat he really enjoys, like duck, bacon and crispy turkey skin.

The holidays can offer opportunities, and perhaps permission, to savor some of our most beloved foods. On Thanksgiving, we might delight in the tartness of cranberry sauce or sample four pies at once.

But eating for pleasure doesn’t need to stop at the holidays, said Dr. Rozin, who studies the role of food in human life. It’s beneficial, and potentially even good for your health, to infuse pleasure into everyday meals.

That idea may seem counterintuitive to many in the United States, who tend to think of eating food they enjoy as “a health compromise,” Dr. Rozin said.

In one study published in the journal Appetite in 1999, Dr. Rozin and his colleagues surveyed about 1,300 people in France, Japan, Belgium and the United States on their feelings about food. Of all the respondents, those in the United States were most likely to say they were trying to cut back on fat and salt, and least likely to say they valued the pleasures of eating. When asked which of two words — “fattening” or “delicious” — best described ice cream, the Americans were more likely to choose “fattening.”

Yet for all of Americans’ obsessions with counting calories, eliminating sugar, hitting sky-high protein goals and following other diet rules, the United States still has higher rates of obesity than these other countries, Dr. Rozin said.

Perhaps it wouldn’t hurt our health — and possibly even help it — to focus more on enjoying food, said Yann Cornil, a behavioral scientist at the University of British Columbia Sauder School of Business. In some limited studies published over the past few decades, Dr. Cornil and other researchers have found that when people pay attention to the sensory pleasures of certain foods — the sweet flavor and smooth texture of chocolate, for instance, or the salty crunch of potato chips — they tend to feel satisfied with smaller portions.

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

That may be because the first few bites of enjoyable foods are often the most pleasurable, Dr. Cornil said. After that, the pleasure of each bite typically fades — a phenomenon called sensory specific satiety — and you may stop eating, Dr. Cornil said.

In his research, Dr. Cornil has also found that when people value the sensory and symbolic aspects of food, including its cultural, traditional and social roles, they generally tend to prefer smaller serving sizes compared with people who don’t have those values. They also have greater well-being, such as agreeing with the statement “I feel that life is very rewarding.”

Other research suggests benefits of intuitive eating, which involves tuning in to hunger and fullness cues and prioritizing satisfying and enjoyable food. Those who practice intuitive eating tend to have better psychological health, including scoring higher on measures of self-esteem and self-compassion, and having fewer anxiety and depression symptoms.

Constantly worrying about tracking macros or following certain diets, on the other hand, can leave you feeling mentally drained, physically deprived and less able to meaningfully connect with others, said Evelyn Tribole, a dietitian in Newport Beach, Calif., who helped name and define the “intuitive eating” framework in the 1990s. It can also lead to disordered eating, she said.

When you outsource your eating decisions to external guidelines, like certain diet plans or the advice of social media influencers, you disconnect from your own needs, preferences and pleasures, she said.

There is even some evidence that people who eat more intuitively tend to have more healthful diets, said Simone Lemieux, a dietitian and professor of nutrition at Laval University in Quebec. One finding from a 2022 review of 14 studies that included nearly 4,000 adults from various countries, for instance, was that those who adopted intuitive eating often ate more fruits and vegetables than those who didn’t.

Such benefits aside, savoring delicious food just feels good — and we deserve to feel good, said Shana Minei Spence, a dietitian in New York City.

Food provides not only nutrients “but also joy and comfort,” she said. In other words, we shouldn’t feel guilty about finding happiness in pecan pie or mashed potatoes with gravy.

“Food is one of the great sources of pleasure,” Dr. Rozin said. “A life of more pleasure is a better life,” he added.

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

The Best Travel Adapters for Power On the Go

Wired November 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.

The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.

Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.

Ceptics

Shop

Amazon

There’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.

For all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. (This video explains grounding well.) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.

I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51), which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40), which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.

Epicka

Amazon

Perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.

When I first tested the 40-watt version ($25), I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any issues with the UK prongs.

Ceptics

Amazon

Shop

This budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones, tablets, smartwatches, and Kindles. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.

There’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.

One Beat

What I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. Offered in several versions (Type C, Type E/F, Type G), this adapter enables you to charge up to six gadgets. I’ve been testing the Type G model in Scotland, and it plugs into a single outlet, giving you three US outlets, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. The USB-C can output up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports are limited to 12 watts—not especially speedy, but fine for overnight charging. The adapter is grounded and has various safety features.

On the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

Mukiya

If you only need USB-C and USB-A ports for charging your mobile gadgets on the go (and no outlet), I recommend this clever, compact travel adapter. I’ve never seen a mechanism like this before, where you twist to extend the prongs. It's a neat feature. The standard US prongs can be angled for Australia, and there are EU and UK prongs (types A, C, G, and I). The USB-C ports can deliver up to 70 watts, enough to charge a laptop (slowly), and there’s a USB-A port. You could charge up to three devices at once, though the wattage is divided between them, and it got a little warm when I did this. It uses gallium nitride (GaN) technology to keep the size down. This is a new brand to me, but I’ve been testing it on various devices for the last two weeks, and so far, so good.

Ceptics

Amazon (Set of 5)

Amazon (Set of 12)

Shop (Set of 5)

Universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. The 12-piece international set from Ceptics is my favorite. It includes types to cover most of the globe, and each is properly grounded. Only visiting a single destination? Just pack the relevant type. These adapters don't have USB ports, so you’ll need the respective charging adapter for your gadgets.

This set is especially good for Europe because it includes Type C, E/F, and G adapters, so you’re covered for any socket. Ceptics offers an even cheaper and smaller five-piece set, but I don’t recommend it. The adapters are flimsy, there’s no grounding, and the European plug’s design doesn’t work well with the recessed sockets you will sometimes encounter. The drawback of plug adapters is that they’re easy to lose, but at least Ceptics includes a small bag for storage.

Ceptics

Amazon

Shop

This kit includes multiple plug attachments that slide and lock into place to keep you powered across most of the world. It is bulky and much bigger than the average adapter but provides two grounded US AC outlets. There is also a built-in USB-C cable, two USB-A ports, and two USB-C ports. The USB-A ports and built-in USB-C cable offer a combined maximum charging rate of 15 watts. The USB-C ports support Power Delivery, with up to 20 watts each. The top charging rate for all of them simultaneously is 55 watts.

There is built-in surge protection, but since this is not a voltage converter, don’t plug in hair dryers or other non-dual-voltage electronics. While the two AC outlets are handy, their proximity means that the shape and size of some plugs can make it tricky to use both simultaneously. But with the ability to charge up to seven devices, this kit is handy. I also like the original Ceptics World Travel Adapter Kit ($35), though it lacks the two USB-C ports.

Mophie

Shop (Mophie)

Amazon

This cute kit comes in a zippered pouch and includes everything you need for a trip. There’s a fold-out charger with a tiltable magnetic Qi2 25W pad for your iPhone or Qi2 Android phone, a 7.5W pad for an Apple Watch, and a 5W pad behind for wireless earbuds. It also includes a 40W power adapter with switchable plugs for the US, UK, EU, and AU—plus a 5-foot USB-C cable. Everything inside comes in color-matched black or cream, unless you opt for the bolder orange-and-teal special edition.

It’s not the most compact option, but I love that everything slots neatly into the included pouch. You can find some great alternatives in my Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.

What Type of Adapter Do You Need?

There are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.

Some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.

If you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.

Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?

Voltage converters are big, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:

Input: 100–220V 50/60Hz

That should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers, irons, and kettles, so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.

If you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.

What About Wattage?

Travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone.

Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?

Yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase. It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags.

Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?

You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.

Some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.

Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?

Seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.

How I Test Travel Adapters

Anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.

There is an endless amount of travel adapters out there you could buy. While I wholeheartedly recommend one of the options above, there are some other travel adapters I've tested that just barely miss the mark.

Epicka Pulse for $30: The beveled edges of this travel adapter from Epicka make it more comfortable to hold. The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. This adapter can deliver up to 45 watts from either USB-C port, while the USB-A ports top out at 18 watts. I also tested the newer Epicka Pulse Duo ($130), which can deliver up to 140 watts across three USB-C and one USB-A ports, has an extra US or Japanese socket in the side and boasts a smart display that shows you the current charging status, wattage, and temperature. Cool as it is, it's overkill for most folks and kinda pricey.

Tessan Travel Adapter 009 for $20: This is a similar design to the Epicka Air I recommend above, but the prongs don’t stay in place as securely when unfolded, and you can only draw a maximum of 20 watts from the one USB-A and two USB-C ports. But it is affordable and compact. Tessan also makes good, traditional, slider universal adapters: There's a 140-watt model ($70), and the most powerful travel adapter I’ve tested, the Voyager 205 ($128), which has six USB-C ports and one USB-A to deliver up to 205 watts. If you don’t care about charging speed, Tessan's 20W model ($23) is very reasonably priced and offers two USB-A and two USB-C ports in a small package.

UGreen Travel Plug Adapter for £17: This travel adapter is for UK folks visiting Europe, and it’s a solid option with a fixed plug (no mechanism). It has only two USB-A and one USB-C port for smaller devices, and it’s very bulky. I prefer the OneBeat above for this type of design.

Statik SmartCharge Pro for $80: This is a nice combo device that includes a 15,000 mAh power bank and a 60-watt wall charger. There are fold-out US prongs and slide-on adapters for the UK, EU, and AU. You also get one USB-A port, one USB-C port, a fold-out USB-C cable, and a wireless charging pad on top that works with your iPhone or Apple Watch.

D-Link 65W Multi-Port GaN Charger (DCP-651) for $30: If two USB-C ports and a USB-A port are enough for your travel needs, this affordable D-Link charger could be for you. It comes with interchangeable plugs for different countries. The 65-watt limit is enough for overnight charging a laptop and a couple of smartphones.

Arsmel VisaPro

Arsmel VisaPro All-in-One Travel Adapter for $80: This chunky power adapter can charge laptops or multiple small devices with a whopping 170-watt maximum output. It works with any outlet in the US, UK, or EU, thanks to sliding plugs that slot in securely, and you can spin the prongs on the US plug to support the total number of countries (more than 200). I love the mecha-inspired paint job, too. There are four ports along the bottom: two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts, with the third USB-C and USB-A ports rated at 18 watts. It supports PD 3.1, QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and SCP, and has a 10-amp fuse.

Satechi GaN Travel Charger for $120: If you only take small gadgets with you when you travel, a compact, multi-port wall charger is all you need and a great way to pack light. It plugs directly into the wall and comes with four interchangeable travel adapters for the EU, UK, and Australia, plus a mesh bag to store them. There are four USB-C ports that you can plug your gadgets into, including laptops like the MacBook Pro, tablets, phones, and wearables. With support for Power Delivery 3.1, the first two ports can supply up to 140 watts, and the bottom two ports up to 45 watts. However, the maximum output when all four ports are in use is 145 watts.

Baseus 70W Universal Travel Adapter With Retractable Cable for $40: This excellent travel adapter is almost identical to our top pick from Ceptics, offering up to 70 watts, sliding prongs to cover more than 200 countries, and a built-in retractable USB-C cable, not to mention a USB-C port and two USB-A ports. It also has a snazzy black-and-yellow finish. It only misses out because it’s slightly more expensive, but if you can snag one on sale or prefer the colors, it’s a solid option.

Epicka Universal Travel Adapter for $20: This travel adapter from Epicka is still a solid option. The sliding plugs cover 150 countries, and there are four USB-A ports on the bottom and a 15-watt USB-C port on the side. There’s also an 8-amp fuse with a spare, and this adapter is RoHS-, CE-, and FCC-certified.

Masterplug Visitor to UK Travel Adapter (3 Pack) for £12: For visitors to the UK, this simple trio of adapters accepts European, American, Australian, and Asian plugs. They are single-outlet adapters with 13-amp fuses inside, and they work perfectly. These are the adapters I use for long-term testing of devices from the US and elsewhere that lack UK plugs. If you forgot to buy an adapter before arriving in the UK, you can find this affordable three-pack at any Argos store.

Anker European Travel Plug Adapter for $16: One of our favorite portable charger brands, Anker, also makes travel adapters. This one plugs into most European outlets to provide a single grounded US outlet, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. Unfortunately, the three USB ports max out at 15 watts total, so it’s best for overnight gadget charging, but I appreciate the temperature and overload protection. There is also a UK version ($16).

Epicka Hybrid European Travel Plug Adapter for $26: This handy adapter turns one outlet into four and includes four USB ports (two A and two C). It has fold-out Type A prongs, but you can also slide on a fold-out Type C plug for use in Europe. While the USB ports support QC 3.0 or PD 3.0, they max out at 20 watts in total. I prefer the OneBeat adapters recommended above.

You can do better than these travel adapters.

EZQuest WorldTravel

EZQuest WorldTravel GaN 5 Port With PD Wall Charger: This travel adapter has a generous four USB-C ports and one USB-A port with a familiar slide-out prong design that covers more than 150 countries. There’s also a built-in 10-amp fuse and a spare. It has RoHS, CE, and FCC certification. It works fine, but it's kinda boxy, and the sliders don't lock in place as securely as some of our other picks. There's also a 65W version ($60).

Rolling Square Pocket Travel Adapter: I admire any attempt to shrink down travel adapters in size, but the three-pronged UK plugs are usually the obstacle. Rolling Square’s solution is to have a flip-out third prong, but you’ll need a good fingernail to unhitch it. This charger has a single USB-C port capable of delivering up to 30 watts and is a compact option that covers the US, UK, and Europe.

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter: This versatile adapter comes with Type A, B, C, E/F, G, and I slide-on plugs. They fit onto the rectangular brick and plug directly into the outlet, or you can attach them to the optional five-foot cable. The brick has one grounded US outlet and a second non-grounded outlet, with one USB-A (30-watt) and two USB-C (65- and 33-watt) ports at the other end. It works fine, and it's affordable, but it's bulky and ugly.

The Gifts Moms Actually Want, Picked by Moms

Wired November 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario. That includes Mother's Day, her birthday, Christmas, Hanukkah, or any other holiday in your family's life that includes gift-giving. The holiday season is now upon us, and I've added a few gift ideas with that time of year in mind.

If you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love. From wellness gadgets that can improve her skin to the best tote bags I've tried, and even a device that puts her digital calendar in an IRL device, moms everywhere can get a ton out of these gifts. Many of these are items I've given to my mother, or other WIRED staffers have given to theirs. Or they might be at the top of my own wish list as a mother of a 4-year-old.

Updated November 2026: I've added Therabody's Theraface Mask Glo, Omnilux's Contour Gloves, WanderFull's HydroBag, and Nuuly's clothing subscription as new gifts to this guide.

Shop

Therabody

Therabody

The must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask. These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red-light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin, and I always get compliments on how nice my skin looks when I'm regularly using it. Therabody's TheraFace Mask Glo has a range of treatments with both red and blue light, a unique vibration therapy feature, and removable eye shields if you don't want the light in your eyes.

Look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.

The Yardsale Day Bag has been my go-to for a variety of needs, from a colorful personal item for a flight to a gym bag to the aerial studio. It's got a waterproof bottom that makes me happy to bring it to the zoo's splash pad, and a magnetic middle separator you can flex to separate the middle of the bag into two medium sections to better divide all your items. Plus, there are a handful of side pockets inside, but none are large enough for my massive Owala water bottle. I have the 30L in Butter, but there's also a smaller 20L version if you're looking for something a little more compact.

If your mom wants something a little more stylish, the Alex Mill totes are always on my mind. They come in a variety of gorgeous colors and are made of coated canvas, so they can put up with daily adventures, and you can customize them with your mom's initials (or even just the word “mom”!) with Alex Mill's hand-painted letter service. It's a simpler tote with no other pockets, but you can use the top snaps to let out the sides or tuck them in, depending on how much space Mom needs on a given day. The weathered color and vibe of these bags also feel perfect for the fall season.

Skylight (With Plus Plan)

My latest favorite family planning gadget is a digital wall calendar. These handy devices take the Google Calendar I live by (and just about any other digital calendar, if your mom isn't a Google girl) and put it on a physical device I can quickly tap into without needing to grab my phone or bark at Alexa. The Skylight Calendar 2 is my favorite, because it not only includes to-do lists, meal planning, and a recipe book but also doubles as a digital photo frame. That means it displays cute photos of my family most of the time, and then, with a simple tap, it opens the calendar or whatever page I was last on to show me what's on my family's schedule. It does have a subscription fee, though, to get the digital photo frame feature and a few other options, like meal planning. But I think it's well worth it to get so many features in a single device. You can also gift her kiddo a Skylight Buddy ($140) so that she doesn't have to remind them to check the main calendar for their chores; it'll appear on their own device if they have a Buddy.

Nuuly

Nuuly ($38 Off First Month)

To me, motherhood is all about change. It's most obvious at the start of motherhood, when your body changes a lot over the course of nine months, but motherhood encompasses the rest of our lives, and our bodies and style change a lot over that time. One of the biggest giveaways that time has gone by is our clothes—how well they fit for our current stage, whether they reflect the time of our life right now, and if we're bored out of our skull with everything but don't want to buy an entirely new closet.

I've been loving renting from Nuuly this pregnancy because the brand has an entire maternity section that lets me find pieces to fit me in this short—but very different size—season of my life. My older mother also loves having a clothing subscription because she gets bored of her outfit options to wear into the office, and I loved it for the same reason when I had my first clothing subscription right out of college. If Mom has been talking about wanting some new looks but feels overwhelmed about what she wants to invest in, these rental services are a fun way to get a lot of new clothes in your life without having to store them or spend as much as you would have (some of my favorite maternity clothes I've gotten through Nuuly would have cost me $200 apiece!) The service costs $98 a month, but your first month is discounted to just $60. There's one piece I miss already that might drive me to pick up a second subscription, which would genuinely be cheaper than buying the piece I want brand new.

For years, the go-to gift for a woman in my family, mother or not, was shopping in the jewelry section of a department store. My mom even helped orchestrate this for the rest of the aunties and grandmas, but now, as a mom myself, I find myself interested in jewelry that tells a story about my family and children instead of just any old set. (Except extra earrings for my earring stack, a gift I'm thrilled to get, because there's never enough.)

I love these pieces from Gorjana and BaubleBar that you can customize. Gorjana has a ton of charms you can add to its necklaces or bracelets to reflect Mom’s kids’ initials, birthstones, or anything else; I paired a charm of my son’s first initial ($50) with the Wilshire Adjustable Necklace ($68). If she's more of a ring gal, BaubleBar's Toi et Moi ring ($78) lets you choose two birthstones to display. I chose my and my son's birthstones, but luckily his sibling-to-be will also have a red birthstone, so it'll remain a perfect reflection of my kids and me for years to come.

This item was literally made for sports moms: a padded stadium cushion with a wearable blanket inside. My son plays on three sports teams, so I do a lot of sitting outside on bleachers and turf sidelines—and often at night, when it’s freezing. I’ve tried many things to keep warm, from heated jackets to HotHands, but nothing has worked as well as this water-resistant blanket, which unfurls to 50 x 70 inches and sports a clip at the front so you can wear it like a cape. It can also be used for picnics or as a spot for younger siblings to sit and read during tournaments. It’s also not hard to fold it back up and fit it inside the seat part (which is 1 inch thick without the blanket inside). It comes in six colors, so you can be sure to find one that matches your giftee’s kid’s team or school colors. —Kat Merck

As a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot. And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them at her fingertips. I have and love both for different reasons.

I love the digital photo frame to add all the photos from a fun weekend at the San Diego Zoo or Renaissance Pleasure Faire for me to relive again and again, but I also love being able to pull a photo book from the bookshelf and relive a specific moment I know is waiting there for me. Aura makes my favorite digital photo frames (followed by Skylight's Calendar 2 if you want a multipurpose device, but Aura has no subscription fee if you only want photos), while Mixbook has been a favorite of mine for a while when it comes to printing photos, and has great starting prices for its photo books.

Once my kiddo is asleep, you can find me parked on the couch playing video games. I upgraded to a Nintendo Switch 2 ($499) earlier this summer so I could finally buy and play Pokopia ($70), since it's exclusive to the new console, and now my husband and I are completely hooked on the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ($60) remake that came out a few weeks ago. It's also quickly become an experience I can share with my son now that he's 4; he was been helping me and my husband replay Tears of the Kingdom, but now he's dubbed Ocarina of Time as “Big Little Link” and is obsessed with using the grappling hook and using up all of our arrows.

If you're not looking to upgrade her console just yet but need a Switch-friendly cozy game for her, Stardew Valley has another big update in the works and only costs $15. I'm also hoping we see Fields of Mistria ($14) come to the Switch eventually, but the full launch came out in August for Steam users and has major quality-of-life improvements if she has played Stardew one time too many. My husband also upgraded his gaming setup this summer with a Steam Machine (from $1,049), and I have big plans to start using it often for Fields of Mistria. If your mom loves games, she'll love any one of these new devices or new games, especially if she already got herself the new gadget as I did.

Look, I love a Kindle, but if you want to get the best e-reader for your buck (or maybe she just wants an e-reader that isn't a Kindle), the answer is actually a Kobo. Kobo also has a page-turner remote ($34), which I love to pair with a pillow stand holder so I can lean back and relax without holding up my e-reader while I read. Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

Wired November 22, 2026

Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.

“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”

Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.

Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

Wired November 22, 2026

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.

They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.

Fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.

Now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine said.

The experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” said Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”

When he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined quickly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.

When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.

Convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.

They considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.

Through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining showed no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.

By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.

For six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.

When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples showed higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.

During metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.

He devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.

It was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv. org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.

According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.

For Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he said. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.

The idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.

“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran said.

Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, said Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.

“This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he said of the new work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.

Another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, said Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.

Ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he said. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.

However, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet said. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.

For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.

“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet said, “right there under our feet.”
